PREFACE 

The Eighth Edition of this book, completely revised after six extremely depressed years in the building industry, has been brought up-to-date in every respect. 

Many new materials and methods of construction developed during the past few years have brought great changes in the building industry and these have all been covered in this new edition. Many trade associations have revised and standardized their methods of installing work and the revised cost data applying thereto reflect these changes.

The construction industry has been mechanized to a greater extent than ever before in an attempt to keep costs within reason in spite of increased wages and shorter working hours. These new methods are described and comparative costs given in many instances. 

The author believes the user will find this the most complete and authentic manual of cost data obtainable and if intelligently used, will result in more accurate estimates with a considerable saving of time in their preparation. 

The data in this book has been condensed as far as practicable for ready reference but the author has never become converted to the idea that accurate labor costs could be obtained from charts or tables, without considering the methods to be used in executing the work or the conditions under which it would be performed. With the best estimating data available, it still requires experience, good judgment and common sense to prepare accurate estimates.

The author wishes to thank the many contractors and manufacturers of specialized building products who have assisted in the revisions of this book and credit is given in the footnotes relating to the subject matter. 

Suggestions and constructive criticism that will tend to increase the value of future editions are always welcomed by the author.

May 1, 1937. 

FRANK R. WALKER iii

PREFACE TO THE FIRST EDITION 

The building contractor and estimator engaged in computing the costs of our modern buildings must eliminate the item of guesswork from the estiinates as far as possible. 

This is not an easy matter, as building construction methods can hardly be reduced to the scientific basis of factories and shops, with their fixed surroundings and control of weather vagaries. When the many unforeseen conditions entering into the cost of modern buildings are taken into consideration this is readily seen-weather, rain, snow, cold, etc., all capable of causing inestimable damage and expense, not including the overhead charges for superintendence, etc., which must be paid regardless of weather conditions. A concrete mixer, hoisting engine, derrick or some other piece of equipment may break, causing delays, overtime, or other unforeseen expense. These are all items over which the contractor or estimator has little control, and he must therefore use his best judgment as to costs and methods of construction. 

In 

The costs given in this book are from the best sources and are thoroughly reliable, as in most cases the author was on the work during con. struction and compiled all cost data during the progress of the work. other cases it was obtained from the actual cost sheets coming in from the job each week and compiled at the completion of the work. No cost or data is included that the author is not convinced of being absolutely trustworthy so that the contractor and estimator may refer to it with perfect confidence. 

Illustrations are freely used, as the author believes that a good picture is better than a volume of explanation, and for this reason actual photographs, taken during the progress of the work, are included to show the conditions existing on the job, the methods and plant employed, through which the labor costs on the various branches of work resulted. 

In several instances no mention is made of the particular building from which the costs were obtained, as the data was given in confidence, but they comprise inside figures on many of the largest and finest structures in the country.

To the casual observer, or one not understanding building conditions, the prices may appear indefinite or with too great a variation of labor quantities and costs.

This is easily explained. A brick mason will lay more brick on a bright warm day than when the thermometer is at freezing. A carpenter will lay more hardwood flooring in one large room than in ten small rooms requiring the same amount of flooring, but with five to ten times the amount of cutting; a marble setter will set more base in a long straight corridor than in one cut up with many pilasters and with from three to five times the number of pieces containing the same number of lineal feet of base. 

These conditions can be multiplied indefinitely. The estimator should study his plans carefully and base prices accordingly. 

The superintendence of the job will have much to do with the final cost of the work. No two executives employ the same methods of construction or of handling men and few individuals produce the same quantity of finished work. When business is dull good men are easily obtained, but during periods of building prosperity the superintendent has a smaller range of choice and must exercise his best judgment in the selection of men. 

For these reasons the labor cost of any piece of work is a variable item and all future estimates can only be based on past experiences. 

The actual costs of work performed as given in this reference book are invaluable to the estimator and contractor. 

All costs have been reduced to actual hours per unit of measure, so that the costs may be applied to any rate of wage. 

A number of manufacturers have generously furnished much information regarding the prices of their various products, which will be of convenient reference to the reader.

The author also wishes to thank his friends and acquaintances in the building trades who have so generously assisted in the compilation of the various branches of work included. 

FRANK R. WALKER.

IMPORTANT How to Obtain the Best Results From the Estimating and Cost Data in This Book 

In compiling a book of estimating and cost data that is used in all parts of America and many foreign countries, it is impossible to quote material prices and labor costs that will apply in every locality without some computation on the part of the user.

For this reason all labor costs state the quantity of work a man will perform per hour or per day, together with the number of hours required to complete a certain unit of work. In each instance a certain basic price has been used, but the user is urged to insert local wage scales and material prices, as by so doing accurate estimates are sure to result. 

This method of tabulation has been used throughout the book, making it easy for any person to insert local prices and obtain absolutely dependable estimates. 

An example of the method used is given below, taken from page 773 under the heading "Framing and Setting Floor Joists."

THE BUILDING  CHAPTER I ESTIMATING 

Estimating is one of the most important phases of a contractor's business because in nearly every instance it is necessary to submit an estimate on the cost of a job before the contract is awarded. If the estimate is too high, the job goes to a competitor, and, if too low, the contractor who is awarded the contract must complete it without profit if not at an actual loss in both time and money.

There are thousands of contractors in business to-day who are no better off than they were ten or twenty years ago because they take work so low they are barely able to make a living; many of them would be far better off working for "day-wages" for a competent contractor, These contractors not only ruin the business for competent builders but they are not improving their own condition.

It is unfortunate, but true nevertheless, that contractors (as a class) are not considered good business men. This is due to a number of causes, but chiefly to the fact that so many contractors are men who have “risen from the ranks," and although they were exceptional mechanics, foremen or superintendents and possessed a thorough understanding of how the work should be done, they were sadly lacking in business training and the ability to estimate the cost of their work accurately. 

As an example, let me quote from an address delivered at a convention of builders by Mr. W. L. Thompson, vice-president of the First National Bank of Portland, Ore. He said: "The average contractor's account is not particularly attractive to the bankers. I think there are well-defined reasons for this attitude. 1.

I do not say that the contractor is entirely to blame; I believe the banker is partially to blame. But that attitude has been brought about by the looseness of methods of so many men who are engaged in the contracting business. I am sure that the average contractor's account could be made much more attractive if this looseness of method were eliminated. I refer particularly to the looseness with which your accounting systems are maintained." "My observation over a period of years in the banking business has been that most failures in all lines of business can be definitely traced to loose methods and the fact that the man in charge of the business did not know where he was at." 

This is further emphasized by the reply of the manager of a large bonding and insurance company, as to just what the companies considered the most important requisites of a contractor or corporation desiring a surety bond.

The answers are given in the order of their relative importance:

First: The ability of the party requesting the bond. Whether or not he understands his business thoroughly. Is he capable of preparing a correct estimate or if he employs an estimator, is he capable of checking the estimator's figures and judgment. 

Second: The general reputation of the contractor for honesty, meeting his financial obligations promptly and his reputation among those with whom he does business. 

Third: The financial ability of the contractor. Whether he possesses sufficient capital to carry on his business efficiently, meet his pay-rolls, current expenses, etc. "You would be surprised," he said, "to see some of the estimates that are brought to our office to pass on, and the contractor really expects us to go on his bond on the strength of them. A contractor recently came to my office and wanted my company to go on his bond covering the construction of a certain building. Upon asking for his estimate covering the contemplated work, he pulled an old, soiled envelope from his inside pocket with a few figures on the back of it and said that was his estimate. Perhaps he had 'cubed' the cost-not more -and we wonder why contractors 'go broke.' 

Sometime later the manager of the Surety Bond Department of another large Bonding Company, said, "You know the bonding company seldom gets the opportunity of bonding the best contractor. It is always the lowest bidder and in a majority

ESTIMATING 

3 of instances the lowest bidder is the weakest financially because some of them must take work at any price in order to exist. 

Again it is due to mistakes in estimating caused by carelessness or ignorance of the proper method of preparing correct estimates."

The above instances illustrate the fact that somebody besides the contractor really attaches importance to a correct and detailed estimate. A well prepared estimate has just as much to do with the success of a contractor as the manner in which he purchases his materials, lets his sub-contracts or handles his work on the job. 

Too much emphasis cannot be placed upon the necessity of measuring the plans and listing the quantities as carefully as possible. They should be listed in as much detail as is consistent with sound construction practice The methods used by many contractors in "lumping" their estimates is a serious mistake for it takes the estimator or contractor away from the fundamental principles of construction and gives the wrong perspective regarding the importance of estimating. 

What Is the Correct Method of Preparing an Estimate? 

If twenty estimators or contractors were furnished the same set of plans and specifications and told to prepare an estimate of cost from same so that the different methods might be com pared, it is safe to assume there would not be more than two estimates in the entire twenty that had been prepared on the same basis or from the same units. 

This is wrong. Why should there be such a variation in methods with only one result to be obtained? It is due to the absence of a uniform method of estimating; the lack of detailed information regarding the cost of the work to be performed with the result that each contractor has developed a system of his own, making it almost impossible for one contractor to check another's figures. This usually results in the "successful" bidder being so ridiculously low that if awarded the contract he will be compelled to complete it at a loss or so unreasonably high as to be completely out of the "running." 

When measuring the plans and listing the quantities on the estimate sheet preparatory to pricing and making up the estimate, it is important that the quantities of the different classes of work should be estimated so far as practical in the same manner in which the work will be constructed on the job. It is

only by observing and learning the costs of the various operations on the job that the estimates will prove dependable. 

As previously mentioned, the practice of "lumping" an estimate is not only a serious mistake but sooner or later it will cause the user a substantial loss, perhaps one that will put him out of business entirely. In more than one instance a life's work has been ruined to save an hour or two in the preparation of an estimate. Is it worth the price?

The Value of Detailed Estimates 

The author has never found any of the so-called “short-cuts" in estimating accurate enough to use in competitive bidding. 

They are all right when preparing preliminary estimates or approximate figures, but when submitting a proposal on a job that you are anxious to obtain-at a profit-take a little extra time and figure the work in as much detail as is necessary to provide accurate and dependable quantities and costs. 

As an example of this practice, take a section of wood floor for an ordinary building, consisting of wood joists, bridging, sub-flooring, deadening felt or building paper, wood furring strips or screeds and the finish flooring. Many contractors will price this work at a certain price per sq. ft. of floor, including all of the above items.

To construct this floor requires six different materials and labor operations. First, the wood joists must be cut to length and placed in position; the bridging placed between the joists; the sub-flooring or sheathing placed; and when the finishing of the building is under way, the deadening felt or building paper is laid, the furring strips placed and then the finish flooring is laid and sanded.

Each of the above requires a distinct labor operation and should be estimated as such because in this way it is possible to compare actual and estimated costs on each class of work. 

This enables the contractor to tell where the money is being made or lost and should prevent similar mistakes on future work.

Short-cuts in estimating have probably "broke" more contractors than they have ever made money for, and with competition as it is to-day a difference of 5 to 10 per cent is the profit or loss on the job. 

The old saying, "Better be safe than sorry" can be followed to advantage by every building estimator.

5 

What Percentage Should the Contractor Add for Profit? 

The author is frequently asked by contractors in various parts of the country, what percentage should be added to the actual estimated cost for profit. 

There is no certain percentage that can be added. It all depends upon local conditions, competition, and how badly you want the job.

On small jobs, alterations, remodeling and similar work, a contractor is justified in adding 20 to 25 per cent to the actual cost for profit, but whether he is able to obtain this amount each contractor must decide for himself. 

On new work, where it is possible to estimate the cost with a fair degree of accuracy, a contractor is entitled to 10 per cent on the actual cost of the work (job overhead included in the actual cost of the job) but when submitting competitive figures it is safe to say there are more jobs let on a 5 per cent than on a 10 per cent basis. A contractor is entitled to 10 per cent "profit but getting it is another matter. 

What About Contingencies?: 

Another item that has caused considerable discussion is, should a contractor add a certain percentage to his estimate to take care of contingencies? Yes and No.

Yes, because it is not necessary to be quite so careful in the preparation of the estimate and if any items have been overlooked, there is a fund to take care of omissions. But a contractor who is not careful in the preparation of his estimates never knows how much should be added to provide for forgotten items or "contingencies."

No, because if you add a percentage for contingencies, it is 10 to 1 that your competitor has not-and you lose another job. 

The only safe way is to be as careful as possible in listing the items from the plans and specifications-include them all and then it will not be be necessary to add for contingencies. This includes everything you will be called upon to furnish, estimate your labor costs accurately, including your job overhead expense, and to this estimated actual cost, add one legitimate profit.

What Are the Qualifications of a Good Estimator? 

The estimator is the most important man in any contractor's organization because it is up to him to prepare estimates that

will either "make or break" the contractor. The most efficient job organization or the best purchasing department in existence can not make money on contracts taken below cost. 

On the other hand, it does not take a good "salesman" or contract man to obtain all the work you can handle if your estimates are way below your competitor's. Remember, the low man is wrong more often than he is right, so the efficient organization is one that can "get the work at the right price." 

It is not an easy task, but a business built-up on the principles of Service, Dependability, Good Materials and Workmanship, and Fair Price, will be in business many years after the "get the work at any price" contractor has made his last assignment in favor of his creditors. 

The dependable estimator should be a practical man. He should possess a thorough understanding of job conditions; how the work will be carried on in the field; the operations necessary to assemble the materials and put them in place in the structure. He must be able to visualize. He must be able to take a set of blue prints and draw a mental picture of the building in construction. How every branch of the work should be handled; the materials required and the labor operations necessary to convert a pile of gravel, sand, brick, cement and lumber into a completed building. 

On the other hand not every visualizer can be a successful estimator. Your job superintendent or foreman may be able to take a set of blue prints and lay the entire job out in his mind; picture the building progressing from the foundation to the finished structure, but unless he possesses the knowledge necessary to compute the quantity of materials and the labor cost of putting them in place, he will never be able to prepare an accurate estimate of cost.

The following seven requisites are essential for the making of a good estimator:

First: He should be able to read plans and measure them accurately.

Second: He should possess a fair knowledge of arithmetic, including addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, together with a knowledge of the decimal system. Nearly all measurements and computations in the average building estimate are made in lineal feet, square feet or yards, and cubic feet or yards. These material quantities are then usually multi-

Third: He should be able to visualize,-that is, he should be able to take a set of blue prints and draw a mental picture of the building; how it will look during construction and at completion. He must be able to place his equipment so that the work can be handled economically. In short, he must first construct the building on paper.

Fourth He should possess an intimate knowledge of job conditions, the most practical methods of handling materials and labor on the job; the most economical methods of construction. While the estimator is an "inside" man he must possess much the same knowledge of construction methods as your superintendents or foremen.

Fifth: The knowledge and ability to assemble materials into workable units. A thousand brick in the wall means more than just the brick. It means a certain amount of sand, lime or cement, and probably mortar color, to make the mortar. A cubic yard of concrete means the exact quantities of cement, sand and gravel must be computed. The same applies to nearly every complete unit in the building. The competent estimator must have this knowledge at his finger tips. 

Sixth: He should possess an intimate knowledge of labor performances and operations and be able to convert them into costs in dollars and cents. This requires a working knowledge of "what a man will do" under given conditions and is obtained only by a careful study of different jobs completed under varying conditions.

Seventh He should be endowed with at least an average amount of common sense.

Listing the Quantities On the Estimate 

When measuring the plans and listing the quantities on the Estimate Sheet, all quantities should be listed in the same manner, and the same units of measure in which the work will be constructed on the job; also, the job costs should be reported in the same units as the work is estimated. This is essential if the job costs are to be of value to the estimator in preparing future estimates on similar work. 

Material and Labor Costs should be estimated separately, because there is usually more variation in labor costs than in material costs.

Correct Method of Listing Quantities on Estimate Sheets.

The illustrations are intended to show how the various items should be listed on the estimate sheet. After all measurements have been taken from the plans, the quantities are extended and reduced to workable units. 

GENERAL OVERHEAD EXPENSE 

The item of overhead expense has long been neglected by most contractors, but it is of such importance that every contractor should give it careful consideration.

Every contractor has a certain fixed expense that must be paid regardless of the amount of work done or contracts received, and these items should be charged to Overhead Expense. 

This includes such items as office rent, fuel, lights, telephone and telegraph, stationery, office supplies, advertising, trade journals and magazines, donations, legal expenses not directly. chargeable to any one job, fire and liability insurance for the office, club and association dues, office employees, such as bookkeeper, stenographer, clerks, estimator and salaries of executives.

These items should be estimated for a year and then reduced to a certain percentage of the total annual business, as follows:

SURETY BOND AMOUNT OF BID AMO Summary of Estimate or "Cap" Sheet for Summarizing the Complete. Estimate on One Sheet.

For example, suppose you have an overhead expense of $15,- 000.00 per year, and do an annual business approximating $500,000.00. On this basis your overhead or general expense would average 3 per cent of the total annual business. 

With some concerns the overhead may run 3 per cent and with others 8 or 10 per cent of the total annual business but every contractor can approximate his overhead based on his average yearly business. Even an approximate is far better than not making any attempt in this direction.

Many smaller contractors do not maintain an office and probably attend to the greater part of their office duties themselves, so only such items of expense as they actually incur should be included.

The following schedule was presented at a meeting of the Associated Building Contractors of Illinois, and is based on a contractor doing a $50,000.00 annual business. You will note the overhead expense is 16 per cent of the total annual business.

OVERHEAD EXPENSE

Should a Contractor's Overhead Expense be Added to His 

Estimate?

Any contractor who attempted to add this percentage to his bid would probably remain without work for a long timebut there is no doubt that the contractor is entitled to a certain amount of overhead expense that should not come out of the "profits" of the business.

All manufacturers, jobbers and retailers add their overhead expense to the cost of their products when computing the selling price and there is no reason why contractors should not do the same except that the man who "doesn't" will probably get the job.

It is not the general practice among contractors to include their office overhead as a portion of the job cost-in fact many contractors do not even figure job overhead when making up their estimate, so until this practice is more generally adopted by contractors, it is not safe to add for this item, especially on work let on competitive figures.

Office Furniture and Equipment 

All expenditures for office furniture, typewriters, calculating machines, filing cabinets, etc., should be kept as a separate account and a certain percentage of this amount charged off each year as depreciation. The depreciation, however, should be charged as a part of the overhead expense of conducting the business, as the cash value of the equipment decreases each year.

Construction Plant and Equipment 

The investment in construction plant and equipment should not be charged to Overhead Expense because this account represents tools and equipment that have a cash value.

When tools or equipment are purchased they should be charged to this account and as used, each job should be charged with a rental or proportionate share of the cost. 

Each year a certain amount of depreciation should be charged off because as the equipment gets older its value is less. 

JOB OVERHEAD EXPENSE 

An important item in making up every estimate and one that does not ordinarily receive the attention it deserves, is the allowance for Job Overhead Expense. 

This should include all items of job expense which are not directly chargeable to any other branch of work, such as salaries

and transportation for superintendent, time-keeper, foremen, and watchmen, the allowances for temporary buildings, tool sheds, hoisting engines, derricks, concrete mixers, fire and liability insurance, surety bond, and all items enumerated on the following pages.

Many contractors figure a certain percentage of the cost of the job to take care of all overhead expense and plant charges, but this is not the correct method to use and does not give the contractor or estimator a reliable basis for computing the cost of this work.

Each item entering into the cost of job overhead expense should be estimated separately the same as any other branch of work.

Superintendence.-This should include the salary and traveling expenses of the job superintendent, time-keepers, material clerks, labor foremen, carpenter foremen, mason foremen, concrete foremen, structural steel foremen, plastering foremen, etc., and in fact all of the foremen required on the job whom it will be necessary to send from one town to another. 

The proper method of computing these costs is to estimate the salaries of the different men required at a certain price per week or per month for the entire time they will be required on the job.

Temporary Buildings and Enclosures.-This should include temporary fences, bridges, or platforms; temporary sheds, store rooms, and water closets; temporary enclosures over hoisting engines, concrete mixers, etc., temporary runways and stairs in the building before the permanent stairs are installed, temporary partitions or screens for enclosing building before the permanent windows or enclosures are in place; also temporary heat or light required during construction. 

Temporary Office. This should include the temporary job office for use by the contractor and architect during construction, together with all necessary expense in maintaining same, such as telephone, heat, light, stationery, and other small items. 

Watchman and Signal Lights.-This should cover the cost of day and night watchmen during construction, cost of maintaining signal lights, etc.

Repairing Streets and Pavements. This item should cover the repair and replacement of all sidewalks and pavements damaged or destroyed during construction.

OVERHEAD EXPENSE 

15 

Damage to Adjoining Buildings.-There is always a chance of a certain amount of damage to adjacent structures, such as breaking windows, damaging foundations and walls improperly shored, damaging skylights, etc., and these items should be considered whẹn making up the estimate.

Protecting New Work from Damage During Construction.— 

During construction there are certain classes of work that must be protected from damage, such as cut stone, marble, terra cotta, granite, etc., also covering newly finished cement or wood floors to prevent damage pending the acceptance of the work by the owner.

Cutting for Other Trades. Many specifications require the general or mason contractor to do all cutting and patching of walls and floors for the plumbing, steam heating and electrical contractor, where it is necessary for the mechanical trades to place sleeves or pipes through the floors or walls after the permanent work is in place. 

Removing and Replacing Water Hydrants, Etc.-In the larger cities it may be necessary to remove water hydrants, poles and wires of telephone, telegraph, or electric light companies, sewers and drains, or other underground pipes pending the installation of certain portions of the new construction work and in such instances it will be necessary for the contractor to pay for any damage incurred. ,, די

Removing Rubbish, Cleaning Floors, Windows, Etc.-During the construction of every building there is always a certain amount of rubbish, such as old concrete, broken brick, tile, etc., that must removed at intervals. The most satisfactory method is to estimate so many loads of rubbish at a certain price per load.

If finish floors are to be swept or scrubbed before acceptance of the building by the owner, it is advisable to make a certain allowance to take care of this work. 

Some architects require the contractor to clean all windows before the building will be accepted. To arrive at this cost, count the windows and allow a certain price for cleaning each window. 

Building Permits. The cost of building permits varies with the city in which the work is to be performed. Some cities base the cost of the permit on the total cost of the building, while others make a charge for the water consumed, the street frontage occupied by the building, and the number of plumbing fixtures, for which an inspection charge is made.

As a general rule a building permit will cost from to of 1 per cent of the total cost of the building. 

In Chicago the cost of a building permit is computed on the following items: 8 cts. per 100 cu. ft. of concrete; 6 cts. per 

100 cu. ft. of rubble stone; 5 cts. per 1,000 brick; 5 cts. per 100 cu. ft. of hollow tile partition or back-up tile; $1.50 per 1,000 sq. yds. of plaster, plus 20 cts. per 1,000 cu. ft. for all area occupied by the building, measured from basement floor to average height of the building. An inspection charge of 50 cts. is also made for every water-closet, urinal, sink, drinking fountain, bath tub, lavatory, etc., in the building.

Surveys. Where the contractor must furnish a survey of the property on which the building is to be erected, a charge of $25.00 to $50.00 is usually made for a lot up to 100' x 100'.

In the downtown sections of large cities this charge will be increased. 

Photographs. Where it is necessary to have photographs taken at intervals to show the progress of the work, the cost will vary with the number of views made at one time. 

In the larger cities it will cost $4.50 to $5.00 for the first photograph and $3.00 to $3.50 for each additional negative. Additional 

8"x10" prints mounted on muslin about 50 cts. each.

In the smaller towns and cities this cost may be reduced onehalf.

Tools and Equipment.-When preparing an estimate on any job, the item of tools and equipment should be figured as carefully as any branch of work in the structure. 

First, make a study of just what equipment will be required to execute the work economically, such as the number and size of concrete mixers, hoisting engines, hoisting towers, derricks, compressors, etc. Also the number of wheelbarrows, concrete barrows or carts, quantity of scaffolding, cables, picks, shovels, etc.

If the job is out of town it will be necessary to add freight and drayage to the job and for its return upon completion. 

On some jobs it may be advantageous to rent or lease certain pieces of equipment, such as concrete mixers, hoisting engines, compressors, etc., and in such instances the rental should be based on the length of time required by each piece of equipment.

Contractors' Insurance 

The following rates for all forms of Fire, Marine and Casualty insurance were furnished by W. W. Durham & Co., Insurance Brokers, 231 S. La Salle St., Chicago, Ill., established 

1901 and serving the best interests of its clientele. This firm will, without obligation, furnish any additional rates, information or service that may be required. 

Fire Insurance.-If provision is not made either in the specifications or contract that Fire insurance will be carried by the owner during construction, it is important that the contractor protect his interests and also the interests of any of his subcontractors, if desired, by carrying adequate insurance. A policy may be arranged and the rates vary based on type of construction, and should be obtained locally. 

Tornado Insurance. This feature of protection is advisable especially when the building is of frame or wooden construction and in a territory frequented by windstorm, cyclones or tornadoes. Standard rates govern which may be obtained locally, and a specific policy may be arranged. 

Automatic Builders Risk Insurance. This form of policy is most desirable and complete as it can be written to cover Fire only, or to include Tornado, Hail, Riot, Civil Commotion and

Explosion at a nominal additional cost. The cost of this policy varies as to territory and type of construction, and could be written on a monthly reporting basis so as to reduce the cost for insurance.

Contractor's Equipment Floater. The successful contractor has established a record for faithful performance; but there are a number of risks over which control cannot be exercised. This may cause a financial strain serious enough to wipe out profits and be responsible for a default in the contract. A Floater form policy could be arranged to cover all equipment against loss or damage by fire and lightning only, or extended to include explosion, tornado, flood, collapse of bridges, transportation perils, theft, collision, landslide, upset or overturn, riot, strike and civil commotion. Rates range from 50 cts. to $1.75 per $100 of insurance depending upon perils insured against and the individual merits of each risk.

Contractor's Performance Bonds.-Surety bonds guaranteeing the faithful performance of a contract for general building and

miscellaneous construction costs 11% on the total contract price for 24 months and the minimum premium is $15.00; thereafter the annual premium is of 1% on the remaining incompleted work. Several types of construction are specially rated as follows: Railroad and Public Utility Construction (except dams) costs 1% on the contract price for the term of the contract with a minimum premium of $15.00; Gasoline Service Stations cost 1% on the contract price for the term with a minimum premium of $15.00; Levee Work and/or Flood Control (except dams) costs 1% on the contract price for the term with a minimum premium of $15.00; Wrecking and Shoring contracts cost 

11% per annum on amount of bond and the minimum charge is $15.00.

Street Paving, Highway, Culvert and Bridge Construction Bonds. For Federal, State, County, Borough, Township. and 

Municipal owners the cost of a performance Bond is 1% on the contract price for 24 months and the annual renewal premium is of 1% on the unfinished work with a minimum premium of $15.00; Sidewalk Bonds cost of 1% on contract price with a minimum premium of $5.00; Curbing and Guttering Bonds when not included in either Street Paving or Sidewalk Contracts cost 1% on contract price with a minimum premium of $10.00 

(When included take Street Paving Rate). 

Iron or Steel Work for Bridges.-Performance Bonds on iron or steel contracts for bridges including assembling or erecting cost of 1% on contract price for the term with a minimum premium of $15.00; Contract for furnishing and delivering metal superstructures only without assembling or erection costs of 

1% on the contract price with a minimum premium of $5.00.

Iron or Steel Contracts on Other Structures Including Build ings. Performance Bonds for furnishing and delivering only without fabricating, assembling or erecting cost of 1% on contract price with a minimum premium of $5.00; Furnishing 

Iron or Steel fabricated to contract specifications without assembling or erecting cost of 1% on contract price, with a minimum premium of $15.00; where such contracts include assembling and erecting, figure $15.00 per $1,000 on contract price with a minimum premium of $15.00.

Supply Bonds. Bonds guaranteeing the furnishing and delivery of stated quantity material or supplies of a standard nature from the sellers' regular stock cost of 1% on the

19 amount of the aggregate contract price. (If the amount of the required bond is less than one-fourth of the aggregate contract price the premium is 1% on the amount of bond) with a minimum premium of $5.00; Bond for specially ordered and designed material or supplies cost of 1% per annum on the contract price with a minimum premium of $15.00.

Labor and Material Bonds. On contracts where State re quirements call for labor and material bonds in conjunction with a performance bond there is no premium charge. On PWA projects where a separate labor bond is required, the cost is of 1% on penalty of the bond for the term. The minimum premium for bonds up to $200.00 is $5.00 and over $200.00 is $10.00. 

Contract Price for Bond Premium Computation.-Initial pre miums and subsequent premiums are computed on the contract price as then established but are subject to adjustment upon completion of the contract. If the original price is increased through extras, there will be additional premium due and if decreased by deductions, corresponding return premium will be allowed.

Maintenance Bonds.-Where no corporate surety bond is required for either construction or supply contracts the cost is of 1% per annum on penalty of the bond with a minimum charge of $7.50 for the term. If the contract or specifications call for a maintenance guarantee extending over 12 months, bond premium for maintenance is computed at $1.50 per thousand per annum on the value of the guaranteed work in the case of miscellaneous construction, whether the maintenance is included in the construction bond or whether a separate bond is required upon completion of the contract. f 

On Highway Construction Maintenance Bond the rate is $2.00 per $1,000 per annum in advance on the cost of the work with a minimum of $1.00 for each year of maintenance; on Supply 

Bonds (maintenance) the rate is $0.62 per $1,000 per annum on the contract price with the minimum premium for supply and maintenance $10.00; Sidewalk, Curbing and Guttering Maintenance Bonds which are 15% or less of the contract price cost $10.00 per $1,000 per annum on amount of bond with a term minimum of $5.00. Where maintenance requirement is included in contract bond and specifications, maintenance extending beyond one year, for Sidewalk, Curbing and Guttering Contracts cost $1.50 per $1,000 per annum on the contract price.

Bid Bonds.-A Bid Bond on supply contracts cost $2.50 flat, all other classes $5.00 flat.

Contractor's Insurance.-In connection with a Workmen's Compensation and Employers' Liability Policy, the following coverages should be obtained: Contractors' Public Liability and Contractors' Contingent or Protective Liability. The former assures protection for claims arising from accidents suffered by others than employees of the contractor, due to negligence on the part of the contractor or his employees resulting from his direct operations, whereas the latter provides protection for claims brought against the contractor resulting from accidents caused by sub-contractors or their employees, for which the contractor may be held liable by the court. Often times the contractor will be required to assume all liability of the owner, thus holding him harmless. In such cases, it is best to consult your insurance broker, or W. W. Durham & Co., Insurance Brokers, 231 S.

La Salle St., Chicago, in order to secure the proper insurance coverage. 

Owners' Contingent Policy.— In connection with Contractors' Employers' Liability and Workmen's Compensation insurance, all contractors should carry what is known as an Owners' Contingent Liability Policy. Some of the insurance companies will write a blanket policy on this kind of insurance running to the Owners of the premises on which the work is being performed. 

The rate is 60 cts. per $1,000 for the first $500,000; 40 cts. per $1,000 for the next $500,000, and 20 cts. per $1,000 for the amount in excess of $1,000,000, based upon the total amount of the con tract. The Workmen's Compensation or Employers' Liability 

Policies assume all liability imposed upon the contractor by law, but do not assume any contractual liability. Inasmuch as the contractor generally agrees to hold the Owners harmless from all accidents resulting from the prosection of the contract, he thus assumes a liability not contemplated by the Workmen's 

Compensation and Employers' Liability Policies. The issuance of a Contractual Liability Policy will provide protection against such a contractual obligation whereas an Owners' Contingent Liability Policy will provide protection to the owner against legal liability imposed upon him by law for accidental bodily injuries or death suffered by the public growing out of the prosecution of work by a contractor.

OVERHEAD EXPENSE 

21 

Contractual Liability Policy. This form of policy provides protection to the contractor in accordance with the provisions of the contract and the issuance of such a policy obviates the necessity of an Owners' Contingent Liability Policy. The rate for contractual coverage is based on the coverage assumed and each contract must be referred to the insurance company for rating.

Occupational Diseases Coverage.-In some States there are 

Workmen's Occupational Diseases laws in effect, and if a contractor is engaged in a class of work that may result in a disease suffered by his employees, said coverage can be added by an endorsement to be attached to a Workmen's Compensation Policy, the rates being exceptionally low. 

A General Contractor should carry a Contractor's Contingent 

Liability Policy protecting himself against any claims for bodily injury or death suffered by any person other than those in his employ, growing out of accidents caused by subcontractors for which accident the General Contractor may be held responsible. 

Accidents of this nature are not covered under the Public Liability Policy of the General Contractor, as that specifically provides protection for public accidents growing out of his immediate operations, and not that of a subcontractor. The rates for this form of coverage is 10 cts. per $100 of total cost of contract work sublet up to $500,000; 6 cts. per $100 for the next $500,000; and 4 cts. per $100 for any amount in excess of $1,000,000 on each specific contract.

Estimating the Cost of Employers' Liability and Workmen's Compensation Insurance 

The rates given in the following pages are based on each $100 of payroll applicable to such classifications. 

In the State of West Virginia Workmen's Compensation in surance rates have a base rate and a sliding scale of rates based on merit. An employer's merit rate shall be the sum of his loss ratio and a loading of 20 per cent of the base rate, the minimum rate to be 65 per cent and the maximum rate 220 per cent respectively of the base rate. 

In the State of Washington, Industrial Insurance and Medical Aid rates are based on a certain number of cents per workman hour instead of the usual rates per $100.00 of payroll.

Summary of Job Overhead Expense 

When preparing estimates the items listed under Job Overhead Expense should always be included in the cost of the building, as they are a part of the direct cost of the job. 

The following items should be included in the estimate: 

Building Permits, Street Permits, etc... . . . .$. 

$250.00 

Superintendent, 6 months at $300.00.. 1,800.00 

Timekeeper and Material Clerk, 6 mo. at $150

Temporary Job Office... 

900.00 150.00 

Cement and Tool Sheds.. 300.00 

Watchman, 6 months at $100.00... 600.00 

Cutting for other trades (approximated).. 75.00 

Removing rubbish. Approx. 200 loads at $2.50 500.00 

Photographs during construction... 50.00

Fire and Tornado Insurance.. 

75.00 

Plant and Equip. Conc. mixer, 3 mo. at $100 300.00 

Hoisting engine, 6 months at $100.00.... 600.00 

Constructing hoisting tower.... 500.00 

Small tools, wheelbarrows, shovels, scaffolding, etc. 500.00

590.00 

Surety Bond, 11% of $150,000.00. 2,250.00 

Total Job Overhead Expense.... 

.$........$9,440.00

It will be noted from the above figures that unless all overhead or general expense items are included in the estimate, the margin of profit must be unusually large to provide for them. 

A REMINDER WHEN MAKING UP ESTIMATES 

The following list includes nearly every item encountered in the construction of present day buildings.

It is intended as a reminder for the estimator, in order that the estimate may be compared with this list to see that all items have been included. 

Forgetting has cost many a contractor his profit.

MENSURATION 

The tables given on the following pages will enable contractors and estimators to estimate quantities and costs accurately and in a minimum amount of time. 

In a number of tables, the quantities are stated in decimals, as by using decimals, it is possible to state the fractional parts of inches, feet and yards, in a smaller space than where regular fractions are used.

For the contractor or estimator who is not thoroughly familiar with the decimal system, complete explanations are given covering the use of all classes of decimal fractions, so that they may be used rapidly and accurately.

Estimating is nearly all "figures" of one kind or another, so it is essential that the contractor and estimator possess a fair working knowledge of arithmetic, if his estimates are to be accurate and dependable.

Most of the estimator's computations involve measurements of surface and cubical contents and are stated in lineal feet (lin.ft.), square feet (sq.ft.), square yards (sq.yds.), squares (sqs.) containing 100 sq. ft., cubic feet (cu.ft.) and cubic yards (cu.yds.). These quantities are often further reduced to thousands of brick, feet of lumber, board measure (b.m.), etc.

HEIGHT HEIGHT LENGTH SQUARE LENGTH RECTANGLE LENGTH PARALLELOGILAM To Compute the Area of a Square, Rectangle or Parallelogram.-Multiply the length by the breadth or height. Example: 

Obtain the area of a wall 22 ft. (22′-0″) long and 9 ft. (9′-0″) high. 22x9=198 sq. ft.

To Compute the Area of a Triangle.-Multiply the base by the altitude or perpendicular height. Example: Find the area of the end gable of a house 24 ft. (24′-0″) wide and 12 ft. (12′-0″) high from base to high point of roof. 24 ft. x 6 ft. ( the height) 144 sq. ft.

To Compute the Circumference of a Circle.-Multiply the diameter by 3.1416. The diameter multiplied by 34 is close enough for all practical purposes. Example: Find the circumference or distance around a circle, the diameter of which is 12 ft. (12'-0"). 12x3.1416=37.6992 ft. the distance around the circle or 12x34=374 or 37.714 ft.

How to Use the Decimal System of Numerals in Estimating 

In construction work nearly all figures are either feet and inches or dollars and cents but inasmuch as it is convenient to use the decimal system in making many computations, a brief description of this system is given for the use of contractors and estimators who are not familiar with it. 

A decimal is a fraction whose denominator is not written, but is some power of 10. They are often called decimal fractions but more often simply a decimal.

Example: We know 50 cents is for of a dollar. Writing the same thing in decimals would be $0.50.

Numerator Denominator 

50 100 When written as .50 or .5, it is a fraction whose denominator is not written, it being understood to be 10 from the fact that 5 occupies the first place to the right of the decimal point.

Therefore we have the following: 0.5 means 

0.25 means 5

0.125 means 15, for the 125 extends to the 1000dth's place.

The orders beyond the ten thousandths are hundred thousandths, millionths, ten milliont.s, etc., but in figuring construction work it is seldom necessary to carry the figures beyond three or four decimal points.

A whole number and a decimal together, form a mixed decimal. Example: 2.25 is the same as 2 or 21. 95 The period written at the left of tenths is called the decimal point. Example, 0.5 = 1%; 0.25 = 

4; 0.375 = 

100%, etc. 375 It is not necessary to write a zero at the left of the decimal point in the above examples, for 0.5 means the same as .5. The zero is often written there to call attention more quickly to the decimal point.

In the construction business, decimals are used chiefly to denote feet and inches, hours and minutes, the fractional working units of the various kinds of materials, and in money, which is dollars and cents or fractional parts of 100.

Similar Decimals.-Decimals that have the same number of decimal places are called similar decimals. Thus, 0.75 and 0.25 are similar decimals and so are 0.150 and 0.275; but 0.15 and 

0.275 are dissimilar decimals.

To reduce dissimilar decimals to similar decimals, give them the same number of decimal places by annexing or cutting off zeros. Example, 0.125, 0.25, 0.375 and 0.5 may all be reduced to thousandths as follows: 0.125, 0.250, 0.375 and 0.500.

To Reduce a Decimal to a Common Fraction.-Omit the decimal point, write the denominator of the decimal, and then reduce the common fraction to its lowest terms. 1000, Example: 0.375 equals 35, which reduced to its lowest terms, equals . 25 375 1000 |15 = 5 = 40 

How to Add Decimals.-To add number's containing decimals, write like orders under one another, and then add as with whole numbers. Example, add 0.125, 0.25, 0.375, and 1.0. 

The total of the addition is 1.750, which equals 

15%, and which may be further reduced to 12 750 1000, 0.125 0.25 0.375 1.0 1.750 

How to Subtract Decimals.-To subtract one number from another, when either or both contain decimals, reduce to similar decimals, write like orders under one another, and subtract as with whole numbers. 

Subtract 20 hours and 37 minutes from 27 hours and 13 minutes, both being written in decimals. The difference is 6.6000 or 6.6 hours, which reduced to a common fraction is 63 hours or 6 hours and 36 minutes. 27.2167 20.6167 6.6000

How to Multiply Decimals.-The same method is used as in multiplying other numbers, and the result should contain as many decimal points as there are in both of the numbers multiplied.

47 In making the above multiplications, you will note there are 2 decimals in both the multiplicand and the multiplier of all the amounts multiplied, so the result should contain as many decimals as the sum of the multiplicand and multiplier, which is 4. 

You will note all the totals contain 4 decimal places. You know the correct result is $7.9575, but suppose by mistake you counted off 5 decimal places. The result would be $.79575 or $0.80 per cu. yd. or just about enough; or if you made a mistake the other way and counted off just 3 decimal places, the result would be $79.575 or $79.58 per cu. yd., or just about 10 times too much. Watch your decimal places.

CHAPTER II EXCAVATING AND BACK-FILLING, CAISSONS, SHEET PILING, WOOD AND CONCRETE PILES 

Excavation is one of the easiest branches of work to obtain quantities or actual amount of earth to be excavated but one of the most difficult to estimate the labor costs accurately.

It is not a difficult matter to compute the number of cu. yds. of earth to be excavated or removed from the premises but it is quite another matter to estimate the actual cost of performing this work, on account of the many hidden items entering into the cost. This includes such items as kind of soil, whether or not water will be encountered, pumping, whether the banks of the excavated portion will be self-supporting or whether it will be necessary to brace and sheet-pile them, disposal of excavated earth, length of haul to dump, etc.

Estimating Quantities of Excavation.-Excavating is measured by the cu. yd. containing 27 cu. ft. 

When computing the cubical contents of any basement or portion to be excavated, take all measurements from outside of basement walls and add 1'-6" to 2'-0" on each side of wall to allow for placing and removing concrete foundation wall forms, painting outside of basement walls with damp-proof paints or for back-plastering same.

On large structures where the concrete footings or piers project a considerable distance beyond the line of the outside basement walls, it will be necessary to excavate the full width of the projection on all sides. Example: Assume you are figuring a building 100′-0″x100'-0" on the ground. The outside footing and pier foundations extend 2'-6" beyond the face of the foundation walls on each side, so it would be necessary to figure the size of the excavation 100'-0"+2′-6″+2′-6″=105′-0″.

The size of the excavation should be figured 105'-0"x105′-0″, multiplied by the depth. 49

When estimating the quantity of excavation in any basement or area to be excavated, it is customary to have the general excavation extend from the natural grade (grade of the ground as you receive it) to the underside of the basement floor. Where cinders or other filling is to be placed under the concrete floor, the excavation should be measured from the natural grade to the underside of the basement floor fill. 

When estimating the quantities of excavation for trenches, take the actual width of the footing as the width of the trench. 

This is seldom less than 1'-4" or 1'-6" and may be 3'-0" or 

4'-0" wide. A man needs 1'-6" to 2'-0" in width to work in a trench, and the deeper the trench the more width required to shovel and throw out the excavated earth. 

To obtain the quantity of excavation in any trench, multiply the length by the width by the depth. The illustration of the estimate sheet on the opposite page shows just how the dimensions should be listed and extended. 

When estimating the quantities of excavation for piers or abutments, take the outside dimensions by the depth, as the bottom course of the footing is usually placed without forms. 

Where foundation walls are of stone, brick or rubble, it will be necessary to excavate sufficient width for the men to work alongside the wall.

Estimating the Labor Cost of Excavation.-Before an exca vating estimate is made up or a bid submitted, the estimator should visit the site and ascertain the exact conditions surrounding the work to be performed. The natural grade of the lot should be noted to compute the depth of the excavation from grade to underside of floor line; the nature of the soil should be determined, whether sand, loam or clay, and whether or not you are likely to strike water. Water usually means an additional cost-pumping out the hole day and night until the foundations are completed.

The safest method of determining the kind of soil is to dig a test hole the approximate depth of the basement, and from this you should obtain a fairly accurate idea of the conditions to be encountered.

If the lot is low and the basement does not cover the entire lot, part of the excavated soil may be used for filling. On the other hand, if the natural grade of the lot is above the sidewalk or established grade, it may be necessary to remove a certain amount of soil from the entire lot.

In many instances the top soil will be a rich black loam which may be sold at a price that will more than pay for the excavation, and frequently where sand is encountered in the excavation, it may be used for masonry mortar. 

If it is necessary to remove the excavated soil from the premises, locate the nearest available dump, and ascertain just how the soil may be handled at the dump, whether it is necessary to spread it, etc.

These are all items that affect the cost and should be given careful consideration by the estimator.

In most localities there are contractors who make a specialty of excavating and are familiar with the kind of soil encountered in different parts of the town. These contractors usually quote a price per cu. yd. for all of the general excavation or they may quote a lump sum for the entire job. 

Trench and pier excavating is usually done by the building contractor.

The cost of cutting down and removing trees will vary with their size and the method used in cutting them down and disposing of them. If their roots run through the portion to be excavated it will increase the labor cost of excavating and removing the soil.

Methods of Excavating 

Excavating costs will vary with the kind of soil and the method used in loosening and removing same. If the lot is low and the excavated soil can be placed in piles or spread over the lot 25 to 50 ft. from excavation, a drag scraper should be used. Drag scrapers contain 3, 5 or 7 cu. ft. when filled but for ordinary work figure only 75 to 80 per cent of capacity.

In small basements where the excavated soil must be removed from the premises, it is customary to load the dirt into wagons by hand or use a small tractor scraper that excavates and loads the wagons or trucks. It will also be necessary to have a “snatch" team to help pull the loaded wagons out of the hole.

In excavations large enough to warrant the use of a steam or power shovel, this is the most satisfactory and economical method to use. The shovel will load the trucks as fast as they can be handled in and out of the hole and will enable the job to proceed much faster.

The tables of quantities and costs given on the previous pages are "average." It is true experienced excavators will perform more work than given in the tables but an inexperienced man will perform less, so average conditions have been used throughout.

Capacity of Shovels, Wheel Barrows, Dump-Wagons and Trucks 

It requires about 150 shovels full (No. 2 shovel) for one cu. yd. 

A 2 horse dump wagon has 40 cu. ft. (1 cu. yds.) capacity of loose material. Horses travel about 200 ft. per min. or 2 mi.per hr. with a load of 4,000 to 6,000 lbs. over paved streets and 11 miles per hr. over unpaved streets and country roads. 

An auto truck will hold 4 to 7 cu. yds. of loose material. 

Steam or Power Shovel Excavating 

The cost of steam or power shovel excavating will vary with the size of the job, the size of the shovel, and the speed with which the trucks are handled in and out of the hole, as it is seldom that the shovel can work to capacity, due to the congestion of trucks waiting to get in or out of the excavated section or due to trucks being held up and delayed at the durnp.

The size of the job also has considerable bearing on the costs, as it costs just as much to get the shovel to the job and remove it at completion for 1,000 cu. yds. as for a 10,000 cu. yd. job. 

Where it is possible to use a 1-cu. yd. shovel to capacity, it should excavate 50 to 60 cu. yds. an hr. but this will prove the exception rather than the rule, as there are always delays

EXCAVATING 

55 due to bad weather, delays in loading, moving shovel from place to place, etc., so that the daily average will probably run about half the rated capacity of the shovel. 

Removing Excavated Earth in Dump Wagons.-This cost will vary with the method used in loading the wagons, whether by hand or power shovel, and upon the length of the haul. 

If the excavating is done by a power shovel and the wagons loaded in the same manner, it should not require over 10 minutes time for a wagon at the job loading and 5 minutes at the dump, providing there are no unnecessary delays.

If the dump wagons are being loaded while the team stands waiting, it will require 6 men about 15 minutes; 4 men 22 minutes; 3 men 30 minutes; 2 men 45 minutes, and one man 11 hrs. to shovel and load 2 cu. yds. of loose earth into the wagon. 

Allowing 5 minutes to dump the wagon at destination and 15 minutes to load it, it will require about 20 minutes per load, in addition to traveling time. 

Where two wagons are used with each team, one wagon being loaded while the other is being hauled to the dump, it should not require over 10 minutes to change wagons, and with 5

minutes to dump, it will require only 15 minutes per load, in addition to traveling time.

Example: A truck carrying 4 cu. yds. per load makes 18 loads containing 72 cu. yds. per day. With the truck costing $30.00 per day, what is the hauling cost per cu. yd.? $30.00÷72-42, or $0.42 per cu. yd. 

Trenching and Ditching Machine Excavation 

The cost of excavating using trenching or ditching machines will vary with the size of the job, width and depth of trenches, etc., as the machines are manufactured to dig certain standard width trenches, so that trenches a little narrower or wider will not make any appreciable difference in the daily output. 

When figuring operating costs, include one operator and helper, daily fuel and oil consumption, depreciation, interest on investment, repairs and replacements, etc. For ordinary figuring, the life of the machine should be figured at 5 years or 

60 digging miles, which is equivalent to 316,800 lin. ft. of trench.

While the following table gives the rated capacity of the machine, it will be necessary to allow for time lost moving machine, bad weather, waiting for trucks where it is necessary to load the material, etc., so that except on very large jobs, such as pipe lines, etc., it is not advisable to figure rated capacity as the average daily output. 

Operating Cost of Ditching Machines.-Taking as an example, a machine costing approximately $4,000.00; interest for 5 years at $240.00 $1,200.00; annual repairs and replacements 5 years at $350.00 $1,750.00, or a total of $7,000.00.

Dividing $7,000.00 by 316,800 lin. ft. of trench (estimated life of machine) gives $0.02 per lin. ft. operating costs. Fuel and oil figured at $6 to $7 per day, averages $0.00 per lin. ft. making a total operating cost of $0.03 per lin. ft. exclusive of labor.

Road Speeds are: Low, 4-mi. per hr.; 2nd. 1-mi. per hr.; high, 2-mi, per hr.; reverse, 1-mi. per hr. 

When ditchers are digging the transmission is normally required to run in 2nd speed.

With this in 2nd speed the bucket runs 182 ft. per min. on a standard machine and 291 ft. per min. on the pipe line model. 

Ordinarily a standard ditcher is fitted with a 22-tooth sprocket, and the 15-tooth sprocket is shipped extra. A Pipe Line Special is fitted with a 15-tooth sprocket, and the 11-tooth sprocket is shipped extra. Changing these sprockets does not change the speed of the digging line.

To dig 24" wide, a special steel extension with tooth sprocket taking a straight tooth is furnished with the 18" bucket. 

To dig 21" wide the 18" buckets are furnished with reversible side-cutting teeth.

Actual Costs of Excavating 

The following costs are taken from work actually completed, giving methods used, kind of soil encountered and conditions under which the work was performed. 

Excavating in Tough Clay or "Texas" Gumbo.-Rice Institute,

Houston, Texas. This excavation was in very tough clay known in Texas as "gumbo." The job consisted of piers and trenches 

1'-6" to 4'-0" wide and 5'-0" deep.

On account of the extreme toughness of this soil, it was necessary to loosen all clay with picks or use shovels having blades about 5″ wide and 20″ long, called "sharpshooters."

This is the only practical shovel to use in soil of this kind and even then it requires a man experienced in this class of excavating to accomplish much in a day. Ordinary building laborers would loosen and remove only 3 cu. yds. per 9-hr. day, but experienced "well diggers" would loosen and remove as much as 6 cu. yds. per 9-hr. day. The average for the job was 

4 cu. yds. per 9-hr. day. Colored labor was used throughout.

CAISSONS 

Caissons are ordinarily used to support very large structures or where soil conditions are unsatisfactory to support a heavy structure. Their size and depth varies with the weight to be

CAISSONS 

71 carried and the depth to bed rock. Chicago caissons average from 90'-0" to 100'-0" in depth.

The cost of excavating varies with the diameter and depth of the caisson, and whether or not water or quick sand are encountered. It is practically impossible to estimate the cost of excavating in quick-sand. 

There are contractors who specialize in foundation work and the several types of caissons. On jobs of any size, it is advisable to obtain figures from these concerns covering the work, as they are equipped to perform it much more economically than the contractor who has only an occasional job. 

Estimating Caisson Quantities. When estimating excavating quantities, take the diameter of the caisson as shown on the plan and add 6″ to allow for the space required by the lagging. 

Example: Find the number of cu. yds. of excavating in a caisson 6'-0" in diameter and 106'-0" deep.

By adding 6" to the diameter to allow for lagging, the diameter would be figured as 6'-6". To obtain the area of a circle, multiply the square of the diameter by .7854. 6'-6″-6.5'. 

6.5x6.5=42.25, the square of the diameter.

Multiply the square of the diameter by 7854 to obtain the area of the caisson, i.e., 42.25x.7854-33.183150 or 33.18 sq. ft.

Multiply the area of the caisson by the depth to obtain the cubical contents, i.e., 33.18x106=3517.08 cu. ft. 3517.08÷27 =130 cu. yds.

After the excavating quantities have been obtained, the next step is to obtain the amount of lagging necessary to wall up the sides of the caisson until the concrete is placed. Either 

2"x6" or 3"x6" tongue and grooved maple in 5'-0" lengths is usually used for lagging. On account of the tongue and groove in the lumber it is necessary to add about 15% to the actual circumference of the caisson to obtain the number of feet of lagging required. 

It requires 23 ft. b. m. of 2″x6″ and 31 ft. b. m. of 3″x6″ lagging to cover one sq. ft. of wall surface. 

To obtain the wall area of the caisson, multiply the circum ference of the caisson by its depth. Example: Obtain the number of feet of lagging, b.m. required to wall up a caisson 

6'-0" in diameter and 106'-0" deep. To obtain the circumference of the caisson, multiply the diameter by 3.1416, i.e., 6x3.1416= 

18.8496, or for all practical purposes 19′-0″. 19x106=2,014 sq. ft. of wall area in the caisson. Using 2"x6" lagging, 2,014 x23=4,699 ft. b. m. of lagging required.

Labor Required for Caissons 

The labor cost of caisson excavating varies with the diameter and depth of the caisson, whether hand or pneumatic shovels and picks are used, the kind of soil, and whether or not water or quick sand is encountered. The smaller the caisson, the higher the cu. yd. cost on account of the crowded quarters in which the men are compelled to work. The number of men required on each caisson varies with the size and the distance the excavated earth must be wheeled or hauled to a dump. 

The average caisson requires 6 to 7 men, distributed as follows: 

2 or 3 men in the well as "diggers", excavating, filling buckets and placing lagging; one man on top operating windlass or "nigger-head" and hoisting the excavated earth from the bottom of the caisson, and 3 or 4 laborers handling lagging, dumping buckets, and loading the excavated earth into wagons. On many well managed jobs, small tractors are used to haul the excavated earth from the caissons to the dump, which reduces labor costs considerably.

Caisson Excavating.-Two men working together as "diggers" should excavate and load into buckets 1 to 14 cu. yds. an hr. or 8 to 10 cu. yds. per 8-hr. day, depending upon soil conditions. 

Estimating the labor cost of placing lagging as a part of the excavating cost, a laborer should excavate and place lagging for one cu. yd. in 2 to 2 hrs. or 3 to 3 cu. yds. per 8-hr. day. 

When excavating by compressed air, a man with a pneumatic digger will loosen and load into buckets 9 to 11 cu. yds. per 

8-hr. day, depending upon the toughness of the clay and the working space.

After the excavated earth has been hoisted from the caisson, it is either necessary to dump the buckets and load the excavated earth into barrows or wagons, or it may be dumped direct into small one-man tractor hoppers and hauled to the main dump. When handled by hand, it requires about 3 hrs. labor time to handle a cu. yd. of excavation from the time the bucket reaches the top of the caisson until the excavated earth is loaded into barrows or wagons. This is at the rate of 21 to 2 cu. yds. per 8-hr. day. 

Where small one-man tractors are used, the buckets are usually hoisted and dumped direct into the tractor hopper, eliminating about half of the hand labor required.

To compute the cost of hauling the ex avated earth from the job to the dump, use the same metho. as described on the previous pages for "Hauling by Motor Truck."

In addition to the above, it will be necessary to allow for time of foreman, time-keepers, material clerks, engineers, cost of setting up and removing equipment, etc., which will cost from 50 to 75 cts. per cu. yd. or it may be estimated separately under overhead expense and a certain amount allowed to cover the entire job.

Wood Lagging.—It requires 23 ft. b. m. of 2″x6″ lagging or 

33 ft. b. m. of 3″x6″ lagging per sq. ft. of wall surface. 

The labor cost placing lagging will vary with the size of the caisson but an average job having caissons 5′-0″ to 8′-0″ in diameter will require 20 to 25 hrs. labor time per 1,000 ft. of lagging, b.m. including time placing iron rings. 

Caissons 5'-0" to 6'-0" in diameter will require 23 to 25 hrs. labor per 1,000 ft. of lagging, b.m.; 6'-6" to 8'-0" caissons 20 to 

22 hrs. and caissons over 8'-0" in diameter will require 19 to 

20 hrs. labor per 1,000 ft. b.m.

The cost of lagging a caisson 6'-0" in diameter and 100'-0” deep, having a wall area of 1,885 sq. ft. and requiring 4,400 ft. b. m. of 2"x6" lagging, should run about as follows:

Actual Costs of Caissons

 ESTIMATING THE COST OF MAKING SOUNDINGS FOR LOCATING STRATAS ON WHICH TO SET FOUNDATIONS 

When preparing estimates on many structures, it is often necessary to make drillings or test holes to ascertain just what class of soil will be encountered and whether or not water will be found and at what depth.

There are several methods of making these tests, which vary according to the information required regarding the soil and the composition of same. The five different methods commonly used for making soundings are Hollow Rod, Core Drilling, Jetting, Churn Drilling, and boring by means of a hand augur.

Method of Making Soundings for Building Foundations. 

The most authentic samples of clay, sand, silt, gravel, etc., can be secured by driving two strings of pipe, preferably 3". 

The 3" pipe should be driven in about 5'-0" lengths. This length of 3" pipe should be cleaned out and a 2" pipe with an improved valve in the bottom, driven through the 3" pipe into the undisturbed stratas and a core or slug collected inside of the 2" pipe. The 2" pipe is then removed and the sample thus obtained, is placed in a bag or jar and properly labeled. 

The sample that is thus taken is in its natural state and contains all clay, silt, etc., and is more true than washed borings 1000

SOUNDINGS 

79 01 churn drill samples. The 3" pipe is then driven another short distance, cleaned out and a sample is taken as before. 

This manner of testing costs about $3.00 per lin. ft. depending upon quantity of work.

The Company* listed in the footnotes maintains drilling equipment in all parts of the Country and will gladly furnish estimates on all classes of test holes, water wells, etc., upon receipt of your inquiry.

Hollow Rod Work. This system of making borings and tests is operated with a churn drill through which the stratas are pumped to the surface and caught in a screen. The most common size holes drilled with hollow rods are 2", 21" and 

3" in diameter.

With this system a very definite description of the stratas may be secured to a depth of 500 feet. 

The cost of drilling holes by the hollow rod method will vary with the amount of drilling necessary and the distance it is necessary to ship tools and equipment.

Hand Augur Drilling. This method of drilling consists of the use of a hand augur which resembles in appearance a large augur used for boring wood. DRILLING WATER WELLS 

The pollution of streams by various manufacturing concerns, due to the fact that the streams are the natural drainage, is driving many municipalities and industries to wells for their water supply.

Where glacial stratas are found, the large quantities of water are found in the sand and gravel. The quality of gravel water is always harder than sand rock water and usually of lower temperature.

Casings, Screens and Pumps Used in Modern Water Wells. 

blank

When a large quantity of water is desired it is customary to drill a test hole to determine if the strata is suitable for water to travel through it, and if it is, then blank pipe, is driven to the top of the water bearing strata and a screen set through the water strata. A turbine pump is the best type of pumping equipment.

The travel of water through a well screen has a tendency to precipitate the solids from the water and close the screen as well as close up the openings in the gravel, some water closes the screens readily, while other screens remain open indefinitely. 

When screens do close they can be opened easily and quickly by an improved acid treatment, which the Ohio Drilling 

Company has protected.

Rock wells are drilled by driving the pipe or casing to the rock and continuing with open hole the inside diameter of the casing through the rock.

It is possible to increase the quantity of water from a rock well by shooting when the water rock is massive, close grained and not creviced. However, if the water bearing strata is loose, porous and creviced the shooting is not beneficial. 

The best type of pump for a rock well is an electric driven turbine pump.

Gravel wells, cost including pipe and screen, from $1.50 to $2.00 per inch in diameter, per lin. ft. of vertical depth, i.e., a 

12" well in gravel would cost from $18.00 to $24.00 per lin. ft. in depth.

Rock wells cost about $0.50 per inch of diameter, plus cost of pipe, per lin. ft. of depth, as follows: a 6″ well would cost $3.00 per lin. ft. of vertical depth, plus the cost of the pipe. Of course in rock, pipe is not used but if there is 100'-0" of earth or gravel over the rock, it would be necessary to figure pipe for this portion, then when rock is struck, the pipe would no longer be necessary. 

Turbine pumps cost from $1,000.00 to $4,000.00, depending upon capacity and head of water.

There is no appreciable difference in the lineal foot cost of water wells according to their depth. As a rule, the larger wells run from 100′-0″ to 400′-0″ in depth and a higher price per inch of diameter would apply to shallow wells, due to the cost of the screens. *Ohio Drilling Company, Massillon, Ohio.

SHEET PILING 

83 The Company* furnishing this information maintain drilling equipment in all parts of the country and will gladly quote prices on any project. 

WOOD SHEET PILING AND BRACING 

Wood sheet piling and bracing is usually estimated by the square foot, taking the number of sq. ft. of bank or trench walls to be braced or sheet piled, and estimating the cost of the work at a certain price per sq. ft. for labor and lumber required.

Sheet piling or bracing is required where the soil is not selfsupporting or where the excavation adjoins a property line. 

In ordinary soil an excavation 8′-0″ or 9′-0″ deep will be selfsupporting unless the excavation is in sand or water. There is usually considerable vibration adjacent to railroad or street car tracks, etc., which will cause the banks to cave in. Unless there is ample space on all sides of the excavations, the banks should be sheet piled to avoid damage to streets, alleys or adjacent buildings.

Trench or foundation piers 5′-0″ to 8′-0″ deep and 3′-0″ or 4'-0" wide may require bracing or sheet piling but this is much simpler than is ordinarily required for basement excavations.

The cost of this work will vary with the kind of soil, depth of the excavation, amount of bracing or sheet piling required and the method used in placing same. 

In ordinary excavations where no water is encountered, 2″ or 3" square edge planks may be used but if running sand or water is encountered, tongue and grooved planks should be used, as it is easier to keep them in line and they are more water tight than square edge planks. It is customary to cut the bottom edge of each plank on a slight angle, so that in driving it is wedged against the preceding plank. The upper corners of the plank should also be cut off so that the effects of the blows will be concentrated along its vertical axis. This reduces splitting.

It requires 2 to 3 ft. of lumber, b.m. to sheet pile one sq. ft. of trench 5'-0" to 8′-0″ deep, but on large deep excavations it will require 6 to 8 ft. of lumber, b.m. per sq. ft. of wall. 

Sheet piling is usually driven with a large sledge or wooden mallet, but the latter is preferable, as it is not so likely to split the planks while they are being driven. *Ohio Drilling Company, Massillon, Ohio.

Where compressed air is available, considerable time and money can be saved by driving the sheet piling with a pneumatic hammer designed especially for this purpose. 

On very large jobs an ordinary pile driver is used for driving the sheet piling but this is done only on jobs of sufficient size to warrant the cost of installing a pile driver and crew. 

Bracing and Sheet Piling Trenches and Piers.-When exca vating trenches and piers 5′-0″ to 8'-0" deep, it is not always necessary to sheathe the walls solid but two or three lines of
