Driving Wood Sheet Piling With a Pile Driver. When wood sheet piling is driven by a pile driver, built-up sections consisting of 3 pcs. of 2"x12" or 3"x12" plank are spiked together, forming a tongue and groove, as illustrated on page 82. 

These sections are sharpened on one end and driven in the same manner as ordinary wood piles, and at about the same labor costs. Including both labor and material, this will average about $0.75 per sq. ft.

Estimating the Quantity of Steel Sheet Piling. When esti mating the quantity of steel sheet piling required for any job, take the entire girth of the basement, cofferdam or piers that are to be sheet piled, and this will give the number of lineal feet required. Example: suppose you have a basement 100'-0"x125′-0″ to be sheet piled. Adding the four sides of the excavation, 100+100+125+125=450 lin. ft. Using M-112 Carnegie sheet piling 16" wide. 450'-0"÷1.33' 338, or it requires 338 pcs. to sheet pile the excavation. Using sheet piling 30'-0" long, 338x30=10,140 lin. ft. weighing 30.6 lbs. per lin. ft. equals 

310,284 lbs.

A shorter method is as follows: 450 lin. ft. around excavation multiplied by 30'-0" long, equals 13,500 sq. ft. of piling at 23 lbs. per sq. ft. equals 310,500 lbs.

Either method is satisfactory, except it is necessary to know the number of pieces to be driven to compute the labor costs accurately.

WOOD PILES 

When estimating the cost of wood piles the item of overhead expense must be considered before the actual cost of

WOOD PILES 

93 driving the piles can be computed. This includes the cost of moving the equipment to the job, setting it up ready to operate and dismantling and removing it at completion. 

This item will remain practically the same regardless of the size of the job, as the equipment charge will be as much on a job having 100 piles as on a job containing 1,000 piles. 

The actual cost of driving the piles will vary with soil conditions, length of piles and the amount of moving necessary.

Driving Wood Piles on a Large Chicago Job

The job actually contained 2,570 piles 55'-0" long and 80 piles 60'-0" long, driven in typical Chicago clay along the river front.

Two pile drivers with 75-ft. heads and single acting steam hammers were employed; driving radius 20'-0"; total weight of hammer 10,000 lbs.; weight of driving ram 5,000 lbs. ; effective distance 3 ft. One driver was the usual timber rig, with steel channel guides instead of the usual 16"x16" timbers. The other had an all steel welded rig, which cost about the same as a wooden rig but the erecting and dismantling costs are about half those of a timber pile driver; and while the latter is usually replaced in 6 to 8 years, the steel rig is considered practically indestructible. 

Each pile driver crew consisted of 9 men: foreman, hoisting engineman, fireman, winch hand, guide man high up in rig, guide man at base of leads, two men handling piles on the ground and one man squaring heads of piles to fit hammer plate.

Loads of 50 piles were lashed on 2 flat cars coupled together and delivered on a spur track adjacent to the site, where 2 men with cant hooks rolled the logs onto storage piles. 

Out of a total of 568 driver-hours, 40 hrs. were spent in moving runs and timbers for driving, 17 hrs. in moving pile butts and debris, and 6 hrs. through breakdowns and other unavoidable delays.

It required a total of 568 hrs. or 71 days for one pile driver, which averaged 4 piles (255 lin. ft.) an hr. or 37 piles (2,040 lin. ft.) per 8-hr. day, at the following cost per pile:

CONCRETE PILES 

Due to the wide variations and conditions under which concrete piles are installed and used, it is difficult to give dependable cost figures without possessing the details of each installation. The different types of piles also vary considerably in cost. When estimating work containing concrete piles, it is always advisable to consult contractors specializing in this class of work. Most of them maintain offices in the principal cities and are usually willing to investigate and quote on any anticipated work. Figures can thus be obtained with more accuracy than can be given in a general way. 

Concrete piles are placed under two different methods, one of which is known as a "premoulded" or "pre-cast" pile, in which a concrete pile is moulded or cast in forms with suitable reinforcement, and after curing for 30 days or longer are driven with about the same equipment that handles wood piles, except that the driver must be strong enough to handle the extra weight of a concrete pile. "Premoulded" or "pre-cast" concrete piles are widely used in connection with work adjacent to or extending into the water. Water jets are usually required to assist in placing these piles since they are apt to be broken by too much driving. 

The Raymond* concrete pile is a tapered pile which is cast in the ground in a sheet metal shell reinforced with spiral reinforcing. A steel core of tapered form covered by the shell is driven into the ground and when the required depth has been reached, this core is collapsed and withdrawn leaving the shell permanently in the ground, thus forming a lining for the hole which is to be filled with concrete. The shell not only retains the soil pressure generated by driving, but protects the "green" concrete from being mixed with the surrounding soil or from being distorted by soil pressure set up by driving adjacent piles. Concrete piles of this type are usually 8" in diameter at the point and the diameter increases at the rate of 0.4" per lin. ft. of length. Refer to illustration opposite page 1. 

Pre-cast concrete piles are cast above ground and dropped into the hole made for them by the steel core or pipe which has been driven to the required depth. The pre-cast pile is 

Raymond Concrete Pile Co. MacArthur Concrete Pile Corp.

aliq Altrosa 

976 asliq 57070NOS. urgh Jeos old,brig bodT ites mer 

Raymond Composite Wood and Concrete Piles.

CONCRETE PILES 

101 smaller in diameter than the pipe, so that it may be inserted within the steel pipe, and after it is in place, the steel pipe is withdrawn and thin grout is poured around the concrete pile to fill any voids or space left by the pipe. MacArthur Straight Shaft Concrete Pile 

The standard MacArthur* concrete pile is a straight shaft pile. A steel cylindrical casing with a core inside is driven into the ground. The core is removed and the casing filled with concrete to a level sufficiently high to take care of compression. 

The core and the hammer, totalling 7 tons in weight, are then lowered onto the concrete and remain so while the casing is withdrawn, thus the concrete is compressed and forced into the space occupied by the casing and any voids in the ground. The finished pile is a cylindrical shaft. 

The MacArthur* pedestal pile differs from the above in that it has a bulb or pedestal at the bottom of the shaft formed in this way: When the core is removed, a charge of concrete large enough to form the bulb is dropped to the bottom of the casing. Then, depending upon the size of the pedestal required, the casing is drawn up a suitable distance varying from 18" to 36" with the core and the hammer resting on the concrete. 

The hammer is then put into operation for a sufficient number

of blows to force this charge of concrete out of its original cylindrical form into a bulb-like pedestal. 

MacArthur Pedestal Concrete Piles 

MacArthur Cased Straight Shaft Concrete Pile and Cased 

Pile with Pedestal 91T

CONCRETE PILES 

103 MacArthur* Cased Straight Shaft Piles are formed by driving the core and casing to the required depth, removing the core from the casing and placing a light gauge corrugated steel shell inside the outer casing. The corrugated casing may be then filled with concrete which may be plain or reinforced; the outer casing is withdrawn leaving the finished pile in the ground. 

MacArthur Cased Composite Wood and Concrete Piles 

MacArthur Pipe Piles with Cast Steel Point are filled with concrete to any length. Economical for driving where headroom is limited; such as for underpinning foundations or making new foundations under existing buildings. 

Composite Piles of Concrete and Pipe have an uncased upper section of compressed concrete and lower section of closed pipe-any length. For use in very soft soils where piles have to be driven to great depths.

Composite Wood and Concrete Piles.-It is not practical to drive concrete piles over 45'-0" to 50′-0″ long and in instances where longer piles are required, composite piles of wood and concrete may be used to a depth of 100'-0". 

The Raymond* Composite Pile has the top 40'-0" of concrete and the balance of wood, as shown in the illustration on page 100. 

The MacArthur Cased Composite Pile has a cased concrete upper section extending to the permanent water level with balance of the pile of timber. The pile is formed by driving the casing

and mandrel to a foot below the joint in the pile at which point the mandrel is withdrawn. Then the wood bottom with the pan on the shoulder is driven through the casing by a recessed mandrel resting on the shoulder of the pile, and the top of the tenon, until the proper resistance is encountered. The mandrel is withdrawn and the permanent shell is passed through the casing and locked to the timber pile. The permanent shell is then filled with concrete and the casing withdrawn. This type of pile is more economical than the all concrete pile and can be driven in lengths up to 100'-0".

Estimating the Cost of Concrete Piles.—When estimating the cost of concrete piles in any of the larger cities where offices and equipment are maintained by the various pile driving concerns, add $1,250.00 to $1,500.00 to cover overhead expense, plant charges, depreciation, advertising, office expense, insurance, etc., as it costs just as much to get ready to drive 100 piles as it does to drive 1,000, so regardless of the size of the job, this item should always be added. 

Where it is necessary to ship plant and equipment from one city to another, it will be necessary to add additional cartage, freight, etc., which will bring the item of overhead expense up to $1,500.00 to $2,000.00.

Labor Driving Concrete Piles.-Before the actual cost of driving the piles can be considered, an allowance must be made for setting up the pile driver, dismantling and removing it from the job at completion, etc. 

After the pile driver has been delivered at the job it should take about 3 days for the crew to set it up ready for driving, as follows:

105 After the pile driver has been set up ready to operate, the number of piles driven per day and the labor cost of driving them will vary with the length of the piles and job conditions. 

For instance, on a recent job where the piles were closely spaced and driven from a flat surface, a pile driver averaged 100 piles per day, while on another job for the same owners, but where the piles were more widely scattered and had to be driven from different elevations, it was with difficulty that 20 piles were driven per day.

A good average for heavy pre-cast piles is about 10 piles per 8-hr. day.

Raymond tapered piles in which the shell is left in the ground can usually be placed at the rate of 20 to 30 piles per day, but other types of cast-in-place piles are usually placed at a slower rate, averaging 10 to 20 piles per 8-hr. day. Mac- 

Arthur pedestal piles can be driven at the rate of 16 to 24 piles per 8-hr. day. Under favorable job conditions all of these averages may be considerably increased. 

The above time does not include supervision, laying out work or "spotting" piles, pumping, shoring, excavating, etc., but includes only the actual time driving the piles. Neither does it include cost of fuel, oil and other supplies, equipment rental, etc., which must be included in the estimate.

CHAPTER III CONCRETE BREAKING, EXCAVATING, WRECK- ING, SAND BLASTING, DRILLING, ETC. BY COMPRESSED AIR. CONTRACTORS'  

Compressed air is being used so extensively on all classes of construction work that the progressive contractor finds new uses for it daily in such operations as concrete breaking, masonry chipping, wrecking old buildings, excavating, tamping, sawing, painting, cement gun work, cutting off piling, driving sheet piling, etc.

The following data on compressed air work has been furnished through the courtesy of the Ingersoll-Rand Company, New York, who will gladly furnish additional information, prices, etc., on all kinds of pneumatic equipment upon request. 

To arrive at accurate costs of performing any of the various classes of work it will be necessary to obtain some idea of the cost of the equipment, interest on the investment, depreciation, repairs, etc.

As a basis for figuring depreciation, 5 years will be taken as the average life of the compressor unit; 6% of the cost will be figured for interest on investment, and $100.00 per year for repairs, miscellaneous supplies, etc.

Fuel and oil will be figured on the basis of 75 cts. per hr. for compressor and tools.

The cost of the compressor units will vary with the size and type of equipment but the following will give an idea of cost of the various units.

Wrecking Old Brick and Concrete Buildings Using Pneumatic Tools bilding elotiuss goodlo

Sand Blast Cleaning of Buildings bus estrandil 

The portable compressor and the sand blast are widely used for cleaning buildings, bridges and other structures, either preparatory to repainting or for the purpose of brightening up the surface.

The cost of this work, however, is contingent entirely upon the condition of the old buildings, as some of them have nothing more than many years' accumulation of dirt while others have been painted numerous times, making it necessary to remove several coats of paint before the surface of the brick or stone can be touched. Also, it is often necessary to repoint all of the old mortar joints. The estimator should consider all of these items when preparing the estimate. 

The process of sand blasting is to force sand against the surface to be cleaned through a small hose connected with the air compressor, and the force of the sand striking the object to be cleaned removes the old surface. Where it requires à maximum pressure of sand and air to remove the old dirt, a 2

" hose is used but where volume is desired more than high pressure, a 1" hose is used.

It usually requires four men to operate a sand blasting machine, as follows: one man attending the machine, one man at the nozzle, and two men on the ground assist ing with hose, scaffold, sand, etc. 

When esti- mating quantities, take the entire area of the surface to be cleaned, making no deductions for door or window openings. 

On court houses, state capitols, postal offices, public libraries, and other orna mental structures, the quantities are 18246 

Sand Blast Cleaning of Buildings computed as above and in addition, balustrades, balusters, etc., are measured on both sides, as it is necessary to go around each baluster separately to clean it. 

With a portable compressor supplying air, the average operator can cover a strip 25'-0" wide and 60'-0" to 75'-0" high per 8-hr. day. The exact area varies with the quality of the stone encountered but the following table shows the speed at which various stones can be cleaned.

Painting by Compressed Air.-Almost any painting job can be done quicker with an air operated paint spray. This is 

Removing Old Rust Scale and Painting Metal Surfaces by Compressed Air or particularly true where large surfaces are to be covered where there are angles and corners that cannot be reached with hand brushes.

Practically all surfaces that are now being painted with a bristle brush can be coated by air painting. On rough surfaces such as cement, stucco, rough plaster, brick, tile, shingles and rough boards, air painting affects a considerable saving in time and labor as well as in the cost of brushes. 

It is now possible to obtain mechanical painting equipment that will apply any paint, varnish, enamel, water paints, graphite, mineral oxides, red lead, etc.

The following information on contractors' plant and equipment will assist the estimator in determining the most economical methods to use when figuring various size jobs. 

Portable Belt Conveyors.-Portable conveyors are used for conveying earth, clay, sand, gravel, stone, bulk cement, concrete, etc., from stock piles or to convey and elevate materials to trucks, etc. They are often used for conveying wet concrete from mixer to elevated structures where the incline is not too steep. Elevating Wet Concrete on a Belt Conveyor

Conveyors are furnished with either plain or cleated belts but the cleated belts should not be used with wet materials, such as wet concrete, wet clay, etc. 

They are made in various lengths from 15 to 60 ft. and are furnished with or without trucks and may be operated either by gasoline or electric motors.

The illustrations show just how belt conveyors may be used for conveying wet concrete from one place to another.

Self-Feeding Loader. This disc-feeding loader is used for loading sand, gravel or other bulk materials by machine, as illustrated. The revolving discs clean-up and feed any loose material into the buckets, where they are carried to hoppers for feeding into trucks, wheelbarrows or other hoppers.

They are furnished with Strike-off Hopper, Standard Measuring Hopper, Wheelbarrow Hopper or with a Balancing Hopper in two different sizes, the smaller one having a capacity of 1 cu. yd. per minute and the larger one a capacity of 1 cu. yds. a minute.

Contractors' Hoisting Towers 

There are a number of methods of hoisting concrete consisting of the ordinary wood constructed tower, towers built-up of sectional steel tubing and steel mast hoists.

The steel towers and mast hoists can be either purchased or rented and are much more quickly erected and dismantled than a wood tower. 

Wood Hoisting Towers-Single wood hoisting towers 50'-0" to 150'-0" high, for hoisting brick, concrete and other building materials, are usually constructed of 4" x 4" or 4″ x 6″ uprights, with the necessary 2″ x 6″ cross bracing, 2″ x 4″ guides, etc. and the cost per lin. ft. in height should average as follows:

Steel Tower Hoists* for Concrete and Building Materials 

Within the past few years a new type of tower for hoisting concrete and other building materials has come into use on account of the ease with which it is erected and dismantled. 

It consists of steel masts in 20' sections having a concrete bucket on one side of the mast and a material hoisting platform on the other, so arranged that both bucket and material elevator can be used at the same time.

They are furnished in a number of different sizes and capacities to meet the requirements of any size job.

Storage Bins and Weighing Batchers*.-Storage bins are used for supplying the mixer with sand and gravel. These bins are equipped with a weighing batcher for weighing the sand and gravel used in each batch. *Butler Bin Co., Waukesha, Wis.

ESTIMATOR'S REFERENCE. BOOK 

A storage bin of sufficient capacity to serve a 14-S mixer sells for about $825.00, while the weighing batcher would cost approximately another $825.00, or $1,650.00 complete.

A larger size bin of about 75 cu. yds. capacity, which would serve one or two 28-S mixers costs about $1,100.00 for the bins and approximately $900.00 additional for the weighing batcher, or $2,000.00 complete.

In some instances, where considerable cement is required on a job, the contractor can effect a considerable saving in using bulk rather than bag cement. In this event, a separate bin for bulk cement storage with a cement weighing hopper may be installed next to the aggregate bin, or one section of the aggregate bin may be used to store bulk cement and a combination aggregate and cement weighing hopper be installed. 

An enclosed conveyor or elevator for elevating the sand and gravel to the bins will cost from $650.00 to $1,000.00, depending upon the size, as they are made to handle 30 to 70 cu. yds. of loose material an hour.

Batcherplants*.-Batcherplants consisting of 2 or 3-compart ment storage bins for the storage of cement, sand and gravel, together with weighing batchers for weighing out the proper amount of each aggregate are furnished in a number of different sizes to meet varying conditions. 

A 35-ton 2-compartment bin of the portable type with hinged legs and weighing batcher for two aggregates of adequate size to take care of any batch up to and including one cu. yd. will cost about $1,495.00*.

A 51-ton 2 compartment bin of the portable type with hinged legs and weighing batcher for two aggregates of adequate size to take care of a one cu. yd. batch will cost about $1,665.00*. 

A 60-ton 3-compartment-in-line bin of the portable type with hinged legs and weighing batcher, scales and all appurtances costs about $1,900.00*.

A 105-ton 3-compartment-in-line bin, with one cu. yd. weighing batcher and pedestal supports instead of hinged leg supports costs about $2,150.00*.

All of the above weighing batchers include beam scales and springless indicator. The bin gates are double clam type with 

12"x18" opening and manual lever operated. The batcher discharge gate is also of the double clam type, lever operated, with an opening 101"x43". *Blaw-Knox Co., Pittsburgh, Pa. All prices quoted are f.o.b. Pittsburgh, and subject to change.

AMERICAN TUBULAR TOWERS* 

American Tubular Towers are extensively used by contractors in all parts of the country for hoisting all classes of building materials and for concreting, on account of the ease with which they are erected and dismantled, their great strength and stability, as well as their economy. 

They have practically supplanted the wood frame hoisting tower in the con struction of our modern buildings. 

American Tubular Towers are designed for handling material and concrete, with or without chuting. 

They are built in any height and with one or more compartments. Their many advantages both in construction and in performance, their durability and low maintenance, and their remarkable adaptability to various jobs, make them ideal as low cost plant and equipment for contractors.

An American Tubular 

Tower consists of a bottom section, the necessary number of intermediate tubular sections, each 6'-6" in height, and a top section containing the cat head with sheaves.

All intermediate sections of a given type of tower are identical and the top and bottom sections can be attached to any one of them.

CHAPTER IV CONCRETE FOOTINGS, FOUNDATIONS AND RETAINING WALLS 

When estimating the cost of mass concrete, such as footings, foundations, retaining walls, etc., there are four distinct labor operations to be considered, in addition to the materials used. 

The first operation is placing the concrete footing. If the trench is in solid ground and the banks self-supporting, a wood form should not be necessary unless specified by the architect or engineer. See illustration on page 155.

After the concrete footing has been placed it will be necessary to construct wood forms or walls to support the wet concrete until it has "set" or hardened. On ordinary walls the forms may be removed as soon as the concrete is self-supporting but walls that are subject to considerable earth pressure should be reinforced with steel rods or mesh. 

The reinforcing steel should be placed after the forms are erected, and the job is then ready to receive the concrete. 

The labor cost of mixing and placing the concrete is also a separate operation and should be estimated accordingly. 

The complete estimate should include the following items: 

1. Cost of concrete forms, including lumber, nails, tie wire, spacers, etc., together with labor cost erecting and removing forms. 

2. Cost of reinforcing steel, if required. Should include cost of reinforcing steel or mesh, tie wire and labor cost of handling and placing. 

3. Cost of concrete for footings and walls, including cement, gravel or crushed stone, sand, together with labor cost of mixing and placing concrete.

Forms for concrete footings, foundation and retaining walls should be estimated by the sq. ft. taking the actual area of the 153

concrete that comes in contact with the wood forms, as illustrated. Also note that wood forms start at the top of the footing and extend to the top of the wall.

Items Affecting the Cost of Concrete Wall Forms.-After the number of sq. ft. of wall forms has been computed, it will be necessary to arrive at the labor and material cost of erecting and removing same.

These costs will be governed by the height of the wall because the higher the wall the more lumber required per sq. ft. of forms and the more bracing required to prevent the forms from spreading while the wet concrete is being placed. 

The shape of the building is also important because it will be much easier and economical to build forms for long straight walls than for irregular walls cut-up with bays, offsets, pilasters, etc., so the estimator should bear this in mind when preparing the estimate.

Concrete Wall Forms Made in Panels or Sections. Many contractors, especially those performing smaller work, use foundation wall forms made up into sections 4'x6', 4'x7' or 4'x8' in size. The frame for these sections is either 2"x4" or 2″x6″ lumber, with intermediate braces spaced 1'-8" to 2'-0" on centers. The corners are reinforced with galvanized straps or strap iron, and the entire frame is sheathed with 1″x6″ lumber, either square edge or dressed and matched. 

It requires 2 ft. of lumber, b.m. per sq. ft. of forms, exclusive of bracing, but forms of this kind can be used a large number of times, especially where the walls are fairly straight. 

The labor cost of making sectional forms will vary with the method used and the number made up at one time. If the lumber is delivered cut to exact length or if an electric hand-saw is used on the job, a carpenter should complete one section (28 sq. ft.) into 1-hr. or 8 to 10 sections per 8-hr. day.

Basis for Computing Labor Costs.-After checking the labor costs on a large number of jobs over a period of years, it has been found that a carpenter will frame and erect about 400 to 450 ft. of lumber, b.m. per 8-hr. day, and will require to -hr. labor time carrying lumber, etc., to each hour carpenter time.

If there are no laborers employed on the job and all lumber is handled and carried by carpenters, a carpenter should handle, frame and erect about 265 to 300 ft. of lumber b.m. per 

8-hr. day.

When removing or "stripping" concrete forms, a laborer should remove 1,200 to 1,400 ft. of lumber, b.m. per 8-hr. day.

REINFORCING STEEL 

Reinforcing steel is estimated by the pound or ton (2,000 lbs.), based on the weight of the steel required in the footings or walls. Obtain the number of pieces and length of each size bar required and multiply this by the weight per lin. ft. The result is the weight of the reinforcing bars required for the job. 

Example: Assume the retaining wall illustrated on page 144, is reinforced with " round bars spaced 6″ on centers both vertically and horizontally. The wall is 40′-0″ long and 15′-0″ high and with bars spaced 6" on centers it will require the following: 

80" rd. bars 15'-0" long 1,200 lin. ft. @ 1.06 lbs.

Labor Placing Reinforcing Steel.-This cost is subject to con siderable variation, due to the class of work, size of bars and the workmen employed on the job.

In many of the larger cities there are concerns making a specialty of setting reinforcing steel. These men become very adept at this work and under favorable conditions can place steel 25% less than the ordinary building laborer or iron worker who has just an occasional job of this kind. For this reason costs are given both ways and the estimator should use his own judgment as to the class of workmen obtainable. 

The size of the bars also affects the labor costs, as it is cheaper to place a ton of heavy bars (" and larger), than small bars (" and smaller). The heavier the bars, the less the labor cost per ton.

Where the reinforcing bars are placed loose in footings and piers, without tying in place, a man should carry and place

CONCRETE 

Concrete should be estimated by the cu. ft. or cu. yd. containing 27 cu. ft. 

The cu. yd. is the most convenient unit to use because all published tables giving the quantities of cement, sand, gravel or crushed stone are based on the cu. yd. of concrete; it is also a more convenient unit to use when estimating labor costs. 

Material Required for One Cu. Yd. of Concrete.-Concrete is usually specified to be mixed in the proportions of 1:1:2, 1:11:3, 1:2:4, 1:3:5, etc., which signifies 1 part portland cement, 2 parts sand, and 4 parts gravel or crushed stone, etc.

A bag of cement weighs 94 lbs. bulks 1 cu. ft. and there are 

4 bags to the bbl. When concrete is specified in the proportions of 1:3:5, it requires 1 cu. ft. (1 bag) cement, 3 cu. ft. sand and 

5 cu. ft. of gravel or crushed stone or multiples thereof, to each batch.

An ordinary contractors' wheelbarrow holds 3 to 3 cu. ft. of dry material, while a concrete or mortar barrow holds 4 to 4 cu. ft. of dry material. When mixed in the proportions of 1:3 :5, each batch requires 1 bag of cement, 1 barrow of sand and 2 small barrows of gravel or crushed stone or multiples thereof. 

The quantity of cement, sand, gravel or crushed stone required per cu. yd. will vary with the size of the coarse aggregate; whether it is of uniform size or whether the small aggregate has been screened out. The more uniform in size the course aggregate, the more small aggregate required to fill the voids. 

Variations in the fineness of sand and the compacting quality of the concrete may affect the quantities 5 to 10 per cent either way.

All tables giving quantities of cement, sand, gravel or crushed stone required for one cu. yd. of concrete, are stated in decimal fractions. Example: One cu. yd. of 1:2:4 concrete requires the following:

Rule for Estimating the Quantities of Cement, Sand and Crushed Stone Required for One Cu. Yd. of Concrete.-On reinforced concrete work it is customary to use crushed stone or gravel" to 1" in diameter. The smaller sizes are used to give the concrete a more plastic form, allowing it to fill around the reinforcing steel, etc., in this way eliminating a "honey combed" or unsightly appearance.

A rule for estimating the approximate quantities of cement, sand, and crushed stone required for one cu. yd. of rammed concrete is as follows: 

Divide 10 by the sum of the parts (by volume) of all the ingredients, and the quotient will be the number of bbls. of 

Portland cement required for one cu. yd. of concrete. After the number of bbls. of cement has been obtained, multiply by the number of parts of sand in the mixture, and the result will be the number of bbls. of sand required for one cu. yd. of concrete. 

To reduce bbls. to cu. yds., multiply the number of bbls. of sand by 0.14 (since a bbl. contains 3.8 cu. ft. and there are 27 cu. ft. in a cu. yd.), and the result will be the number of cu. yds. of sand required for one cu. yd. of concrete. 

To obtain the quantity of crushed stone required per cu. yd. of concrete, use the same method as given for sand. 

Example: Find the amount of cement, sand, and crushed stone required for one cu. yd. of 1:2:4 concrete.

CONCRETE 

171. 

The sum of all the parts of the various ingredients is 1 part cement, 2 parts sand, and 4 parts crushed stone; making a total of 7 parts. Dividing 10 by 7 gives 1.50 bbls. of Portland cement per cu. yd. of concrete. 

As there are 2 parts of sand to each part of cement, multiply 

1.50 bbls. by 2 and the result is 3.00 bbls. of sand required. To reduce 3.00 bbls. of sand to cu. yds. multiply 3.00 by 0.14 (since a bbl. contains 3.8 cu. ft. and there are 27 cu. ft. in a cu. yd.), and the result is 0.42 cu. yds. of sand required per cu. yd. of concreté.

There are 4 parts of crushed stone to each part of cement. 

Multiply 1.50 bbls. by 4 and the result is 6.00 bbls. of crushed stone. To reduce 6.00 bbls. of crushed stone to cu. yds., multiply 

6.00 by 0.14 (since a bbl. contains 3.8 cu. ft. and there are 27 cu. ft. in a cu. yd.), and the result will be 0.84 cu. yds. of crushed stone for one cu. yd. of concrete. 

The same method may be used to compute the quantities of material required for one cu. yd. of rammed concrete mixed in any other proportion.

Rule for Estimating the Quantities of Cement, Sand, and 

Gravel Required for One Cu. Yd. of Concrete.-Where gravel under 1" in diameter is used instead of crushed stone, use 10 as the divisor instead of 10 and proceed as described above. 

The Water-Cement Ratio Method of Proportioning Concrete 

The water-cement ratio method of proportioning concrete mixtures is rapidly being adopted by the leading engineers, architects and contractors throughout the United States. A number of City building codes have been revised or amended to include the water-cement ratio specification. It will be well for contractors and builders to acquaint themselves with the fundamental requirements of a method that appears destined to become the universal standard practice of proportioning concrete mixtures.

The water-cement ratio method of proportioning concrete mixtures is based entirely on the proven theory that for any given set of conditions and materials the strength of concrete is dependent upon the amount of water used per sack of cement as long as the mixture is workable. There is no arbitrary specification for the amounts of sand, gravel or stone to be used. 

All that is demanded is that the mix be workable. 

What is a workable mix? A workable mix is one of such plasticity and degree of wetness that it can be placed in forms

readily, and with light spading or tamping will result in dense concrete. It should be neither too dry nor too wet. In a workable mixture there is sufficient sand-cement mortar to give good, smooth cement surfaces, free from rough spots, called honeycombing, and to bind the pieces of coarse aggregates into a mass so they will not separate in handling.

Quantities of Materials.-The quantities of materials in a concrete mixture may be determined accurately by making use of the fact that the volume of concrete produced by any combination of materials, so long as the concrete is plastic, is equal to the sum of the absolute volume of the cement plus the absolute volume of the aggregate plus the volume of water. 

The absolute volume of a loose material is the actual total volume of solid matter in all the particles. This can be computed from the weight per unit volume and the apparent specific gravity as follows: 

Absolute Vol.= unit weight apparent specific gravity x unit wt. of water (62% lb. per cu. ft.) in which the unit weight is based on surface dry aggregate. 

The method can best be illustrated by an example. Suppose the concrete batch consists of 1 sack of cement (94 lb.), 2.2 cu. ft. of dry fine aggregate weighing 110 lb. per cu. ft. and 3.6 cu. ft. of dry coarse aggregate weighing 100 lb. per cu. ft. and is to be mixed with a water-cement ratio of 7 gallons per sack. The apparent specific gravity of the cement is usually about 3.1 and of the more common aggregates about 2.65. The volume of concrete produced by the above mix is calculated as follows: 94 3.1x62.5 Cement =1 cu.ft. @ = .49 cu. ft. abs. volume

High Early Strength Concrete 

Time is often an important factor in construction, or repair work or for winter construction. Ordinarily, concrete is allowed to stand several days before being used. There are now a number of methods by which strong concrete may be obtained in 1 to 3 days. Several high early strength cements are now on the market which develop the same compressive strength in 72 hours as is ordinarily obtained in 28 days by using ordinary Portland cement. Another method using ordinary 

Portland cement develops the same strength in 3 days as ordinarily requires 28 days to develop.

Some of the various cements and methods are listed below: 

High Early Strength Concrete in 3 Days Using Ordinary 

Portland Cement.-Concrete as commonly used, with proportions, mixing water and mixing time as in line "A," has a strength of 2,000 lbs. or more in 28 days. By well-authenticated methods, a strength of 2,000 lbs. or more, can with standard

Universal Atlas Portland cement, be obtained in 3 days. Using less mixing water and increasing the mixing time, greatly increases the strength of the concrete.

A slump test is made by molding the concrete in a sheet metal conical form (4" top diameter, 8″ bottom diameter and 12" high) and then removing the form and measuring the settlement or slump. Universal-Atlas Lumnite Cement 

A hydraulic cement for concrete and mortar. Mixed with sand, stone and water only, it produces concrete, which has full 28-day strength within 72 hrs. No artificial accelerator is used to hasten the hardening and there is no admixture in 

Lumnite that might affect its permanence.

The rapid hardening of Lumnite cement concrete to its extraordinary high early strength is the result of a natural chem ical action due to the use of aluminum ore (Bauxite) in manufacturing the cement.

It allows ample 

Lumnite cement is not "quick setting." time for mixing, placing and finishing the concrete; the concrete then hardens with great rapidity so that it attains 28-day strength within 72 hrs.

Lumnite cement may be used in the same proportions as ordinary Portland cement, so that the quantity required per cu. yd. of concrete remains the same; however, it costs 3 to 4 times as much as ordinary Portland cement because of the high cost of the principal raw material, which is high-grade alumi num ore (Bauxite) imported from Southern Europe. The

kind of Bauxite that will make Lumnite is rare and expensive. This, with other raw materials, is fused and ground to considerably greater fineness than required by the Standard 

Specifications for Portland Cement. The process of manufac turing is comparatively slow and highly exacting. Price varies according to locality and freight but use $9.00 per bbl. for average conditions. "Incor" High-Early-Strength Portland Cement. For all classes of plain and reinforced concrete and mortar. No new methods are necessary with "Incor" cement, as it is used just like any other Portland cement and produces concrete with the same compressive strength in 72 hrs. as is obtained with ordinary 

Portland cement in 28 days.

Cost varies according to locality but $4.00 per bbl. in paper, is an average price. "Quikard" Cement.-A high-early-strength cement that produces a hard, rigid concrete ready for full service in 72 hrs. It takes its initial and final set normally and produces an impervious, water-proof concrete.

CONCRETE FOUNDATIONS 

181 Quikard cement requires 10 to 15% less mixing water than ordinary cement for necessary workability. The concrete should be cured by keeping wet for at least 24 hrs. and maintained at a temperature of not less than 70° F. for at least 24 hrs. 

The same quantity of cement per cu. yd. of concrete is used as with ordinary cement, which is given in the tables on the previous pages. 

Cost varies according to locality but $4.00 per bbl. in paper, is an average price.

Labor Mixing and Placing Concrete 

The labor cost of mixing and placing concrete will vary considerably according to the size of the job, the method used in mixing and placing the concrete, the proximity of the stock piles to the mixer, and the distance the concrete has to be transported after mixing.

On large jobs using conveyors and bins for feeding the aggregate to the mixer and using spouting systems for carrying the concrete from the mixer to place of deposit, the purchase or rental of the equipment, together with the labor cost of placing same, should be estimated separately and not included in the cu. yd. price of placing the concrete. This plant and equipment cost may be the same whether the job contains 1,000 or 10,000 cu. yds. of concrete, and unless it is kept as a separate item, the resulting labor costs will be misleading and valueless insofar as estimating the cost of future jobs are concerned. 

Weather conditions also influence the labor costs considerably because placing concrete in freezing weather usually necessitates heating the sand, gravel or stone and water, and protecting the concrete from freezing by the use of tarpaulins, straw, manure, salamanders or other artificial means, which all cost money.

With so many small mixers on the market very little concrete is hand mixed to-day, but occasionally a job presents itself where it is more economical to mix by hand, so costs will be given covering all different methods. 

Mixing Concrete by Hand Using One Mixing Board.-The labor cost of hand mixing will vary according to the number of times the concrete is mixed or "turned", together with the methods used in handling and placing the concrete.

Using only one mixing board it is necessary for the men wheeling cement, sand and gravel to wait until the previous batch has been mixed and disposed of before they can dump the material on the board for the next batch. This slows up the work considerably.

A gang of 9 or 10 men should mix and place 5 to 6 batches (approx. -cu. yd. each) an hr. or 40 to 48 batches (20 to 24 cu. yds.) per 8-hr. day, at the following labor cost per cu. yd.: 

Labor  Total 

3 $..... $..... $0.971 $3.26

During extremely warm weather or in warm climates, such as our Southern States, where the summer temperature ranges from 90 to 100 degrees, figure about 4 hrs. labor time per cu. yd. of concrete.

If necessary to load concrete into barrows and wheel from mixing board to place of deposit, add to -hr. per cu. yd. 

The above costs are based on using men experienced in mixing concrete by hand, as the costs may be increased 25% by using inexperienced men.

An average gang should consist of the men distributed as follows: 2 laborers loading and wheeling gravel; 2 laborers loading and wheeling cement and sand; 4 laborers mixing concrete and shoveling into forms or trenches, and 1 or 2 laborers attending water and spading concrete. 

Mixing Concrete by Hand Using Two Mixing Boards.-When two mixing boards are used, the men wheeling gravel, sand and cement can keep one board filled with unmixed materials while the mixing gang is working on the other board. In this way there is no lost time by either gang. 

Where the concrete can be shoveled directly from the mixing board into the trenches or forms, a gang of 11 or 12 men should mix and place 7 or 8 batches (about -cu. yd. each) an hr. or 56 to 64 batches (28 to 32 cu. yds.) per 8-hr. day, at the following labor cost per cu. yd.:

Mixing Concrete in a One Bag (7-S) Mixer.-Foundation con crete is usually mixed in the proportions of 1:2:4, 1:21:5, 1:3:5 or 1:3:6, which is a one bag mix using a 7-S mixer. 

Ordinarily a 1:3:5 mix is used for foundation walls, which requires 1 bag of cement, 3 cu. ft. of sand and 5 cu. ft. of gravel or crushed stone, per batch. Wheelbarrows ordinarily used for dry materials hold 3 to 3 cu. ft. loaded level full, so each batch will require 1 barrow of sand and 2 barrows of gravel or 9 cu. ft. of dry material. 

Where possible to start mixing first thing in the morning and continue all day without delays, a mixer should average 30 batches (6 to 7 cu. ft. of wet concrete each) or 240 batches (54 to 62 cu. yds.), per 8-hr. day. Runs like this on foundation work are exceptional, as there are usually delays caused by moving mixer, building and removing runways, time lost waiting for materials, engine breakdown or other unforeseen delays which occur on every job.

Based on 6 to 7 cu. yds. of concrete an hr. the following men will be required in the gang: 3 laborers loading and wheeling gravel or crushed stone; 2 laborers wheeling sand and cement; 

1 laborer attending mixer; 3 or 4 laborers wheeling concrete from mixer to place of deposit; 2 or 3 laborers dumping barrows, spreading, leveling and tamping concrete; 1 mixer engineer (if required), and 1 mason foreman in charge of work (if required).

If the concrete is mixed in a 21-S or 28-S mixer, fed by wheelbarrows and the concrete wheeled from the mixer to place of deposit or hoisted in a concrete bucket and then distributed by spouts, the labor costs per cu. yd. will run approximately the same as given for 14-S mixers, under similar conditions.

Mixing and Placing Concrete Using Conveyors and Batching 

Bins for Supplying the Mixer and Spouting the Concrete from Mixer to Place of Deposit.—It is not advisable to use a spouting system for placing foundation concrete unless the job covers a large area and contains several thousand cubic yards of concrete, as the cost of erecting and dismantling hoisting towers, concrete hoppers, buckets, spouts, etc., together with the labor operating hoisting engines, handling and raising hoppers, spouts, etc., are all items that run into considerable money and only fairly large jobs can stand this expense. 

On heavy foundations, retaining walls, dams, piers, caissons, etc., where it is possible to use a concrete mixer of to 1-cu. yd. capacity, a spouting system may be used to advantage because it is possible to deposit large quantities of concrete without moving the spouts every few minutes. 

For instance, on a job containing 5,000 to 10,000 cu. yds. of concrete, the cost of building hoisting towers, bins, handling, erecting and dismantling spouting equipment may run as high as $2,500.00 to $5,000.00 or equivalent to 50 cts. to $1.00 per cu. yd. This is in addition to the cost of mixing, hoisting and placing the concrete after the equipment is in place. ·

CONCRETE FOUNDATIONS 

187 After the plant and equipment is in place, the labor cost per cu. yd. of concrete will be considerably less than where the concrete is wheeled from the mixer to place of deposit. For this reason, labor costs, exclusive of plant and equipment charges, should be estimated as a separate item or an allowance added to the cu. yd. labor cost to provide for plant and equipment. 

This allowance should vary with the type of equipment, size and area of the job, number of cu. yds. of concrete to be placed, etc. 

When using a 21-S mixer, which discharges about 4-cu. yd. of concrete per batch, it will probably average about 2 minutes per batch for the entire job, although on days when conditions are favorable it may average only 1 to 1 minutes per batch. Considering the entire job and allowing for short runs, etc., it is not advisable to figure over 30 batches (22) cu. yds.) per hr. or 180 cu. yds. per 8-hr. day. However, on many runs the output may exceed 250 cu. yds. per day but this will not allow for lost time, preparing for and cleaning up after runs, etc., which must be included in the cost.

Ready Mixed Concrete 

When using ready-mixed concrete, all labor in connection with operating the concrete mixer, unloading and handling materials, supplying the mixer with sand, gravel and cement is eliminated, as the trucks dump the ready-mixed concrete into a hopper from where it is distributed by wheelbarrows, concrete buggies or hoisted and spouted.

It is necessary to have a fairly large hopper on the job to receive the concrete from the trucks because the hoisting buckets, wheelbarrows or concrete buggies must be supplied from this hopper. The same amount of labor will be required building and removing runways, cleaning concrete hoppers, buckets, wheelbarrows and buggies as when the concrete is job mixed, so the only labor saved is in connection with the concrete aggregates and operating the mixer. 

The labor handling and placing ready mixed concrete will vary somewhat with the quantity handled and placed per day, as the same number of foremen, hoisting engineers, etc., will be required whether 50 or 150 cu. yds. of concrete are placed per day. The method of distributing the concrete, whether wheelbarrows, concrete buggies or spouting systems will also affect the labor costs. *Where the concrete is hoisted and it is necessary to use a hoisting engineer, add as given in table. *If Union regulations require a mason or cement finisher foreman in charge of gang, add as given in table.

Heating Concrete Aggregates for Winter Work 

During the winter months and extreme cold weather it is necessary to heat the concrete aggregates and mixing water to prevent the concrete from freezing. There are perhaps a dozen different methods that may be used.

Steam jets are often placed in the sand and gravel piles at intervals which thaw and heat the sand and gravel at the same time.

Old hot water tanks or boilers, sections of metal culverts, old iron pipe, etc., are placed on the ground and the concrete materials are shoveled over them, as a wood fire is kept in the old pipes or culverts which heats the sand and gravel. This method requires considerable extra labor shoveling the materials over the pipes and will add 1 to 2-hr. per cu. yd. of concrete. 

On large jobs, a special pipe grillage may be used, where rows of steam pipes are placed on a platform and the concrete materials are dumped from the trucks onto the platform. The live steam running through the pipes keeps the sand and gravel warm at all times. Jobs having 5,000 sq. ft. area on each floor will require an 18 to 25 h.p. boiler for heating the materials but large jobs will require a 50 h.p. boiler.

An economical method of heating concrete aggregates is by using an oil burner that projects into the mouth of the mixer. 

If mixed 2 to 3 minutes, this burner will ordinarily heat the concrete sufficiently to prevent freezing and the only additional labor is the little attention the air tank requires, plus the necessary kerosene for fuel.

Protecting Concrete During Freezing Weather 

Where necessary to cover concrete footings and foundation walls with boards, straw, manure, etc., to prevent freezing, figureto-hr. labor time per cu. yd. of concrete. 

If the concrete is to be covered with straw, figure about 1 bale or 80 lbs. of loose straw to each 100 sq. ft. of surface to be covered. This is sufficient to cover the concrete with 8" to 

10" of loose straw.

Actual Cost of Heating Concrete Aggregates and Protecting Concrete During Freezing Weather 

Illinois Central Hospital Bldg.-It was necessary to heat the concrete aggregates and protect the concrete from freezing after placing. The following costs were obtained which should be of assistance when estimating the cost of winter work. 

Where the sand or gravel has to be shoveled over iron pipes or tubes containing the fire, a man will scoop or shovel 1 to 2

CONCRETE FOUNDATIONS 

207 cu. yds. an hr. or 14 to 16 cu. yds. per 8-hr. day, depending upon the depth the sand and gravel are frozen. This is sufficient material for 10 to 12 cu. yds. of concrete and will add to 1-hr. labor time per cu. yd. 

If the water is to be heated, it will require the attention of one man practically all the time supplying fuel and attending the fire in the water heater. This will add to 3-hr. per cu. yd. of concrete.

The total time heating aggregates and water by the above methods will add 14 to 1 hrs. labor time per cu. yd. of concrete. 

Protecting Concrete from Freezing.—Where necessary to cover foundation concrete with boards, straw, manure, etc., to protect from freezing, figure to -hr. labor time per cu. yd. of concrete.

Actual Costs of Unloading Concrete Materials from Cars 

On the Illinois Central Hospital Bldg., all materials were delivered in cars and were unloaded by hand at the following labor costs:

Unloading Sand from Cars.-A man shoveled and threw out of cars onto stock piles at the side of the track, 10 to 12 cu. yds. of sand per 8-hr. day.

This cost is high because the Laborers' union permitted only a certain size shovel to be used. Under normal conditions this quantity should be increased 20 to 25 per cent.

If sand freezes in the cars it is practically impossible to loosen it and the labor costs will run 2 to 3 times those. given above. 

Unloading Gravel from Cars.—A man unloaded 9 to 10 cu. yds. of gravel per 8-hr. day. The same ruling regarding the shovel size applies here as with the sand, also the note regarding freezing.

Unloading Cement from Cars.-The cement used in the above building was unloaded from cars and stacked in piles about 

9′-0″ high. Stacking this height required 1 extra man.

Four men working together, unloaded, wheeled, counted and stacked 800 bags (200 bbls.) of cement per 8-hr. day, which is equivalent to -hr. per bbl.

CHAPTER V REINFORCED CONCRETE 

Reinforced concrete is one of our most common building materials and on account of its flexibility is easily adapted for use on practically all classes of construction work. 

It is used in all types of structures, from residential, apartment, hotel and hospital buildings, requiring comparatively light floor loads, to the heaviest constructed warehouses, factory buildings, wharves, industrial buildings, etc. 

On account of its flexibility, it is used in a number of ways and in conjunction with clay tile, gypsum tile, wood and metal "pans" or it may be used alone in the construction of floors, roofs and all types of skeleton buildings. 

Regardless of the fact that it is one of our most common building materials, costs on all classes of reinforced concrete construction are subject to wide variation. This is due to a number of causes, such as the type of building, whether flat slab or beam and girder type; whether solid concrete construction or used in conjunction with clay or gypsum tile, wood or metal "pans," etc.

The method used in erecting and removing the formwork, handling, mixing and placing the concrete, and last but not least, the ability of the superintendent or foreman, all affect the final costs of the work. 

Regardless of how carefully or accurately the job has been estimated, if the superintendent or foreman in charge of the work are not proficient, the actual costs are almost certain to run higher than the estimate-not because the work was estimated too low but because it was poorly handled on the job. 

All labor costs given on the following pages are based on efficient management; economical layout and design of all formwork; use of modern labor-saving methods, such as shop fabrication of column, beam and girder forms where possible, 208

REINFORCED CONCRETE 

209 and the use of labor saving tools such as power saws, band saws, electric hand saws, etc. For instance, an electric hand saw will cut off a 2"x12" plank in 4 seconds where it requires about a minute by hand. It takes about 9 minutes by hand to rip a 12'-0" plank 2″ thick but it takes only 40 to 45 seconds using an electric saw. These are just a few of the savings that can be made by using labor-saving tools and equipment. 

In these days of high wage scales, the contractor who meets competition must use methods and tools that will reduce costs to a minimum, otherwise you are out of the running when it comes to obtaining work in competition and of performing it economically after you have obtained the job. Remember, Good Management, Economical Design, Labor-saving Tools and 

Methods are absolutely necessary if you are to keep up with the procession. 

Items to be Included in the Estimate.-Reinforced concrete should be estimated in the same manner and in the same units as the work is constructed on the job. This allows comparisons between estimated and actual costs and enables a contractor to tell where variations occur between estimated and actual costs.

The first operation on any reinforced concrete job is the erection of the temporary wood or metal forms to support the weight of the wet concrete until it has set sufficiently to be self-supporting. The members usually requiring forms are the columns, girders, beams, spandrel beams, lintels, floor slabs, stairs and platforms. Each class of formwork should be estimated separately and are treated in more detail on the following pages.

After the forms are erected, it is necessary to place the reinforcing steel or wire mesh ready to receive the concrete. This may include unloading steel from cars or trucks at the job, cutting steel to length and bending to special shapes for columns, beams, girders and floor slabs, and placing it in position ready to receive the concrete. 

After the reinforcing steel is in place, the job is then ready for concrete. This consists of mixing the cement, sand and gravel into the concrete mass, hoisting, wheeling and placing it in position.

Each of these items should be estimated in detail to include all material and labor operations necessary to make up the completed unit.

Forms for Reinforced Concrete Columns 

Reinforced concrete columns may be either square, rectangular, octagonal or round in shape. The forms for square or octagonal columns are usually constructed of wood while metal molds are used for round columns. 

The wood forms may be constructed of either 1″ or 2″ lumber, although the largest concrete contractors usually use 1" lumber. 

While the 2" lumber has greater salvage value the original cost is nearly twice as much, which probably accounts for the greater use of 1" material. Of course, 1" lumber requires more frequent clamping than 2″ but now that metal form clamps are so generally used, it is not such a large item as formerly. 

Forms for reinforced concrete columns should be estimated by the sq. ft. obtained by multiplying the girth of the column by the height. Example: obtain the number of sq. ft. of forms in a column 18" square and 12'-0" high. Proceed as follows: 

18+18+18+18=72" or 6'-0", the girth. Multiply the girth by the height, 6′-0″x12′-0″=72 sq. ft. of forms. 0:0"

Octagonal columns are seldom used on account of the expense of the wood forms, but occasionally where machinery is to be fastened to the columns, it is necessary to use them.

Method of Measuring Plans and Listing Quantities for Reinforced Concrete Construction.

REINFORCED CONCRETE 

213 An easy method of listing the concrete columns and forms from the plans at one operation is to list the number of columns, dimensions, length, etc., then at the side of the column headed "No. Pcs." place in small letters "F4S," which designates that the column requires "Forms 4 sides," so when extending the quantities on the estimate sheet, the quantity of concrete can be extended in cu. ft. and the quantity of forms listed in sq. ft. 

See illustration of estimate sheet on page 212 showing the method suggested for easy, accurate estimating. 

Labor Cost of Wood Forms for Square Concrete Columns.— 

The labor cost of wood forms for square or rectangular concrete columns will average about the same regardless of the type of building, but the variations are due to the method used in assembling and building-up the column sections, their size, method of clamping, etc.

On jobs of any size it is customary to have a “mill" on the job, where the column forms are built to exact size, including cut-outs for beams or girders, and then sent to the floor on which they are to be used, ready for erection. 

Where 1" sheathing is used with wood column clamps it will require about 2 ft. of lumber, b.m. per sq. ft. of forms. If 2″ sheathing is used, it will require about 3 ft. b.m. per sq. ft. 

of forms. 

The following labor costs are based on a certain number of "man hours" per 100 sq. ft. of forms, regardless of whether the work is performed by carpenters or whether laborers carry and handle the lumber ready for the carpenters, so that the estimator must use his own judgment as to the class of labor to be used on each job estimated.

Wood Forms for Concrete Columns Using Wood and Iron Rod Column Clamps. 

Using any of the better metal column clamps, the labor cost of erecting and removing the column forms will be reduced somewhat, as it is easier to use a clamp already assembled than nailing and wedging wood clamps and removing them after the concrete has been poured. 

Ordinarily, 2 men working together will place one metal column clamp in 3 to 4 minutes or 6 to 8 minutes for one man. Based on an average 12'-0" column requiring 7-or 8 clamps, it will require to 1-hr. for one man to clamp each column, which is about half the time required where wood or wood and rod clamps are used.

Metal Forms for Round Columns 

The cost of metal forms for round concrete columns will vary according to the diameter of the column, height, whether a plain shaft or one having a cone or "bell" top, also whether it is necessary to cut out for beams and girders framing into the metal column molds.

Where it is necessary to cut the metal molds or "heads" to frame into wood forms for concrete beams and girders, an extra labor allowance should be made.

The cost of this work will vary with the method used in erecting the columns. The average contractor sub-lets this work, including rental of the metal molds, erection and removal, at a certain price per column, based on the number of columns per floor and the number of Round Metal Column stories in the building.

Anchor Slots for Brick, Stone and Terra Cotta

The Dovetail* Anchor Slot method of anchoring masonry to concrete consists of a metal slot dovetail in cross section and anchors with dovetail ends for cut stone, brickwork and terra cotta. 

The dovetail anchor slot is nailed to the form with the open side against the wood, the ends are then closed with a bit of paper or wood. After the concrete is poured and the forms removed, the slot remains in the concrete available at any course height to receive the anchors.

The anchors are installed by merely inserting the dovetail end of the anchor edgewise in the slot, then turning anchor crosswise of the slot with the hand, the other end of anchor being imbedded in the facing material or mortar joint. The dovetail slot holds the end of anchor securely, making any other means of fastening, drilling or boring unnecessary.

The Dovetail anchor slot is made of 22 and 24 ga. galvanized iron. It is 1" deep and 1" wide at the back and is furnished in standard lengths of 10'-0". 

Dovetail stone anchors are of black or galvanized steel, 1" wide by " thick and when in place measure 31″ from the face of the *Dovetail Anchor Slot Co., Chicago.

227 W concrete to outside of turned down end. Special length and thickness of anchors can be had on order. 

Dovetail brick anchors are made of No. 12, 14 and 16 ga. galvanized iron and when in place measure 33" from the face of the concrete to the outer end, which is adapted to be embedded in the mortar joint. It is fan shaped, measuring 1" at the outer end. 

Dovetail terra cotta anchors are 1" wide and " thick. They measure 1" from the face of the concrete to outer end. There are two holes in these through which the standard " square iron is hooked. There is a simple lock piece furnished with the terra cotta anchor to prevent it turning in the slot. .$30.00

The installa tion of Dovetail anchor slots consists of driving the nails through the slot into the form. 

A carpenter will nail two pieces, each 10' long to a column and close the ends in approxi- mately 1 minute.

This applies where the slots for a number of columns are being placed at one time.

Concrete Girders, Beams, Spandrel Beams, and Lintels

Forms for reinforced concrete beams, girders, lintels, etc., should be estimated by the sq. ft. obtained by adding the dimensions of the three sides of the beam and multiplying by the length. Example: a beam or girder may be marked 12″x24″ on the plans but perhaps 6" of this depth is included in the slab thickness, so the form area should be obtained by taking the dimensions of the beam or girder from the underside of the slab, i.e., 18″+12″+18″=48″ or 4′-0″ the girth, which multiplied by the length gives the number of sq. ft. of forms in the beam, viz., 4'-0"x18'-0"-72 sq. ft.

A good rule to remember when measuring beam forms is to take the area of all forms that come in contact with the concrete.

Labor Cost of Wood Forms for Concrete Beams and Girders. 

-The labor cost on beam and girder forms will vary considerably on different jobs, due to the amount of duplication, size of beams and girders and the methods of framing and placing them.

On typical buildings where the same size beam and girders are used on several floors, so that the forms may be used several times with only a small amount of labor with each

REINFORCED CONCRETE 

233 re-use, minimum labor costs should prevail. Also, larger beams are more economically framed than very small ones but one of the most important cost factors is the method of fabricating the units and whether they are built-up in a job "shop" using power saws and electric hand saws. These are factors that cut costs and the contractor attempting to compete in to-day's markets without using the most up-to-date methods and equipment available is bound to suffer accordingly. 

The following labor costs are based on efficient management, economical design and labor-saving tools and equipment. If the old "hand-saw" methods are to be used, increase the costs given 10 to 20 per cent.

It requires 2 to 3 ft. of lumber, b.m. to complete 1 sq. ft. of beam and girder forms, which includes uprights or "shores", beam soffits, bracing, etc.

.251* Reinforced Concrete Floors 

Forms for all types of reinforced concrete floors should be estimated by the sq. ft. taking the actual floor area or the area of the wood forms that come in contact with the concrete. 

The same method of measuring the plans and listing the quantities should be used whether the floor is solid concrete or one of the many combinations using clay or gypsum tile or metal or wood "pan" construction.

The quantity of lumber required to construct forms for the different types of floors will vary with the thickness of the concrete slab, ceiling height, etc. Floors of combination tile and concrete joist construction require less lumber per sq. ft. of forms than heavy constructed warehouse, mill, factory and industrial buildings using solid concrete floors. The number of sq. ft. of forms will be the same in both cases but the latter will require nearly twice as much lumber per sq. ft. of forms as the former.

Estimating the Cost of Form Lumber.-When computing the lumber cost per sq. ft. of forms, the estimator should study the plans carefully to determine just how many times it is possible to use the same form lumber in the construction of the building. 

On 8 to 12 story buildings it may be possible to use the same lumber 3 to 4 times while on a 3 story building it might be necessary to buy sufficient lumber to form the entire building. 

These are items that affect the material costs and can only be *Lumber cost based on 33%% depreciation each time used or on using each set of forms 3 times. Labor costs based on using same forms over again by cutting down to size.

REINFORCED CONCRETE 

235 determined by the estimator or contractor as they should be in position to know just how soon the forms can be wrecked and how fast they will be required to carry on the work. 

Example: Assume the forms for an 8 story building are being estimated. It will probably be necessary to buy sufficient lumber to form 3 complete floors. If it requires 3 ft. of lumber per sq. ft. of forms (with lumber at $40.00 per 1,000 ft.), the cost per sq. ft. of forms would be obtained by multiplying 3x.04.12 cts. If the lumber can be used 3 times during the construction. of the job, 12÷3-4 cts. per sq. ft. each time the lumber is used, plus a small charge for breakage, nails, etc., making a total of 4 to 5 cts. per sq. ft. for forms. 

Form lumber that has been used 3 or 4 times will have little salvage value but each contractor should determine this for himself.

An easy method of listing at one operation, both the concrete quantities and the wood forms required is to list the slab dimensions, giving length, width and thickness. Then at the side of the column headed "No. Pcs.", place a small letter "F," which designates that forms are required.

Example: Estimate the quantities in a concrete floor slab, 16'-0" wide, 20'-0" long and 8" thick. 16x20=320 sq. ft. of forms, which is placed in the second column. 320 sq. ft. multiplied by 8" 214 cu. ft. of concrete in the slab. See illustration of estimate sheet on page 212.

Types of Reinforced Concrete Floors.-There are a number of distinct types of reinforced concrete floor construction and on account of the variations in costs, some of the more commonly used types will be described in detail. 

Flat Slab Construction.-Mill, factory, warehouse and industrial buildings designed for heavy floor loads are usually of flat slab construction, which consists of floors without beams or girders, except spandrel beams between columns, on outside walls, and around stair wells, elevator shafts, etc. Buildings of this type usually have square or rectangular columns in all exterior walls and round interior columns. The round columns usually have a "flared" or cone head that extends into a depression in the bottom of the slab. These depressions are usually 

5'-0" to 7'-0" square and 4" to 8" deep. This is necessary

on account of the extra reinforcing steel required to develop the specified strength.

Beam and Girder Type Construction.-This is the oldest type of concrete structure, having square or round columns with beams and girders running between each row of columns and the floor slabs carried by the beams and girders and then to the columns.

Combination Tile or "Pan" Construction with Concrete 

Joists.-Apartment buildings, hotels, schools, hospitals, department stores, office buildings and other structures requiring light floor loads ordinarily use this type of construction, which consists of clay or gypsum tile or wood or metal "pans" in conjunction with concrete joists. This type of floor is used with either round or square columns and beams that run at right angles to the joists.

Inasmuch as this is primarily a light floor construction, the wood forms supporting the wet concrete are equally light. 

Concrete Floors Used in Conjunction with Steel Joists and

Truss Joists.-This is a special type of floor construction where ribbed metal lath is placed over the top of steel joists or truss joists and a thin slab of concrete (usually 2″ thick), is placed over the metal lath, covering the entire floor area. The steel joists or truss joists may be supported by concrete beams or girders, structural steel framework or they may rest on masonry walls. 

Floors of this type do not require wood forms as the joists or trusses are usually spaced 12" to 24" on centers, and selfsupporting ribbed metal lath is placed over the joists. The concrete is then placed directly over the metal lath and while it may cause the lath to sag somewhat, it does not make any particular difference as the ceilings underneath are usually plastered.

Pressure Against the Forms.-This is figured as water pressure and in water pressure the pressure depends upon the height of the column of water. In concrete the same thing holds true because the form for a low wall does not have to withstand as much pressure as a form for a high wall.

The illustration shows the pressure of the concrete against the forms per sq. ft. of wall area for the different heights. The wall illustrated is 6'-0" high and if the concrete is poured in one operation the pressure at the bottom will be 900 lbs. while the pressure at the top will be only 150 lbs. per sq. ft.

Lumber Required for Slab Forms.-The following tables give the approximate quantity of lumber required per sq. ft. of forms for floors of different thickness and with varying ceiling heights. These tables are only approximate as every building is different and the quantities will vary with the span, ceiling height, slab thickness and weight of the wet concrete to be supported.

Also, the tables given below are based on using 4"x4" shores or uprights. If adjustable shores are used it will be necessary to deduct the lumber required for 4"x4"s and add cost or rental of adjustable shores. 

The difference in the quantity of lumber required per sq. ft. for floors having 8′-0″ ceiling heights and those having 20′-0″ ceiling heights is principally in the shoring and bracing. If adjustable shores are used, deductions can be made on the following basis: Floors 3" to 6" thick having 8'-0" ceiling heights, require to ft. of lumber per sq. ft. for shores; 7" to 9" slabs require to ft.; and 10" to 12" slabs require to 

1 ft. of shoring lumber per sq. ft. of floor. 

The above quantities can be used for all 8'-0" story heights, plus the additional lumber given in the tables for higher ceiling heights.

Example: Find the quantity of lumber necessary to shore

Labor Cost of Flat Slab Forms.-Forms for flat slab floors are continuous-without breaks or offsets-except at column heads, stair wells, elevator shafts, etc., where it is necessary to frame for beams and girders.

The sq. ft. labor cost will vary with the amount of lumber required per sq. ft. of forms, as the heavier the slab and the higher the ceiling, the more lumber required per sq. ft. 

Forms for exceedingly light floor slabs cost proportionately more per sq. ft. than heavy forms as the preliminary work is the same with both types. However, on work of this class a man should handle, frame and erect 325 to 360 ft. of lumber, b.m. per 8-hr. day, at the following labor cost per 1,000 ft.:

Labor Labor Framing for Slab Depressions at Column Heads.-On flat slab jobs there is usually a depression at each column head 

5'-0" to 7'-0" square and 4" to 8" deep. The labor cost framing for these depressions will cost about 50% more than for straight slab forms.

A satisfactory method of estimating this additional labor is to figure the entire floor area at the regular price and then measure up the area of the depressions and figure them at 50% additional labor.

Example: Floor contains 10,000 sq. ft. of slab forms, including 40 column head depressions 5′-0″x5′-0″, containing 25 sq. ft. each. 10,000 sq. ft. slab forms @ 10 cts. per sq. ft..... 

Add for 40 depressions (5'-0"x5′-0″) 1,000 sq. ft. at 50% more than plain slab forms or 5 cts. per sq. ft....... .$1,000.00 50.00

This makes a total of 15 cts. per sq. ft. for labor framing depressions at column heads.

Symons Adjustable Shore.**An adjustable metal shore used with 4"x4"s, which may be raised or lowered, having an adjustment of 5′-0″ at 1″ centers.

These shores may be purchased at $3.50 each or rented at 15 cts. per month, with a minimum rental charge of 75 cts. per shore, f.o.b. Chicago. 

Adjustable Shores Versus 4"x4"s.—It is much easier to shore up a floor using adjustable shores instead of 4"x4"s, which require wedging and cutting or adding to for each change in story height. This additional labor all costs money at present wage scales.

However, to offset this, the original cost of the adjustable shores is much more than the 4"x4"s but if they can be used often enough they will eventually show a large saving. This will have to be considered when contemplating a purchase or rental basis.

The Hausman Steel Flat Slab System. This system of flat slab construction uses metal panels. 18" to 24" wide and 4'-0" to 6'-0" long, instead of wood sheathing, while the shores, purlins, stringers, bracing, etc., are wood, similar to ordinary forms. 

Laying Hausman Steel Slab Panels. 

This system of formwork is used to best advantage where the forms may be used a number of times on the same job, and the costs will vary accordingly. 

On the average job where the floor panels may be used 4 to 6 times, and with laborers' wages at 40 cts. an hr. and skilled workmen (iron workers and carpenters) at $1.10 an hr. the costs will vary from 16 to 18 cts. per sq. ft. 

This includes furnishing, erecting and stripping the shoring and panels, together with towers and drop heads for interior columns, but does not include column molds, nor exterior columns, beams, walls. stairs or other miscellaneous forms.

REINFORCED CONCRETE 

251 It is advisable to communicate with the manufacturers* regarding any job you may be figuring, as they will gladly quote prices in any part of the country on any of the following: 

ЛИИИИИИИ The Hausman Steel Flat Slab Forms, Illustrating Construction at Column Heads. 

1. A rental price on steel forms delivered at the City in which the building is located. 

2. A definite bill of material for the lumber to be used in connection with the system. 

3. Erection schedules, drawings, and a service man to aid in the successful installation of the forms. 

4. Quotations on forms erected in any part of the country. 

Forms for Beam and Girder Type Floors 

The labor cost of wood forms for beam and girder type floors will run somewhat higher than flat slab floors on account of the shorter spans, additional framing around beams, girders, etc. However, if the beams run in only one direction and the floor slabs are 15'-0" to 20'-0" wide and 30'-0" or more in length, the costs will run about the same as given for Flat Slab floors.

The same quantity of lumber is required per sq. ft. of forms as given for "Flat Slab Forms" on Page 242. 

*Hausman Steel Co., Toledo, O.

Concrete Floors of the Beam and Girder Type. 

Floors of this type having beams and girders running both ways of the slab, blocking the slab into panels 10'-0"x10'-0" to 

16'-0"x16'-0" in size, will require 10% to 15% more labor than flat slab floors of the same thickness and story height.

Method of Constructing Wood Forms for Concrete Stairs. 

platforms. Also, whether the stair is straight or winding and having square or bull nose treads and risers. The story height will also affect the labor costs on account of the shoring and bracing necessary to support the wet concrete. 

It is rather difficult to estimate the cost of stair forms on a sq. ft. basis as it costs as much to frame a 3'-0" stair as one 

4'-0" wide, while the latter contains more forms per lin. ft. 

Lumber costs based on 33% depreciation each time used or on using each set of forms 3 times. Change to suit local conditions.

The better method is to allow a certain price per flight of stairs of each type as this will result in more accurate estimates than the sq. ft. method. However, where it is desirable to estimate the stair forms by the sq. ft. take the area of the soffit of the stairs and platforms. Example: a stair 4'-0" wide and 18′0″ long, contains 72 sq. ft. of forms. 

Some contractors and estimators estimate the cost of stairs at a certain price per lin. ft. of tread, which includes forms, reinforcing steel, concrete and finishing. 

Wood Forms for Straight Concrete Stairs.-On straight stairs extending from floor to floor without intermediate landing platforms and having an average story height of 10′-0″ to 12'-0", two carpenters working together should lay out the stair, place rough stringers, mark off treads and risers on the rough string boards and set them in place in 5 to 6 hrs.

An 

After the rough strings are in place it will require another 

6 to 8 hrs. for 2 carpenters to sheath the stairs, cut, bevel and place risers, and place all necessary shoring and bracing ready for concrete.
