Reinforcing Steel 

Reinforcing steel is estimated by weight, obtained by listing all bars of different sizes and lengths and reducing the total to pounds. Reinforcing bars may be purchased either from mill or warehouse in mill lengths and all cutting and bending done on the job or it may be purchased cut to length and bent, ready to place in the building.

When purchased in mill lengths, the labor cost of unloading, sorting, handling and storing is less than where sent to the job cut to length and bent. The former method requires less storage space as the different size stock length bars are placed in compact piles, while steel cut to length and bent requires considerable storage space as all bars of each size and length must be placed in separate piles.

REINFORCED CONCRETE 

275 While it costs more to handle and store steel sent to the job cut to length and bent, the shop costs of cutting and bending are usually much less than job costs, especially where the work is done by iron workers at present day wages. On large jobs where power bending machines may be used, job bending costs will compare favorably with shop costs. 

Basis for Estimating Price of Reinforcing Steel.-When estimating quantities and weights of reinforcing steel, all bars of each size should be listed separately to obtain the correct weight. Bars" and over take the lowest price per lb. while bars under " in diameter increase in price on a graduated scale, depending upon the size of the bars. The smaller the bars the higher the price per lb. 

Example: If base price of " bars is $2.10 per 100 lbs. what is price of " bars? The table shows that " bars take an increase of 40 cts. per 100 lbs. over base or $2.50 per 100 lbs.

Prices are usually quoted f.o.b. mills or warehouse, with freight allowed to destination.

Bending Stirrups for Beams and Girders.-Steel stirrups for reinforcing concrete beams and girders should be bent in the shop as this is really a machine operation and can be performed much more economically in the shop than on the job. This bending costs $0.80 per 100 lbs. or $16.00 per ton, f.o.b. shops.

100 lbs. or $35.00 per ton.

Spirals for Reinforced Concrete Columns.-Spirals should always be bent and fabricated in the shop as it is all machine work.

It is worth about $1.00 per 100 lbs. .or $20.00 per ton to bend spiral reinforcing, f.o.b. shops. This is for labor only and does not include reinforcing steel, which will have to be added. 

At the present time, fabricated spirals formed of "hot rolled rods are worth $90.00 per ton, and spirals 3/8" and larger of hot rolled rods cost $80.00 per ton, f.o.b. shops.

Shipping Data on Steel Spirals. When estimating the cost of steel spirals that are to be shipped by freight, the estimator should note the spirals that cannot be shipped knocked down, owing to the pitch being such that they cannot collapse. 

Such spirals are subject to first-class freight rates which greatly increase their cost.

The following table gives the maximum pitch for spirals of various diameters which will collapse for shipment.

Cost of Engineering Service. The cost of making working drawings, bending details, setting plans, etc., will vary with the amount of work involved.

Where the engineers prepare the complete design for a reinforced concrete structure, including working drawings, placing plans, bar lists and bending details, a charge of about $5.00 per ton is made for this work. 

Preparing placing plans from design made by others, including bar lists and all bending details, a charge of $2.00 to $3.00 per ton is made for this work. 

Minimum charge for any engineering work is $15.00.

Detailing and placing plans from designs made by others, cost as follows:

Hauling Reinforcing Bars From Shops or Cars to Job.-The cost of hauling reinforcing steel from warehouse or cars to job will vary with the distance of the haul but will cost from $1.00 per ton in the smaller cities to $2.00 per ton in the larger cities.

Labor Labor Placing Reinforcing Bars.-The labor cost of placing reinforcing steel will vary with the average weight of the bars, the manner in which it is placed; i.e., whether bars may laid loose or whether it is necessary to tie them in place, and upon the class of labor employed. be

In many of the larger cities there are concerns that make a specialty of setting reinforcing steel. These men become very adept at this work and under favorable conditions can place steel 25% less than the average building laborer or iron worker. For this reason costs are given both ways and the estimator should use his own judgment as to the class of workmen obtainable.

Clay Tile for Tile and Concrete Floors 

The labor cost of handling and placing clay tile for combination tile and concrete joist floor construction will vary with the

size of the tile, the class of work and the amount of handling necessary.

On straight jobs having long spans without much cutting for pipes and conduits, a mason will lay far more tile per day than on hospitals, schools, hotels, apartments, etc., requiring cutting and fitting for pipes, sleeves and chases through the floor, etc., as it is the cutting and fitting that requires the time. 

If the tile are laid before the pipe trades have completed their roughing-in, it is usually necessary to go over the floor a second time and straighten the rows of tile before the concrete can be placed. This also adds to the labor cost. 

The following table gives the approximate number of tile a man can wheel per load, using tile barrows for wheeling the tile from stock piles to floor.

Pyrobar Floor Tile in Place Ready for Concrete 

The 19" widths of tile are furnished with one closed end on each tile, but they can also be furnished with both ends closed for "two-way" joist construction or with an extra thick top shell for "no-topping" joist construction.

Labor Handling and Placing Pyrobar Floor Tile. The labor cost of handling and placing Pyrobar floor tile will vary according to the size of the tile, job conditions, etc.

Using 3", 4" or 5" tile, a laborer should load into barrows, wheel to building and place on the floor ready for the mason, 8 pcs. 3″, 7 pcs. 4", or 6 pcs. 5″ tile per load and should make at least 5 loads per hr. This amounts to 100, 87.5 and 75 lin. ft. of tile per hr. or sufficient for 133, 117 and 100 sq. ft. of floor area respectively. 

Using 6″ or 8" tile, a laborer should load into barrows, wheel to building and place on the floor ready for the mason, 6 to 7 pcs. (18 to 21 sq. ft. floor area) of tile per load, and should make at least 4 loads an hr. This is at the rate of 

72 to 84 sq. ft. of floor area per hr. 

If 10" or 12" tile are used, a laborer should load into barrows, wheel to building and place on the floor ready for the mason, 4 pcs. (12 sq. ft. floor area) of tile per load, or 48 sq. ft. of floor area per hr.

Metal Tile or "Pans" for Joist Constructed Floors

On jobs of metal "pan" and concrete joist floors, the variations in the labor cost of handling and placing the pans is not as great as with clay tile. This is due to the light weight of the metal tile and the ease in handling them from the ground to the floor so the depth of the "pans" does not materially affect the labor cost of handling and placing.

Where the same size "pans" are used on a number of floors, they are removed after the concrete has hardened and used again on the same job. Removable "pans" are of 16, 18 or 

20 gauge metal that will stand hard usage and are usually rented from one of a number of concerns furnishing, erecting and removing the "pans” at a certain price per sq. ft. of floor or for a stipulated sum for the entire job. However, on some jobs the pans are left in the floor and in such instances they are usually made of 26 or 28 gauge metal.

It is not always economy to use the lightest gauge tile because the men working over them before the concrete is placed, often dent them so badly that it requires considerable extra concrete to fill in the "dents." 

Metal pans should be tacked to the wood forms to hold them rigid and in line while the concrete is placed. 

After the metal "pans" have been used on a job they should be painted with linseed oil to prevent rusting because when properly cared for they are much easier placed and removed. 

Metal "pans" are furnished 20″ and 30″ wide, 6", 8", 10", 12" and 14" deep and in 1'-0", 2′-0″ and 3′-0″ lengths. They are also furnished adjustable to 8", 10", 12", 14″ and 15" deep.

Filler pans for filling in odd spaces are furnished 10″, 12″, 15″ and 16" wide.

Estimating Quantities of Metal "Pans."-Metal pans are estimated by the sq. ft. obtained by taking the entire area of the floor on which they are to be used. 

The sq. ft. area with all pan companies has been established by taking the inside dimensions of the building for brick bearing wall jobs, and adding 1′-0″ to each dimension. Example: a building 50'-0" x 100'-0" having brick bearing walls 1'-4" thick, would be measured as 47'-4" x 97'-4", plus 1'-0" to each dimension, making 48′-4″ x 98′-4″.

With steel or concrete frame buildings, the area is taken to the outside of the lintel beams. Example: a building 50'-0" x 100'-0" having concrete lintel beams within 4" of the outside face of the wall, would be measured as 49′-4″ x 99′-4″.

Do not make deductions for openings in floors, such as elevator shafts, stair wells, pipe spaces, etc., containing less than 50 sq. ft.

CONCRETE Light Weight Concrete 

There are two types of light weight concrete. One type, in use for a considerable time, is produced by simply combining portland cement and a light weight aggregate. The second is a comparatively recent introduction but has been used by European engineers for some time, and is known as aerated concrete. The process is patented and the cost is little, if any, higher than ordinary concrete. 

Aerated concrete is produced by a process depending upon the introduction of certain chemicals to generate gases which cause the mass to expand. The weight of aerated concrete may be controlled with a variation of from 20 lbs. per cu. ft. to approximately the weight of ordinary light weight concrete. 

For average conditions a weight of 40 to 50 lbs. per cu. ft. with a compressive strength of about 500 lbs. per sq. in. is usually selected.

Aerated concrete is fireproof, has a low moisture absorption rate and provides good insulation against the transmission of heat and sound. It may be sawed or nailed as readily as other light weight concrete.

Aerated concrete is known by several trade names, as 

Aerocrete, Casconcrete, Bubble-stone, etc. "Porete", also a light-weight concrete, has been used in the United States for a number of years but the process is more mechanical than chemical. "Porete" possesses much the same advantages as the aerated type but is more costly in process.

All light-weight concretes are of decided advantage for partition walls and fireproofing, whether in monolithic or precast unit form; for floor fill and for roof slabs. The estimator should consider the combined advantages of each type of light-weight concrete before selection. 

Haydite Concrete.-Haydite concrete uses burnt clay or shale for coarse aggregate instead of gravel or crushed stone. 

*Grid Flat Slab Corporation, Boston, Mass.

This inert, cellular material weighs less than 50 lbs. per cu. ft. and when mixed with ordinary torpedo sand and portland cement, produces concrete weighing about 115 lbs. per cu. ft. instead of 150 lbs. for ordinary concrete. 

Full structural strengths can be obtained with Haydite concrete and in many instances a redesign based on lighter weight concrete and reduced dead load more than pays for the slight additional cost of the aggregates. 

The cost of Haydite coarse aggregate will vary with the locality, freight, etc., but under ordinary conditions does not exceed 10 cts. per cu. ft. more than for ordinary concrete. 

Reinforced Concrete 

After the forms, tile and reinforcing steel are in place, the job is ready for concrete. This should include the cost of gravel or crushed stone, sand and cement used in the concrete mixture as well as the labor cost of handling materials, mixing, hoisting and placing the concrete. 

Concrete used in reinforced construction is usually mixed in the proportions of 1:1:2, 1:14:3, 1:2:4, etc., depending upon the class of work on which it is used. Concrete columns are usually mixed in the proportions of 1:1:2 or 1:11:3 as the columns carry the load of the entire building and for that reason require the "richest" and strongest concrete. 

Concrete for reinforced beams, girders, lintels and floor slabs is usually mixed in the proportions of 1:2:4.

When mixed according to the Water-Cement Ratio Method of Proportioning, these proportions will vary somewhat. See tables on pages 171 to 178.

On nearly all classes of reinforced concrete building work, such as columns, beams, girders, floor slabs, etc., the coarse aggregate (gravel or crushed stone) ranges from " to 1″ in size, as it is absolutely necessary to cover and surround all reinforcing steel to produce a smooth surface on all exposed concrete.

When used on any of the combination tile and concrete joist systems, the coarse aggregate should not exceed " in size or

REINFORCED CONCRETE 

309 it will not fill the voids in the narrow joists and surround the reinforcing bars as it should. 

Estimating the Quantities of Cement, Sand, Gravel or Crushed 

Stone Required for One Cu. Yd. of Concrete

A full description of methods and tables giving the amounts of cement, sand, gravel and crushed stone required for one cubic yard of concrete, mixed in any proportion, are given on pages 167 to 178.

Estimating Quantity of Concrete Required for Combination Clay Tile and Concrete Joist Floors 

When figuring concrete quantities for this type of floor construction, figure the entire floor area of the thickness shown as if it were solid concrete. Then make deductions for the displacement of the tile. Example: A floor slab 20'-0"x60′-0″x0′- 

8" contains 800 cu. ft. of concrete. Using 6"x12"x12" tile spaced 16" on centers and allowing for wall bearing of slab and “T” beams, each row of tile is 18′-0″ long. With joists 16″ on centers there are 45 rows of tile 18'-0" long in the slab. 

45x18-810 sq. ft. or 405 cu. ft. of concrete displaced by tile. 

800-405 395 cu. ft. of concrete in the slab.

Quantity of Concrete Required for Metal "Pan" and Concrete 

Joist Floor Construction.-Floors of this type should be estimated in the same manner as tile and concrete joist construction, i.e., obtain the entire floor area as though of solid concrete and deduct for the displacement of the metal "pans."

The deductions for "pan" area in floors of this type is not quite as simple as for clay tile, as metal "pans" are furnished in a number of different sizes, with tapering sides while the sections at each end of the row are often double tapered. 

Allowances for these conditions have been made in the following tables.

Pans furnished by different manufacturers vary slightly in shape but not sufficient to materially affect the concrete quantities. Meyer* steelforms have been used in the tables as being "typical" for general use. Refer to pages 300 to 302.

"Pans"

Labor Mixing and Depositing Reinforced Concrete 

The labor cost of mixing and placing concrete for all classes of reinforced building work, such as columns, beams, girders, stairs, floor slabs, etc., will vary with the size of the job, the method used in handling the materials to the mixer, size and type of mixer used and the method of hoisting and placing the concrete. 

The number of cu. yds. in the job is a big factor in the labor costs because it is not usually advisable to spend a great deal for plant and equipment, such as hoisting towers, spouts, conveying systems, bins, etc., on a job containing less than 1,000 cu. yds. while a job containing 10,000 cu. yds. would warrant such an expenditure and would enable you to place concrete at a much lower cost per cu. yd.

The various methods of handling, hoisting and placing concrete are fully discussed on page 319 to 335. 

Mixing Reinforced Concrete by Hand.-It is not advisable to mix concrete by hand that is to be used for reinforced work as the uniformity of the mix cannot be relied upon. Labor costs of mixing concrete by hand are given on pages 181 to 183. 

Plant and Equipment for Reinforced Concrete Jobs.-The various methods available for mixing and placing reinforced concrete are given on pages 128 to 148. 

Mixing and Placing Concrete on Small Jobs, Using a One Bag (7-S) Mixer and Wheelbarrows or Concrete Carts.-On small reinforced concrete jobs of light construction, where the floors are of clay or gypsum tile or metal "pan" and concrete joist construction or where metal joists are used, it is necessary to cover a comparatively large floor area to place a small amount of concrete. Jobs of this kind require considerable labor working the concrete around the reinforcing bars in the joists and spreading, grading and tamping a very thin floor slab, usually 2" to 3", as a floor using 8" tile and a 2″ slab over requires only 1 cu. yd. of concrete to 85 sq. ft. of floor. 

It is on buildings of this type that a small mixer can be used to advantage both as to convenience and economy. 

Concrete for reinforced structures is usually mixed in the proportions of 1:1:2 or 1:1:3 for columns and 1:2:4 for beams, girders, and floor slabs. When mixed in 1:2:4 proportions, it

requires 1 bag of cement, 2 cu. ft. sand and 4 cu. ft. of gravel or stone or 1 bags of cement, 3 cu. ft. sand and 6 cu. ft. gravel or stone for each batch.

While it is possible under favorable conditions to mix and discharge a batch about every 1 to 2 minutes, it is seldom done in actual practice, except for short periods, as there is always a certain amount of time consumed washing out mixer, cleaning barrows, moving runways, etc., and this must all be included in the final cost. 

On jobs containing less than 500 cu. yds. of concrete, it is seldom economy to construct a special tower for hoisting the concrete from the ground to the upper floors and for this reason an ordinary double cage brick or material hoist is generally used. While this method costs a little more, it is not sufficient to offset the cost of erecting a special hoisting tower for such a small amount of concrete. .

Where the concrete is discharged into wheelbarrows, the average barrow holds only 2 to 2 cu. ft. of wet concrete, so it will require 3 to 4 barrows to remove each batch from the mixer. In hoisting the concrete, an allowance of 1 minute is made for placing barrow on hoist, hoisting to upper floor and removing the barrow. On this basis it requires about 3 min. per batch of 4 to 7 cu. ft. of mixed concrete; 20 batches containing 3 to 5 cu. yds. an hr. or 30 to 40 cu. yds. per 8-hr. day. 

On jobs of this kind it is often possible to use an automatic hoist, operating two single cages at one time, without the use of a hoisting engineer.

On work handled in this manner, the gang will be distributed about as follows: 3 men wheeling stone or gravel; 2 men wheeling sand and cement; 1 man attending mixer; 3 men wheeling concrete barrows from mixer to hoist; 4 men wheeling concrete from hoist to place of deposit; 4 men dumping barrows, spreading, grading and tamping concrete; 1 man on miscellaneous labor, such as cleaning barrows and mixer, baling cement bags, etc.; 1 mixer engineer and 1 hoisting engineer, if required; also 

1 cement finisher or mason supervising work. 

Based on an average output of 5 cu. yds. per hr. the labor cost per cu. yd. should run as follows:

Mixing and Placing Concrete on Jobs Using a Bucket Hoist and a 14-S Mixer.-Based on 1:2:4 concrete, a 14-S mixer will discharge about -cu. yd. of mixed concrete per batch. 

The labor cost of mixing and placing the concrete will vary with the method used in supplying the mixer and in handling the concrete from the mixer to the floor, also the class of work, whether thick or thin slabs, etc.

Assuming the mixer is fed in the usual way and the concrete hoisted to the various floors in a concrete bucket and then wheeled in concrete carts to place of deposit, the mixer should average 25 to 30 batches an hr. or 200 to 240 per 8-hr. day.

While it is true that many contractors attempt to turn out a batch every 1 to 1 min. it is a known fact that much stronger concrete is obtained by allowing the concrete mixture to remain in the mixer 1 to 3 minutes. Some architects and engineers specify that the concrete mixture must remain in the mixer for a certain length of time.

Clay Tile, Gypsum Tile or Metal "Pan" and Concrete Joist

Construction. The labor cost of placing concrete for floors of this type will run a trifle higher than for solid concrete floors. 

The concrete is usually only 11″ to 2″ thick over the tile.or "pans", which necessitates more labor spreading, grading and tamping and more labor building and removing runways, etc., than when placing a thick slab. Placing concrete in small joists, usually only 4" or 5″ wide also requires time and care to see that all reinforcing steel is completely imbedded and the bottoms on all joists filled with concrete to eliminate voids and "honey combing."

It ordinarily requires to -hr. additional labor time per cu. yd. for slabs 2″ and under in thickness. 

Mixing and Placing Concrete for Thin Concrete Floors 

Placed over Steel Plate or Truss Joists and Metal Lath.-Floors of this type average only 2″ to 3" thick and while it is a simple matter to place the concrete, there is a large area to cover to place a comparatively small amount of concrete. This requires extra labor spreading and grading concrete, placing and removing runways, etc. For floors of this type, add to -hr. additional labor time per cu. yd. of concrete. 

Fireproofing Structural Steel Columns and Beams with 

Concrete.-Buildings having structural steel frames often have the columns and beams fireproofed by covering them with 2" of concrete. This requires forms the same as ordinary concrete beams and columns and the cost is practically the same. 

When fireproofing just the beams and columns with concrete, the labor cost will run rather high per cu. yd. as this is another instance of covering a large area to place a small amount of concrete. Use the same labor costs as given on page 319, under

REINFORCED CONCRETE 

325 "Mixing and Placing Concrete on Small Jobs using Wheel barrows or Concrete Carts." Mixing and Placing Concrete Using "Spouting" Systems.- 

Spouting systems for conveying and placing concrete are used most advantageously on large heavily constructed jobs, such as dams, retaining walls, mill, factory and warehouse buildings, and other structures requiring a large amount of concrete. 

It is seldom economical to use a spouting system on thin concrete floors (2″ and under), as it requires too much labor moving spouts to place a comparatively small amount of concrete. Then too, a spouting system deposits more concrete in one place than can be conveniently handled on floors of this type, necessitating too much hand shoveling. 

However, a system that is often used to advantage on light constructed floors is to mix and hoist the concrete in the usual manner and then spout it from the hoisting tower to hoppers placed at convenient points on the floor. The concrete is then wheeled from these floor hoppers in wheelbarrows or concrete carts to place of deposit. Where a system of this kind is used, the labor costs given on pages 321 to 324 will apply. 

When considering the use of a spouting system, remember there is a considerable cash outlay required for the spouting equipment in addition to the labor cost of raising and moving them for each floor.

A system of this kind is ordinarily used. with a 14-S, 21-S or a 

28-S mixer and the labor cost will be approximately the same with either size mixer, except for a slight difference in the cost of mixing and hoisting.

The cost of setting up and removing concrete mixer and hoisting engine, erecting and dismantling hoisting tower, raising and placing hoppers and spouts should be estimated as a · separate item, as this will remain practically the same whether the job contains 1,000 or 10,000 cu. yds. For this reason it is not advisable to allow a certain amount per cu. yd. for plant and equipment unless the total yardage is known. 

Based on an average of 25 to 30 batches an hr. or 200 to 240 per 8-hr. day, the labor per cu. yd. of concrete should cost as follows:

Ready Mixed Concrete 

When using ready-mixed concrete on all classes of reinforced construction, such as floors, beams, girders, columns, etc., the cost of handling and placing the concrete will run approximately the same as for job mixed concrete, except for the labor handling materials, supplying and operating mixer, etc., as the trucks dump the ready-mixed concrete into a receiving hopper, where it is distributed by wheelbarrows, concrete buggies or hoisted and spouted into place. 

It is necessary to have a fairly large size hopper on the job to receive the concrete from the trucks, as this hopper must be of sufficient capacity to supply the hoisting bucket as fast as it can handle the concrete, otherwise the work will be slowed down and with the gang idle part of the time-up go the labor costs. 

The labor cost of handling and placing ready-mixed concrete will vary with the amount handled and placed per day, the method of handling, hoisting and placing the concrete and the class of work, as it will cost less to place concrete in heavy floors than in thin floor slabs 2 to 2-in. thick.

"Pumpcrete"* or Placing Concrete by Pipeline 

The development and perfection of a pump for transporting freshly mixed concrete through pipelines has revolutionized the placing of substantial yardages of concrete in dams, tunnels, retaining walls, bridge decks, mill, factory and warehouse buildings where concrete is required at rates varying from 15 to 65 cu. yds. an hr. This machine for pumping concrete is called a "Pumpcrete" and pumps concrete through a pipeline in much the same manner that a piston pump pumps water. It will transport freshly mixed workable concrete to distances of 1,000 ft, and to heights in excess of 100 ft. Many instances are known where the pumpcrete has delivered the concrete to the forms 1,400 ft. away. 

The Pumpcrete will handle efficiently concrete of any slump from" to 7" but the ideal slump for pumping is from 4" to 6".

The concrete is delivered to the forms in better condition than when discharged from the mixer due to the added mixing received in the remixing hopper which receives the concrete from the mixer and keeps it in a uniform condition as it is fed through 

*Chain Belt Company, Milwaukee, Wis.

the cylinder of the Pumpcrete to the pipeline. During the pumping operation, the pipeline is full at all times which keeps the concrete from segragating, thereby eliminating one of the major objections found in most methods used to transport concrete to the forms. The troweling action of the walls of the pipeline in contact with the concrete as it passes through improves the quality of the concrete. 

NSYLVANIA "Pumpcrete" Equipment in Operation 

The smooth even flow of concrete into the forms reduces the stresses in the bracing and ties. Danger of "honeycomb" is reduced as there is no "slug" of pebbles dumped in, as in the case of a buggy, at the end of a batch which might not be properly spaded. Walls 120 ft. long and 15 ft. high have been made at one pour in 3 ft. lifts without signs of longitudinal jointing or uneven surfaces due to the dumping of wheelbarrows or buggies in such a way as to splash the form above the point of placement.

REINFORCED CONCRETE 

331 Runways for wheelbarrows or concrete buggies are not required when placing concrete by pipeline, although it is necessary to provide supports for the pipelines, which usually consists of "horses" or "trestles," similar to those shown in the accompany illustrations. 

Concrete can be placed with the Pumpcrete in 2" sections, thin walls, footings or in large masses.

Cost of Placing Concrete by Pipeline.-The cost of placing concrete by pipeline varies widely as do other methods of distribution, and is governed by the size of the job, area covered, the yardage of concrete that can be placed at one set-up of the pipelines, whether thick or thin walls, slabs or large masses of concrete are being placed. 7018

Placing Concrete by "Pumpcrete" Showing Pipeline Supported on Horses 

When placing concrete by ordinary methods, the cost of erecting and dismantling the hoisting tower and spouts must be considered, also raising the concrete hopper and moving spouts for placing the concrete. 

The same conditions must be considered with Pumpcrete distribution, which includes original cost of the equipment, total yardage of concrete in the job, cost of setting up and removing pipelines, etc.

REINFORCED CONCRETE 

333 On large jobs containing 10,000 to 50,000 cu. yds. of concrete, the cost per cu. yd. will be very small but on jobs of 1,000 cu. yds. or less and up to 5,000 cu. yds. all cost factors must be carefully considered.

Always bear in mind, the cost of mixing the concrete will be the same regardless of the method of distribution because where the concerte is mixed and dumped into a hoisting bucket using ordinary methods, it is deposited in the Pumpcrete hopper under the Pumpcrete method. It is only the method of handling, hoisting and placing the mixed concrete that should be considered. 

This also applies where ready-mixed concrete is used. 

The crew operating the Pumpcrete unit will vary with the size, area and yardage in the job. An operator is required on the Pumpcrete, a foreman and 8 to 10 laborers should place and remove pipelines, handle, spread and level the concrete, and the quantity will vary from 15 to 45 cu. yds. an hr. depending upon the class of work, as follows:

Actual Cost of Placing Concrete by Pipeline.-On a large sewage disposal plant, size 370′-0″x380′-0″, containing 15,000 cu. yds. of concrete consisting of heavily reinforced concrete in slabs and thin walls, all of the concrete was placed by pipeline. 

The concrete plant was placed midway of one side where a railroad spur provided for delivery of cement in cars, which eliminated a second handling. The sand and gravel was dumped

directly into the charging hopper of concrete mixer by "batching" trucks, which eliminated all handling of aggregates on the job except one man dumping trucks. The mixer discharged into the remixing hopper of a single Pumpcrete which was placed below grade in the excavation made for the plant addition. 

From this point the concrete was pumped through 7" pipelines to the point of placement. 

Placing Concrete in Thin Walls Using "Pumpcrete" Equipment 

The floors of the aerating basins, 30 ft. wide and 120 ft. long were poured by radial spouting from the end of the pipe line, which was supported on horses. The line was taken up as the concreting progressed and laid in the next basin. 

Staging, as illustrated, supported on the forms permitted erection of the pipeline, pouring 112 cu. yds. of concrete in the wall and removal of the pipe line and forms in one day. The walls of the aerating and settling basins were 15 ft. high and were

REINFORCED CONCRETE 

335 poured in 3 ft. lifts. Valves at 20 ft. intervals were inserted in the 120 ft. of distributing line which permitted the withdrawal of concrete at these points. Elephant trunks directed the concrete into specially constructed chutes that led the concrete down through the maze of steel to the level being poured where it was discharged without spattering the forms above that point. Pouring was started from the valve nearest the Pumpcrete. When enough concrete had been withdrawn at a valve, it was closed and the next valve opened for concreting at this point. This procedure was continued until the lift was completed at the end of the pipeline

With the aid of internal vibration, these high long walls were poured without blemishes or jointing.

Slab Forms for Clay Tile and Concrete Joist Construction 

Illinois Central Hospital Building.-The floors in this building were of clay tile and concrete joist construction. The "open" deck system of forms was used on the first floor with 2"x8" plank spaced about 8" on centers. This system has both its advantages and disadvantages, as it requires more care in spacing the deck boards and in setting the tile because if a tile is knocked out of place, it allows the concrete to leak through the forms onto the floor below. All of the forms above the first floor were sheathed solid with 1"x8" sheathing. Ceiling heights varied from 9'-0" to 15'-0", with no typical floors. 

The forms were constructed with 4"x4" uprights or "shores" spaced 6'-0" on centers one way and 8'-0" the other so that each shore supported 48 sq. ft. of floor. Purlins of 4"x6" lumber were placed on top of the shores, and 2"x8" joists spaced 2'-0" apart received the 1"x8" sheathing. It required about 3 ft. of lumber, b.m. per sq. ft. of forms.

Slab Forms for Metal "Pan" and Concrete Joist Construction 

Three Story Office Building.—The floors in this building were of metal "pan" and concrete joist construction. The pans varied from 6" to 10" deep and 20" wide with joists spaced 25" on centers. 

The ceiling heights were 10'-6" in the first story; 12'-6" on the second and 11'-0" on the third story. All forms were of "open" deck construction. 

The uprights or "shores" were 4"x4"'s spaced 5'-0" to 6'-0" on centers, depending upon the span. The stringers or purlins were 2"x12" plank spiked to the sides of the shores, and 2″x6″ joists were spaced about 2'-6" on centers. The first floor or "deck"

sheathing was 2″x6″ planks spaced 1'-9″ on centers. An item that added considerably to the cost of these forms were the concrete braces or bridging running at right angles to the metal "pans." On each span over 16'-0" it was necessary to frame for a concrete joist or brace 4" wide by the depth of the joist. 

It was also necessary to frame a tight "deck" for the "T" beam supports, as all slabs had a concrete "T" beam projecting l′-0″ to 1'-6" from the walls the entire length of the slab. The labor fitting and filling in for these joists and "T" beams added considerably to the labor costs. 

All form lumber was old material that had been, used on other jobs, which also increased the labor costs. It required about 2 ft. of lumber, b.m. per sq. ft. of forms, and there were 

15,900 sq. ft. of slab forms in the job.

Reinforced Concrete Dome Arkansas State Capitol Building.-The dome on this building had a structural steel frame that was entirely covered with concrete and which served as a base for the stone placed on the exterior. This was an exceedingly difficult piece of form work as it was necessary to imbed all of the structural steel members. On account of the shape of the dome it was necessary to cut all forms to a double radius, both horizontally and vertically and it was also necessary to place forms on both the inside and outside of the steel framework, making practically a wall form. These forms were built in sections about 4'-0" square and the inside and outside sections were wired together. 

This work was 200′-0″ to 250'-0" above ground, without intermediate floors, necessitating a large amount of scaffolding. 

There were 11,340 sq. ft. of forms in the job (measurement taken on both sides) and the labor cost per 100 sq. ft. of forms was as follows:

363 Schulze Baking Company Building.-Illustrated on page 366. 

This job was 160'-0" wide and 320'-0" long. The front portion was 5 stories high, with 18'-0" ceiling heights and 10" flat slab floor construction. The rear portion was 1 to 3 stories high of regular beam and girder construction, with unusually large beams and girders.

There were 6,800 cu. yds. of concrete in the job, all of which was mixed in two -cu. yd. batch mixers. One mixer was placed near the front of the building to pour the 5-story portion and the other one was placed about half way back to take care of the 3-story portion. It was seldom that both mixers were running at the same time.

The sand and gravel was piled in the street adjacent to the mixers, and was then loaded into wheelbarrows and wheeled to the mixers. The concrete was discharged from the mixer into a bucket hoist, hoisted to the floor being poured and dumped into a hopper on the floor. The concrete was then wheeled in concrete carts from the hopper to place of deposit. 

The runways for the carts were built in 8'-0"x4'-0" sections with 15" legs, and had the appearance of low tables. It was an easy matter to move these runway platforms after the concrete was poured, enabling the use of the same runways over and over again. Each runway section had 6 4″x4″ legs spaced about 

4'-0" on centers and the tops were covered with 2" plank.

Illinois Central Hospital Building.-Illustrated on page 389. 

The floors in this building were of clay tile and concrete joist construction, with most of the tile 6″ or under in depth, 4″ wide concrete joists and only 11" of concrete over the tile. 

Fully 75% of this concrete was mixed and placed during freezing weather, necessitating heating the mixing water and all aggregate. After placing, it was necessary to protect the concrete from freezing by hanging salamanders 4'-0" to 5'-0" below the ceilings and covering the entire floor area with tarred felt and about 12" of loose straw.

Placing Concrete on Gable Roofs Rice Institute Buildings.-Ilustrated on page 580. This building had a gable roof which required considerable extra

labor. The concrete was hoisted in concrete carts, wheeled to the high point or "ridge" of the roof, where the carts were emptied and the wet concrete flowed from the ridge of the roof down toward the sides. When placing concrete on sloping surfaces, it has a tendency to run down the sides and into the gutter, which requires extra labor banking, leveling and tamping to hold the concrete in place.

Arkansas State Capitol Building.—Illustrated on page 377. The dome of this building was covered with a 4" shell of concrete, which also fireproofed the structural steel framework. The labor cost of mixing and placing this concrete was extremely high as there were only 200 cu. yds. of concrete in the dome, which did not warrant a large expenditure for plant and equipment. The concrete was only 4″ thick, which necessitated a great deal of spading to cover the reinforcing steel and prevent "honey-combing."

The manner in which it was necessary to operate also increased the labor cost. One section of forms about 4′-0″ high entirely circling the dome was placed at one time, so that it was necessary to circle the dome for each 4'-0" in height. 

The concrete was mixed in a -cu. yd. batch mixer, dumped into concrete carts and wheeled about 30'-0" where it was dumped into a bucket, which was picked up by a stiff leg derrick on the pediment of the building. The bucket was then lifted to the platform on either side of the pediment, where it was placed on a small car running on a track. This car was then

Reinforced Concrete Stairs Arkansas State Capitol Building.-Illustrated on page 379. 

There were 4 flights of main stairs in this building about 10′-0″ wide, 29'-0" long and containing 20 cu. yds. of concrete per flight or 80 cu. yds. total. 

These stairs were not installed until after the floors were poured, which added to the labor costs. 

The concrete was mixed in a -cu. yd. batch mixer, wheeled in concrete carts 50'-0" to 100'-0", and then hoisted to the second and third floors where it was again wheeled about 50′-0″, and then dumped from the edge of the stair well into chutes extending to the stair proper. 

After the concrete had been emptied into the chutes it was necessary to spread it with shovels and hoes because the long wheel had settled the concrete in the carts, making it difficult and expensive to handle.

CHAPTER VI , SLAG, CINDER AND HAYDITE CONCRETE FLOOR FILL, NAILING CONCRETE 

Concrete floors, sidewalks, and slag, cinder or Haydite concrete floor fill are estimated by the sq. ft. taking the number of sq. ft. of any given thickness, as 2", 3", 4", 5″, 6″, etc.

The quantities are easily computed by obtaining the area of the various rooms or spaces to have concrete floors and stating the number of sq. ft. of each thickness. 

When preparing an estimate for concrete floors or sidewalks placed on the ground, there are eight distinct material and labor items to be considered when arriving at the sq. ft. price, as follows: 

1. Labor grading and removing surplus earth under floors or filling where present grade is too low. 

2. Cost of cinders, sand or slag to be placed under concrete floor; labor spreading and tamping same in place. 

3. Labor placing wood or metal screeds or forms. 4. 

Cost of cement, sand and gravel for concrete sub-floor. 

5. Labor mixing and placing rough concrete sub-floor. 6. 

Cost of cement and sand for finish top, also cost of floor hardening compound, if specified. 

7. Labor mixing, placing and troweling cement finish top and blocking off into squares, if required. 

8. Cartage of plant and equipment, insurance, profit, etc.

Grading for Concrete Floors and Walks.-On practically all cement floors and walks placed directly on the ground it is necessary to do a certain amount of grading before the bed of cinders, sand or slag can be placed.

If the space is large and it is not necessary to remove the excavated soil from the premises, a team and drag scraper is probably the most economical method to use or a small tractor scraper might be used to advantage. 395

· 

A team and driver, with one extra man on the scraper should excavate and place in piles, 28 to 32 cu. yds. per 8-hr. day, at the following labor cost per cu. yd.:

This cost will vary with the kind of soil encountered, i.e., sand or loam, ordinary black soil, heavy soil or clay. Detailed excavating costs are given on pages 52 to 70.

To obtain the cost of grading one sq. ft. of any thickness, divide the cu. yd. cost by the number of sq. ft. obtainable from one cu. yd. and the result is the sq. ft. cost for grading. Example: With excavating at $0.53 per cu. yd. find the sq. ft. cost of removing 5″ of top soil. The table shows that one cu. yd. contains 65 sq. ft. of 5″ fill. $0.53÷65=.00815 or approx. of a cent per sq. ft. for grading.

The cost of any other thickness is obtained in the same manner.

Mixing and Placing Concrete for Floors and Walks 

Mixing Concrete by Hand.-On the average sidewalk or basement floor job, it is possible to mix the concrete by hand on a mixing board close to the place of deposit and it is then only necessary to shovel the mixed concrete from the board directly into place.

As with other classes of concrete work, the cost of mixing and placing the concrete will depend upon the number of times it is turned on the board and the method used in mixing and placing; but on the smaller jobs it will require 3 to 4 hrs. labor time to mix and place one cu. yd. of concrete, as this class of work does not proceed as fast as foundation work. 

On work of this kind, the gang usually consists of 5 or 6 men, so it is not possible for one man to work at the same class of work all day, but must alternate between wheeling sand, gravel, cement, and mixing concrete, as the job may require. 

Five men working together should handle all materials, mix, place and tamp 20 to 24 batches (-cu. yd. each) or 10 to 12 cu. yds. per 8-hr. day, at the following labor cost per cu. yd.: 

3/1/2 $... $.

$0.97 $3.41

Labor Mixing and Placing Concrete for Floors and Walks 

Using a Small Mixer.-A small concrete mixer of or 1 bag (31-S or 7-S) capacity is ordinarily used for floor and sidewalk work.

Where possible to use a full gang of men and keep the mixer in operation steadily, a mixer should discharge a batch every 2 minutes, but as in all other kinds of construction work there are always delays, such as engine adjustments, repairing mixer, delays caused by non-delivery of sand, gravel or cement, moving and placing runways, cleaning concrete barrows, etc., so the average for a job will be about 20 to 25 batches an hr. or 

160 to 200 batches per 8-hr. day.

On the above basis, using either a 34-S or 7-S concrete mixer, the labor cost per cu. yd. should run as follows: 

Labor  Total 

3 $..... $..... $0.971 $2.93

Using a larger mixer will increase the output but the labor cost will increase in direct proportion. Many of the largest contractors have found that a one bag mixer is the most economical unit for floor and sidewalk work.

Estimating the Labor Cost Per Sq. Ft. of Floor or Sidewalk. 

-The labor costs given above for mixing and placing rough concrete are based on a cu. yd. while floors and sidewalks are usually estimated by the sq. ft. 

After the labor cost per cu. yd. has been obtained, divide this by the number of sq. ft. of floor obtainable from a cu. yd. of concrete and the result will be the labor cost per sq. ft. of floor. Example: Find the labor cost per sq. ft. of 4″ floor. The table on page 399 shows that 81 sq. ft. of 4" floor can be obtained from one cu. yd. of concrete. If the labor cost is $2.93 per cu. yd. $2.93÷81=.0362 or 3 cts. per sq. ft. 

Any other thickness is obtained in the same manner. 

Rule for Obtaining the Quantities of Cement and Sand Required for One Cu. Yd. of Plastic Mortar.-Use the following rule to obtain the approximate quantities of cement and sand sufficient for one cu. yd. of plastic mortar : 

Divide 10 by the number of parts (by volume), of sand and cement in the total mixture, and the quotient will be the number of bbls. of Portland cement required for one cu. yd. of mortar. Multiply the number of bbls. of cement by the number of parts of sand required, and the result will be the number of bbls. of sand required for one cu. yd. of plastic mortar. To reduce bbls. to cu. ft., multiply by .14 (since a bbl. contains 3.8 cu. ft. and there are 27 cu. ft. in a cu. yd.), and the result will be the quantity of sand required for one cu. yd. of plastic mortar. 

Example: Find the quantity of cement and sand required for one cu. yd. of Portland cement mortar mixed in the proportions of 1 part cement and 2 parts sand.

Adding 1 part of cement and 2 parts of sand equals 3 parts in the mixture. Dividing 10 by the number of parts, which is 3, the result is 33; therefore it requires 3 bbls. of cement for one cu. yd. of cement mortar. Multiply the number of bbls. of cement, which is 33, by the number parts of sand, which is 2, and the result is 63, or it requires 63 bbls. of sand to each cu. yd. of cement mortar. To reduce the sand from bbls. to cu. yds. multiply 63 by .14, and the result is .93; so it will require .93 cu. yds. of sand for one cu. yd. of cement mortar mixed in the proportions of 1:2. 

Estimating the Number of Sq. Ft. of Cement Finish Top 

Obtainable from One Cu. Yd. of Cement Mortar.

-To obtain the

number of sq. ft. of cement finish top obtainable from one cu. yd. of cement mortar, use the same method as described on page 399. i.e., take one cu. yd. of mortar in the form of a cube, 3'-0" long, 3'-0" wide and 3′-0″ (36″) high. The surface of this cube contains 9 sq. ft. and the number of sq. ft. of topping obtainable from same will vary with the thickness of the finish. By dividing 36″ (the height of the cube) by the thickness of the finish top, ", 1", ", etc., the result will be the number of slabs, each containing 9 sq. ft. obtainable from the cube. 

Example: Find the number of sq. ft. of 3" finish top obtainable from one cu. yd. of cement mortar. 36″÷3″=48. 48x9=432, or it is possible to obtain 432 sq. ft. of 3″ finish top from one cu. yd. of mortar.

Labor Applying Cement Finish Top on Sidewalks.-Concrete for sidewalks is usually of a very dry mix and stiff consistency so that the finish may be applied immediately after a section of the rough base has been laid. After allowing sufficient time for the topping to set, the finisher can return and trowel this section of the walk while the next section is being laid. 

Overtime may be materially reduced by using this method. 

On nearly all classes of finish it requires 2 to 3 men in the gang. Where it is possible for the finisher to trowel and finish all day long, he will require a helper to assist in screeding and troweling the floor and a laborer to mix and deliver the finish topping. 

If the sidewalk is blocked off into 4'-0" to 6'-0" squares, a finisher and helper should finish 700 to 800 sq. ft. per 8-hr. day. 

These quantities will often be exceeded but by making allowances for lost time, etc., it will prove a fair average because on nearly every job one-half the finisher's time is non-productive. 

It is often necessary to wait 2 to 4 hrs. after the finish topping has been placed before it sets sufficiently to be troweled. The brand of cement used will have considerable bearing on this as some cements set much more quickly than others. 

Based on conditions as described above, the labor per 100 sq. ft. of finish should cost as follows:

Labor Applying Cement Finish Top on Concrete Floors on the 

Ground. The labor cost of placing finish top on concrete floors laid directly on the ground will run much the same as for sidewalk work, as it is possible to mix the concrete rather dry and place the finish immediately after the rough concrete has been placed over a sufficient area. However, there is some lost time due to waiting for the finish topping to take its initial set. 

During the past few years it has been demonstrated that the strength of concrete is vitally affected by the amount of mixing water used and for this reason there is a tendency to use as little water as possible to obtain a workable consistency. This applies to both the rough concrete and the finish top, and the less water used, the sooner the finisher is able to start finishing. 

Where possible to start finishing floors the first thing in the morning and continue all day, a finisher and helper should complete 100 to 125 sq. ft. of floor an hr. but instances of this kind are so rare as to be almost negligible. 

On the average job it is necessary for the gang to place concrete for two or three hours in the morning before a sufficient area is covered to warrant placing the finish top. After the finish has been placed and leveled, it is necessary to wait from 1 to 3 hrs. until it sets sufficiently to allow the finisher to commence troweling. In this way practically half a day has been spent by the finisher without completing any floor. 

Where the gang placing the rough concrete works until the regular quitting time, it will be necessary for the finishers and helpers to work far into the night to place the finish top. 

While some cement finishers may finish 175 to 200 sq. ft. of floor an hr. under favorable conditions, the average will be 

85 to 100 sq. ft. an hr. or 700 to 800 sq. ft. per 8-hr. day.

Labor Applying Cement Finish Top on Reinforced Concrete 

Floors. The cost of placing finish top on reinforced concrete floors is subject to wide fluctuations. One of the reasons is the custom of placing the rough concrete over as large an area as possible and then allowing the concrete to stand until the water disappears from the surface before placing the cement topping. 

This allows the finish top to take its initial set in the least possible time. However, the time required for cement to take its initial set depends upon the brand of cement used, as some cements are noted for being either "quick setting" or "slow setting."

The amount of water used in the concrete mix also has considerable bearing on the finishing cost because if "sloppy" concrete is used it requires much more time for the floor to set sufficiently to receive the finish top than if concrete of a rather "stiff" consistency is used.

Many architects and engineers specify that the finish top must be applied and finished at the same time the rough concrete is placed, and in such instances it necessitates a large amount of overtime for finishers and helpers.

Where the gang places rough concrete right up until quitting time, it is a foregone conclusion that the finishers and helpers will have to work far into the night.

The item of overtime should be carefully considered by the estimator for as a usual thing the cement finisher starts work when all other trades have quit for the day.

While under favorable conditions, some finishers and helpers may finish 175 to 200 sq. ft. of floor an hour on certain classes of work, the general average for a reinforced concrete job will vary from 75 to 80 sq. ft. an hr. or 600 to 640 sq. ft. per 8-hr. day.

It will also require the time of a man mixing the finish topping and placing it on the floor ready for the finisher and helper. 

The labor costs given are for straight time but the estimator should bear in mind that overtime costs time and a half or double time.

Use 9 lbs. of cement color* to each bag of Portland cement used in the topping.

It is advisable to establish the mixture from samples built up under job conditions and allow to dry because by this method you will know in advance what the job will look like when completed.

Final troweling should be done after the concrete has stiffened, as this assures a smooth, polished finish. Integral waterproofing hardener can be added to mix materials, also polishing or a surface treatment can be applied, if desired. 

Measure every ingredient in each batch of color mortar, including water and always use clean sand.

Cerox Colored Cement.*-A ready-mixed cement made in various colors to be used wherever a colored cement surface is required.

It is a combination of imported oxide colors, Ceresit Waterproofing Compound and Portland cement, accurately proportioned, reground and machine mixed.

Cerox is used in the same manner as Portland cement. Make proportions 1 part Cerox colored cement to 2 parts clean, well graded sand. Add no additional material. Thoroughly mix for at least 3 minutes and deposit over the concrete base before the base has appreciably hardened. Float and trowel in the customary manner. Troweling must be carefully done and timely troweling is an essential part of finishing, but excess troweling should be avoided.

Resurfacing Old Concrete Floors and Patching Floors Having 

Holes, Ruts and Breaks

Many concrete floors subject to trucking and heavy service become full of holes and ruts and require patching or a complete new topping. A new concrete topping is difficult on account of the labor involved in removing the old floor and the additional thickness required to bond the old and new concrete. 

Stonhard Resurfacer* is a material having an emulsified asphalt base and is used for this purpose. It is mixed with sand and cement and applied directly over the old floor or used to fill holes and ruts where a complete new floor is unnecessary. 

Clean the old floors to remove all loose particles, grease and grime. Oakite or other caustic solutions may be used for cleaning the floors of grease, etc.

The resurfacer is applied about " thick. Where the floor is subject to hand trucking, " crushed stone, trap rock, grits or pebbles should be mixed with the sand and resurfacing materials but if subject only to power trucking, sand only is mixed with the resurfacing materials. *Stonhard Company, Philadelphia, Pa. 

*Ceresit Waterproofing Co., Chicago

Stonhard Resurfacer will harden ready for use in about 36 hours but if the floor must be ready for service in 12 to 15 hours, "Resmix" is used instead of Portland cement to hasten the hardening action.

A 3-man crew, consisting of foreman, cement finisher and helper should place about 500 sq. ft. of floor per 8-hr. day.

Cinder, Slag and Haydite Concrete Floor Fill 

Concrete made of light weight aggregates, such as cinders, slag or Haydite is often used for floor fill under marble and tile floors, between wood floor sleepers, screeds, etc. 

The labor cost of placing concrete floor fill runs considerably higher than for ordinary concrete because the fill is usually only 2" or 3" thick, which necessitates covering a large floor area to place a comparatively small amount of concrete. In many instances it is necessary to hoist the concrete to the upper floors

in wheelbarrows or concrete carts and then wheel it to the different parts of the building where it is to be used. 

When placing concrete fill between wood floor sleepers or screeds, it is important that every precaution be taken to prevent the sleepers from being knocked out of level when wheeling over them. As this work is usually done after the partitions and rough door bucks are in place, care must be used to prevent knocking wheelbarrows into door bucks and partitions. 

When placing concrete floor fill, it is not advisable to use a large mixer because of the necessity of covering a large floor area to place a small amount of concrete. It usually requires considerable leveling and tamping, making it impractical to handle the concrete in large quantities. A concrete mixer of 1 or 2 bag capacity is best adapted for this class of work. 

Mixing and Placing Concrete Floor Fill-On account of the additional labor required spreading, grading and tamping concrete floor fill, the cu. yd. labor costs run higher than for foundation or sidewalk work.

There is also more labor required wheeling concrete from the mixer to the hoist and from the hoist to place of deposit, as floor fill is usually placed after the structural portions of the building have been completed, and it is not possible to carry on the work with as much speed as before door bucks and partitions were erected. 

A gang of 18 to 20 men on a 7-S or 10-S mixer should handle materials, mix and place 15 to 20 batches (containing 6 to 7 cu. ft. each) or 4 to 5 cu. yds. of concrete an hr. with the men distributed as follows: 2 men wheeling cinders, slag or Haydite from stock piles to mixer; 2 men wheeling sand and cement to mixer; 1 man attending mixer; 1 laborer placing and removing runways; 3 men wheeling concrete from mixer to hoist; 4 men wheeling concrete from hoist to place of deposit; 3 men dumping barrows, leveling, grading and tamping concrete; 1 mixer engineer and 1 hoisting engineer, if required.

Nailing Concrete 

Nailing concrete is used instead of wood sleepers, screeds or nailing strips for floors, roofs, partitions and grounds. The nails are driven through the wood floors, slate, tile or metal roofing directly into the nailing concrete. 

Nailing concrete is usually applied about 2" thick, the same as other concrete floor or roof fill, although this varies with its use.

There are several kinds of nailing concrete on the market and this data does not consider the merits of any of them but merely describes their uses, covering capacity, quantities, costs, etc. 

Nailcrete. A patented all mineral nailing concrete suitable for use as a nailing base for floors and various kinds of roof covering. Nailcrete is used on floors without sleepers, underflooring or sheathing.

Methods of Using Nailing Concrete 

At 2003 and

Nailcrete is packed 100 lbs. to a bag or 20 bags to the ton. 

It costs $2.35 to $2.50 per bag on jobs having 40,000 sq. ft. or more, while smaller quantities cost $3.00 to $3.25 per bag. These prices vary according to location and governing freight rates. 

The mixtures and quantities depend on the use to be made of the materials.

As a nailing base for floors, it requires 1 bag of Nailcrete, 21 bags of cement and 7 cu. ft. of sharp sand to cover 60 sq. ft. of surface 2" thick.

As a structural slab on roofs, it requires 1 bag of Nailcrete, 2 bags of cement and 4 cu. ft. of sharp sand to cover 42 sq. ft. of surface 2″ thick.

When used on roofs over a concrete roof slab, it requires 1 bag of Nailcrete, 2 bags of cement, and 8 cu. ft. of sharp sand to cover 60 sq. ft. of surface 2″ thick.

The above covering capacities are based on a level concrete base course and will vary if applied to uneven surfaces.

Surfacing Concrete Walls and Ceilings by Machine.-Where necessary to remove fins, board and form marks and all other surface irregularities from concrete work, the Berg Concrete Surfacer and Finisher may be used with satisfactory results. 

It may also be used for surfacing synthetic or concrete stone, concrete blocks; surfacing walls and ceilings, columns, bridges, stadiums, power plants, etc. With attachments, it cuts brick walls in preparation for stucco application, grinds paint from brick and cleans all kinds of stone surfaces.

This machine consists of a cutting tool, driven by a light weight electric motor or compressed air. It weighs only 21 lbs. and may be swung from the shoulders of the operator. The cutter head, which may be used either flexibly or rigidly cuts through the outer surface to expose the aggregate, and the fine cutting action produces a surface that forms a perfect bond for float or other finishes.

CHAPTER VII CONCRETE CURB AND GUTTER, CONCRETE, BRICK AND WOOD BLOCK PAVING 

This chapter is not intended to cover road building as it is conducted to-day but only average size jobs of concrete curb and gutter, and small jobs of concrete, brick and wood block paving.

Large jobs of this kind require a vast amount of equipment and the costs vary widely according to the amount of cut and fill required, method of receiving materials, etc., as many jobs have their own gravel crushing and screening plants, while others maintain elaborate plants at the nearest railroad siding for unloading materials from cars, loading trucks, etc. 

When making up an estimate on curb and gutter work, concrete, brick or wood block paving, it should include all items of overhead expense, such as superintendent, foremen, timekeepers, watchmen, etc.

The item of plant and equipment should include the cost of transporting equipment to the job and removing same at completion, and includes the following items: steam or power shovels, power rollers, trucks, tractors, dump wagons, ditching machines, self-feeding loaders, belt conveyors, concrete mixers, concrete carts or tractors, wood or metal forms for curb and gutter, templates for street grades, tar kettle and pots, tool boxes, etc. These items should be estimated on the basis of total transportation costs both ways and a rental charge for plant and equipment. The total should be divided by the number of sq. yds. of pavement in the job, as it is customary to submit bids on paving at a certain price per sq. yd. including profit.

Hauling Sand, Gravel, Crushed Stone, Etc.-The cost of hauling paving materials will vary with the length of haul from pit or cars to point of delivery, Tables of hauling time for both teams and trucks are given on pages 55 to 59.

Hauling Cement, Paving Brick and Wood Blocks.-The cost of unloading and hauling any of these materials will vary with the method of unloading, length of haul, etc. 

Ordinary paving brick are 21″x4″x8″ in size, weigh 7 lbs. each, and the average load for horse drawn wagons is 700 to 750 brick over unpaved streets or roads or 900 to 1,000 brick over paved streets and roads. A truck will carry from 300 to 

1,500 brick, according to capacity. 

Brick paving blocks 34"x4"x81″ or 3″x4″x9″ weigh 10 lbs. each and a horse drawn wagon will carry about 500 blocks per load over unpaved streets or roads and 600 blocks over paved roads. 

A truck will carry from 200 to 1,000 blocks, according to capacity. 

Creosoted wood paving blocks, 31"x4"x8", weigh only about one-third as much as brick, so that a horse drawn wagon should carry 800 to 1,000 blocks per load over paved streets or roads, while a truck should carry from 2,000 to 10,000 lbs. depending upon capacity of truck.

When hauling cement over unpaved streets or roads, a horse drawn wagon should haul 4,000 to 6,000 lbs. (40 to 65 bags)

per load, although the ordinary load is 40 bags. Over paved streets, the average horse drawn load will run from 6,000 to 

7,500 lbs. (65 to 80 bags).

A truck will carry all the way from 2,000 to 10,000 lbs. depending upon capacity.

The most practical method of loading wagons is to have either 2 or 3 wagons, so the men at the car will have a wagon to load at all times and the men at the other end of the line will have a wagon to unload. In this way a team will either be hauling a loaded wagon or returning with an empty wagon. 

If the team is kept waiting at the car or job while the wagon or truck is being loaded and unloaded, it requires much more time per load and it will not be possible to make as many loads per day.

Concrete Curb and Gutter 

When estimating the cost of forms for concrete curb or curb and gutter, the size and shape must be considered, amount of materials required, etc.

Combined curb and gutter is usually 12" high at the outside edge (including pavement thickness), 24" to 30" wide and 6" to 71" thick.

Integral curb is formed as a part of the concrete pavement and is usually 6"x6"x7" in size, as shown in the illustration. 

Separate concrete curb is usually 6" wide at the top, 8" to 

9″ wide at the bottom, and 24″, 30″ or 36″ high.

.061 Concrete Roads and Pavements 

Concrete roads and pavements are usually thicker in the center than at the sides, so it will be necessary to obtain the average thickness of the pavement when estimating quantities of concrete materials. 

To obtain the average thickness of a pavement, take twice the center thickness, plus the side thickness divided by 3 equals the average thickness. Example: Pavement 8" thick in center and 6" thick at sides. 8+8+6=22÷3=7.33" average thickness.

Mixing and Placing Concrete Base Course. The labor cost of mixing and placing concrete base course will vary with the size of the mixer, the method used in feeding and discharging same, access to materials, length of haul, etc. 

Where a regular paving mixer is used having side loader that may be loaded by trucks or tractors and having an extension boom for discharging the concrete, minimum labor costs may be obtained, as it requires only a small gang of men to operate the mixer.

On the other hand if the mixer is fed by wheelbarrows and the concrete is wheeled from the mixer in horse drawn carts, the labor costs will run higher, so the method to be used should be known if accurate labor costs are to result.

The length of mixing time should also be considered because in the past few years it has been determined that the strength of concrete is dependent upon the amount of mixing water used and the length of time the concrete remains in the mixer. 

Many engineers specify the concrete must remain in the mixer 1 to 2 minutes, so when these conditions prevail, the output is restricted but the quality of the concrete is increased. 

If the concrete must remain in the mixer 1 minutes, a fair average for a job will be 30 batches of concrete an hour and the following costs are based on that assumption.

Using a mixer fed by hand with the concrete taken from the mixer in wheelbarrows or concrete carts, the labor per cu. yd. of concrete should cost as follows:

CONCRETE CHAPTER VIII MASONRY, PARTITION UNITS, TILE AND CONCRETE , CONCRETE JOISTS 

The term concrete masonry is applied to block, brick or tile building units molded from concrete and laid by masons into a wall, the same as brick or tile manufactured from shale or clay.

The concrete is made by mixing portland cement with water and other suitable materials, such as sand, pebbles, crushed stone, cinders, burned shale or clay. 

Concrete masonry units should always be manufactured in a cement products plant where facilities for manufacturing, curing, etc., are uniform so as to obtain high quality products, which is seldom, if ever, obtained under job conditions. 

The quality of all concrete masonry units should conform to the standards set by the American Concrete Institute in their standard specifications for concrete block, building tile and concrete prick.

Weight of Concrete Masonry.-Concrete masonry is manu factured in two weights of concrete, one weighing approximately 145 lbs per cu. ft. (sand, pebbles, crushed stone or slag aggregates) and the other weighing approximately 100 lbs. per cu. ft. made of burned clay or cinder aggregates. 

Estimating Quantities of Concrete Brick.-Concrete brick are manufactured in just one size, i.e., 21″x3"x8", weighing about 

5 lbs. each.

They should be estimated by the sq. ft. of wall of any thickness or by the cu. ft., if all wall thicknesses are combined. 

For instance, if there are only 8" walls in the job, it will be satisfactory to take the number of sq. ft. of walls but if the job contains 8", 12" and 16" walls, then it will be easier and more 441

satisfactory to reduce the quantities to cu. ft. and multiply by a certain number of brick per cu. ft. of wall. 

The number of concrete brick required per square or cubic foot of wall will vary with the size of the mortar joints used in laying them up. A brick 24"x8" on the face contains 18 sq. in. but the difference comes in the width of the mortar joints, whether "," or ".

Each brick is 3" thick, and with an allowance of " for mortar joint, each brick measures 41″ thick. An 8″ wall would be 2 brick thick; a 12". wall 3 brick thick, etc., adding one brick for each 4" of wall thickness. 

In drawing plans, some architects mark the walls 12" and others 13" thick. This makes no difference in estimating, so always figure your walls 4" thick or multiples thereof, as 4", 8", 12", 16", 20", etc.

When measuring the plans and listing the quantities of brick required, always take exact measurements and deduct all openings in full. Do not count corners twice but have your estimate show as accurately as possible the actual number of brick required to complete the job.

Mortar Required for Concrete Masonry.-Portland cement mortar should be used in laying up all concrete masonry units below grade, where exposed to severe moisture conditions or where supporting concentrated loads. For such construction the mortar is usually mixed in the proportions of 1 part portland cement to 3 parts sand, with 10 per cent of lime added. 

For ordinary construction above grade, the mortar should be mixed in the proportions of 1:1:6, i.e., 1 part portland cement, 1 part lime, and 6 parts sand.

Labor Handling and Laying Concrete Brick 

The labor cost of handling and laying concrete brick will vary with the class of work, thickness of the walls, number of openings, etc.

On buildings having long straight walls without many openings, such as basement walls, garages, factories, etc., a mason should lay 1,200 to 1,400 brick per 8-hr. day, while on dwellings and other structures having 8″ walls, cut up with numerous openings, pilasters, etc., a mason should lay 1,100 to 1,300 brick per 8-hr. day.

Concrete Blocks and Partition Units 

Concrete blocks and partition units are manufactured in two weights of concrete, one weighing approximately 145 lbs. per cu. ft. (sand, pebbles, crushed stone or slag aggregates) and another of fighter weight concrete weighing about 100 lbs. per cu. ft. of burned clay or cinder aggregates. 2 These two types of units may be used interchangeably for all purposes although the light weight units afford a saving of weight to secure economy in design; they afford increased heat and sound insulation and provide a satisfactory nailing base without the use of grounds.

Estimating the Quantity of Concrete Blocks and Partition 

Units.-Concrete blocks and partition units should be estimated by the square foot of wall of any thickness and then multiplied by the number of blocks per 100 sq. ft. as given in the following tables.

When estimating quantities, always take exact measurements and do not count corners twice.

Make deductions in full for all openings, regardless of size. 

The result will be the actual number of sq. ft. or number of blocks required for the job.

Mortar. The same kind of mortar should be used in laying up concrete blocks as given for concrete brick on page 443. 

Celite* in Mortar for Setting Concrete Blocks.-Used to make cement and lime mortar work better under the trowel, increases plasticity, and gives the mortar exceptional spread and "fatness." 

*Johns-Manville Sales Corporation, New York.

Mortar Joints.-Hollow concrete blocks or tile should be laid with broken joints to secure the maximum resistance to moisture and heat penetration. Sufficient mortar is spread on the inner and outer shell bed and end joints to cover and to provide a joint of the required thickness when pressed into place. Solid units, brick, etc., are laid in solid beds. 

Labor Laying Concrete Masonry 

The labor cost of laying the various types and sizes of concrete blocks and tile will vary with the size and weight of the blocks, the class of work, whether long straight walls or walls cut up with numerous openings, etc.

Cinder Concrete Building Units 

Cinder concrete building units are made from washed cinders and cement and are sold under various trade names, such as 

Cincrete, Straub Blocks, etc.

One hundred sq. ft. of 8" cinder concrete wall weighs 3,520 lbs. The blocks have a 2" web for mortar, enabling the mason to run the bed joint ahead of the course and then the blocks may be buttered on the ends and laid up rapidly to line, as shown in the accompanying illustration. 

Method of Running Bed Joints When Laying Concrete Blocks 

The data given on the previous pages under "Light Weight Concrete Units" is applicable to cinder concrete units. 

Plaster may be applied directly to the wall without furring or lathing. Cinder blocks are damp-proof because of the cellular structure of the unit as no condensation takes place and no water is drawn through the wall by capillary attraction. 

Haydite Concrete Blocks 

Haydite concrete building units are made from Haydite (burned shale or clay aggregate in accordance with the patent granted Stephen J. Hayde in 1918) and cement.

CONCRETE MASONRY 

453 Haydite makes one of the lightest concrete masonry units used for building purposes. An 8"x8"x16" Haydite block meeting standard specifications weighs 26 lbs. as against 45 to 50 lbs. for standard concrete blocks of the same size. Haydite blocks have the added advantage of nailability, increased heat and sound insulation and extremely low capillary absorption. 

Plaster may be applied directly to the wall without furring or lathing. 

Method of "Buttering" End Joints of Concrete Blocks 

The data given on the previous pages under "Light Weight Concrete Units" is applicable to Haydite concrete units. 

Manufacture of Concrete Masonry Units 

⚫ Concrete Masonry units are most efficiently and economically manufactured in a concrete products plant. Units thus produced are dependable due to the positive control over all factors entering into manufacture-design of mixtures, machine operation, curing facilities to produce maximum strength, and storage

periods. This control assures the purchaser of a full strength masonry unit of consistent high quality. 

It is recommended that the estimator select concrete masonry units produced by modern, well equipped plants, except where the size of the job or future markets justify the expense of the proper equipment to assure adequate control of quality. As high quality, dependable concrete masonry units, block, tile and brick, are widely manufactured, the estimator will find that he is usually close to the source of supply and that accurate costs are readily obtainable. This close proximity to the source of supply is especially desirable where a few extra units are required on short notice.

Concrete Block and Tile Manufacture. The quantity of material will vary with the size of the unit, whether solid or hollow, and if hollow, upon the size of the air spaces, as each manufacturer of block machinery has his individual molds requiring different quantities of materials. The majority of concrete block or tile are manufactured with a 35 per cent core or air space. If desired to estimate the number of block or tile produced from a cubic yard of concrete use the following table and for sizes not shown, figure the cubic content solid and subtract the percentage of core volume.

Labor Making Concrete Blocks.-As previously stated, con crete blocks are usually manufactured in a concrete products plant and the labor costs will vary with the size of the plant, equipment, etc., as modern machinery is essential for favorable costs.

The labor costs will be materially reduced where the blocks are manufactured in a well equipped cement products plant, as modern power machinery will turn out several blocks at a

time and the direct labor costs can be reduced accordinglybut to equip a plant of this kind will cost from $10,000 to $25,000, so unless the job is of considerable size the blocks should be bought direct from a cement products plant equipped for manufacturing in quantity.

Concrete Storage Bins and Silos 

Concrete storage bins and silos are used for storing grain, coal, sand, gravel, etc., in addition to those used for feed storage on the farm.

There are numerous types of silos, such as wood, concrete stave, monolithic concrete, cement block and glazed tile, and the

cost varies with the size, height, and kind of materials to be stored.

Practically all silos are round or circular shape as it gives more capacity for the least material and it packs better. 

Excavating for Silo Foundations

The size and depth of the necessary foundation will vary with the size and height of the silo but in all instances they should extend below the frost line, which is from 4'-0" to 5′-0″. 

The quantities of excavation a man will perform per day in the various kinds of soil are given under "Trench Excavation”.

Monolithic Concrete Silos 

The estimating data given below is applicable to and based on the circular type storage silo.

The labor schedule includes the time required for all construction operations, including setting, raising and removing forms, mixing and placing concrete, but does not include any time for placing reinforcing steel. This has been omitted, as the type of storage contemplated greatly varies the amount of reinforcing required and the time of placing. The estimator may use the same unit cost per ton as given for placing reinforcing steel in the average wall construction. 

Forms for Monolithic Concrete Silos.-Circular forms for monolithic concrete silos are made either of wood or metal, in sections 3'-0" to 6'-0" high that can be raised as the height of the wall progresses.

An ordinary gang consists of 3 to 4 men who erect forms, mix and place concrete, raise the forms, etc., until the silo is completed, and the costs are given on that basis. 

Metal Forms are furnished in sections for each inside and outside wall diameter and may be used a large number of times but a set is required for each diameter.

Wood forms should be made in the shop and the job labor consists of setting, raising and removing only.
