Concrete Stave Silos 

Concrete stave silos are built-up of cast concrete staves 10" wide, 30" long and 21" to 3" thick. Every other stave in the top and bottom circles are half height staves, each circle adding 

2'-6" to the height of the silo.

The quantity of staves required per silo may be based on the number of staves per circle with the height of the silo governing the number of circles. 

Labor Setting Staves.-The setting of 500 10"x30" staves may be considered a fair day's work under average conditions for a 4-man crew, consisting of two men on the ground, one setting staves, and a foreman to follow-up, leveling staves and inspecting the tension of hoops. This includes the raising of the necessary scaffolding, placing and tightening hoops, etc.

Number of Staves Required Per Circle for Concrete Stave Silos 

The number of staves are for complete circles with no allowance made for door frames. Deduct 3 staves when figuring doors.

Concrete Block Silos 

On account of the popularity of concrete stave and monolithic concrete silos, concrete block silos are not used to any great extent. The blocks are 8"x8"x16" on the face and require 110 blocks per 100 sq. ft. of wall. 

The blocks should be manufactured with a groove in the top, providing for a steel rod to run around the complete circle every first, second or third course, to hold the wall together. 

The blocks may be made of ordinary cement concrete or light weight concrete of cinder or burned shale aggregates.

Size and Weight of Units. For manholes or catch basins having 48″ inside diameter, 10 units are usually required for

each course; for 42" 9 units; 36" 8 units, and 30" require 7 units. However, one popular type of block requires 12 units per course in 48″ structures and 9 units in 36″. A block 73″ high and 6" thick weighs approximately 50 lbs. and a block 53" high and 6" thick weighs approximately 35 lbs.

Method of Construction.—The concrete base is placed and then the first course of blocks is embedded at least 3" in the plastic concrete, leveling the units at once, as this construction insures a watertight joint at the base.

PRECAST CONCRETE JOIST FLOORS 

Within the past few years precast concrete joist floors have been extensively used in schools, residences, apartment buildings and other structures requiring light floor loads. 

The concrete joists are manufactured in a cement products plant and delivered to the job ready to set in place. The joists for each floor of a building should be laid out separately, showing size of joists, spacing, etc., which varies from 20 to 32 inches, depending upon depth of joists, span, floor load, etc.

To develop maximum strength, a reinforced concrete slab 2 or 2 inches thick is placed over the tops of the joists with the 

Setting Precast Concrete Joists on the Wall joists imbedded into the concrete slab to a depth of to -inch. 

Effective bond shall be obtained between the joists and slab. 

Concrete for both joists and slab shall have an average compressive strength of not less than 3,000 lbs. per sq. in. at age of 

28 days, which is the equivalent of 1:2:31 or 1:2:4 concrete. 

Concrete joists are manufactured 8, 10 and 12 inches deep and various strength requirements of each size may be obtained by increasing the amount of reinforcing steel. For instance, 8-inch concrete joists are manufactured using ", " or " round rein-

forcing bars at the bottom of the joists and §″ round reinforcing bars at the top, with 1″ round steel stirrups spaced according to the load requirements of the particular job. The strength of 10 and 12-inch joists is determined in the same manner.

Method of Constructing Precast Concrete Joist Floors 

The formwork usually consists of short pieces of 1x6 or 2x6inch wood "spreaders" as shown in the illustration, cut to bear on the bottom flange of the concrete joists. These "spreaders" are placed between the concrete joists and wood floor boards, 1x4, 1x6 or 1x8-inch boards are placed on top of the "spreaders" to receive the concrete. The joists are usually spaced so that full width boards can be used without cutting. 

The forms may often be rented but in any event all of the lumber used for floor boards can be used again in the building

for sub-flooring, sidewall or roof sheathing, so that actually the only lumber cost is for the "spreaders." 

On forms of this kind, it will require about 11 feet of lumber b. m. per sq. ft. of floor area.

When placing forms for precast concrete joist floors, a carpenter should place forms for 375 to 425 sq. ft. of floor per 8-hr. day, at the following cost per 100 sq. ft.:

Placing Concrete for Precast Concrete Joist Floors. --The labor cost of placing concrete for thin concrete floors 2 to 2 in. thick runs considerably higher than the cost of placing foundation concrete or concrete for heavier floors on account of the extra labor required to spread and grade so many sq. ft. of floor to place one cu. yd. of concrete. 

One cu. yd. of concrete covers 162 sq. ft. of 2-in. floor or 129 sq. ft. of 2-in. floor.

1:2:4 to develop a compressive strength of 3,000 lbs. per sq. in. at age of 28 days.

Wood Screeds For Use With Precast Concrete Joist Floors.- 

Where wood floors are used with precast concrete joist floors, it will be necessary to place 2x2 or 2x3-in. wood strips or "screeds" in the concrete for nailing the wood floors. These strips should be spaced about 16 in. on centers and should rest on top of the steel stirrups that project above the concrete joist. 

The screeds are secured to the joists by wiring around the screed and through the top of the steel stirrups. Care must be taken when placing the concrete to see that the strips are level to receive the finish wood floors. 

The floor strips should be beveled or nails driven into the sides at short intervals to provide anchorage into the concrete, otherwise after the concrete hardens and the wood strips dry out and shrink they become loose and cause squeaking floors. 

Where wood strips are placed over the tops of the joists without leveling, a carpenter should place 400 to 500 lin. ft. per

CHAPTER IX INTEGRAL AND MEMBRANOUS WATERPROOF- ING, DAMPPROOFING PAINTS, PLASTER BONDS AND CEMENT FLOOR HARDENERS 

Nearly every building requires water and dampproofing, plaster bonds or floor hardeners of one kind or another, and with the great number of preparations on the market, it is impossible for the best informed contractor or estimator to familiarize himself with even a small proportion of them. 

No attempt has been made here to pass on the relative merits of the various preparations, but this data deals strictly with information that is of interest to the estimator, namely,—use of the material, covering capacity, and cost of applying same. 

The prices quoted will not apply to all localities, but are basic prices quoted by the various manufacturers, and will be close enough for average use.

Methods of Water and Damp-Proofing.-There are several methods used by the different manufacturers for mixing and applying their products to produce a waterproof wall or surface. 

In some instances, the waterproofing compounds are incorporated with the cement, sand, and gravel while the concrete is being mixed, and by filling the voids in the cement and sand produce a water proof mixture. Where the various powders or pastes are mixed in the concrete mass it is called the Integral method of waterproofing.

Some water and dampproofing preparations are furnished in mastic form, and are applied with a trowel. Others are mixed with portland cement and sand and applied as a plaster coat to the surfaces to be waterproofed.

There are also numerous water and dampproofing compounds in the form of heavy paints, which are applied to the concrete or masonry walls, floors, and ceilings with a brush or mop. 

One or more applications of these materials are supposed to penetrate and fill the pores in the concrete or masonry surfaces to such an extent that the treated surfaces will be impervious to dampness or moisture. 

Where there is considerable pressure or a heavy head of water, 484

one of the most satisfactory methods is known as Membranous waterproofing. This method consists of applying several coats of hot asphalt or other preparation with a stiff brush or mop, in conjunction with a prepared felt or treated burlap. Waterproofing of this kind is applied in much the same manner as a built-up roof. It usually requires two, three, four or more thicknesses of felt or burlap, held in place by as many applications of hot composition. After the last ply of felt or burlap is applied, the entire surface is mopped with a heavy application of hot compound.

Estimating Quantities of Water and Damp-Proofing. When estimating quantities of the various plaster coats, paints and membranous waterproofing compounds required for any job, the entire area of the walls or surfaces to be treated should be measured and the quantities stated in sq. ft., sq. yds. or by the square (100 sq. ft.).

Integral waterproofing is usually estimated by the cu. ft. or cu. yd. of concrete to which the waterproofing liquid, paste or powder is added.

Water Required for Mixing Concrete.-When mixing concrete sufficient water should be used to produce a plastic mix-no more and no less. A plastic concrete can be readily molded, but which, when the mold is removed, flows sluggishly and without segregation of the water or the fine materials from the coarse. 

Concrete should be mixed at least 2 minutes in a mechanical mixer after all materials have been dumped from the skip into the mixer.

Remember there is nothing more injurious to good concrete than too much mixing water.

Refer to water required for mixing concrete as given under the "Water-Cement Ratio Method of Mixing Concrete," pages 

170 to 180.

Waterproofing by the Integral Method 

When using the integral method, the waterproofing compounds are usually mixed with the cement, sand or gravel and form a part of the concrete mass. The quantities are based on the specifications of the various manufacturers. 

Material prices given are approximate, as it is impossible to quote prices that will apply to every locality. Wherever possible the contractor or estimator should obtain local prices on the materials specified.

Liquid Waterproofing 

Liquid waterproofing consists of (1) calcium chloride solutions, (2) oil waterproofings and (3) other integral mixtures which flow freely from a drum. 

The cost of hauling the barrel to the mixer, setting it up on blocks and drawing off the liquid by spigot into a measuring container will cost from 2 to 3 cts. per gallon of waterproofing. 

The cost of integral waterproofing liquids varies from 35 cts. per gal. for accelerators to $1.25 per gal. for the integral waterproofings. They are generally used on the basis of 1-gal. of waterproofing liquid to each barrel of portland cement, with the exception of oil waterproofing which is used in the proportions of 2 gals. of waterproofing to each barrel of cement. This is true for practically all manufacturers for the use of this material in either concrete or mortars. Oil waterproofings cost about $1.25 per gal, and use 2 gals. per bbl. of cement. Using 

1:2:4 concrete which requires about 6 bags of cement per cu. yd. the cost of oil waterproofing will run about $3.75 per cu. yd. of concrete.

Integral Liquid Waterproofing 

Prices given are approximate, as it is impossible to quote prices that will apply to every locality. One gallon lots will cost considerably more than barrel lots. On large jobs it is recommended that quotations be obtained from the manufacturer for each particular job.

Water and Damp-Proof Plaster Coats 

There are numerous preparations on the market to be mixed with portland cement and sand and applied as a plaster coat for waterproofing concrete and masonry walls. There are other preparations in mastic form that are applied with a trowel the same as ordinary cement mortar. 

The materials described on the following pages include many of the better known preparations used for this purpose. 

Quantity of Water Required in Mixing Portland Cement 

Mortar. As many waterproofing preparations are added in proportion to the amount of mixing water used, some definite basis for computing the amount of water required per cu. yd. of mortar must be established. This will vary with the condition of the sand (whether wet or dry) and the consistency to which the mortar is mixed. 

A cu. yd. of cement mortar requires more water than a cu. yd. of concrete. It requires about twice as much sand and two to three times as much cement as mass concrete; and obviously, it is the cement and sand that require the water. 

Neat cement will absorb 20 to 22 per cent of water by weight to produce a normal consistency. A quick setting cement requires more water than a slow setting cement, on account of having a larger amount of lime in its composition. 

The more sand used in proportion to the amount of cement, the less water will be required in the mortar.

Cleaning and Washing Old Masonry or Concrete Surfaces.— 

Where old masonry or concrete surfaces are to be given a waterproof plaster coat, it will first be necessary to prepare the old surface to receive the cement plaster. 

On some jobs it will be necessary to rake out the old brick joints to form a key for the plaster and on others it will be necessary to thoroughly brush the old surface to remove all surface dirt and then wash the surface with clean water or a solution of muriatic acid and water mixed in the proportion of 1 part acid to 10 parts water.

Where the surfaces are to be brushed and washed with water or acid and water, the cost of cleaning 100 sq. ft. of surface should average as follows:

Labor Applying Waterproof Plaster Coats.-The labor cost of applying waterproof plaster coats to exterior masonry or concrete walls will run somewhat higher than plastering above grade, on account of the crowded quarters in which the men are often obliged to work. 

In the larger cities this work is usually performed by cement finishers or plasterers but in the smaller cities and towns without union labor restrictions the work can be performed by common laborers.

When applying waterproof plaster coats it is not necessary to give the surface a float or brush finish, but it must be reasonably smooth and without uneven projections that would prevent the water from running down the sides of the walls. 

Most manufacturers specify the mortar to be mixed in the proportions of 1:1 or 1:2, and the material is usually applied in one or two coats by a cement finisher or plasterer. 

A man should apply 500 to 550 sq. ft. of first coat per 8-hr. day, at the following labor cost per 100 sq. ft.:

Membranous Waterproofing 

Membranous waterproofing consists of several thicknesses of waterproof felt or fabric applied with asphalt or other compound. The asphalt or compound is first mopped over the surface and then a layer of felt or fabric is applied between each subsequent mopping. The number of thicknesses required will depend upon the water pressure. 

There are several patented methods of membranous waterproofing on the market which are applied according to manu facturers' directions. 

Estimating the Quantity of Felt or Fabric Required for Membranous Waterproofing.-When estimating the quantity of felt or fabric required for waterproofing masonry or concrete walls, pits, floors, etc., it will be necessary to add a certain percentage for lap and waste. If the felt is applied to walls, it will be necessary to allow about 6" to lap over the footings at the bottom, also a small allowance at the top of the walls above grade. This will average from 7 to 10 per cent of the total area to be waterproofed.

If the walls or floors are covered with a single thickness of felt or fabric, it will be necessary to lap each strip of felt 

4" to 6", depending upon the specifications. As most felts are put up in 36" rolls it will be necessary to add about 12 per cent for waste for a 4" lap, and 17 per cent for a 6" lap. 

If the lap is 4" wide and only a single thickness of felt is used, it will be necessary to add about 20 per cent to the actual area to allow for laps and the additional felt required at the top and bottom of the wall. On floors it is customary to run the felt or fabric up the sides of the walls from 4" to 6". 

If the lap is 6" and only a single thickness of felt is used, add about 25 per cent to the actual wall or floor area for laps, etc. 

When 2, 3, 4 or more plies of felt are used, it will not be necessary to allow for laps except at the ends of the wall or floor, as one thickness of felt overlaps the next without waste. 

However, extra material will be required at the tops and bottoms of the walls and where the paper runs up the sides of the walls from 4" to 6". On work of this kind, add about 10 per cent to the actual floor or wall area.

Weight of Asphalt Felt for Membranous Waterproofing.- 

Asphalt felt for waterproofing is furnished in 4 sq. rolls of 432 sq. ft. weighing 60 lbs. per roll of 14-lb. felt and 65 lbs. per roll of 15-lb. felt.

When specifying the grade or weight of felt to be used, it is customary to state that "felt shall weigh not less than 15 lbs. per square" or per 100 sq. ft. Inasmuch as felt is furnished in 

4 sq. rolls of 432 sq. ft. there are 32 sq. ft. per roll or 8 sq. ft. per 

100 sq. ft. allowed for laps.

Asphalt saturated membrane or saturated burlap is usually sold by the sq. yd.

The itemized estimates on the following pages are based on using waterproof felt weighing 15 lbs. per 100 sq. ft., or 65 lbs. to the roll of 432 sq. ft.

To obtain the number of lbs. of waterproof felt or fabric required to cover a given surface, multiply the number of squares by the weight per 100 sq. ft., and the result will be the total number of lbs. required for the job. 

Estimating the Quantity of Asphalt or Compound Required for Membranous Waterproofing.—The quantity of asphalt or compound required will vary according to the thoroughness with which the surface is mopped or coated and the number of moppings necessary. 

On concrete or masonry walls or floors, it is customary to figure 30 to 40 lbs. of asphalt or compound per 100 sq. ft. for each application but this will vary with the class of work. 

Many special coatings are sold under trade names. Some are furnished solid, making it necessary to heat and melt them before using, while others are furnished in the form of a heavy black paint that can be either mopped or brushed on cold. The

manufacturers usually specify how their materials shall be applied.

Engineers and architects usually specify the quantity of asphalt or compound to be used for each 100 sq. ft. of surface.

Applying Membranous Waterproofing.-Membranous water proofing consists of several applications of hot compound and prepared waterproof felt or fabric, and the labor operations are similar to applying a built-up roof. This work is considerably more expensive than roofing on account of the limited working space and the difficulty in making the felt stick to a vertical surface.

An asphalt primer should first be applied uniformly over the surface to be waterproofed and thoroughly brushed. When the primer has dried sufficiently (slightly tacky), the surface shall be mopped with hot asphalt compound. 

Imbed in hot asphalt or other special compound, two or more layers of asphalt saturated felt or fabric, lapping all sheets 19 in. over previous sheet, each layer to be imbedded in hot compound, so that in no place shall felt touch felt or fabric touch fabric.

Mop the entire surface with a finishing coat of hot asphalt or other compound.

Reinforce all angles at corners, walls, etc., by cementing with hot compound, two or more sheets of standard asphalt saturated felt or fabric cut to extend at least 6 in. each way from angles, to the underlying construction. 

A waterproof protection course (cement, brick, mortar or other suitable materials) shall be placed over the waterproofing for best results.

Larson Pre-Formed Waterproofing Units.-These units installed during construction, on new work, as a preventative measure of waterproofing, and take the place of spandrel beam waterproofing and dampproofing to the interior surface of walls. 

These units are made of a specially developed material which is extremely tough and resilient enough to withstand the preforming processes and the handling and setting without injury.

The standard units are about 18-in. high and 36-in. long and weigh about 2 lbs. so that application is extremely simple. Only 

5 shapes are required to meet any condition ordinarily encountered.

The cost of Larson units is about 15 cts. per sq. ft. of wall area covered.

The Iron Method of Waterproofing 

The iron method of waterproofing uses an exceedingly fine metallic powder, containing no grease, asphalt, oil or other substances subject to disintegration.

The waterproofing is applied to the inside or outside surfaces of walls after all forms are removed, and to the tops of rough footings and floor slabs, in the form of brush coats or in combination of brush and plaster coats.

Applied either upon the inside or outside of walls, this type of waterproofing will resist any hydrostatic pressure which the wall is capable of withstanding. 

It usually requires 2 to 6 coats of iron waterproofing, depending upon the density of the concrete and the conditions encountered.

Some of these materials are mixed with sand and water and applied as a brush coat while others are furnished already mixed ready to apply by the addition of water.

Damp-Proof Paints for Exterior Concrete or Masonry Surfaces 

Where a heavy head of water is to be overcome, the concrete or masonry should be waterproofed by the integral method, membranous method, iron method, or by the use of waterproofed plaster coats. Where only a damp-proofing material is required, there are a number of paints on the market for this purpose. 

The application of one, two or more coats of paint to the exposed surface is intended to make the walls impervious to dampness.

Labor Applying Water and Damp-Proofing Paint to Exterior 

Surfaces Below Grade. Where the water or damp-proofing consists of applying one or more coats of heavy black paint to exterior concrete or masonry surfaces below grade, it is customary to use an ordinary roofers' brush or a mop. On foundation walls below grade, the men are usually obliged to work in cramped quarters which reduces output. 

To make these paints effective, they must be thoroughly brushed into the surface and all voids and pin holes filled, otherwise water and moisture will seep through. 

On work of this kind, a man should apply 650 to 750 sq. ft. per 8-hr. day, at the following labor cost per 100 sq. ft.: Labor

Back-Plastering and Back-Painting Cut Stone and Marble to Prevent Staining 

When marble, limestone, brownstone or sandstone are used in building work, considerable difficulty is encountered in preventing the moisture in the brick or concrete backing from penetrating the surface of the stone or marble and staining or discoloring the face. This is due to the open grain or porous nature of the stone or marble. 

To overcome this condition it is customary to paint the back of the stone, beds and end joints up to within 1" of the face to prevent staining and discoloration. White or non-staining

cement is also used for this purpose. The stone is set in nonstaining cement mortar and the back of the stone is plastered with the same mortar.

In many instances the backs, beds, and joints of the stone are painted and then back-plastered with non-staining cement which acts as a double preventative. 

Estimating the Cost of Back-Painting Cut Stone and Marble. 

-Inasmuch as it is customary to estimate the cost of cut stone by the cu. ft. the cost of back-painting should be estimated in the same manner.

Plain stone ashlar is usually 4" to 8" thick or in alternating courses of 4" and 8" stone so as to provide a bond with the brick or masonry backing. Where just a veneer of cut stone is required, the stone is usually 4" thick and is bonded into the masonry backing by metal anchors.

If cut stone is furnished in alternating courses of 4" and 8", the stone for the entire job will average 6" thick. It will therefore be necessary to back-paint 2 sq. ft. of surface to each cu. ft. of stone. Including beds and joints, it will double the above quantities or it will be necessary to back-paint 4 sq. ft. of surface to one cu. ft. of stone. 

If the stone averages 4" thick, it will be necessary to backpaint about 5 sq. ft. of surface to each cu. ft. of stone, including the backs, beds, and joints. 

If the stone averages 8″ thick, it will be necessary to backpaint about 4 sq. ft. of surface to each cu. ft. of stone. 

Back-Painting Cut Stone and Marble.-When back-painting limestone, sandstone, marble, etc., the stone is often painted in the yard before delivery, although on many jobs it is painted after delivery. It is customary to paint the stone a few days before setting, although the backs are frequently painted after the stone has been set. 

Care must be exercised to thoroughly brush the paint into all the pores and not drop any paint on the face of the stone. 

When painted at the building site, a man should paint 600 to 700 sq. ft. of surface per 8-hr. day, at the following labor cost per 100 sq ft.:

Cement Floor Hardeners

There are many preparations on the market for waterproofing, dustproofing and wearproofing cement finished floors by hardening the surface. These preparations consist of chemicals in liquid or powder form that are either mixed with the dry cement before the sand and water are added or metallic powder that is applied as a dust coat.

Liquid hardeners consist of liquid chemicals applied to the floor and swept or brushed into the surface. The action of the chemicals on the cement is supposed to harden and densify the floors, making them both dustproof and waterproof. 

Metallic Floor Hardeners

Metallic floor hardeners consist of pulverized iron ground to pass through a 20 mesh screen and retained on a 40 mesh screen and is dusted over the cement finish topping before it has taken its initial set and troweled to a smooth, even finish. It is mixed with the dry cement in the proportions of a certain amount of powder to each bag of cement. 

Mixing iron powder with the cement makes the floor much harder, as it fills the voids between the sand and cement and makes a dense mortar that both waterproofs and hardens the floor. Floors treated in this manner will not wear down nor dust as quickly as where plain cement and sand are used. 

Manufacturers, architects and engineers specify different methods and amounts to be used, which is usually a certain number of pounds of hardener mixed with an equal amount of cement and "dusted" over the floor surface before the finish topping has taken its initial set. These quantities vary from 15 to 50 lbs. per 100 sq. ft. of floor, depending upon the traffic which the floor will have to withstand. 

It is not necessary to add anything to the labor costs of applying the regular cement finish top. It merely means that

CEMENT FLOOR HARDENERS 

511 the finisher dusts the floor with the metallic powder while it is still too wet to trowel. By adding this dust coat it is possible to trowel the floor sooner than it would be without it, as it absorbs a portion of the surface water. 

If the cement finish top is applied after the rough concrete base has set, it will be necessary to hack or roughen the surface and then thoroughly wash same with muriatic acid and water in the proportions of 1:5. The rough concrete base must be thoroughly soaked with water until it can absorb no more.

While the concrete base is still damp, apply a thin coat of grout mixed in the proportions of 1 part hardener, 1 part portland cement, 1 parts clean water. This should be applied with a brush, using a scouring motion and taking care to coat all the surface.

To clean the old surface, flush same and apply the grout coat, estimate as follows per 100 sq. ft.:

Ferricon Floor Hardener.-A super metallic floor hardener

CEMENT FLOOR HARDENERS

The Zilicon prevents the metallic parts of the hardener from sinking, instead it floats and carries the iron particles near the top, where hard metal surface is most needed to take the wear.

Portland cement per 100 sq. ft. of floor. 

Total requirements: 35 lbs. of Ironite per 100 sq. ft. of floor. Price 6 cts. per lb. 

Liquid Chemical Floor Hardeners

As concrete wears down it is ground into dust and a great deal of trouble has been encountered with cement finished floors where the wearing and grinding process has been in progress. 

This condition has had an especially detrimental effect in mills and factories where the dust from the floors has been carried into the bearings of machinery, motors, engines, etc., causing considerable damage and expense in the upkeep of the equipment.

To overcome this condition, there have been a number of chemicals in liquid form placed on the market that create a chemical action in the cement and lime in the floors and cause a complete transformation of the lime so that it solidifies the entire concrete aggregate into a hard, flint-like, homogenous mass that prevents dusting and wearing of the floors. 

These liquid chemical compounds are swept over the floor until all of the pores in the surface are filled. It is usually necessary to treat the floors two or three times with the liquid to secure satisfactory results. When using any of these preparations, it is necessary to treat the floors with them at stated intervals, as the chemical action they create on the cement and lime is not permanent.

When using these liquid chemicals care must be exercised to see that the floor is absolutely clean and free from all grease, dust, dirt, oil, or other foreign matter.

The compounds are usually applied to the floor and spread with a long handled brush having stiff bristles. The floor should be thoroughly scrubbed and should be permitted to absorb as much of the liquid as possible, as it is by penetrating the surface of the floor that the chemical reaction takes place and hardens and densifies the surface. 

Different manufacturers specify varying numbers of applications of their materials but all of them must be applied just as often as the floor shows signs of dusting.

Bonding Old and New Concrete 

The problem of bonding new concrete to old so that the new concrete will remain permanently in place, is one that has received considerable attention among users of concrete. Unless the utmost care is exercised in preparing the old surface, the new concrete will invariably come loose where it is joined to the old concrete.

Different methods have been used to overcome this fault, but the basic condition of all of them is that the old surface must be thoroughly cleaned and washed, and the old aggregate must be exposed, which means that the thin film of cement that covers the surface of the concrete must be removed. One of the methods of preparing the old surface consists of hacking or picking it, and then washing or turning a steam hose under pressure to remove all dust and dirt from the old floor so as to present a perfectly clean surface. 

Another method is to wash the concrete surface with a solution of muriatic acid and water to remove the old film of cement and then thoroughly wash the surface with clear water. 

After this has been done, the old concrete surface should be given a slush coat of neat portland cement and water, and the new concrete applied.

Adensite Bonding Coat.-Rough the old concrete slab with a pick and chisel and thoroughly clean it of all loose particles as

previously described. The surface should then be given a coat of Adensite grout mixed in the proportion of 1 gal. Adensite and 

3 parts water, with sufficient portland cement (to -bag) added to give the mixture a creamy consistency.

Repairing Leaks Against Hydrostatic Pressure 

When repairing leaks in basement walls or floors, tunnels, pits, etc., where water pressure exists, the following methods and materials may be used.

Sika Waterproofing Compound.-Leakages occurring at iso lated spots only can be stopped by the application of a mortar consisting of neat portland cement and neat Sika No. 4A, having the consistency of a putty. It is necessary that the area to be treated is first properly hacked, cleaned and wetted. Cracks in the masonry and the joint between floor and wall should be cut back "V" shaped about 14" deep, and then filled flush with the above described mortar. The leaking joints in brick masonry should be raked out to about twice their width and also filled with this Sika No. 4A mortar. One gallon of Sika No. 4A used with neat Portland cement will stop infiltrations on a honeycomb area of about 40 square feet. Sika No. 4A costs about $6.00 a gallon.

If whole areas call for waterproofing, same should also be thoroughly hacked, and infiltrations stopped as previously described. The area is then covered with a key coat consisting of one part portland cement, one part of sand, activated by Sika No. 4A, diluted with 10 parts of water. This procedure is fol-

lowed by the application of an intermediate and final coat of one part portland cement, two parts of sand, activated by Sika No. 1, diluted with 12 parts of water, finished off with a steel trowel.

A gallon of Sika No. 4 used in the above described key coat, applied thick, will cover 400 sq. ft. A gallon of Sika No. 1, diluted 1:12, used in the above described 1:2 mortar, applied 1" thick, will cover 100 sq. ft. Sika No. 1 costs about $1.70 a gallon and Sika No. 4, $5.00 a gallon.

The first and intermediate coats are not scratched by wire, but a bond is secured by throwing a mortar of the same mixture, but a little thinner consistency, against same. This bond is applied in order to avoid the destroying of the fresh waterproof film. 

If strong infiltration exists, the insertion of bleeder pipes is advisable. The concentration of the water to these bleeders is accomplished by the use of the previously describd Sika No. 4A mortar. The bleeders can be removed about 24 hours later, and the bleeder holes plugged with a mortar consisting of neat Sika No. 2 and neat portland cement, which sets in seven or eight seconds. The latter procedure, however, is not usually called for in average waterproofing, as it is only used where very strong infiltration exists. A gallon of Sika No. 2 would be sufficient to plug between 20 and 70 bleeder holes, depending upon the strength of the infiltration. Sika No. 2 costs about $7.00 a gallon.

Sika waterproofing on top of concrete floors is usually laid in one operation, 1″ thick and should consist of a 1:2 cement mortar, activated by Sika No. 1, diluted with 12 parts of water. It is essential to see that floors are laid on a structurally sound base, which must be strong enough to withstand the existing pressure. The infiltrations on such floors are taken care of, as stated for walls. Care should be taken that the joint between floor and wall is well filled, and the waterproofing carried around continuously. 

Regarding elevator pits, it is most essential to see that the waterproofing is carried continuously behind the bumper-channel guard rails, bolts and other attachments which penetrate the waterproofing coat, so that every attachment is put into a little waterproof "pit." 

Stonhard Stontite.-A material for sealing leaks in walls and masonry or correcting dampness on basement walls. Stontite

CONCRETE ADMIXTURES 

523 makes it possible to waterproof a wall on the free or open side without removing the hydrostatic pressure from the reverse side. 

It is used in maintainance work in subways, reservoirs, sea walls, basement walls, elevator pits, dam breasts, tunnels, manholes, tanks, etc.

When mixed with neat portland cement and applied "thick, 1 gal. will cover approximately 12 sq. ft.

Concrete Admixtures 

Concrete admixtures are added to the concrete mix to improve the plasticity, workability and finish of the concrete, to prevent segregation of the aggregate and to a certain degree provides integral waterproofing qualities by filling the small voids in the concrete mixture. 

In manufacturing concrete of any type, it is necessary to form a paste of water and cement sufficient in volume to fill the voids and uniformly coat the particles of aggregate. Due to the difference in specific gravity of the components of concrete, it is necessary to provide a water-cement paste of sufficient viscosity to prevent segregation of the concrete particles. It is the function of these admixtures to supply not only sufficient body to the water-cement paste to prevent segregation, but also to uniformly distribute the cement and coat the aggregate. Their purpose, therefore, is to preserve desirable uniformity of the concrete mix, considerably improving the strength, finish and waterproof qualities. The improved workability imparted to the concrete mix by the addition of these admixtures will alone often justify their use. Other advantages include lowered labor costs, less form leakage and the elimination of honeycombing and patching. 

Aquagel.-Aquagel is a hydrous silicate of alumina of volcanic origin and its chemical analysis shows it to be composed of the ordinary constituents of portland cement, except lime. Physically, it is extremely active and it will form with twenty-five times its weight of water a jelly-like mass and possessing strong lubricating values.

The rendering of concrete more impermeable is affected by the mix, the aggregate, water-cement ratio, job conditions, methods

and care used in placing, etc., and that Aquagel has a certain relation to all of these factors. 

Segregation and workability values are best obtained when 1 to 2 lbs. of Aquagel is used to each bag of cement, while the best waterproofing values occur when 3 to 4 lbs. of Aquagel is used to each bag of cement. 

Aquagel costs from 2 to 2 cts. per lb. according to quantity and locality and when used in ready-mixed concrete, it adds 15 to 50 cts. per cu. yd. 

Celite.* A light weight mineral powder (diatomaceous silica) used in portland cement and concrete for increasing workability of the mix and for improving uniformity, strength, water-tightness and appearance of the final concrete. 

Extended use over a period of years has shown that Celite is a positive mechanical means of insuring better concrete under average field conditions. Being practically pure silica (SiO2) it is the most permanent element in concrete and does not affect the setting time.

Waterproofing Mortar 

Many waterproofing compounds and admixtures are used in mortar for brick, stone and tile work to waterproof the mortar; prevent shrinkage and leakage in the mortar joints and make a smoother mortar that will work better under the trowel. 

These preparations are added with the mixing water or cement and lime and are incorporated in the mix. 

Adensite. The mortar shall be composed of 1 part portland cement and 3 parts clean sand, tempered with a liquid composed of 1 part Adensite to 12 parts water.

Emulsified Asphalt 

Emulsified asphalt may be used as a floor surfacer, a bonding coat, or a quick-setting, hard-drying and durable patching material. It may be used with satisfactory results over either old or new floors. The following procedure is generally used. 

First, clean the old surface free from dirt, grease and foreign matter; second, cutting out the worn spots or cracks with perpendicular sides to avoid the formation of feather edges; third, a bonding coat of emulsified asphalt is applied, consisting of 1 part clean water to 4 parts of emulsified asphalt, dry overnight; fourth, the mixture of portland cement, sand, gravel and emulsified asphalt is applied and rolled.

When applied direct to a concrete surface, 1 gallon will cover about 75 sq. ft. one coat or 50 sq. ft. two coats. 

When used instead of water as a material for binding cement, sand and gravel the quantity will vary with the thickness applied and will require 4 to 5 gallons per bag of cement. 

Aquabar Emulsified Asphalt.-A pure, unadulterated asphalt scientifically emulsified so that it may be used cold without heating when mixed with aggregate for repairing cement floors, roads and by itself as a bonding and waterproof agent. 

One gallon covers approx. 75 sq. ft. 1 coat or 50 sq. ft. 2 coats. 

Price, $1.15 per gal. in drums; $1.20 per gal. in half drums; $1.30 per gal. in 5-gal. pails and $1.40 per gal. in 1-gal. cans. 

Elastex. This material has been developed to meet the requirements for an emulsified asphalt that may be used as a floor surfacer, a bonding coat or a durable patching material. 

Covering capacity, approx. 75 sq. ft. per gal. 1 coat or 50 sq. ft. 2 coats.

Price $1.25 per gal. in drums; $1.30 per gal. in half drums; $1.35 per gal. in 5-gal. drums and $1.60 per gal. in 1-gal cans.

CHAPTER X BRICK MASONRY 

To prepare an accurate estimate on the cost of brick masonry requires a knowledge of the various factors entering into the work. This includes the type of building, thickness of walls, kind of mortar, style of mortar joint, class of workmanship, ability of workmen, and last but not least, the ability of the foreman in charge.

Estimating brickwork is more than a matter of referring to a table or chart to obtain the prevailing wage scale and from that determine the labor cost of laying a thousand brick. If accuracy is important in the preparation of your estimates then all of the above items should be considered when determining the unit costs. If this were not so, any inexperienced person could become an expert estimator in a week's time. 

The type of building plays an important part in the costs because a mason can lay far more brick on a factory or warehouse building having long straight walls than on a school or office building, cut up with numerous windows, which require straight walls, plumb jambs, pilasters, etc.

A mason can lay far more brick on a 16" wall than on an 8″ wall and he can lay more brick in smooth working lime mortar than in coarse portland cement mortar. He can also lay more brick by merely cutting the mortar joints than by striking them with the point of his trowel.

The class of workmanship plays an important part. Many of the cheaper constructed speculative buildings have crooked walls, open mortar joints and present an all round slovenly appearance, while the best grade of workmanship requires full slushed mortar joints, straight walls, plumb jambs and corners, etc.,-in other words, good workmanship.

Weather conditions also affect labor costs. A mason can lay more brick on a clear, dry day than when it is cold and wet, 528

BRICK MASONRY 

529 or when it is necessary to heat materials during freezing weather. 

The demand for mechanics also affects their output. When there is an abundance of work, many (not all) mechanics take advantage of this condition and do just as little work as possible to hold their jobs. On the other hand, when work is scarce and there are two mechanics for every available job, they do a much better day's work when they know there is another man eagerly waiting to take his place. 

The ability of the foreman in charge of the work has much to do with the final costs; his ability to plan, schedule and lay out his work in addition to obtaining a full day's work from the men under his supervision are equally important. 

If accurate costs are to result, then all of these matters should be considered when making up your estimate.

COMMON BRICK 

When estimating the number of common brick required for any job, obtain the length, height and thickness of each wall, stating the totals in cu. ft. 

In present day estimating, all openings should be deducted in full, regardless of their size, as the estimate should show as accurately as possible the exact number of brick required for the job. The old method of counting corners twice, doubling the number of brick required for pilasters, chimney breasts, etc., is no longer used by progressive builders because they know they would never get a job using obsolete methods—and if they did get it, they would have no idea of the actual number of brick required to build it. Actual quantities and costs is the only sure method of getting your share of work at a profit. 

The thickness of brick walls increases by 4″ or 41″. A standard common brick is 8"x24"x3" in size, but will vary from "to" in length, depending upon the burning. The brick in the center of the kiln are usually more thoroughly burned than the ones on the outside, which accounts for the variation in size. 

Brick walls are usually designated on the plans as 4" or 41″; 

8" or 9"; 12" or 13"; 16" or 17", etc., increasing by 4" or 41" in width. This variation in thickness need not be considered by

TIMATOR'S 

the estimator because a wall marked 13" on the plans does not require any more brick than one marked 12", as both walls are 

3 brick thick. A 4" or 44" wall is 1 brick thick; an 8" or 9" wall is 2 brick thick; a 12" or 13" wall is 3 brick thick; a 16" or 17" wall is 4 brick thick, etc. The easiest method for the estimator is to mark all walls, 4", 8", 12", or 16" and then reduce the totals to cu. ft. After the number of cu. ft. has been obtained, multiply by the number of brick required per cu. ft. of wall and the result will be the number of brick required for the job.

When brickwork is estimated on the above basis, it is advisable to add 1 to 2 per cent to the total to take care of salmon brick, broken brick, bats, etc., and the waste should not exceed this amount unless very poor brick are used. 

In the "good old days" contractors figured their common brickwork on the basis of 7 or 7 brick per sq. ft. of 4" or 41" wall; 14 or 15 brick per sq. ft. of 8" or 9" wall; 21 or 22 brick per sq. ft. of 12" or 13" wall, etc.

This method is no longer used by progressive contractors because modern business practice, sometimes called "competition" demands that actual quantities be figured. Work is being estimated too closely to-day to permit a 10 to 20 per cent overrun on the brickwork, especially when many contractors are figuring on a 5 to 10 per cent margin of profit. 

After the number of cu. ft. of brickwork has been obtained it will be necessary to determine the number of brick required per cu. ft. of wall. This will vary with the size of the brick and the width of the mortar joints. The standard size adopted by the Common Brick Manufacturers Association is 8"x24"x31″, but not all manufacturers have changed their molds to this size. 

However, this is the most common size and the only one that can be used as a basis for figuring without knowing the exact size of the brick used in each locality. 

A standard brick is 8" long, 21" high and contains 18 sq. in. on the face. If laid dry without a mortar joint it would require 8 brick per sq. ft. of wall (144-18-8). How- 2400 ever, the thickness of the mortar to joint must be added, and this will 2 bied

General Description of Lime for Structural Purposes.-Quick lime for construction purposes is supplied in bulk or packaged in barrels, cartons or bags, at the option of the purchaser. The 

Federal Lime Barrel Act prescribes that barrels for packaging lime shall contain 180 lbs. net (200 lbs. gross) for the small barrel or 280 lbs. net (300 lbs. gross) for the large or export barrel. Lime sold in bulk or packaged in cartons or bags is generally quoted on the basis of a ton (2000 lbs. net) while barreled lime may be quoted on either a ton or barrel basis and the cost of cooperage is included in the price for lime. (Note: 

11 small barrels 180 lbs. net each (1980 lbs. net) or 7 large barrels 280 lbs. net each (1960 lbs. net) are usually considered as one ton.)

Quicklime may be secured in any of the following forms at the option of the purchaser: Lump lime, pebble lime, crushed lime, ground lime, granular lime or pulverized lime. The principal difference being in the size of the particles. All quicklime must be slaked prior to use and manufacturers directions for slaking should be followed to secure best results. During recent years there has been a definite trend toward the use of finely divided types of quicklime due to the greater ease with which complete slaking is secured. Slaked quicklime putty should be screened, run off and permitted to age until all the lime particles are completely slaked. The aging period may vary from a few hours to several days according to chemical and physical properties of the quicklime used and the skill of the operator in slaking the lime. 

*Quality Lime Institute, Philadelphia, Pa.

BRICK MASONRY 

533 Hydrated lime for structural use is furnished in the dry powdered form usually packaged in 50 lb. net paper bags and sold by the ton, (2000 lbs. net). It may be had in bulk where proper facilities are provided for handling and storage. Hydrated lime need not be slaked prior to use, but its plasticity or workability is enhanced by making it into a paste or putty form after which it is soaked for several hours. The preferred method for soaking is to sift the hydrated lime evenly into a watertight box or vat which has been previously half filled with clean water. Do not stir, mix, or agitate the mass, but allow the hydrated lime to settle naturally and continue to add hydrated lime slowly and evenly over the entire surface of the water until a thick paste is formed after which the mass is permitted to soak until required for use.

All lime should comply with the requirements of the Standard Specifications for Lime for Structural Purposes as promulgated and adopted by the American Society for Testing Materials. 

Storage of Lime and Lime Putty.—Prior to slaking, or use, all quicklime and hydrated lime previously delivered to the site of the work should be stored in a clean, dry place. 

Quicklime furnished in bulk, cartons or bags, should be slaked immediately after delivery to assure maximum yield and avoid loss. Quicklime in barrels may be stored in a dry properly ventilated warehouse, but it is not advisable to so store it in excess of 30 days.

Hydrated lime in bulk or packed in bags may be stored for relatively long period of time provided it is placed in clean, dry, properly ventilated warehouse.

Lime putty should be aged and stored in clean, tight vats and should be well protected from direct contact with the atmosphere by maintaining a thin film of water over the surface. 

Commercial plants for the production of scientifically prepared, well aged putty, are in operation in many markets. The use of commercially prepared lime putty eliminates all necessity for slaking and aging or soaking of lime on the job, and has the further advantage of providing the estimator with reliable figures for estimating purposes since purchase order is based on net quantity of lime putty required for the operation. Other advantages of commercially produced lime putty include flexibility during construction, eliminating lost time awaiting preparation of lime putty and admitting of expansion in operations

on short notice, reduction in storage space required for materials at the site of the work and improved quality of putty due to careful supervision during slaking and aging of lime putty. 

Lime Putty and Its Preparation.-Job specifications generally require mortar to be mixed in definite predetermined proportions by volume and the lime proportion is usually determined in volumes of lime putty, therefore, some knowledge of putty yield of lime is necessary in preparing estimates of quantity of lime required. The putty yield of different limes varies over a relatively wide range according to chemical and physical properties of the lime, methods of processing etc. However, the quantities given in the following table may be used as a sound, conservative average for estimating purposes.

On jobs using common brick only, a mortar maker should slack lime and make sufficient mortar to supply 7 to 9 masons, depending upon thickness of joints, width of walls, etc. 

On an average job consisting of 4" of face brick backed up with 8" to 12" of common brick, a good mortar maker should supply 10 masons without difficulty.

On face brick work alone, a mortar maker should supply 16 to 24 masons with mortar, depending upon the class of work and the width of the mortar joints. 

On jobs employing 10 or more masons, a considerable saving is made by using a mortar mixing machine, as it produces a more uniform mortar that is more easily spread. It not only enables a mason to lay more brick but also results in a saving of approximately 10 per cent in labor required mixing mortar and attending masons. 

Quik-Slak Masons Lime.-A lime furnished in pulverized form that slacks the instant it hits the water. Put up in 50 lb. paper bags and the manufacturers say that 4 bags are sufficient to lay 1,000 brick under average conditions. Price $15.00 per ton; 37 cts. a bag or $1.50 per bbl. of 4 bags. 

Bricklayers' Cement.-There are a number of special bricklayers' cements on the market, such as Brixment, Carney's, Kosmortar, Hy-Test, Medusa-Mix, Wifco, Utica, etc., that are used instead of lime or portland cement mortar.

When used without the addition of lime they work harder than a straight lime mortar but are "fatter" and consequently work easier under the trowel than pure portland cement mortar. 

The amount required per 1,000 brick is a variable and somewhat debatable quantity, as practically all manufacturers recommend a 1:3 mixture and state that 4 to 6 bags are required per 1,000 brick when laid with a " mortar joint. The author has letters from contractors where they state they used only 4 to 5 bags per 1,000 brick but we have never been so fortunate on our own work and the memory of the last job is still very vivid, and it required 9 bags per 1,000 brick. 

The quantities given below are those recommended by most manufacturers, and on that basis sufficient cement mortar to lay 1,000 brick (15 cu. ft.) with 1″ mortar joints should cost as follows:

Some manufacturers of masonry cement now specify that the mortar should be mixed in the proportion of 1:21 instead of 1:3.

In our experience, we have found that it requires closer to 18 cu. ft. of mortar per 1,000 brick than 15 cu. ft.

Labor Laying Common Brick 

There are so many factors entering into the labor cost of laying common brick that an explanation is necessary to use the following data intelligently.

There are no set quantities of brick that a mason will lay per hr. or per day, and with 10 men laying brick on the same wall and on exactly the same class of work, no two of them will lay exactly the same number of brick. For this reason averages must be taken. There are good mechanics and poor mechanicsthere are conscientious mechanics who desire to do a full day's work and there are unscrupulous ones who do only enough to "get-by". There are others who never "get-by" and are on one job only long enough for the foreman to see they are incompetent and off they go.

The class of work also has a great deal to do with the variation in labor costs, as it costs much more to lay brick in an 8" wall with struck joints than in a 16" wall having cut joints on one side of the wall and struck joints on the other. Also, it costs more to lay brick in portland cement mortar than in lime mortar because the lime mortar spreads far more easily than cement mortar.

It costs more to lay brick in cold, wet weather when the brick are slippery and the mason's hands cold than in fair weather with all conditions favorable.

It requires more labor to lay brick in the winter when the brick and mortar must be heated and salamanders placed along the floor or scaffold, requiring additional labor attending salamanders, removing ice, snow, etc., than in the summer when conditions are favorable.

It costs more to lay brick on a job having straight walls, plumb corners, and the brick laid in a good bed of mortar than on cheaply constructed speculative buildings having crooked walls and practically no mortar between courses-a "sloppy" job that will require repairs as soon as the building is finished. 

The quantities and costs given on the following pages are based on a good grade of workmanship applicable to the type of building on which it is to be used. The same class of workmanship has not been figured on the bungalow and apartment building that is required on a high grade school, university building, a U. S. Government Post Office or buildings of that

543 type, but neither has the cheapest grade of workmanship been figured. Judgment and common sense are necessary when applying any figures, otherwise anyone could be a "successful" 

estimator and contractor. 

The quantities given are based on the performances of experienced masons working regularly at their trade under present conditions—not conditions that existed during the boom times of a few years ago. Today's motto is "a full day's work for a full day's pay." They will not hold good in small communities where the mason does the cement work and plastering as well as the bricklaying and stone setting of the community. 

The costs are based on efficient management and supervision, the use of modern tools and appliances, machine mortar mixers, etc., on jobs large enough to warrant their use. On jobs of sufficient size to require a mason foreman, it will be necessary to add for this time on the basis of a certain price per 1,000 brick or at a certain price per week, based on the estimated duration of the job.

The Ideal Brick Wall 

The Ideal wall is the general name used to describe all types of hollow walls built with standard solid brick. There are three types of Ideal walls, as follows: Ideal Rolok-bak walls; 

Ideal all-rolok walls, and Ideal all-rolok walls in Flemish 

Bond. 

Only in the all-rolok types does the exterior appearance of the Ideal wall differ from the standard and traditional brickwork with which all are familiar. In the other type-the rolok-bak wall-the face of the wall may be worked out in any bond and joint to suit the builder's taste, and the complete wall has the same appearance as a wall of solid brickwork. 

The 8" Rolok-Bak Wall.-A general utility wall that may be used both for exposed and unexposed walls and basement construction. It forms a satisfactory base for stucco where that finish is desired and for plaster in interior walls. 

The exterior 4" is laid with brick placed flat in the usual manner and the backing is laid of brick on edge. The wall may be 8" thick or in multiples of additional 4" thicknesses.

This wall requires 7 exposed brick and 3 backing brick, a total of 10 brick per sq. ft. of 8" wall. 

In walls having the average number of openings and corners,

a mason should lay 600 exposed brick backed up with 300 backing brick, or a total of 900 brick per 8-hr. day. 

For rough work in side, rear and unexposed walls, a mason will lay 950 exposed brick backed up with 475 backing brick, or a total of 1,425 brick per 8-hr. day.

The 12" Standard Rolok-Bak Wall.-The six flat courses out side are first placed as for the 8" wall. The center and inside withes are then built together according to the ordinary practice in the backing of brickwork, each four courses high. The center withe is built close to the outside withe, which acts as a guide.

For rough work in side, rear and unexposed walls a mason should lay 715 exposed brick, backed up with 910 backing brick, or 1,625 brick per 8-hr. day.

The 12" Heavy-Duty Rolok-Bak Wall.-This wall is con-

BRICK MASONRY 

545 structed exactly like the 12" standard wall except the center and inside withes are built only 3 courses high. Next place the header course tying these two withes together. This is a continuous course of rolok headers. The brick in the header course need not have the vertical joints between them filled with mortar. As with the center withe, see that the bed joints are full and that the vertical joints are filled to a distance of about 

1" from the inside face of the wall. Then the flat header course is placed, consisting of a continuous header course on the outside face with a course of stretchers behind it. 

This wall requires 7 exposed brick and 8.8 backing brick, a total of 15.8 brick per sq. ft. of wall. Six courses of brick laid flat and four courses of brick on edge bring the wall level on top, ready for the header course.

In walls with the average number of openings and corners, a mason should lay 480 exposed brick backed up with 603 backing brick, a total of 1,083 brick per 8-hr. day.

For rough work in side, rear and unexposed walls, a mason should lay 650 exposed brick backed up with 817 backing brick, or a total of 1,467 brick per 8-hr. day.

The All-Rolok Wall 

The all-rolok wall may be employed for exposed and unexposed walls, both bearing and nonbearing, and for basement construction. The wall is built of two courses entirely of stretchers on edge, alternating with one course of flat headers. 

The 8" All-Rolok Wall.-This wall requires 9 brick per sq. ft. of which 6 brick are exposed in outside walls.

Method of Laying 12" Standard Rolok-Bak Brick Wall 

In walls with the average number of openings and corners, a mason should lay 1,000 brick per 8-hr. day, in front and other carefully faced walls, and 1,150 brick per 8-hr. day in rough work for side, rear and unexposed walls. 

The 12" All-Rolok Wall.-In the 12" wall, the 3 withes are constructed, each 3 courses high. The header course consists of pairs of headers laid flat, basket weave bond, with a stretcher placed alternately on the inside and the outside of the wall. 

This wall requires 13 brick per sq. ft. of wall, of which 6 are exposed and 7 used for backing up.

547 In walls with the average number of openings and corners, a mason should lay 1,080 brick in front and other carefully laid walls and 1,600 brick per 8-hr. day in rough work, such as rear, side and unexposed walls. 

The All-Rolok Wall in Flemish Bond.-This wall is primarily intended for exposed walls. It is very strong construction and is much used for basement work and for interior walls. 

It is constructed entirely of brick on edge laid in Flemish bond for the outside 8" thickness. For thicker walls a withe of stretchers on edge is added for each additional 4" thickness. 

Method of Laying 12" All-Rolok Brick Wall 

The 8" All-Rolok Wall in Flemish Bond.-This wall is built by laying headers and stretchers alternately, and backing up at every course. The headers of each course are placed over the center of the stretchers of the course below. The 8" thickness of wall must be laid "pick and dip" fashion and hence is slower to lay than the other types of Ideal wall. 

It requires 9 brick per sq. ft. of 8" wall. 

In walls with the average number of openings and corners, a mason should lay 650 brick per 8-hr. day. 

The 12" All-Rolok Wall in Flemish Bond.-In building the 12" wall the outside 8" thickness is built the same as the 8" wall, three courses high. One course is then placed on the outside

withe consisting of stretchers and bats alternately, the bats being used to preserve the bond. The inside withe is then built three courses high entirely of stretchers and a solid header course of brick on edge is then placed to tie the inside withe to the outside 8" thickness. 

This wall requires 13.75 brick per sq. ft. of wall, of which 6 brick are exposed and 7.75 used for backing up. do? 8519

Brickwork for Incinerators

Incinerators are used in residences, apartments, apartment hotels, hotels, hospitals, schools, industrial plants, etc., for burning garbage, waste papers, etc.

With many types the refuse may be fed into the chimney at each floor, the deposited material dropping to the incinerator in the basement, or they may be fed direct to the incinerator in the basement.

Practically all incinerators require a separate flue or stack, which should be estimated in the regular way, figuring fire brick, flue lining and common brick as shown on the plans. 

The number of fire and common brick required for the various sizes and types of incinerators will vary with the different manufacturers.

However, the following data will assist the estimator in computing the number of brick and labor hours required to construct the brickwork for the different size incinerators, where they are not detailed on the plans.

When preparing an estimate on the cost of face brick work many of the same factors influence the costs as described under "Common Brick."

The size of the brick and the width of the mortar joints must be known to accurately estimate the number of brick required per sq. ft. of wall and the quantity of mortar necessary to lay them. 

To estimate labor costs accurately, the style of bond

MA which the brick are to be laid should be known, whether Common, Dutch, English, Flemish, etc.; the kind of mortar joint, whether cut flush, struck, weathered, raked out or rodded, as there is a vast difference in the number of brick a mason will lay in the different bonds

. 

and mortar joints. Also, whether the brick are laid in lime or cement mortar in long, straight walls or walls cut up with numerous piers, pilasters, door and window openings, etc. 

Estimating the Quantity of Face Brick.-When estimating the number of face brick required for any job, obtain the length and height of all walls to be faced with press brick, and the total will be the number of sq. ft. of wall. 

Always make deductions in full for all openings, regardless of their size, as the estimate should show as accurately as possible the exact number of brick required to complete the job. 

When making deductions for door and window openings, always note the depth or width of the brick jambs or "reveals”.

If they are only 4″ deep, deduct the full size of the opening as the 4" end of the brick forms the "reveal" or jamb.. 

If the jamb is more than 4" wide, the full depth of the jamb or "reveal" should be deducted. Example: Deduct for a 5′-0″x 

7'-0" opening in a 12" brick wall where the face brick jamb or "reveal" returns the full thickness of the wall. It will be necessary to deduct for the 12″ jamb or "reveal" on each side of the opening, i.e., 2″x12″=24″ or 2′-0″. Deduct this from the width of the opening, i.e., 5′-0″-2′-0″-3'-0". The opening deducted should be 3′-0″x7′-0″ instead of 5′-0″x7′-0″, as shown on the plan. 

A standard face brick measures 8"x24"x3", but sometimes, due to special conditions in the clay or the kiln burn, the brick may vary slightly from the dimensions given. 

After the number of sq. ft. of wall has been obtained, it will be necessary to determine the number of brick required per sq. ft. This will vary with the size of the brick, width of mortar joint, style of bond in which the brick are laid, frequency of header courses, etc. 

A standard face brick is 8″ long, 24″ high and contains 18 sq. in. on the face. If laid dry it would require 8 brick per sq. ft. of wall. However, the thickness of the mortar joint must be added, and this will vary from " where "buttered" joints are used to 1" where extremely wide joints are used. The average mortar joint for face brick work is ".

BRICK MASONRY 

557 

A brick 8" long, plus " mortar joint, makes 8". A brick 21" high, plus 1″ mortar joint, makes a height of 2§″ for each brick course. On account of uneven burning of the brick, a course usually varies from 2" to 23" high. 81″x21″=22 sq. in. To obtain the number of brick required for one sq. ft. of wall, 144÷22=61 brick per sq. ft. of wall.

If the brick are laid in running bond without headers, the above quantities will prove sufficient but if there is a full course of headers every 5th, 6th or 7th course, it will be necessary to allow for the extra brick required. Also, if the brick are laid in 

English, Flemish, English Cross or Dutch Bond, it will be necessary to make an allowance for extra brick where full header courses are required.

Brick Bonds 

Bond in brickwork is the overlapping of one brick upon the other, either along the length of the wall or through its thick- *Add 10 to 15 per cent extra brick for waste in cutting.

BRICK MASONRY 

559 ness, in order to bind them together into a secure structural mass. Units are shifted back and forth so that the vertical joints in two successive layers or "courses" do not come into line; in other words, the brick are laid so as to break the joint, the whole forming a natural bond or a structural unit giving strength to the wall.

Running or Stretcher Bond. The wall surface is made up of stretcher courses having a header at the corners which appears as a stretcher on the return side. This bond is very strong longitudinally, but lacks transverse strength, consequently it is modified into what is called Common or American Bond.

Common or American Bond. This bond is obtained by laying a course of headers about every sixth course. To maintain the effect of the running bond, a special double header bond is sometimes used. This method of using headers as in Common or American Bond, in order to secure transverse strength of wall, can be treated in a way to produce more pleasing effects, as may be seen in Flemish or English Bonds.

English Bond.-English Bond is made up of alternating courses of stretchers and headers. Ordinarily half brick are used for the header courses, except every sixth course a full header course is used to tie the face and common brick walls together. Garden Wall Bond.-Garden Wall Bond is merely a modifica tion of Flemish Bond, secured by laying courses with two to four stretchers alternating with a header, and requires the same number of brick per square foot as Flemish Bond.

Labor Laying Face Brick 

The labor cost of laying face brick will vary with the grade of workmanship, style of bond in which the brick are laid, width and kind of mortar joint, type of building, whether long, straight walls or walls cut up with pilasters, door and window openings, etc., and last but not least, the ability of the foreman in charge-a good foreman will probably have competent masons and vice versa.

Costs are given on two classes of work, Ordinary and First 

Grade. 

Ordinary workmanship should be used for all buildings of average construction, such as brick dwellings, store and apartment buildings, ordinary school buildings, factory and warehouse buildings, speculative apartment buildings, apartment hotels, etc.

First Grade workmanship is intended to cover all of the better class of buildings, such as high-grade fireproof hotel and apartment buildings, fireproof office buildings, fine residences, Bank buildings, Court Houses, U. S. Post Offices and other 

Federal Government structures, State Capitol buildings, School and University buildings, and all structures where the best grade of workmanship is required.

Common bond is the most economical method of laying face brick, and other styles, such as English, Flemish, Dutch and

Garden Wall bond, require more labor on account of the various patterns and the additional cutting required. This is especially so on First Grade work where all vertical mortar joints must be plumb.

BRICK MASONRY 

565 

Concave Convex V-Tooled Stripped Rodded Raked Out Weathered 

Struck 

Flush Cut Styles of Mortar Joints. 

The mortar joints have considerable bearing on the labor costs. The flush cut joint is the most economical because the bricklayer cuts off the excess mortar with his trowel and the joint is finished. For 

Concave, V-tooled, Weathered and Struck joints, it is necessary to cut off the excess mortar with the trowel and then another operation is required, using a trowel for the

Weathered or Struck joints or a jointing tool for Concave and V-tooled. For raked-out joints, a bricklayer must rake out the mortar " to " back from the face of the brick, and for a rodded joint, the bricklayer must rake out the excess mortar and then strike the joint with a jointer. These operations all require time and cost money with bricklayers' wages at their present level.

The stripped joint is the most expensive of any illustrated, as it is necessary to place narrow wood strips in the mortar joints between each course of brick, and these strips must remain until the mortar has set, so it will not squeeze out toward the face of the brick.

It is slow work laying brick where the joints are stripped. 

If face brick are laid with 3" or 1" bed mortar joints, the work proceeds very slowly and requires a stiff mortar because the weight of the top brick courses squeeze the mortar out of the lower mortar joints, producing an uneven appearance. For this reason the work cannot be carried up many courses at a time. Where the joints are struck, it is necessary for the mortar to take its initial set before the joints can be struck to produce a workmanlike job. Brickwork of this kind is very expensive.

The quantities and costs given on the following pages are intended to cover all kinds of face brick work, whether laid in veneer in frame buildings, in solid brick or brick and tile valls.

Labor Laying Face Brick in English, Flemish, Dutch, Garden Wall and Diamond Bonds 

Face brick laid in any of the above bonds with the courses consisting of various arrangements of headers and stretchers requires considerable extra labor cutting brick on account of the large number of "bats" or headers required for each course. Ordinarily, a full header course extends through the wall every 5th, 6th or 7th course, and the other headers are only half brick or "bats." On First Grade workmanship it is necessary to plumb all vertical mortar joints in order that the various patterns will work out accurately. 

For a description of the labor involved in obtaining the various styles of mortar joints, refer to the preceding paragraph. 

Skintled Brickwork

Skintled brickwork consists of laying common brick irregularly, with random projecting brick at intervals and using clinkers or irregular and other off-colored brick to produce a variegated wall.

These brick are laid in a number of different ways to produce the desired effect. In some of them the mortar projects beyond the face of the brick just as it has been squeezed out of the joint; in others the joints are cut flush or raked out to produce shadows, etc.

The labor cost will vary with the design and care used in laying up the brick.

When laying common brick without regard to color of wall and with uncut mortar joints or joints cut off flush with the face of the wall, a mason should lay 500 to 550 brick per 8-hr. day, at the following labor cost per 1,000: Mason

Vitrified Face Brick 

17 12 * 20 There are a number of light gray vitrified face brick on the market that are so hard it is almost impossible to cut them. 

On account of their denseness and brittleness they do not absorb water from the mortar and for that reason it requires more time for the mortar to take its initial set. It is impossible to lay up many courses of brick at one time because the weight of the upper brick courses forces the mortar from the joints of the lower courses, causing an unsightly wall. It is also difficult to hold the brick in the wall and keep the wall plumb, as the brick slide out of place very easily. 

Brick of this kind are ordinarily laid with "buttered" mortar joints or with " mortar joints struck flush. They are fur-

Brick Fireplace Linings.-A mason should complete the lining for a brick fireplace having an opening 3'-0" to 4'-0" wide, 2'-6" to 3'-0" high, and 1'-4" to 1'-9" deep, in 4 to 6 hrs. all depending upon the class of work.

If the fireplace linings are laid in common bond and do not require an excessive amount of cutting and fitting, a mason should complete one fireplace lining in about 4 hrs. but where the back-hearths are of irregular shape and require considerable cutting and fitting at angles and at tops for dampers and smoke chambers, it will require about 6 hrs. mason time for each lining. 

Fireplaces having an opening 3'-6" to 4'-0" wide, about 4′-0″ high and l′-9″ deep, lined with firebrick laid in herringbone pattern, requiring cutting and fitting at all edges and corners, will require 16 hrs. mason time to line one fireplace. 

Labor Laying Brick Hearths and Back-Hearths.-If brick hearths and back-hearths are laid in square or basket weave pattern, a mason should complete one back-hearth in 2 to 3 hrs. and the front hearth will require the same length of time, or 

4 to 6 hrs. for both.

If laid in herringbone pattern with cut brick at all edges, it will require 3 to 4 hrs. mason time for both the hearth and back-hearth, or 6 to 8 hrs. mason time for both.

Figure about -hr. labor time to each hr. mason time, except where only one mason is on the job when it will figure hour for hour.

Cleaning and Pointing Face Brick Work 

The cost of cleaning face brick work will vary with the kind of brick, as it is much easier to clean a smooth face vitrified brick than one having a rough texture. 

When estimating tuck pointing, the cost of the work may be figured either by the thousand brick or by the sq. ft. of surface. 

When estimating by the sq. ft. do not make deductions for door and window openings unless very large.

Where smooth face brick are used and it is not necessary to do any pointing but merely wash the wall with muriatic acid and water, an experienced tuck pointer should clean 6,000 to 

6,500 brick (850 to 950 sq. ft. of wall) per 8-hr. day, at the following labor cost per 1,000 brick, or approximately 150 sq. ft. of wall:

Plastering old Brick Walls and Blocking off to Represent

Face Brick. It is an expensive job to plaster over old common brick and block it off to represent face brick. 

While the material cost is insignificant, the labor costs run high, as it is necessary to use experienced tuck pointers. 

Cement mortar should be used and may be of any color to represent face brick. It should not be applied over" thick. 

The mortar joints are then worked in, being either white or

a color that shows a contrast between the brick and the mortar. 

The mortar joints are usually made to project a little beyond the face of the brickwork. 

The labor cost of making mortar is expensive because it must be made in small quantities by the tuckpointers themselves. 

It is mixed, worked up, and then allowed to stand to season, and just before using it is worked up again. 

After the mortar has been made, a tuck pointer should complete 125 to 150 sq. ft. of wall per 8-hr. day, at the following cost per 100 sq. ft.:
