Reinforced Brick Walls As Protection Against Earthquakes 

A two story dining hall and kitchen built for the United States Government at Helena, Montana, required 100,000 face brick and 190,000 backup brick. All bearing walls were solid brick, faced with select common brick, laid in mortar consisting

BRICK MASONRY 

607 of 1 part lump lime putty, 1 part portland cement and 6 parts sand.

The first story walls were 16″ thick and were completed without reinforcing at the time the earthquakes occured in October, 1935. 

Reconstruction was resumed the following March. The first story walls 12" thick were reinforced with " round bars spaced 24" on centers horizontally and 17" on centers vertically. " dowels were placed in the first floor slab 17" on centers. The vertical bars extended through the wall beams at the roof slab into the parapet walls. All reinforcement was placed 4" from the inside face of the walls. 

All brick were laid in a full bed of mortar with shoved joints, with each course completely flushed with mortar. Facing brick were laid with "weathered joints, with a full header course every 6th course to bond with the backing.

Glass Masonry or Building Blocks 

Glass blocks are hollow, partially evacuated, translucent units of water clear glass. They are suitable for functional uses as light-transmitting walls of high thermal resistance and offer a wide range of decorative possibilities. 

They are furnished in a number of different sizes, all 33-in. thick, and with variations in the prismatic patterns impressed upon the faces of the blocks, which result in light transmitting values and diffusing properties over a wide range, with an absence of glare, affording light comparable to that from northerly exposed windows or skylights. 

Method of Laying Glass Blocks 

The partial vacuum of dry rarefied air prevents condensation inside the blocks. They are non-absorbent to liquids or odors and are easy to clean and maintain. 

Glass blocks admit diffused light of desirable character without allowing heat flow and for that reason are desirable for use in air-conditioned and artificially heated buildings. 

Their sanitary properties make glass masonry desirable for use in such buildings as hospitals, dairies, bakeries and breweries. They are also used for store fronts, windows, and for many interior purposes, such as corridor and dividing partitions,

counters, bars and interior walls and columns where many attractive designs and lighting effects may be worked out. 

They offer many possibilities for patterns, either used alone or combined with ordinary brickwork or other masonry. 

Mortar for Glass Blocks.-Materials used in making mortar for laying glass blocks shall be measured by volume. For this purpose 25 lbs. of quicklime or 40 lbs. of hydrated lime shall equal one cu. ft. of portland cement. 

All mortars shall be composed of 1 part portland cement, 1 

part lime and 4 parts sand. It shall be mixed in a watertight box and hoed from end to end until thoroughly incorporated. 

Consistency shall be such that the hoe is clean when withdrawn from the mortar. 

Calking Glass Blocks.-Where called for by details or specifications, use a plastic non-hardening, water-repellant calking compound of approved brand. 

Reinforcement.-Use 20 gauge x 12-in. x 6-ft. strips with 1-in. diameter perforations 12-in. on centers, galvanized after shearing. Place reinforcing strips in all glass masonry panels over 

6-ft. wide, every fifth course. Lap strings 8-in. allowing ends to act as anchors to the masonry piers by projecting into the masonry at least 18-in.

Labor Laying Glass Blocks.-Fill all joints uniformly and completely and allow the mortar to set after each 5 courses. 

Compress or point joints on both surfaces with metal pointing tool. Tool when set. If block must be disturbed after laid, clean it and relay.

All openings must have steel lintels except those spanned by a glass unit.

As described above, glass blocks should be laid with full mortar joints or 1-in. wide and the joints should be tooled on both sides of the wall with a jointing tool after the mortar has set sufficiently.

Inasmuch as glass blocks do not absorb water, the mortar must be as stiff as possible and still be workable, otherwise the blocks will be inclined to slide and it will be difficult to lay up a straight wall and very few courses can be laid at a time as the weight of the glass blocks will squeeze the mortar out of the joints.

CHAPTER XI , WALL BEAR- ING TILE, FLOOR ARCHES, PARTITIONS, WALL FURRING, ROOF TILE, ETC. 

Hollow tile are furnished in many styles, sizes and shapes. 

They are used for both interior and exterior structural walls. 

On exterior work they are usually finished with stucco although some tile are furnished with finished faces, similar to face brick. 

They are also used for backing-up face brick work and on account of the dead air cells in the tile are supposed to make a building cool in summer and warm in winter-and dry at all times, providing moisture does not penetrate through the mortar joints from the outside of the wall. 

Hollow tile are also used for structural floors in steel skeleton buildings and for fireproofing structural steel beams, girders, columns, etc.

They are also used for furring exterior masonry walls to prevent moisture from coming through the plaster, and for partitions in nearly all types of fireproof buildings. 

Book tile are used for roof construction where a dry ceiling surface, free from condensation, is important. 

Furring and Partition Tile 

Furring and partition tile are furnished 12"x12" square and 

2″, 3″, 4″, 6″, 8″, 10″ and 12″ thick. Each piece of tile covers one sq. ft. of wall.

Furring and partition tile should be estimated by the sq. ft. taking the area of all walls to be furred or partitions to be constructed, stating the number of sq. ft. of each size tile. 

Make deductions in full for all openings, and add a small percentage (2 to 5%) to cover waste and breakage, although this should be largely overcome by the mortar joints, unless a very poor grade of tile is used. 615

A tile is nominally 12"x12" in size, although this varies somewhat on account of burning in the kilns. Allowing for mortar joints, makes 12"x12", covering 156 sq. in. or 1 sq. ft. so unless the breakage is unusually large, the mortar joints should offset it.

Labor Handling and Setting Hollow Tile Furring and Par titions. The labor cost of handling and setting hollow tile furring and partition tile will vary with the length and height of the walls and floor plan, i.e., whether straight walls having an average number of openings or short and irregular walls having an unusually large number of pilasters, openings, etc. 

The height of the wall has considerable bearing on the labor costs, as one scaffold is sufficient for a 10'-0" or 11'-0" wall, but higher walls require two or more scaffolds, and additional labor. 

Handing the tile from the floor to the second scaffold requires the services of one extra man. 776 

Ted W Website brit Hollow Clay Partition Tile. 

Waise 8860 barimi

Bricklayers usually set all furring and partition tile but in the larger cities there are masons who specialize in setting tile partitions. 

The labor handling and wheeling tile, building scaffold and helping bricklayers will average about 1 hr. labor time to each hour bricklayer time. If partitions are two or more scaffolds high, figure 1 to 1 hrs. labor time to each hour mason time.

It is not generally practicable to use 2" tile for partitions, except for closets, shafts, etc.

Partitions of 3" tile can be safely used up to 12'-0" in height; 

4" to 16'-0", and 6" to 20'-0".

In office buildings it is good practice to have all main corridor partitions and stairway and elevator enclosures of 4" tile and partitions between rooms of 3" tile. Partitions should be bonded where meeting and anchored to wood bucks or brick walls by using ten-penny nails or metal wall ties in each second joint. 

Tile should be set on end, except top course, which may be set on side. 

Hollow Tile Partitions Reinforced with Wire Mesh. 

Split furring tile are 13" or 2" thick and 12" square. The ribs being set against the wall form an air space which checks the passage of moisture. Where walls must be straightened or furred out to line with the face of piers the 2" tile cannot be used but 3" or 4" partition tile should be used, depending upon the ceiling height.

Tile Girder and Column Covering 

The purpose of beam, girder and column covering is to place a fire retardant over the structural steel frame of buildings and to provide a surface on which to plaster. This goes under the general name of "Fireproofing of Steel."

Structural steel columns are economically protected by encasing them with at least 3" of hollow tile. Some jobs require bullnose tile where corners are to be rounded and others require radial tile for round columns. 

Hollow Tile Fire-Proofing for Round or Circular Columns. 

The radius of 3" circular tile covering is 10" on the outside and is suitable for columns 16" to 28" in greatest dimension. 

This material is sold at a price based on the square foot of exterior surface.

The labor cost of setting tile column fireproofing will vary with the size and height of the column, scaffolding, etc. The smaller the column the higher the labor cost per sq. ft. of surface on account of the extra corners.

How to Select and Order Proper Clip and Angle Tile for 

Beam and Girder Covering.-To figure the exact sizes of tile required for fireproofing any members, proceed as follows:

Obtain the width of the beam flange, either by field measurement or from manufacturer's handbook. 

Select from the following table clip tile having the "F" dimensions nearest to the width of the flange. 

Figure two pieces of clip tile for each lin. ft. of beams when the flange is covered on both sides. Example: A beam having a flange 6″ wide will require a G-30, since of 61″ is 31"; and G-30 has "F" dimension equal to 3".

Angle tile should be selected so that the “G” and “F” legs are long enough to cover the special condition for which it is needed.

Labor Fireproofing Beams and Girders.-The labor cost of fireproofing steel beams and girders will vary with the sections required per lin. ft. of covering, the accessability of the work, etc. *Add hoisting engineer time only if required.

GYPSUM TILE FIRE-PROOFING 

Gypsum tile are used for wall furring, partitions, and for fireproofing structural steel columns, beams and girders. They are 12"x30" in face dimensions. The large units are light in weight and require a minimum of labor for erection. 

Estimating Quantities of Gypsum Tile.-Gypsum tile should be estimated by the sq. ft. taking the area of all walls or partitions and making deductions in full for all openings. 

Gypsum tile are easily handled and may be cut with an ordinary hand saw, reducing waste to a minimum. 

The average mortar joint is " to " thick. 

Special shaped gypsum tile are furnished for fireproofing steel columns, beams and girders. This class of work should be estimated in a manner similar to that used in estimating partition tile.

GYPSUM TILE FIREPROOFING 

631 tile set, it requires more labor time handling and getting them to the mason.

Gypsum tile are set by bricklayers or tile setters (bricklayers who specialize in setting tile) and the labor costs will vary with the experience of the men setting them. There are concerns which specialize in the erection of gypsum tile partitions and fireproofing, and their workmen are skilled in this branch of work. 

Naturally they set more tile per day than a bricklayer, who lays brick today, clay tile tomorrow and gypsum tile the day after. To offset this increased labor efficiency, it is necessary to add their overhead expense and profit, so the total costs will probably offset one another.

Experienced tile setters should set 15 to 25 per cent more tile than inexperienced men.

FLAT ARCH TILE FLOORS 

Flat arches as adapted to floors and roofs are made up of various shaped tile, as illustrated. The tile resting against the beams are called "skews" and the protection for the beam known as the "soffit" tile is held in place by the bevel on the "skews." The intermediate tile are called "inters" and the center one is the "key."

Flat arches are used principally in steel frame constructed buildings, where speed of erection and light weight are the determining factors. A majority of all city "skyscrapers" have flat tile floor arches.

The outstanding advantage of the flat arch is its adaptability to speed in construction independent of temperature. Centers need remain in place but one-tenth to one-fourth as long as required under concrete construction.

Typical Wall Sections Using Natco Heath Cubes 

2 Cubes build 1 sq. ft. of 8" wall.

Heath Cubes. 

-Heath Cubes are standardized hollow structural clay tile units, cubical in shape, dimensioned according to the established measurement of brickwork. Their size, 7"x72"x72", exactly that of 6 brick, permit their substitution wherever brick have been figured.

The wall is built up in consistently formed tiers of load bearing members formed with the webs and shells in fixed alignment. 

Cubes are generally scored but they may be obtained smooth on as many faces as desired. 

Webs and shells are " thick. A cube contains 

52% solids and 48% voids. One cu. ft. of 

Heath Cube masonry weighs 60 lbs.

Heath Cubes are fur nished in whole and fractional units. 

2 Half-Cubes build 1 

sq. ft. of 4" wall. 

2 Cubes and 2 halves build 1 sq. ft. of 12" wall. 

3 Cubes and 2 halves build 1 sq. ft. of 16" wall. 

4 Cubes and 2 halves build 1 sq. ft. of 20" wall. 

3 Cubes equal 1 cu. ft. including mortar. 

1 Cube equals 6 brick, including mortar.

167 Cubes equal 1,000 brick in the wall. 

1,000 Cubes require 1 cu. yd. of mortar.

Interlocking Tile.-Used for load bearing and closure walls, either in combination with brick or stucco, or without facing. 

The units are light enough to handle with one hand and are easily laid. They measure 8″x61"x12", which is 61″ high, 8" thick and 12" long.

When ordering jamb tile state the total number of vertical feet for both sides of all openings and the thickness of the wall. 

When ordering corner tile, state the total height of all corners and the thickness of the wall. 

When used in solid tile walls 2.2 tile lay 1 sq. ft. of 8" wall; 

3.4 tile lay 1 sq. ft. of 12" wall, and 4.1 tile and 7 bond tile lay 

1 sq. ft. of 16" wall.

When used for backing up face brick, 2 tile lay 1 sq. ft. of 12" wall, consisting of 8" tile and 4″ brick; 3.1 tile lay 1 sq. ft. of 16" wall, consisting of 12" tile and 4″ brick. 

Interlocking tile weigh 60 lbs. per cu. ft. of wall, including mortar.

When laid in the wall with " mortar joints, it is 12" long, 63″ high on the broad face and 31″ high on the narrow face. It is equivalent to 6 common brick laid in the wall. 

When laid in 8" tile walls, it requires about 7.8 cu. ft. of mortar per 100 sq. ft. of wall, and when used in backing up face brick in a 12" wall, it requires about 19 cu. ft. of mortar per 

100 sq. ft. of wall.

TILE ROOF CONSTRUCTION 

There are several types of hollow clay, gypsum and cement tile used for roof construction. Roofs of this type are especially desirable where the underside of the roof must be perfectly dry and free from condensation.

Book Tile Roof and Ceiling Construction 

On account of their shape these tile are called "Book Tile", and they are made especially for roofs to be covered with concrete, tar and felt or any composition roofing. They are furnished in any length from 3"x12"x18" to 3"x12"x24", weigh 18 lbs. per sq. ft. and are made with a tongue or lip so that one tile slips into the other forming a continuous bond. Book tile should be laid in portland cement mortar and it requires 1 cu. ft. of mortar per 100 sq. ft. of tile. 

Light weight "T" irons, 21"x24" and weighing 4.1 lbs. per lin. ft. should be used to support the book tile, as shown in the accompanying illustration. The book tile are then laid to rest on the bottom flanges of the "T" beams and form a continuous roof.

Labor Laying Short Span Gypsum Roof Tile.-When laying short span gypsum roof tile, the tile are laid directly on the steel supports without mortar, and with sides tight together. 

The grouting joints are then filled with gypsum mortar and the roof deck is ready for the application of the roof covering. 

The labor cost of placing the tile will vary according to the height and pitch of the roof because the labor handling and hoisting the tile has considerable bearing on the total cost. 

On flat roofs where the tile may be hoisted on a hoist and wheeled to the setter, a setter should place 1,040 to 1,120 sq. ft. per 8-hr. day.

On pitch roofs or where there is considerable cutting and fitting around dormers, hips, valleys, etc., a tile setter should place 640 to 700 sq. ft. per 8-hr. day.

GYPSTEEL PLANK* 

Gypsteel Plank is a solid slab of extra dense, nailable gypsum, bound on sides and ends with galvanized copper-bearing steel, tongued and grooved like ordinary lumber. The gypsum core is reinforced with wire mesh. 

It is designed for roof decks of industrial and other steel frame buildings and for structural sub-floors in buildings of light load occupancy such as schools, libraries, theatres, hotels, stores, apartments and residences. 

M Method of Placing Gypsteel Plank 

It is made in two standard sizes: Junior Plank, 2" thick, 15" wide and 6'-0" long, is suitable for floors on spans up to 3'-0" and roofs up to 4'-0"; and Senior Plank, 2" thick, 15" wide and 

10'-0" long, for floors up to 5'-0" spans and roofs up to 7'-0" spans. The two types of Plank are identical except for length and thickness of binding. Each weighs 12 lbs. per sq. ft. 

*Trade Mark Registered. American Cyanamid & Chemical Corp.

GYPSTEEL PLANK 

663 Plank is handled and installed just like lumber, except that instead of splicing end joints over the supports they are laid at random without regard to the spacing of the purlins or beams. 

This method, which permits the use of standard length units, is possible because the meshing steel members enclosing the Plank form a steel I-beam that carries the load. 

Tongue and Groove Jointing of Gypsteel Plank 

Plank is readily cut, sawed or bored with ordinary carpenters tools. A short piece left over from one row is used to start the next, so that there is little waste. The Plank is secured to the steel supports by means of clips which are nailed to the steel binding.

A safe allowance for estimating purposes on the average job with fairly large unbroken areas is one to two percent more than the net area. Junior Plank, in carload lots of 3,300 sq. ft. or more, including fastening clips, cost 15 cents per sq. ft. f.o.b. destination to most rail points east of and including Pennsylvania and north of and including Virginia. On the same basis 

Senior Plank cost 18 cts. per sq. ft. 2 15"

Section Through Gypsteel Plank Labor Placing Gypsteel Plank. The labor cost of handling and placing Gypsteel Plank runs about the same as given on the following page under the heading "Labor Laying 22" Tongue and Groove Tile." Also note additional time required where laid on pitched roofs.

Precast Concrete Roof Slabs 

Precast concrete roof slabs are of three general types: Rib, Flat and Channel. They are adapted to all roof decks, flat or sloping, are fireproof and with caulked joints, present a smooth surface for the application of built-up roofing. Where slate, ornamental tile or copper covering is specified, slabs with nailing surfaces can be furnished, permitting direct application. 

Precast concrete roof slabs are furnished made with regular concrete aggregates or where a light weight slab is desired, they are made of light-weight (Haydite) aggregate. 

The rib tile is self-weathering and its attractive red color provides an architectural feature that is very desirable and so often lacking in industrial buildings. Auxiliary pieces are furnished to suit the particular design required, as ridges, sawtooth ridges, gable end finishing tile, monitor flashing tile and

other specials such as would be required in connection with a hip or valley.

Tile of the same standard stock sizes, but having a glass insert, may also be furnished where additional light may be required. On this type of roof slab it is necessary to obtain prices from the manufacturer* due to the fact that the amount of trim varies with each project.

CHAPTER XII RUBBLE STONE, CUT STONE, GRANITE AND TERRA COTTA 

There are many kinds of stonework used in building construction and each must be estimated separately and in detail, if accurate estimates are to result.

Rubble work consists of irregular sized stones and is ordinarily used for foundations and rough masonry walls. 

Rustic or Cobble stone work is used for chimneys, porch piers, etc., in residential construction, also for rustic fences and walls.

Ashlar or cut stone is usually cut in the mill and sent to the job ready to set in place, as it requires modern machinery to produce this class of work economically. 

Coursed ashlar is set in regular courses while random or irregularly coursed ashlar is furnished in irregular shapes and sizes and usually requires considerable fitting and jointing at the job.

Within the past few years a great deal of rough faced rubble stone work has been used in many high class buildings. This stone is set in both regular and irregular coursing. In some instances the stone is cut to fit in the yard but frequently all backing and vertical joints are cut on the job. These are discussed in more detail in another part of this chapter. 

RUBBLE STONE WORK 

Rubble stone work may be estimated by the cu. yd. containing 

27 cu. ft. or by the perch containing 24 cu. ft. A perch of stone is nominally 16 ft. long, 1 ft. high and 1 ft. wide, but is often computed differently in different locations. In many states, especially west of the Mississippi River, rubble work is figured by the perch containing 16 cu. ft. Before submitting prices 678

RUBBLE STONEWORK 

679 on rubble work by the perch, be sure to find out the common practice in your locality.

Cost of Rubble Stone.-The cost of rubble stone will vary with the locality, kind of stone used, distance of quarry from the job, etc.

The method of buying and selling rubble stone also varies with the locality, as in some places it is sold by the ton containing 2,000 lbs. while in others it is sold by the perch containing 24 cu. ft. or by the cord containing 100 cu. ft. and weighing 13,000 lbs. which is about 130 lbs. per cu. ft. In some localities it is sold by the cu. yd. containing 27 cu. ft. 

Mortar for Rubble Stone Work.-The quantity of mortar required for rubble stone will vary with the size and shape of the stone and the thickness of the walls, but a fair average is 7 to 9 cu. ft. of mortar per cu. yd. of wall. Mortar costs are given under "Brick Masonry."

Cost of Setting Rubble Stone.-When handling and setting rubble stone in walls up to 1'-6" thick, a mason and laborer should handle and set 80 to 100 cu. ft. per 8-hr. day. 

On heavy walls, 2′-0″ to 3′-0″ thick, a mason should set 115 to 135 cu. ft. per 8-hr. day, and will require about 14 hrs. labor time to each hr. mason time.

RUSTIC OR COBBLE STONE WORK 

Rustic or cobble stone work is used extensively for chimneys, porches, fences, ornamental work on residences, bungalows, and other buildings of this type. 

Ordinary cobble stones or boulders 4" to 18" in diameter are used on this work. The face of the walls, piers, etc., are of stone backed up with common brick. 

The smaller stones cost more to lay than the larger ones, as a mason can handle and lay a 12" stone almost as fast as a 4" one, providing the stone are not too large for one man to handle. 

Cobble stone work should be estimated by the sq. ft. of surface or by the cu. ft. or cu. yd., the latter method being pre ferable. 

Mortar Required for Rustic Stone Work. It requires about cu. ft. of mortar to each cu. ft. of stone, due to the unevenness and irregularity of the stone.

Labor Setting Rustic or Cobble Stone Work.-On residences, bungalows and other buildings having rustic or cobble stone chimneys, piers, etc., built of 4" to 8" stone, (average 6″), a mason and laborer should handle and lay 80 to 100 sq. ft. (40 to 50 cu. ft.) of stone per 8-hr. day. 

Where larger stones 8" to 18″ (average 12″) in size are used, a mason and laborer should handle and lay 120 to 140 sq. or cu. ft. per 8-hr. day.

RUBBLE OR SPLIT FACED ASHLAR 

The past few years has witnessed a revival in the use of rubble stone in the construction of churches, college and university buildings, fraternity and sorority houses, chapels, residences, etc.

This stone is commonly known as Lannon (Wisconsin), Briar Hill (Ohio), Crab Orchard (Tennessee), as well as other similar stones quarried in different parts of the country and used in the same manner. 

The stone is usually furnished in slabs from 4" to 8" thick and 1″ to 15″ high, depending upon the class of work. 

When the stone is to be backed-up with common brick it is usually furnished 4" to 8" thick to bond with the brickwork but when used as a veneer on residences, etc., it is usually furnished 

4" to 6" thick and is tied to the wall by metal wall ties. 

The cost of setting this stone varies widely, depending upon the size of the stone and the amount of cutting required. On some of the more intricate jobs it requires as much mason's time trimming and cutting the stone as is required to set it. 

The entire success of the use of this rubble ashlar depends upon the artistic manner in which the work is performed, and the labor costs will be governed accordingly. 

Labor time handling stone and helping masons varies widely, depending upon method of handling stone at job, access of material piles, size of stone, etc. 

To show the variations in the cost of setting, six different classes of work are described. 

Estimating Quantities of Split Faced Ashlar.-Split faced ashlar stone is usually sold by the ton and is furnished with rough beds, backs and joints. The stone weighs 160 to 165 lbs. per cu. ft. and there are 12 to 12 cu. ft. of stone to the ton. 

Stone 4-in. thick produces 36 to 38 sq. ft. of wall to the ton and when laid with a -in. mortar joint should lay up 40 to 42 sq. ft. of wall.

Stone 5-in. thick produces 29 to 30 sq. ft. of wall to the ton and when laid with a -in. mortar joint should lay up 32 to 33 sq. ft. of wall.

Where the stone is backed with common brick, the stone is usually furnished 4-in. to 8-in. thick to bond with the brick

backing. Based on an average of 6-in. thick for the job, one ton is sufficient for 24 to 25 sq. ft. of wall and when laid with a 1-in. mortar joint should lay up 26 to 28 sq. ft. of wall.

When estimating the cost of plain door and window sills, lintels, steps, platforms, copings, etc., the quantities are sometimes estimated by the lin. ft. for sills and coping and by the sq. ft. for platforms, but the cu. ft. method is more generally used.

Setting Cut Stone Using Power Derricks. On large jobs where it is necessary to use stiff leg or guy derricks for hoisting and handling the stone, the costs will vary with the size and weight of the stone, quantity, and with the method of handling the stone on the ground.

On work of this kind it is usually necessary to use stiff leg or guy derricks, or by having the boom of the derrick placed in a boom seat and bolted to the steel frame of the building. 

On jobs covering a large area, it will be necessary to use a number of derricks, so regardless of the method used in setting the stone, the cost of setting and removing derricks, hoisting engines, etc., should be estimated separately, as this charge will remain the same whether there are 5,000 or 50,000 cu. ft. of stone to be set.

After the derricks and equipment are in place, a stone setter should set 240 to 280 cu. ft of stone per 8-hr. day. It will require about 2 laborers helping to land the stone and set it, 4 or 5 laborers on the ground sorting and handling the stone from stock piles to derricks, 3 derrickmen giving signals and operating nigger-head and one hoisting engineer.

In connection with work of this kind, there is always a certain amount of lost time caused by delays in delivery of stone, repairs to derricks and hoisting engines, oiling and

attending derricks, moving and raising derricks, inspecting cables, tightening guy lines and many other items that require attention and which must be charged against the cost of stone setting.

Including contingencies as enumerated above, the labor setting 100 cu. ft. of cut stone should cost as follows:

Carving Sand or Limestone.-The cost of carving cut stone is usually figured from full-size details or models furnished by the architect. This cost will vary with the amount of detail and the method used in carving, i.e., whether performed in the shop before setting or after the stone has been set on the job. 

Where you are sure of a first class job of setting, it is more economical to have the carving done in the shop as all carved work consisting of a number of pieces is set up with wood strips forming the thickness of mortar joints and accurately fitted before shipping to the job. 

Many architects who previously had their carving done on the job are now having it done in the mill before shipment.

Cost of Models for Stone Carving.-On the better class of work, clay or plaster models for all carving are usually furnished by the architect or a stipulated sum is allowed for models.

Figuring on a sq. ft. basis, models in clay will run around $8.00 per sq. ft. while plaster models will cost about $10.00 per sq. ft. A small rosette or head cast in plaster will cost about $20.00. The models quite generally cost more than the carving, and often twice as much where models are made, for an individual piece. It will often require a week's work for a skilled artisan to produce a carefully made model for a carved plaque or panel, 3′-6″ to 4′-0″ in diameter.

The sq. ft. price of models should be based on the sq. ft. of model required and not on the sq. ft. surface of carved stone, as one model may often be used for carving 10 or 15 pieces of stone, or one lin. ft. model of carved molding in plaster may often be used for carving hundreds of lin. ft. of stone.

Setting Stone on the Dome of the Arkansas State Capitol 

Building. This work was 200 to 250 ft. above the ground, so that it required considerable handling and hoisting to bring the stone from the cars to the top of the building. 

When the stone setting was first started, a stiff leg derrick was placed on the pediment over the front entrance and the stone was lifted from the cars to the wood platform that extended the entire length of the building. In some instances it was possible to unload the stone from the cars and hoist it for immediate use. When the stone was ready to set, it was picked up by the stiff leg derrick over the front entrance and hoisted to the platforms on either side of the derrick, as illustrated on page 377. There were narrow gauge tracks extending from each platform to the rear of the building and dome, and the stone was placed on small hand cars on the front platforms and pushed by hand to the nearest point of operation. It was then picked up by the setting derrick and lifted into place. 

When this work was first started, three steel boom seats were placed on different parts of the steel framework of the dome, and three different booms were used for setting. On account of the height of the derricks and the strong wind encountered, it was almost impossible to swing the booms so that the stone could be set, and after a few days' trial this method was

CUT STONE 

699 

Marble Carving on Rice Institute Buildings, Houston, Texas.

abandoned. When setting by this method a stone setter set only 85 to 115 cu. ft. of stone each 8-hr. shift. 

After the booms and boom seats had been removed, a guy derrick was placed on the extreme top of the dome, having a mast 60 ft. long and a boom 55 ft. long. This derrick was held in place by 6 guy lines about 750 ft. long. 

The boom on the guy derrick was operated by a hoisting engine located on the ground in front of the building, as illustrated on page 377, while the derrick circled the dome by means of a bull wheel operated by hand on the top of the dome. 

After the guy derrick was in operation the labor costs took a decided drop. On days when setting large column sections or the large stone lintels resting on same, a setter would set 500 cu. ft. of stone each 8-hr. shift.

Data on Indiana Limestone .12

Indiana limestone is probably more favorably known and more generally used in all parts of the United States than any other stone used for building purposes. This is doubtless due to its appearance, as well as the ease with which it is worked, its freedom from stratification and cleavage plane, and while it is a sedimentary stone, it is to all intents and purposes a free stone, having about equal strength in all directions.

CUT STONE 

705 

Three Story Brick and Concrete Office Building, Harvey, Ill.

It is used for the exterior facings of buildings, as well as all kinds of trimmings, such as sills, lintels, coping, steps, plat forms, etc. 

Indiana limestone can be produced in any reasonable quantity and size. A vast amount of this stone is cut ready to place in the building by the mills located adjacent to the quarries, but the rough quarry blocks and sawed slabs may be shipped to any locality where the proper facilities are available and be cut by mills located near the job. In fact, about 

75 per cent of the total annual output of the quarries is cut by the local plants throughout the country. 

Kinds of Indiana Limestone.-Indiana limestone is furnished in a variety of different grades and color-tones, a brief summary of which is given below:

Select stock is uniform in color and texture, more so than is required for ordinary building construction. It is recommended for entrance work and those portions of a building within ready range of vision, carving, interior and other exceptional uses. 

Standard stock is sound stone with a range of variation in color shades and texture not found in Select but necessarily confined within limits that make it impossible to determine at a distance of a few feet whether it is Standard or Select stock. In fact, the capillary attraction of the Standard stock is less than of the Select, so that the Standard stock, if anything, acts better under the weather than the Select. 

Rustic stock is of more or less coarse grain but strictly sound and harder than either Standard or Select stock. Rustic stock is used to a considerable extent for country residences and terrace work, hence its name. It is recommended principally for sawed ashlar. When used for molded work the treatment should be bold as it cannot be machined as readily as the other grades.

Variegated stock is an irregular mixture of Buff and Gray produced from the blocks that are quarried where the Buff and Gray color-tones adjoin in the quarry. It shows variation in texture as well as color. Variegated stone when cut into building units will exhibit, in these, units of each color-tone and a small percentage of units with both color-tones in one piece. 

Variegated stone is unusually effective in giving variety to plain surfaces and is a desirable class of material for trim as well as for facing.

CUT STONE 

707 There are certain grades of Indiana Oolitic limestone especially adapted for grade courses, steps, buttresses, floor tiling, etc., or any position in the building exposed to abrasion. Some are available in different color-tones and may be identified by the following names: Special Hard Gray Indiana Limestone, Special Hard Cream White Indiana Limestone, and Special Hard Buff Indiana Limestone. 

The following are the Trade terms by which the different grades of Indiana limestone are commonly known: 

Select Buff Select Gray 

Indiana Travertine

Standard Buff Standard Gray Old Gothic Variegated 

(both Buff and Gray) Rustic

Old Gothic is a new classification, used largely for roughsawed random ashlar work, for residences, and for field work in churches, school and college buildings, etc. 

The Old Gothic stone is ungraded and is usually furnished in short length blocks. It has the full range of variation with most of the select or fine grain stock removed.

Finishes of Indiana Limestone.-The following finishes are ordinarily used on Indiana limestone: Any finish desired except bush-hammering and other hard stone finishes can be used. 

Some of the machine finishes are sawed, smooth planed and tooled two, four, six, eight or ten bats to the inch. The class of tooling in common practice is understood to cover what is properly termed fluting, that is, concave depressions. Convex tooling is sometimes used effectively, but is never applied unless specifically designated. Two bat tooling has been successfully applied (and always vertically) in construction requiring large ashlar facets. Two bat tooling, however, is expensive because it must be superimposed or matched, as wide tooling should not be applied promiscuously, the lines must be continuous from course to course.

It is generally recommended that all molded work be finished smooth. If it is tooled at all, the tooling should run in the direction of the mold and not across it, unless largely increased expense is of no consequence. As to tooled ashlar, some architects contend vertical tooling is preferable, others prefer the horizontal.

Indiana Oolitic limestone will take most hand finishes which under certain conditions are considered preferable to machine finish. Notable examples of this class of work are crandalling

and tooth chiselling, but a number of the hand finishes can now be simulated by machine work.

A smooth finish is not commonly furnished other than in the form it comes from the planers. If sand rubbing is desired, it should be specified, and in such event the sand rubbing should be by the wet process and not with carborundum. It is contended by many that sand rubbing is the best finish for smoky city atmospheres because a surface so treated offers no lodging place for grime.

Back-Painting Indiana Limestone Not Recommended by 

Quarrymen and Producers.-Painting the backs and sides of

Indiana limestone is condemned by the producers of the stone, not only because it involves useless expense but primarily because it tends to create conditions which it is supposed to counteract.

Painting stone on five sides to within an inch or less of the exposed face compels the impurities in the backing and mortar to proceed along the joints towards the face of the stone where it finally finds egress within an inch or less of the face and spreads fanwise and promptly shows its effects. There is the further condition that the quarry sap contained in all stone can evaporate only at the face and when this occurs while the building is in course of erection, dust, dirt, and other impurities readily cling to the face. Furthermore, waterproof paint is frequently thinned with gasoline, which carries some of the heavy substances of the paint into the stone and tends to create undesirable discolorations. 

In connection with the application of limestone facing to re-inforced concrete structures or concrete fire-proofing, it is essential that some form of stain prevention be used. In such instances the damp-proof coating should be applied to the face of the concrete members and not to the backs of the stone. A full inch space should be allowed between the back of the stone and finished face of the concrete when detailing this work, while in actual practice it will give an average -inch backing joint. 

Contractors should also use the utmost precaution during construction to prevent drippings and wash from the concrete floor construction, during rains, from running down on cut stone or into the backing of the walls below. Carelessness during construction is often the cause of unsightly discoloration that sometimes appears on limestone buildings.

CUT STONE 

709 

Mortar for Setting and Back-Plastering Indiana Limestone.— 

Mortar made in the following proportions is recommended for setting and back-plastering limestone: 

All Indiana limestone should be set in lime tempered with stainless cement. The mixture to consist of one part lime to not over three parts of clean sharp sand, and stainless cement equal to ten per cent (10%) by volume of the lime putty used. 

The lime should be first slacked with cold water and screened through a-inch mesh into a settling box, following the practice employed in preparing lime for plastering. The lime putty so prepared should stand in the settling box not less than one week and then be prepared with sand and cement for use in setting the stone. The sand must be clean, washed sand, free from all vegetable matter, salts, and other impurities. The water must be clear and devoid of salts and all injurious chemical elements.

The mixture of lime recommended above should give entire satisfaction. A percentage of cement is included in order to hasten the setting of the mortar. While lime has the tendency to set more slowly than ordinary cement mortar, the latter is more likely to crack in time, and many years' experience has shown that there is nothing better than good lime mortar when properly used.

Another mortar mixture which has been successfully used after considerable experimentation consists of one-half part lime putty, one part of a well known white cement and two parts of clean sharp sand.

Too much emphasis cannot be laid on the need of having clean sharp sand and pure water.

Weight of Indiana Limestone.-Indiana limestone weighs 200 lbs. per cu. ft. when furnished in rough quarry blocks and 180 lbs. per cu. ft. in scabbled quarry blocks. These figures include 

2 bbls. white portland the weight of rough excess stone. 

Sawed slabs or other squared material weighs 170 lbs. per cu. ft. The weight of the finished cut stone ready to set in the building is figured at 150 lbs. per cu. ft. If there are any large round columns in the job, they may be figured at 140 lbs. per cu. ft. of stock. The actual net weight of a cu. ft. of dry seasoned stone is 144 lbs.

Average Prices of Indiana Limestone.-Where the cut stone for any job consisting of ashlar, sills, steps, coping, plain.machine moldings, etc., is furnished by any of the mills in the 

Bedford or Indiana limestone district, the price will vary from $2.75 to $3.75 per cu. ft. f. o. b. cars at the mills.

CUT STONE 

711 

Considerable variation in price is due to the following reasons: 

Stone consisting of light weight pieces, such as 4" or 6" ashlar, small molded courses, small turned columns, bases, sills, coping, etc., require a comparatively small amount of stone but involves considerable cutting and finishing expense, and even higher costs will prevail.

On other jobs consisting of fairly large stone, 8″ or more thick, large molded pieces, bases, columns, etc., the cubical contents are a deciding factor, and the cu. ft. price of this stone, even for more elaborate work will usually average less in cost than the lighter stone described above. 

Jobs containing many large pieces of stone will take the minimum price.

To the above prices it will be necessary to add freight from the Bedford district to destination on the basis of 150 lbs. per cu. ft. 

Always remember that the cube of the largest dimensions must always be used when computing the quantity, cost and weights of stone of any kind.

Cutting Beds and Joints.-When cutting beds and joints the cost will vary with the size of the stone. The smaller the stone the higher the price per cu. ft. and the larger the stone the less the price per cu. ft. For instance, a piece of ashlar 8" thick contains twice as many cu. ft. of stone as a piece 4" thick, while the cost of cutting the joints will not be much more on the larger piece than on the smaller. 

Where the joints are cut by hand, the cost will vary from 40 to 60 cts. per cu. ft., depending upon the conditions stated above.

On the second sawing, where sawed slabs are used and it is necessary to run them through the saw the second time for top and bottom beds, it will cost 35 cts. per cu. ft. for this work. 

Where the jointing is done on the saw, figure 40 cts. per cu. ft. for cutting joints.

CUT STONE 

713 Smooth or Planer Finish.-When Indiana limestone is wanted with a smooth finish as it comes from the planer, the cost will vary from 20 to 25 cts. per sq. ft. of surface planed. 

The slabs are usually furnished sawed to the correct thickness and then the stone is run through the planer to remove the saw marks, which is not a very expensive process on straight work.

On the cheaper classes of work, and on some of the higher grade work where a sawed finish is desired, the sawed slabs are jointed and the stone is sent to the building without having been run through the planer. Work of this class is a little cheaper than stone having a first class finish. 

Tooled Finish.-If the stone has a tooled finish, having 4, 6, 8 or 10 bats to the inch, the cost of horizontal tooling on plain surfaces will cost 25 to 30 cts. per sq. ft. (not cu. ft.) of surface tooled, or about 15 cts. per cu. ft. more than planer finish. 

Hand vertical tooling in connection with machine molded work will add about 25 cts. per sq. ft. of surface finished. 

Cross or vertical tooling on curved surfaces will add 50 cts. per sq. ft. of surface finished. 

Two bat tooling, which is always used vertically, can be done for almost the same cost as given above if it is not made to register. This tooling, however, usually has to be made to register and for that reason is generally more costly than 4, 6, 8 or 10 bat work.

Sand Rubbed Finish.-If the stone is to have a sand rubbed finish, making it necessary to rub the surface with sand and water, add 25 cts. per sq. ft. for all surface to be rubbed. 

Rustication. If the stone is to be furnished with rustication or a "rabbet" along the edges of the stone, the cost will vary according to the depth of the "rabbet." This is all planer work, so the width of the "rabbet" does not make as much difference as the depth to which it must be cut.

Stone Moldings.-The cost of stone moldings will vary greatly according to the size of the stone, the type of mold, breaks, heads, jointing, etc. The two kinds of moldings most commonly used are plain or Classic moldings and Gothic moldings

CUT STONE 

717 When cutting stone moldings on a planer, the smaller the piece of stone the higher the price per cu. ft., on account of the additional labor involved and the small amount of stone required. 

Tools for cutting moldings vary from 3" to 8" wide, so when the moldings are over 8″ in width, it is necessary to run them through the planer a second time.

The moldings that are the cheapest to run are similar to the illustration of plain moldings, where a large amount of stone is required on which no special work is necessary. On work of this kind the actual cost of running the moldings averages only slightly more than the average cu. ft. prices given on the previous pages.

Plain Moldings. 

Gothic Moldings. 

When estimating plain moldings, take the largest dimensions of the stone to obtain the cubical contents and figure at the average price as given on the previous pages, as this will cover most jobs where the molded courses do not form too large a proportion of the total stone in the job. 

Gothic Moldings.-Gothic Moldings are much more expensive than plain or Classic moldings, as in almost every instance it is necessary to run the stone through the planer twice or perform a certain amount of hand labor in connection with same. Gothic moldings cost at least twice as much to run as plain or Classic moldings. The cutting of heads for Gothic moldings will run much higher than plain moldings, or from $1.00 to $5.00 each, depending upon the size and character of the molding. 

Where entire jobs consist of elaborate Gothic stone, they frequently will run from $6.00 to $10.00 per cu. ft. On work of this kind it is advisable to obtain figures from a reputable concern covering the stone delivered ready to set.

Turned Balusters.-When estimating the cost of slender turned stone balusters, the item of breakage requires consideration, as there is a large percentage of waste in this class of work. The balusters usually break after they are about 

75 per cent completed.

On plain turned balusters, without hand work, take the cubical contents of the largest dimensions, and price same at about 15 cts. per cu. ft. more than the average prices given on the previous pages. 

After the contents have been estimated by the cu. ft., the following allowances should be made to take care of the extra labor involved in turning each baluster on the lathe. 

This applies to jobs having about 50 balusters. Where there are more the turning cost will be reduced and where there are fewer, the cost will be increased.

Round Stone Columns. When estimating the cost of plain turned columns, the cubical contents should be obtained by taking the cube of the largest dimension (measured square) and price as follows: 

Obtain the cu. ft.

cost of the grade of stock to be used, whether Select Buff, Standard Buff, Select Gray, etc., and add seven times the cu. ft. cost of the rough quarry blocks. This will give the cu. ft. price at which the columns should be estimated. 

For instance, a turned column 3′-0″ in diameter and 36′-0″ long would contain, 3'x3'x36′ or 324 cu. ft. of stone. Select Buff is worth 80 cts. per cu. ft. in rough blocks. Multiply 80x7 gives $5.60 per cu. ft. 324 cu. ft. @ $5.60 equals $1,814.40, the cost of one column.

A stone column 38'-0" long is the usual limit of present day machine capacity, so when the column shaft is over 36'-0" long, it is best to get them out in three sections.

Ilco Riplstone 

Ilco Riplstone which is extensively used in residence construction, is produced by sawing the Old Gothic, Rustic Buff or Variegated Indiana limestone using steel shot for the abrasive instead of the customary silica sand. This produces a riple finish that has considerable variation and tends to bring out the color in the stone, ranging from almost a rust-brown and grays of various shades to a mellow creamy buff.

Ilco Riplestone is furnished in strips sawed on 4 sides, ends left rough, in lengths ranging from 3'-6" to 6'-5″ and is broken to length at the building site. Breaking to length is a simple operation and the only tools really necessary are a square, a carpenter's hand saw and a mason's hammer. A groove about

CUT STONE 

721 "deep is sawed in the face of the stone and then a sharp tap on the back with the hammer breaks the stone squarely in line with the cut on the face. A common laborer can break about 

18 cu. ft. per hr. by this method. The strip can be broken to length easier and somewhat faster by using a portable electric carborundum saw for grooving the stone. In breaking the stone for the wall there is some waste, which should not exceed 5%. 

The strips of Ilco Riplstone cost from $0.75 to $0.85 per cu. ft. at the quarry. One cu. ft. of stone 4" thick will cover approximately 3 sq. ft. of wall surface. Freight is estimated on the basis of 170 lbs. per cu. ft. 

Ilco Riplstone is used for the exterior wall facings of churches, schools, residences, and other buildings of informal character. 

Labor Laying Ilco Riplstone.-When laying Ilco Ripstone in veneer work, a mason should set 100 to 125 sq. ft. of 4" stone per 8-hr. day, but if backed up with masonry the costs will be about the same as given on previous pages for "Setting Random or Split Faced Ashlar." BUILDING GRANITE 

Granite for building purposes is generally used for base courses, ashlar extending from the first to the second or third floors (from which point terra cotta or cut stone is usually substituted), for steps, curbing, columns, bases, caps, etc. 

It requires considerable time and care to make up an estimate on granite work, as the different operations on each piece must be figured separately, and there are frequently five or six operations on each.

Granite is delivered from the quarry in rough blocks-some already split to approximate dimension sizes and others in random sizes to be drilled and split to dimension or sawed into slabs for ashlar or polished work. Pneumatic drills are universally used for drilling up rough stock or slabs and pneumatic hand tools for cutting the edges, moldings and for carving. 

Pneumatic surfacing machines rough down large surfaces and point or cut them to the form and finish required. Surfacing machines are also used to bush sawed slabs to the various cut finishes, core and rough out heavy checks or moldings, recess for panels, rough and finish the surface of columns, rough out the flutes and similar work. 

Polishing machines are used for producing rubbed, honed or polished work from surfaces prepared either by surfacing machines or saws. Steel shot, carborundum or emery are used for grinding down the surfaces and heavy felt faced wheels gloss the surface, using oxide of tin and water. Small surfaces, moldings, etc., are polished by hand.

Balusters, columns and other round work are usually turned on specially built lathes, using disc cutters. Lathes are also used for polishing round work.

Carborundum machines are quite generally used for cutting rabbets, checks and for freeing flutes and moldings.

Practically every piece of granite requires hand work. 

Standards of Quality in Building Granite 

The quality of workmanship on granite work has been graded into three classifications as follows:

BUILDING GRANITE 

725 

Monumental Building Grade.-This grade of workmanship is required for permanent buildings of the highest type, such as state houses, court houses, library or public memorial buildings. 

Good Commercial Grade.-This grade of workmanship is required for high class buildings, such as banks, insurance buildings, high class office buildings, churches, schools, etc. 

Ordinary Commercial Grade.-For buildings where architectural appearance is subordinate to utility. Workmanship will meet the requirements of structural safety, but not carried beyond the point of good appearance to the casual observer. 

Weight of Granite.-Granite weighs 180 lbs. per cu. ft. when furnished with a pointed or polished finish, and 200 lbs. per cu. ft. when furnished with a rock face. These weights should be used when estimating freight on granite from quarry to destination. 

Labor Setting Granite.—Granite weighs 180 to 200 lbs. per cu. ft., or 15 to 20 per cent more than cut stone and on account of the finish and cost of most kinds of building granite, it requires very careful handling and perhaps an additional man to help handle and set the granite. 

Where exceedingly large pieces are used, such as columns, etc., it may require extra heavy derricks and equipment to handle and set it.

On an average the labor costs given on the previous pages for setting cut stone should be increased 20 to 25 per cent. 

Mortar Required for Setting Granite.-Use the same quantities of mortar for setting granite as given on the previous pages for "Cut Stone."

Methods Used In Estimating the Quantities and Costs of Granite 

As mentioned in the first part of this chapter, estimating granite is a highly specialized business, and for that reason the methods given in the following pages can only be approximate. 

Wherever possible, the granite company should prepare their own estimate and submit a bid on the granite delivered at the job or f.o.b. cars.

There are two distinct methods of estimating granite; the one given on the following pages is used by many of the older concerns in the business, while the other estimates only the actual thickness of the granite slabs, whether 2 or 12 inches thick and prices the granite and the various finishing operations on the actual surface to be finished. 

One of the largest and most progressive granite quarriers and manufacturers in the United States, says "During the past few years we have made great changes in the manufacturing of building granite and have modernized our plant far beyond any of our competitors, and due to this modernization, have compiled a system of estimating granite work, which as far as we know is applicable only to our method, and for that matter would be 'Greek' to many concerns which might attempt to use it. Due to this, we do not feel justified in having this information appear in print, where it would be an open book to all of our competitors."

The above is self-explanatory. If those engaged in the actual manufacture of building granite do not agree on a definite method of estimating, what is the estimator who prepares only an occasional estimate supposed to do?

Estimating Quantities and Costs of Granite 

When estimating the quantity of granite, each piece should be figured by taking the cube of the largest dimensions, but as a general thing no piece of granite is figured as less than 12" thick or containing less than 1 cu. ft. to the running foot. 

If the granite is over 1′-0″ thick, figure the actual thickness. 

This method of measurement applies to sills, steps, etc., where the granite may be 12" thick, but only 5" to 7" high. In such instances the height should be estimated as 12".

The illustration on the opposite page gives the correct method of listing the different pieces of granite on the estimate. Note that it is necessary to list every labor operation separately, if accurate estimates are to result.

The costs given on the following pages are approximate and are for use only where it is impossible to obtain prices from the producers. Granite cutting is a highly skilled industry and estimates on jobs of any size should be prepared only by those in intimate touch with the industry and for that reason it is

Estimating Cutting Quantities.-When estimating the differ ent operations required to produce a piece of finished granite, all surfaces, such as plain beds and joints must be estimated as being at least 1′-0″ thick and l′-0″ high. Actual measurements are used on larger dimensions. The number of sq. ft. of beds and joints should be obtained according to the above method and multiplied by the rate per sq. ft. 

Inasmuch as 75 to 90 per cent of the cost of finished granite is labor, the utmost care should be exercised to estimate all labor operations accurately.

Surface Finishes for Building Granite.-The surface finishes most frequently used for building granite, arranged in the order of their relative cost, are rock faced, pointed, four-cut, six-cut, eight-cut, rubbed and polished.

Rock face is generally the least expensive, but the cost varies with the grade of work required, whether having uniform projections, beds, joints and arrises, and sometimes with rusticated or tooled margins.

Pointed work is furnished in fine, medium and coarse. 

Peen-hammered finish is used for rougher work such as steps, curbings, sills and thresholds or on portions of high class work requiring level finished surfaces, but which are not exposed to the eye. In general peen-hammered finish is somewhat coarser than four-cut work.

Four-cut, Six-cut, and Eight-cut.-These surfaces are finished by bushing with a patent bush-hammer. This is all hand work. 

The surface is first pointed, then further smoothed by cross bushing with either a peen-hammer or four-cut. 

Six and eight-cut finishes are continuations of the four-cut process, each coarser hammer being used consecutively until the required finish is reached. 

Ten and twelve-cut work are seldom used for building work. 

Rubbed and honed work is produced by grinding a pointed or sawed surface under the polishing mill. The grade of rubbing is determined by the extent to which this grinding process is carried from coarse rubbed to a honed finish, which is the last stage before glossing or polishing.

BUILDING GRANITE 

729 Polished work is produced by glossing under a heavy felt coated wheel, a surface previously rubbed and honed.

Estimating Granite Ashlar, Base Courses, Etc. 

When estimating granite ashlar, base courses, etc., the same rule of measurement applies as given on the preceding pages, viz., do not figure any piece of granite as being less than 1′-0″ thick, 1'-0" high or containing less than 1 cu. ft. of granite per running foot. All granite 4", 6", 8" or 10" thick should be figured as 12" when computing the rough stock. When larger than 1′-0″ thick or high, use actual dimensions.

The above method of measurement also applies when estimating the labor cost of cutting and finishing granite to obtain the number of sq. ft. of beds and joints, finished surfaces, etc. 

Figure all heads and reveals at 1 times the cost of straight work.

Estimating Plain Molded Courses, Cornices, Plain Column and Pilaster Bases, Caps, Etc.-When preparing estimates on granite work involving molded courses, plain cornices, plain column and pilaster bases and caps, which do not require carving, particular attention should be paid to the different members making up each molding, cap or base.

RELATIVE VALUE OF WASH OR CHAMFER IN TERMS OF PLANE SURFACE Method of Estimating Granite Moldings. 

The above illustration gives the value of the different members and how they should be estimated. In general every 4" or fraction thereof, is counted as one member. One lin. ft. of member is approximately equal to the cost of one sq. ft. of plain work.

When there are returns on square members, such as pilaster bases, caps, etc., add 1 lin. ft. for each member stop. 

For members cut on a radius or circling members, add to the value of straight members.

For water drips under sills or coping, add 1 member for each lin. ft. of drip. 

For breaks on washes or members, add 1 member for each break.

When preparing an estimate on granite work requiring moldings, always count the number of members in the height and then multiply the length of the molding in lin. ft. by the rate per ft. As an example, assume there are 50 lin. ft. of molded course consisting of 10 members (measured as per schedule). 

Six-cut finish is worth $2.75 per lin. ft. per member or a molding containing 10 members would be worth $27.50 per lin. ft.; 

50 lin. ft. at $27.50 per lin. ft. equals $1,375.00, the cost of labor in connection with the molding. To this add the cost of the rough stock together with the labor cutting beds and joints.

Philadelphia Building Blocks* 

Philadelphia Granite building blocks are used for broken or range ashlar in the construction of houses, apartments, churches, schools, or any structure using this type of wall. The blocks may be set in a number of different ways, as shown in the accompanying illustrations.

They are furnished in two sizes as follows: Singles are furnished in blocks 14" to 19" long, 6" to 7" high and 3" to 4" thick. Doubles are furnished in blocks 14" to 19" long, 13" to 

15" high and 3" to 4" thick.

TERRA COTTA 

Terra cotta is a building material made of a high grade clay (usually a mixture of several different kinds), to which is added a percentage of calcined clay to uniformly control the shrinkage and prevent undue warping. 

Terra cotta is used for the same purposes as other building materials, like sandstone, limestone, granite, press brick, etc.; i.e., for interior or exterior trimmings or for entire fronts. It is also used extensively as glazed terra cotta for light courts, for the interior walls of swimming pools, operating rooms in hospitals, clinics and patients' rooms, corridors, vestibules and stair halls (full height of wainscot) and in large kitchens where a ceramic material is required for sanitary purposes as well as for fire resisting advantages. It is used for service stations, power houses and rooms housing machinery on account of the ease with which it can be kept free from dust, dirt and grease. 

Its unlimited possibilities in color effects make it an ideal material for store fronts. It is used as a lining for the interior of restaurants, palm courts, hotels, residences and railroad stations. In stations and public buildings it is also used in the construction of ceilings and domes. In fact, it is a universal building material and has the advantage over other materials in that it may be produced in almost any color and may be glazed or unglazed with any surface treatment desired. It furnishes unlimited possibilities to the architect not only in color effects, but *Varies according to distance from quarry. *North Carolina Granite Corp., Mount Airy, N. C.

in the beauty of the original modeling in the plastic clay, an effect that cannot be obtained in carved stone except at tremendous cost.

Method of Manufacturing Terra Cotta.-Models for the dif ferent pieces of terra cotta to be produced are made in plaster to a shrinkage scale; i.e., to an increased size to allow for the shrinkage in drying and burning. If the piece is ornamental, such ornament as may be required is modeled in clay by artists and attached to the plaster model. From this model a mold is made in plaster, and the number of pieces required are "pressed" from the mold in the soft clay mixture. The pieces are then thoroughly dried and burned to a temperature of approximately 

2,300 degrees Fahrenheit. Obviously, the more pieces there are exactly alike the lower the cost will be. 

Fifty pieces is about the limit that can be successfully produced from one mold, but if more are required additional molds can be made from the original model at small cost. 

Terra Cotta wall ashlar is made by extruding the soft clay from a die. After this stage the process of manufacture is about the same as for hand pressed terra cotta so that a high grade accurately sized material results. It is usually made with enamel or glaze finish but can be unglazed and offers the same choice of colors as the hand pressed terra cotta. As the cost of dies is considerable, duplication is an important item of cost. The manufacturers furnish catalogues showing standard shapes and sizes. 

Special pieces can be readily furnished by making models and moulds and pressing by hand. It is customary for the manufacturers to furnish complete layout drawings for the work. 

Cost of Terra Cotta. In estimating the cost of terra cotta there is no unit that may be taken as a definite basis for estimating. All estimates are usually made by the manufacturer in a lump sum price for the entire amount of terra cotta to be used on the building.

To arrive at the cost of the terra cotta it is necessary to figure same from the architect's plans and specifications. These should include floor plans, elevations, sections, and scale details. The elevations should indicate the character and amount of modeling. 

To estimate the cost of terra cotta a careful list of quantities is made from which is figured the cubical contents in much the

TERRA COTTA 

745 same way as in estimating cut stone. The weight is ascertained and this is used as a partial factor in ascertaining the cost. The determining factors, however, are the design of the work, character and amount of ornamentation, amount of duplication, sizes of pieces, supply and demand, etc. For this reason it is always advisable to obtain prices from the manufacturers wherever possible, as it is the custom of manufacturers to give exact bids from the plans and specifications furnished by the architect or contractor.

However, it is possible to figure an approximate cost of the terra cotta f.o.b. cars at the factory, to which it will be necessary to add freight and cartage from factory to destination. 

The cost of terra cotta in comparison with cut stone is a variable item, and will depend upon the locality in which the work is performed and the amount of carving in the job. 

On jobs having considerable ornamental work, terra cotta is frequently more economical material to use, especially where there is a reasonable amount of duplication of the ornamental parts; because by making one model for an ornamental portion it is possible to reproduce 50 to 100 pieces, while if cut stone is used each ornamental piece must be run through the machine separately or each carved piece must be completed by hand, which involves a great deal of extra labor. 

The cost of making models for terra cotta is always included in the terra cotta manufacturer's bid except in rare instances where the architect specifies that models will be supplied to the manufacturer, and then an allowance is usually made to cover this work.

Estimating Quantities of Terra Cotta.-When estimating quantities of terra cotta from the plans or details, all measurements should be squared; i.e., all molded courses, cornices, round columns, column caps, bases, coursed ashlar, sills, copings, etc., should be figured from the extreme dimensions and reduced to cubic feet.

The weight of terra cotta varies from about 80 lbs. per cu. ft. for plain 4" thick ashlar to 60 lbs. per cu. ft. for large moulded courses. For an average job about 72 lbs. per cu. ft., equivalent to 28 cu. ft. per ton of 2,000 lbs. may be used. 

After the quantities have been taken off the plans and reduced to cu. ft., they may either be priced in that manner, or multi-

1 plying the number of cu. ft. by 72 lbs. will give the total weight of the terra cotta required for the job. 

Terra Cotta wall ashlar 2" thick weighs about 16 lbs. per sq. ft.; 4" thick (2 cell block) about 23 lbs. per sq. ft. and 4" thick (wall bearing block) about 32 lbs. per sq. ft. 

Cost of Unglazed Terra Cotta.-Plain unglazed terra cotta is worth about $110.00 a ton, or $3.90 to $4.50 per cu. ft. f.o.b. factory, based on 28 cu. ft. to the ton. 

This price is the average price per ton for an entire job. It includes manufacture and fitting to exact sizes at the factory so that no cutting is necessary at the building, except where the dimensions are changed after the drawings have been approved by the architect. It includes the cost of plain mouldings and the simpler kinds of ornament, which in the case of cut stone work must be added to the basic price. It allows for lugs, water bars, and drips and washes for cornices and coping. 

The above price per ton applies to an average job where a reasonable amount of duplication of individual pieces occurs. 

The addition of simple repeating ornament allowing the same amount of duplication of individual pieces will not add greatly to the cost. Where there is little duplication either of plain or ornamental pieces it is advisable to apply to the manufacturer for prices.

Cost of Terra Cotta Wall Ashlar.-Terra Cotta wall ashlar is generally priced on a sq. ft. basis, counting the total exposed surface including reveals of openings. On an average job requiring a relatively small number of specials, 2″ thick material in glaze finish will cost from $0.70 to $0.80 per sq. ft. and 4″ thick material from $0.80 to $1.00 per sq. ft. including the necessary specials.

Cost of Glazed or Enameled Terra Cotta.-Glazed or enameled terra cotta is furnished in dull or shiny finish. The enamel finish is often mottled. The cost is about 10 per cent higher than that of unglazed terra cotta. 

Cost of Unglazed Granite Terra Cotta.-Unglazed granite terra cotta is made in various colors to resemble the different natural granites. The cost is about 10 per cent higher than that of one color unglazed terra cotta. 

Cost of Glazed Granite Terra Cotta.-Glazed granite terra cotta having a smooth glaze finish resembling polished granite

TERRA COTTA 

747 will cost about 15 per cent more than one color unglazed terra cotta. 

Polychrome, Ceramic Gold and Ceramic Silver.-The term polychrome is used when two or more colors are applied to the same piece. Polychrome terra cotta may be either glazed or unglazed. The additional cost is figured by the sq. ft. and depends upon the intricacy of the color scheme (number and distribution of colors) and may vary from $0.25 to $1.50 per sq. ft. 

Ceramic gold and ceramic silver finishes consist of the pure metals applied to glazed terra cotta after it has been burned. 

They require a second burning. The additional cost is figured on the actual surface to be covered and runs from $1.50 to $4.00 per sq. ft.

Drawings for Terra Cotta.-Manufacturers of terra cotta make a point of rendering special service to the architect in the matter of preparing drawings. Shop scale drawings are prepared from the architect's small scale drawings, and are submitted for approval before proceeding with the work. The terra cotta manufacturer usually makes, at his own expense, all of the full sized details. In addition, photographs showing the modeling of the ornament are made by the manufacturer and submitted for the architect's approval. 

Handling and Setting Terra Cotta. The labor cost of hand ling and setting terra cotta will vary with the sizes of the different pieces, the amount of duplication and the method used in handling and setting same.

Terra cotta weighs about one-half as much as stone, so that it is seldom necessary to use derricks in handling and setting, as it is usually furnished in sizes that can be conveniently handled by 2 or 3 men. Considerable space is usually required on the job for storing the terra cotta, as it is sent to the job each piece marked to show its exact position in the building and must be carefully handled and placed in convenient piles for use as required. When handling the terra cotta on the job it is customary to load it into wheelbarrows or stone barrows and wheel it to the location where it is to be used. However, if it is necessary to hoist it to the upper floors or roof of the building the barrows can be placed on the material hoist, raised to the proper floor and then wheeled to the location where it is to be set. 

Inasmuch as a great deal of terra cotta consists of trimmings

or 4" ashlar, it requires considerable handling to set a cubic foot. For instance, most ashlar being 4" thick, it is necessary to set terra cotta in 3 sq. ft. of wall to set one cu. ft. This also applies to sills, lintels, etc. 

Based on the average job consisting of ashlar, sills, lintels, ornamental trimmings, etc., a mason will set about 45 to 50 cu. ft. (135 to 150 sq. ft. wall) per 8-hr. day, at the following cost per 100 cu. ft.:

In general, terra cotta is only filled as far out as the face of the wall, projecting portions being left unfilled, thus cutting down the weight of the overhanging construction. 

Filling is not generally regarded as either necessary or desirable in free standing work, such as for example, balusters, etc. 

All supporting iron should be firmly imbedded in masonry and

TERRA COTTA 

749 completely covered with mortar to prevent rusting. Bronze or other non-corrosive metal or cadmium coated steel anchors should invariably be used for suspended features or for anchoring or bracing free standing work. 

Cost of Setting Terra Cotta.-Most any mason or stone setter experienced in the construction of present day buildings is able to set terra cotta satisfactorily. 

Most manufacturers of terra cotta are able to supply a mechanic experienced in handling and setting terra cotta who will work under the local trade union rules. This man will sort the material as it arrives at the building and plan the erection of same in the most expeditious manner. The manufacturers usually charge the current rate of brick layers' wages in the larger cities plus traveling expenses from headquarters to destination and return for this service. Many contractors have found this method satisfactory, and find that it effects a considerable saving in time and money.

Mortar Required for Setting Terra Cotta.-Under average conditions it will require about 4 cu. ft. of mortar to set one ton of terra cotta, or about 4-cu. yd. of mortar per 100 cu. ft. 

The following proportions are recommended as being suitable for making satisfactory mortar for setting terra cotta: One part standard portland cement, one part lime putty and six parts sand.

Do not under any circumstances use plaster of Paris or salt in the mortar.

All exposed joints in projecting and overhanging features, parapet work, and work standing free, should be raked out and pointed with a good asphaltic elastic cement. 

Never use a cement that swells in setting for filling the voids in terra cotta. Use only the best quality of cement.

Cleaning Down or Washing Terra Cotta.-Broadly speaking, there are three different surface finishes in Terra Cotta; lustrous glazed, matt glazed and unglazed. The glazed surfaces are the easiest to clean.

For both lustrous and matt glazed finishes a good abrasive soap or washing powder is best. Where required, there can be added to the latter a slight proportion of sharp sand. A stiff lather should be made and the surface scrubbed hard, allowing the lather to remain long enough to soften the dirt and then rinse off with clean water. Acid is not necessary for cleaning glazed surfaces.

In cleaning unglazed terra cotta the addition of a slight proportion of commercial muriatic acid is recommended. The proportion of acid to water may be varied. One quart of acid to 4 gallons of water is sufficient in ordinary cases. In no event should it exceed 13 pints of acid to one gallon of water and care should be taken to rinse off shortly after applying. 

Where acid is employed use only wooden pails and fiber brushes. Metal pails cause a chemical reaction under which the solution becomes a yellow stain instead of a cleaning fluid. 

Do not permit hydrofluoric acid to be used. Many cleaners in order to save hand labor employ strong solutions of this which are highly injurious.

When washing down unglazed terra cotta, a tuck pointer should clean 400 to 500 sq. ft. of surface per 8-hr. day, at the following cost per 100 sq. ft.:
