Pointing Terra Cotta.-Recommended practice today is to strike the joints as the work progresses. Pointing mortar applied afterward is usually of different composition and accordingly of questionable permanency.

CHAPTER XIII ROUGH CARPENTRY 

To estimate carpentry quantities and costs accurately, the estimator should possess a working knowledge of the trade and be familiar with job conditions. He should know how the various classes of work are constructed; where joists and studs should be doubled; where to place wood furring strips for walls and floors; openings requiring wood bucks, and where it is necessary to place wood grounds. These may appear to be small items but they are important, nevertheless. I recall on one job where the estimator taking off the carpentry quantities had figured wood bucks for all exterior window frames. He could read plans but was an “inside” man and did not know how work was constructed on the job. Your estimator is like your fire insurance-an expense until you have a fire—and then it is the most highly treasured document in your possession. 

When taking off lumber quantities from the plans, always estimate as closely as possible the exact quantity of each kind of lumber required. Some contractors estimate the cost of wood floors at a certain price per sq. ft. including joists, bridging, sub-floor, deadening felt, furring strips and the finish wood flooring. Entering into the construction of such a floor are materials and labor operations of widely varying costs; yet certain contractors are content to estimate their work in this haphazard manner, and at the completion of the job have no more idea of their labor costs than before they took the job.

When estimating labor costs of rough carpentry, bear in mind the costs will vary with the class of work performed, with the ability of the carpenters employed and with the experience and executive ability of the foreman or superintendent in charge of the work. 

Modern tools, such as electric hand saws, electric drills, sanders, etc., play a big part in reducing labor costs. For 751

instance an electric hand-saw will cut off a 2″x12″ plank in 4 or 5 seconds while it takes about a minute to do it by hand; it takes 4 to 5 minutes to rip a 12'-0" plank 2″ thick when sawing by hand while an electric handsaw will do the work in less than a minute. In other words, an electric saw will cut 

10 to 20 times as fast as can be done by hand. The handling cost remains the same in either instance but when sawing for any length of time, a man can turn out three or four times as much work with an electric saw as by hand. 

Another thing that should be considered is the cost of filing saws where there are a number of carpenters working. This will vary with the condition of the saw but on an average it will require -hr. to file a saw by hand, while an automatic saw filer will do the same work in 4-hr. The same applies to circular saws used on saw rigs or electric hand saws, as these can be filed in to -hr. by machine, while hand filing requires nearly twice as much time. 

The same thing applies to the use of electric drills, electric sanders, etc., so the contractor who is going to keep up with the procession must use modern, labor-saving tools and equipment wherever possible.

Here is another thing that should be remembered by every contractor. No matter how carefully the plans have been measured and how much consideration they have been given before pricing, if the work is not executed in a businesslike manner, careful estimating will not avert losses.

Estimating Lumber Quantities 

When estimating the quantity of lumber required for any job, the only safe method is to take off every piece of lumber required to complete that portion of the work. This is seldom done, however, and the following tables are given to simplify the work as much as possible and at the same time provide accurate material quantities.

Estimating Wood Joists.-When estimating wood joists, always allow 4" to 6" on each end of the joist for bearing on the wall.

To obtain the number of joists required for any floor, take the length of the floor in feet and divide by the distance the joists are spaced apart, then add 1 to allow for the extra joist required at end of span.

ROUGH CARPENTRY 

753 Example: If the floor is 28 ft. long and 15 ft. wide, it will require 16-ft. joists to allow for wall bearing at each end. 

Assuming the joists are spaced 16" on centers, one joist will be required every 16" or every 13 ft. In other words it will require as many joists as the length of the span, plus one. 

Three-quarters of 28 equal 21, plus 1 extra joist at end, makes 

22 joists 16 ft. long for this space.

Joists 16'-0" to 20'-0" long will require 2 double rows of bridging or 4 pcs. to each joist.

Framing Wood Houses To Prevent Plaster Cracks, Sagging Floors, Sticking Doors and Damage Caused by "Settlement" 

or Shrinkage

One of the greatest defects in wood house framing and the one causing the most trouble for contractors and builders is the damage caused by "settlement" of the building. Fully ninety per cent of this damage is caused by the shrinkage of lumber used in framing the house and is not due to faulty foundations, as is commonly believed. 

Lumber shrinks in width and thickness but the shrinkage lengthwise is negligible, so to prevent the unsightly and costly damage caused by lumber shrinkage, avoid the use of "sidegrain" bearing lumber.

There are three general types of house framing used in this country, i. e., (1) platform framing, (2) the braced frame and (3) the balloon frame, the merits and defect of each are discussed in the following paragraphs:

One Defect Common To All Types of Framing.-One defect common to all types of house framing is the practice of using a wood beam or girder through the center of the house to support the first floor joists because when this beam or girder shrinks in width, it causes the entire interior of the house to sag toward the center, which in turn ruins decorations, causes plaster cracks at wall and ceiling intersections, in the corners of rooms and over doors, pulls the interior door frames out of square, necessitating planing the tops and sides of doors so they will open and close and requires the adjustment of lock strikes. 

Never use a wood beam or girder through the center of the house to support the ends of the first floor joists but instead use a steel or concrete beam or a masonry wall. 

Where the Greatest Amount of Shrinkage Occurs In House 

Framing. The greatest amount of shrinkage occurs in the floor joists and in the wood plates used at the top and bottom of the wood partition studs. When the floor joists shrink, everything resting on them settles down equal to the amount of shrinkage in the joists and plates and this further increases the damage to the interior of the house, damage that is practically impossible to repair satisfactorily, regardless of cost. 

Methods of overcoming the shrinkage damage caused by joist shrinkage are fully described in the following paragraphs.

Roof boards

The Western or "Platform" Method of Framing Uses More Side-Grain 

Bearing Lumber than any other and Develops the Greatest Amount of Shrinkage

ROUGH CARPENTRY 

765 

The Platform Frame.—The platform frame is extensively used. 

It is similar in construction to the Braced Frame except that it has boxed sill construction at each floor line. This makes for greater shrinkage but it is equalized on each floor when a similar type of construction is used under bearing partitions. 

The disadvantages of the Platform Frame are as follows: (1) 

requires more lumber than any other method; (2) requires more labor to frame; (3) weakest frame because the first and second stories are not tied together at the first story ceiling line; (4) offers less resistance to wind and cyclone than the balloon frame; (5) uses more side-grain bearing lumber than the balloon type frame; (6) develops more shrinkage than any other type frame, and (7) no space is provided for heating ducts without cutting top and bottom plates, which reduces stiffness of walls and partitions. 

The Braced Frame. This type of frame is an outgrowth of

New England solid timber post and girth construction. Instead of heavy posts set 8 or 10-ft. apart, the walls are built of 2x4-in. studs set 16-in. on centers. Diagonal bracing is inserted at the corners. This is a better type of framing than the Platform 

Frame but it still requires more lumber than the balloon type frame, as well as more labor to frame. On account of the studs running only one story in height, it offers less resistance to wind and cyclone because the first and second stories are not tied together at the first story ceiling line. It also develops slightly more shrinkage than the balloon type frame and does not provide for heating ducts in the walls without cutting top and bottom plates, which reduces stiffness of walls and partitions.

The Balloon Frame. This type of frame has many things to recommend it. The one piece studs, extending the full height of the wall and tied together by the ribband at the second floor line reduce to a minimum the shrinkage factor. It is strong and rigid but requires careful fire stopping.

The Walker "Shrink-Proof" Method of Framing. This method of framing incorporates the advantages of the Balloon Type frame and eliminates shrinkage damage by using light steel members to support and reinforce the wood framing at vulnerable points. For instance, non-shrinkable steel ribbands are used to support the second floor joists instead of shrinkable wood rib-

bands. Non-shrinkable steel plates are used on the top of interior bearing partitions instead of shrinkable wood plates, with the result that all shrinkage in the length of the outside stud walls and interior bearing partitions is eliminated. ition and Stud Wall Bracing 10 

The Walker "Shrink-Proof" Method of Framing Which Develops a 

Minimum Amount of Shrinkage

Interior wood partitions are usually set on top of the wood floor joists. This is very bad practice because the greatest amount of shrinkage usually occurs in the joists and when the joists shrink, down come the partitions and everything bearing on them, resulting in more costly damage. The Walker "Shrink- 

Proof" Method prevents this destructive damage by placing pressed steel shoes over the top of the joists, which extend to

ROUGH CARPENTRY 

767 within 1-in. of the bottom, where they are secured by nails. The wood partition studs are set on top of these shoes. When the joists shrink, the partitions cannot settle with them because they are held up at their original height by the steel shoes, thus maintaining the interior of the building in perfect condition. It is very simple and inexpensive and can be used on the lowest cost houses and apartments.

ROUGH CARPENTRY 

769 There are 39 inches of side-grain bearing lumber used in this construction, and when using lumber kiln-dried to 12 per cent moisture content, it will still shrink about -in. in width. When using thoroughly air seasoned lumber containing 15 per cent moisture content, the shrinkage will be about 1 inches in width. 

If the lumber contains 18 per cent moisture content it will shrink 1 inches in width and if it contains 20 per cent moisture content, the shrinkage will amount to 13 inches. 

Just think how this shrinkage damages the house. It causes stucco to crack and buckle off the outside walls at the first and second floor level where shrinkage is the greatest and causes brick veneer to dislocate door and window frames and throw them out of plumb.

The damage to the interior of the house is even greater because the shrinkage causes unsightly plaster cracks in the corners of rooms and at the intersection of walls and ceilings. 

It causes the floors to sag toward the center of the house, throwing door frames out of square, causing the doors to stick at the tops and sides, necessitating planing them off so they will open and close—in fact, it causes damage that is practically impossible to repair satisfactorily, regardless of cost. 

Compare This With the Walker "Shrink-Proof" Method.— 

Note how the Walker "Shrink-Proof" Method eliminates the use of side-grain bearing lumber at vulnerable points, thus preventing all of the costly damage enumerated above.

When the Walker "Shrink-Proof" Method of framing is used the shrinkage in the length of the outside stud walls and main bearing partitions amounts to only 1/20 of an inch against to 13 inches when ordinary methods are used. 

The slight cost of the Walker "Shrink-Proof" method of framing pays for itself many times over the first year the house is completed by reducing repair bills, eliminating plaster patching, planing off tops and sides of sticking doors, adjusting locks, redecorating, etc., plus the added satisfaction to the owner, architect and builder during the entire life of the building.

Labor Framing Lumber in Building Construction 

The labor quantities and costs given in the following pages are intended to include all classes of frame construction, such as houses, bungalows, barns, stables, apartment buildings, store and apartment buildings, country clubs, school houses, and in fact all buildings that are constructed entirely of wood or have brick, stone, tile or cement block walls and wood joists, rafters, stud walls, partitions, wood sub-floors, wall and roof sheathing, finish wood floors, etc.

Costs are given on two classes of workmanship. The classification "Ordinary Workmanship" is intended to cover the grade of workmanship encountered in most of our present day buildings where price is a factor.  designates the grade of workmanship demanded where quality is a factor as well as price, and is usually found in high-grade residences, apartments, hotel and office buildings, public buildings, high school, college and university buildings, etc. 

The estimator must use his own judgment as to the grade of workmanship required, depending upon the type of building, the reputation of the architect, and the requirements of the 

Another thing that is going to govern labor costs is the kind of equipment used, as the contractor who uses electric hand saws, drills, etc., will not have any trouble in outdistancing his competitors who are still doing business on the old "hand-saw" 

basis.

Framing and Erecting Exterior Stud Walls for Frame Build ings. The labor cost of framing and erecting stud walls is subject to wide variation, depending upon the type of building, height and regularity of the walls, etc. 

The framing on square or rectangular buildings, such as colonial type houses and buildings of similar shape and construction will cost much less to frame than English type houses, having walls of irregular shape and height. 

When you consider that the average house requires only 1,500 to 2,500 ft. of lumber, for outside stud walls, it shows just how much labor is required to frame it.

WOOD SHINGLES 

The labor cost of laying wood shingles will vary with the type of roof, whether a plain gable roof, a steep roof or one cut up with gables, dormers, etc. Also with the manner in which they are laid, whether with regular butts, irregular or staggered butts, or thatched butts.

The costs given on the following pages are based on the actual number of shingles a man will lay per day and not upon the number of squares covered, as this will vary with the spacing of the shingles. It does not make any particular difference to the shingler whether the shingles are laid 4", 4" or 5″ to the

weather, as he will lay practically the same number either way. 

It does make considerable difference in the number of sq. ft. of surface covered, which will vary from 10 to 40%. 

The number of shingles laid will vary with the ability of the workman and the class of work, as ordinary carpenters will not lay as many shingles as carpenters who specialize in shingle laying. On the other hand, experienced shinglers usually demand a higher wage rate than ordinary carpenters. 

Some carpenters claim to be able to lay 16 bunches, (4,000 shingles) per 8-hr. day, but this is unusual and is generally found only on the cheapest grade of work where only one nail is driven into each shingle instead of two that are necessary to secure a workmanlike job.

Estimating the Quantity of Wood Shingles.-Ordinary wood shingles are furnished in random widths, but 1,000 shingles are equivalent to 1,000 shingles 4" wide.

Dimension shingles are sawed to a uniform width, being either 4", 5" or 6" wide. 

Stained shingles, such as Creo-Dipt, Weatherbest, etc., are usually sold by the square based on sufficient shingles to lay 100 sq. ft. of surface, when laid 5″ to the weather. 

When estimating the quantity of ordinary wood shingles required to cover any roof, bear in mind that the distance the shingles are laid to the weather makes considerable difference in the actual quantity required.

There are 144 sq. in. in 1 sq. ft. and an ordinary shingle is 4" wide. When laid with 4" exposed to the weather, each shingle covers 16 sq. in. or it requires 9 shingles per sq. ft. of surface. There are 100 sq. ft. in a Square. 100×9=900, and allowing 10% to cover the double row of shingles at the eaves, waste in cutting, narrow shingles, etc., it will require 990 shingles per 100 sq. ft. of surface.

WOOD BOWSTRING TRUSSES* 

Wood bowstring trusses are extensively used for roofs in any type of building requiring clear floor space, such as automobile garages, airplane factories and hangars at air ports, gymnasiums, auditoriums, bowling alleys, dance halls, and other buildings where a large, unobstructed floor space is essential. 

When designed by a competent truss engineer they give entire satisfaction and can be used on spans from 30 to 130 ft. with absolute safety. On moderate spans the truss can be designed to carry lath and plaster ceilings on the lower chords and where necessary, small balconies for light storage. 

A wood truss costs much less than a steel truss and is better in case of fire, as a wood truss withstands heat for a considerable time and water can be applied without danger of the truss or roof collapsing, whereas in steel, failure occurs at 1100° F. 

Wood Bowstring Truss.

The price of wood bowstring trusses varies considerably in different parts of the country, due to the building ordinances, as some cities require only 25 lb. live load while others require a 

50 lb. live load, which requires heavier construction and consequently costs more.

Prices on roof trusses are governed by the following conditions: 

1. Cost of material and labor. 

2. Loading conditions and spacing. 

3. Difficulties of erection.

Spacing of wood roof trusses is usually 16′-0″ to 20′-0″ on centers, but the prices given are based on 18'-0". 

It is advisable to obtain prices from the manufacturers* either for the trusses delivered at the building site or erected in place, as they are familiar with conditions in practically all 

American Roof Truss Company, Inc., Chicago, Ills.

Labor Erecting Wood Bowstring Trusses.-A gin pole is ordinarily used for erecting wood bowstring trusses. 

The labor cost of erecting them will vary with job conditions, as deep excavations, piles of brick, mortar boxes, lumber piles, etc., in the way of the derricks, will prevent the erecting crew from making as good time as where a clear unobstructed space is available.

Framing and Erecting Exterior Stud Walls. The exterior stud walls for the two English type houses illustrated on pages 568 and 805 were very irregular, as can be plainly seen from the illustrations, requiring an unusually large amount of cutting and framing for the various height walls, offsets, irregularities, etc.

One thing that made this work cost so much was the method used in framing all stud walls and partitions. The studs were not set on top of the rough floors as is usually the case, but run through the rough floors and the ends of the 2"x4" studs either rested on masonry walls or steel "I" beams. This was done to eliminate plaster cracks due to shrinkage in the lumber. While it was very expensive, it was well worth while

because the completed buildings showed practically no plaster cracks. 

There were 8,000 ft. b.m. of 2"x4" studs in the job, and a carpenter framed and erected only 150 ft. b.m. per 8-hr. day, at the following labor cost per 1,000 ft.:

 Carpenter Labor

Rules for Grading Hardwood Flooring.-In many instances the specifications of the architects and owners are confusing and not in accordance with the standard rules for grading as adopted by the manufacturers. The rules adopted by the flooring manufacturers are given below, so that they may be compared with the architects' specifications, and the proper grade of flooring figured.

Hard Maple Flooring 

First Grade.-Shall have one face free of all defects, but the question of color shall not be considered. Standard lengths in all widths in this grade shall be trimmed 2 ft. and up; the proportion of lengths, 2 to 3 ft. shall be what the stock will produce up to 15 per cent. 

Second Grade.-Will admit of tight, sound knots and slight imperfections in dressing, but must lay without waste. Stand-

WOOD FLOORS 

821 ard lengths in all widths of this grade shall be trimmed 11 ft. and upward; the proportion of lengths, 1 to 3 ft., shall be what the stock will produce up to 30 per cent. 

Third Grade.-Must be of such character as will lay and give a good serviceable floor, with some cutting. Standard lengths in all widths of this grade shall be trimmed 1 ft. and up; the proportion of lengths, 1 to 3 ft., shall be what the stock will produce up to 50 per cent. 

Beech and Birch Flooring 

Clear Red.-Shall show 75 per cent red on the face, free from all defects, and is manufactured in " and " thickness. 

Standard lengths 2 ft. and up. 

Clear. Shall have one face free from all defects, but the question of color shall not be considered. Standard lengths in all widths in this grade shall be trimmed 2 ft. and up; the proportion of lengths, 2 to 3 ft., shall be what the stock will produce up to 15 per cent.

Oak Flooring 

Effective January 1st, 1931, the Oak Flooring Manufacturers

Association changed the grade names of oak flooring that are more fittingly descriptive of the special qualities and particular uses of the various grades of lumber. 

Quarter Sawed Oak Flooring.-Quarter sawed oak flooring is now furnished in three grades, Clear, Sap Clear and Select. 

There has been no change in the existing grading rules except for the names.

Plain Sawed Oak Flooring.-Plain sawed oak flooring is furnished in four grades, Clear, Select, No. 1 Common and

No. 2 Common. There has been no change in the existing grading rules except for the names.

Laying and Finishing Wood Floors 

The following pages contain detailed itemized costs of laying and finishing all kinds of soft and hardwood floors. 

In the larger cities there are carpenters who make a specialty of laying and finishing floors and they seldom do any other kind of work. Due to their long experience, they not only do a much better job but accomplish far more work per day than the average carpenter and they expect to be paid accordingly. 

For this reason costs are given for floors laid and finished by both carpenters and floorlayers.

Some floorlayers agree to lay and finish floors at a certain price per sq. ft., and when taken on this basis the men usually work harder than when paid by the day. An allowance of 25% should be added to all floorlayers' time to provide for this bonus. 

Costs are given on two classes of workmanship. The first or 

Ordinary Workmanship includes the grade of work found in moderate priced homes, apartments, stores, etc., where the floorlaying permits of some hammer marks and is not a "bangup" job in every respect. 

 includes all classes of high class buildings where the best in workmanship is required, with all flooring closely driven up, laid free from hammer marks and with all nails set.

The same thing applies to sanding and finishing floors. 

Ordinary workmanship consists of scraping and sanding the floor to produce a presentable job but under manship, the floors are scraped, traversed and sanded to produce a fine smooth finish. The Highest Grade workmanship requires that the floors be planed, traversed, scraped by hand and then brought to an absolutely smooth finish with fine sand paper. 

This class of work is usually found only in quarter sawed oak or parquetry floors. 

Removing Wax or Varnish From Old Hardwood Floors.- 

Where necessary to remove old wax or varnish finish from old hardwood floors, a floorlayer should remove the old finish from 700 to 800 sq. ft. per 8-hr. day, depending upon the condition of the old floors and the thickness of the finish. One gallon of varnish remover should be sufficient for 250 to 300 sq. ft. of floor.

Surfacing Floors by Machine

The cost of sanding and finishing wood floors by machine is subject to the same conditions as hand work, i.e., kind of flooring, whether old or new work, class of workmanship, size of rooms, and amount of hand finishing around edges of rooms. 

With some machines it is necessary to hand finish from 6" to 12" around the edge of each room while others will surface to within an inch or two of the edge. 

The class of workmanship also governs production but where just an ordinary grade of workmanship is required in average size rooms in houses, apartments, offices, etc., a good machine and operator should finish 900 to 1,100 sq. ft. per 8-hr. day, at the following cost per 100 sq. ft.:

Parquetry Flooring 

When laying wood carpet or parquetry floors in residences, apartments, ballrooms, or other buildings where a floor of this kind is desired, experienced floorlayers should be used where possible.

While a carpenter may be able to lay the floor if given sufficient time, an experienced floorlayer will accomplish more work in a more satisfactory manner and at less expense than when carpenters are used.

It is advisable to have a hardwood flooring firm perform the work, as the job will not only be much more satisfactory to the owner and architect, but will be completed at less expense to the contractor than where he attempts to perform the work with ordinary carpenters.

The costs given on the following pages are for First Grade workmanship, and are intended to include rooms of average size with not too much cutting and fitting for irregular sized rooms, bays, pilasters, etc.

When estimating work of this kind in the smaller cities and towns where floorlaying contractors are not to be found or where it is not possible to obtain experienced floorlayers, it will be necessary for the architect or contractor to add transportation for floorlayers from the nearest city where they may be obtained, or from Chicago where good men are to be found at all times. Also make an allowance of $12.00 a week for board of men while performing the work. 

How to Lay Wood Carpet or Parquetry Floors.-The follow ing rules for handling, laying, and finishing wood carpet or parquetry floors were furnished through the courtesy of one of the largest manufacturers* of hardwood and parquetry flooring in the United States. 

*Wood Mosaic Company, Louisville, Ky. 

*Hand finishing time will vary with size of rooms and kind of machine used.

Before attempting to lay wood carpet or parquetry floors in a building, see that the building is perfectly dry, as flooring of this kind is kiln dried, and if placed in damp buildings, it is subject to great damage.

How Parquetry Flooring is Furnished.-The flooring that can be laid with the greatest ease and economy is" thick with square edge. The most popular and best designs in this thickness are shown on the following pages. These patterns can also be purchased ", ", or " thick if desired. The fancy designs are furnished glued to a backing, and the plain ones are furnished in separate pieces of solid oak with tongue and groove on edges. 

The borders are made up in 12 ft. lengths. The fancy fields are made up in convenient sized slabs for laying. The simple oak designs are composed of 13″ or 2″ slats assembled in squares, hexagons, etc., on canvas. This canvas is simply to hold together the carefully selected slats or short strips in a convenient form for handling until the flooring is nailed down. 

The herringbone pattern (No. 706) is supplied in separate pieces. 

How to Lay the Floor.-Nail all loose boards in underfloor to the joists. Wide boards curl and shrink, and so affect the parquetry.

It is therefore necessary to nail these with particular thoroughness.

Traverse the floor with a jack plane until all inequalities are taken out. Unless the thin parquetry be in contact with the lower floor in every part, it will break when heavy furniture is placed over the hollow places. 

Square the room with a chalk line and mark the boundaries of field and border upon the floor. In doing this, leave the space for the field of such a size to necessitate as little cutting of the sections as possible. Lay out the goods along one side and end of the room to see how they are coming out. 

If the room is out of square, divide the inequalities between the opposite sides by putting in more or fewer wall strips as occasion requires.

As to which part should be laid first there is a diversity of practice, and much may be left to the judgment of the mechanic. 

Some prefer this order: (1) the wall strips, (2) the border, (3) the field. Under some conditions it may be best to reverse the order and lay the field first, but we think it best, generally, to lay first the wall strips and border along one side and one end of the room, then the field, and finally the border and wall strips on the remaining end and side. All sections must be pressed up as tightly as possible by chisel driven into the floor below. In laying thin strips an easy method is to lay down, ahead of the layer, enough to cover about 18 inches

or 2 feet. Nail down a small waste piece beyond this breadth, and drive a wedged shaped bit of wood between this piece and the breadth of strips. This enables operator to use both hands to nail the strips instead of holding the pried over chisel with one hand. 

We may say that thin strips 13" wide are much easier to handle and squeeze up in breadths than the 2" width. This width also requires fewer nails per sq. ft., and consequently less setting (or punching) and less puttying (or cementing) of nail holes. 

Use steel wire brads 13" long of 15 gauge. On another page, we show the number of nails required for the different varieties of thin goods. We may say that it is not advisable to put in all the nails as you go.

About one-fourth of the entire number of nails should be put in at once as you lay the floors. After the floor is laid complete go over the whole floor promptly, and thoroughly nail as per directions. 

Set nails about one-sixteenth-inch below the surface, using set (or punch) no larger than the head of the nails. 

In making a mitre you may have a small block that is not large enough to nail. In such a case glue the block in and lay the next section close up to it. 

How to Finish the Floor.-All flooring leaves the factory perfectly smooth. After nailing down, however, it will be necessary to go over the whole floor and smooth it perfectly, as it will certainly not be absolutely true and free from projecting edges or corners. One who is accustomed to the use of a plane and unfamiliar with the Stanley Veneer Scraper will doubtless prefer to use the plane. This scraper is so much easier to use if one knows anything of turning over the edges of the blade that we certainly recommend its use. A small cabinet maker's scraper is used to finish off the scraping, and goes into the corners, etc., where the veneer scraper cannot reach. If the entire floor is gone over with this (after the veneer scraper) less sandpapering will be required. 

Sandpapering.-Go over the floor thoroughly with No. 1 sandpaper. A block of wood or cork about 2"x4"x6" in size is a good thing to wrap sandpaper around while rubbing floor.

Filling. Fill with a good wood filler colored to match the wood or a little darker. The use of a somewhat darker filler on quartered oak causes the pores of the wood to fill dark while the filler rubs off the quartered figure, enhancing the prominence with which it stands out. This greatly improves

the appearance of the floor. We supply dry filler mixed to shade and requiring only binder of oil and thinning with turpentine to be ready for use. Fillers should be reduced to the consistency of a thin paint. Apply with rag, rubbing thoroughly into pores of wood. 

Some of the silex fillers must be left only a few minutes or they will set too hard. Our filler may be left for an hour or more. The rubbing off may be done with the scraper shavings, final rub being given with a piece of burlap. 

The filled floor may well be left over night, but we do not consider it necessary to wait more than an hour or so before a very much diluted coat of finish can be put on. This coat of finish, diluted with alcohol, is for the purpose of fixing the color of the filled floor before puttying nail holes. 

Burn all rags and shavings used around a floor at once, or you may have a case of spontaneous combustion. 

Puttying.-Next fill the nail holes with putty colored to match the wood. Do not have the putty too thin lest the oil be absorbed by the wood around the nail holes, thus making these more conspicuous. We will supply coloring matter to match the different woods in dry form, which must be worked into putty until desired shade is reached. A dash of finish over the first few holes puttied will prove if you have the right shade of putty. It is well now to go over the floor with a small piece of clean sandpaper, removing possible putty smudges from around the edges of the nail holes.

The procedure when laying thicker flooring (" to 3") with tongue and groove is the same, excepting that the puttying of nail heads is omitted. Different sized nails for varying thicknesses are used to nail down each piece through the tongue. 

Finish. Two good coats of finish should now be given to the entire floor, leaving suitable time for drying between the coats. Rub down surface of the last coat slightly with No. 1 steel wool to get rid of the objectionable varnishy shine; "rubbing flat" this is called.

In bath rooms where it is impossible to keep water off the floor, we have recommended Liquid Granite as it is water-proof. 

Like all varnishes, however, it covers and disguises the grain of the wood. We only recommend it in such extreme cases.

At first the wax will not flow, but the heat of the hand and the friction will soon cause a thin film to be deposited on the floor. See how little you can put on and yet know that it is there. A slight coating polishes best. Let the wax stand for half an hour or more and rub with weighted brush. Rub first in one direction and then at right angles thereto. Method of Laying Parquetry Floors.-If house, location, and general atmospheric conditions are dry, nails may be omitted in smaller maple, mahogany, and other colored blocks and fewer nails used in the larger colored blocks. In very damp seashore localities it would be well to put an occasional nail in colored woods in designs such as No. 711. The oak blocks should always be nailed just as shown. Strips may be nailed every 6″ under favorable conditions as above mentioned.

Plank or Colonial Decking 

Plank or Colonial decking is extensively used for finish floors in fine buildings. It is more expensive than ordinary "square edge flooring and is furnished 13" thick and in random widths from 4" to 8" and in random lengths. It may be laid either with keys or plugs or with "cracklines of dark wood, as preferred.

The boards are made 3-ply" thick, with a cross core and veneer top and bottom which run lengthwise of the piece. 

They are also furnished in solid boards (not veneered), " thick and in various widths, the same as veneered, and while the solid decking furnishes a satisfactory floor, for a real high grade job the veneered decking is preferable. 

The illustrations on pages 849 and 850 show the different methods of laying this decking.

Mastic Wood Block Flooring 

Mastic wood block flooring consists of wood blocks, embedded in a special mastic adhesive, laid directly on concrete. The mastic itself is similar in appearance to tar or pitch, but it, however, remains slightly plastic. This assures a thorough and lasting bond between the wood blocks and the concrete. 

By the use of mastic wood block flooring, wood sub-floors are eliminated but the concrete sub-floors must be troweled perfectly level and smooth to receive the wood flooring. 

The flooring is usually furnished in sizes 24"x13"x18", with tongued and grooved edges and with both ends grooved for laying in separate, individual pieces in Herringbone design. 

The blocks should also be provided with flat backs and with mastic grooves on all four lower edges to prevent surplus mastic from squeezing up to the surface of the floor. 

Grades of Mastic Wood Block Oak Flooring.-Mastic wood block Oak flooring is furnished in four grades, in standard size blocks, 2"x13"x1" face, for laying in Herringbone designs or squares. 

First Grade, "Clear".-Clear heartwood, free from sap, for use where light colored or almost natural colored finish is required. 

Second Grade and Better, "Residential".-Approximately 35% of blocks permitting clear sap (2nd grade), but otherwise clear. The modern finish of almost all floors is somewhat dark; therefore shade and color are not considered in this grade. 

Recommended for most residences and finer apartment buildings. 

Third Grade and Better, "Commercial".-Approximately 45% first grade; balance 2nd and 3rd grades. In addition to clear sap, the 3rd grade blocks permit other minor defects such as stained sap, dark streaks, occasional small pin knots and now and then a pin worm hole. This grade is recommended for many houses, for most apartments and office buildings. 

Fourth Grade, "Sub-Floor".-This grade was originally intended for laying in mastic, on concrete as a base, to which surface floors in period designs, fancy parquetry, etc., would

PARQUETRY FLOORING 

855 be nailed. It contains knots, imperfections in milling, worm holes and even knot holes. Considerable quantities of this grade have been used by floor-laying concerns for use in Sunday school community rooms, cafeterias, basket ball rooms, etc. 

Usually from 5 to 10% of the blocks have to be thrown aside to make a solid, serviceable floor.

CHAPTER XIV MILL WORK AND INTERIOR FINISH 

When estimating the labor cost of erecting mill work and interior finish, it is advisable for the estimator to ascertain the grade of workmanship required by the architect or owner, as the quantity of work a man will perform per hr. or per day will vary considerably with the grade of workmanship required. 

The costs given on the following pages embody two distinct grades of workmanship. The grade termed "Ordinary Work" is by far the most common and is usually found in medium priced residences, bungalows, "flat" or apartment buildings, apartment buildings with stores underneath, factory and warehouse buildings, non-fireproof store, office and school buildings, and other buildings of this class. 

The other grade, known as "”, is usually required in finishing fine residences, high-class fireproof apartments, hotel, bank and office buildings, high grade store buildings, fire-proof school and university buildings, Court Houses, City Halls, State Capitols, Post Offices, and other buildings of this type. The interior finish in buildings of this class is usually selected birch, selected gumwood, plain or quarter-sawed oak, mahogany, walnut or other first class hardwoods.

The Difference Between "Ordinary" and "First Grade" Work manship.—There is considerable difference between the two grades of workmanship listed above and the estimator must be able to determine the grade required. 

When placing wood base, chair rail or picture mold where just an ordinary grade of workmanship is required, the miters are not always perfect, the base does not hug the plastered wall closely at the top, which would not be tolerated where first grade workmanship is required. Also, the doors may not show the same margin at the sides and top, nails are not always set, and a close inspection of the trim will reveal some hammer marks. 858

MILL WORK 

859 Where first grade workmanship is required, the doors must be hung to show the same margin on all edges, the trim must be absolutely straight and plumb, all nails set and free from hammer marks, and with perfect fitting miters. 

These same differences apply to the erection and installation of all classes of mill work and interior finish. 

Methods of Estimating the Labor Cost of Erecting Mill Work and Interior Finish.-Different contractors use different methods of estimating the labor cost of erecting and setting mill work and interior finish, but the system generally used is to add a certain percentage of the cost of the mill work to cover the labor cost of erection. While this method is the easiest one known it does not produce the best estimates. Example: suppose you are estimating the cost of a building on which you receive 4 millwork bids ranging from $4,000.00 to $5,000.00. After receiving the bids you add the customary percentage to the lowest acceptable bid to take care of the labor cost of handling and erecting the millwork. This percentage usually runs from 

40 to 50% of the cost of the millwork. Taking 40% of $4,000.00 gives $1,600.00 for labor to handle and erect all millwork and interior finish. Suppose a competitor received a bid for $3,- 

500.00 from a mill which did not quote you. If your competitor added 40% to his bid, he would have only $1,400.00 to erect the same amount of millwork on which you figured $1,600.00. 

Why this difference of 121% on such a small item?

While this method saves a great deal of time and is almost universally used, it does not produce the most accurate estimates.

The only accurate method is to list each item separately; i.e., the number of lin. ft. of wood base, chair rail, picture mold, etc., the number of door jambs to set, the number of sash to fit and hang, together with the number of window openings to be cased or trimmed; the number of wardrobes, linen cases, buffets, kitchen units to set, etc. Estimating labor costs by this method produces more uniform and accurate estimates, reduces risk to a minimum and enables the contractor to check actual and estimated costs during construction.

Interior Window Trim Total 

$2.03 1.02 

The labor cost of placing interior window trim will vary considerably with the type of building, thickness of walls, style of trim or casings, etc. Frame buildings, stucco buildings, brick veneer buildings, etc., having walls 6" to 8" thick will not require inside wood jamb linings, as the wood window frames usually extend to the inside face of the plastered wall and the wood casings, window stools, aprons, stops, etc., are nailed directly to the wood frame. 

Buildings having walls 10", 12″, 16″ or more in thickness will require a wood jamb lining to extend from the inside of the

MILL WORK 

869 wood window frame to the face of the finished plaster. It will also require wood blocking and grounds to nail the jamb linings, window stools, aprons, etc.

The style of trim will affect labor costs considerably and for that reason costs are given on 4 distinct types of interior casings, as follows: 

Style "A" consists of 1-member trim with either a mitered or square cut head or "cap". This is the simplest trim it is possible to use.

Style "B" consists of 1-member trim for sides and a built-up cap trim for window heads. Caps may be put together in the mill or assembled and put together on the job. See page 900. 

Style "C" consists of 2-member back-band trim, consisting of a one-piece casing with a back-band of thicker material. See illustration on page 898.

Style "D" consists of any type of window trim that are assembled and glued together in the mill and set in the building as a unit.

The class of workmanship will also have considerable bearing on the labor costs, as in ordinary structures the casings are nailed to the frames or jamb linings and the trim may show some hammer marks but where "" is required, the utmost care must be used in cutting and fitting all casings, miters, etc. All nails must be carefully driven and set, casings must show the same margin on all sides and must fit closely to plastered walls. In other words, it must be a first class job in every respect.

Fitting and Hanging Wood Doors.-The labor cost of fitting and hanging doors will vary with the class of workmanship, weight of door, whether soft or hard wood, and upon the tools and equipment used, as there are power planes, hinge butt routers and lock mortisers that enable a carpenter to turn out 3 to 5 times as much work per day as where the doors are fitted and hung by hand. This must be considered when making up the estimate.

Where just an ordinary grade of workmanship is required, the doors do not always show the same margin at the top and sides, the screws are frequently driven instead of placed with a screw driver and in many instances the doors are "hingebound" so they will not open and close freely. 

Where doors are fit and hung by hand, a carpenter should fit and hang 11 to 12 doors per 8-hr. day, (although some carpenters will fit and hang 16 doors per day), at the following labor cost per door:

Carpenter 

Hours Rate 

Rate

Carpenter 

Hours Rate 

Rate

The above costs will vary with the ability of the carpenter, as a power planer should plane off a door in 5 to 10 minutes; a hinge butt router should do all the way from 60 to 75 openings per 8-hr. day, while a lock router should mortise out for a lock in about 1-minute, after it has been set on the door. The labor handling the doors is the same for both hand and machine work.

In the better class of buildings, the doors must show the same margin between the door and jamb at the top and sides; the hinges must be set even and flush with the jambs and the edge of the door and the doors must be free from "hinge binding" so they will fit well and work easily at the same time On this grade of work a carpenter should fit and hang 4 to

Placing Wood Wainscot or Paneling.—The labor cost of placing wood paneling or wainscoting will vary with the height of the wainscot and the manner in which it is delivered, i.e., whether assembled or knocked down.

It takes nearly as long to place wood wainscoting 4′-0″ high as 7'-0" high, as the top and bottom members are identical and the only difference is the height of the panels. 

If the wood wainscot is put together in the mill and the carpenters on the job do what little fitting is necessary, set it against the walls and nail it to the grounds, 2 carpenters working together should place 30 to 40 lin. ft. of wainscot per 8-hr. day, at the following costs for the different heights:

Erecting Wood Stairs in a Fine Residence. This residence was erected in Highland Park, Ill., and was a first class job in every respect.

The main stair consisted of 2 short flights leading from the first to the second floor and 2 short flights from the second floor to the attic, both having intermediate landing platforms. 

These stairs were half box and half open stringer. The wall stringer was housed out to receive the treads and risers while

the open stringer was cut out and the treads projected beyond the face of the stringer.

The stringers were birch about 12" wide and the risers were 7" high. The treads were clear white oak having return nosings.

The main stair contained 4 short flights, having 8 risers in each flight or 32 risers in the 4 flights. The landing platforms were erected by carpenters and were not included in the stair costs.

HOW TO OBTAIN "NET" PRICES OF OPEN OR GLAZED SASH 

The prices quoted on the following pages applying to open or glazed sash are "list" prices, subject to discount. This applies to all "Extras" on wood sash, unless otherwise mentioned.

When sash are purchased in stock sizes as listed, in full bundles of one size, the "stock" discount applies.

When sash are purchased in stock sizes in quantities of 100 or more openings of one size, a larger discount applies, which is usually stated. 

When "odd" or special sash are wanted, as listed under "Sash Extras," then the Odd Discount applies. When odd size sash are ordered in quantities of 10 or more windows of one size, then the regular stock discount applies. 

Discounts will vary according to mills in different localities but the following approximate discounts will prove a fair average for use:

SASH EXTRAS 

Note "A"-List Extras apply to either the open or glazed list. Where the extra is based on a percentage, it applies to the "open" list only and should be added before adding for the glazed list. Where a net extra is provided it applies to the net cost of either the open or glazed Window and Sash. 

Note "B"-These extras are intended to enable the forming of a list which shall be subject to the "odd work” discount, except when ordered in stock quantities. 

Note "C"-For smaller than listed and intermediate sizes, use same list as next larger listed size. 

Note “D”—All unlisted sizes when ordered in “Stock Quantities" apply stock discounts.

(b) Bottom rails wider than 3 inches to glass rabbet, add for each additional ½ inch or part thereof to the entire sash or window list..... 10% 5% (c) Check rails higher than 1% inches and not over 134 inches, either for 13% or 14-inch thick windows, add to the entire window list..... 10% (d) For 2 inches or 24 inches high check rails, for 134 inches thick windows, add to the entire window list 30% (e) Bars or muntins wider than standard sizes for each 14-inch or part thereof on each bar or muntin, add of the entire sash or window list for each such wider bar or muntin..... 12%

CHAPTER XV WALLBOARD, INSULATION, SOUND DEADEN- ING, BUILDING BOARD AND SHEATHING, CORK INSULATION AND WEATHER STRIPS 

The numerous types of wallboard, building board, hardboard, presdboard, tileboard, tile, planks, etc., now being extensively used for both new and remodeling work in all classes of structures, renders it highly important that every carpenter and contractor possess a thorough knowledge of this important subject if he is to prepare accurate estimates of both materials and labor.

Estimating wallboard is more of a task than merely computing the number of sq. ft. of surface to be covered. 

Each room should be laid out to obtain certain panel effects as the design of the panels will govern to a certain extent the amount of cutting and fitting necessary. 

Wallboard is furnished in three standard widths, 32″, 48″ and 64″* and may be applied to studs spaced 16″ or 24" on centers. It is furnished in lengths from 6′-0″ to 12′-0″, although a few manufacturers* make it in 14'-0" and 16'-0" lengths. It is also furnished in ", " and " thickness. 

The labor cost of applying wallboard depends upon three things the cost of placing headers and nailing strips between wood studs to which wallboard and decorative strips are nailed; the cost of installing the wallboard and the cost of placing the decorative panel strips. When installing a relief ceiling, furring must be applied to provide nailing pieces for all edges of the decorative strips. 

Decorative or panel strips are " thick and 3″, 4″, 6″, 9″ and 

12" wide and are furnished in lengths of 12′-0″, 14′-0″ and 16′-0″ 

*The Upson Co., Lockport, N. Y. 

956

WALLBOARD 

957 In modern decorative treatments, metal mouldings of plain or polished chromium, copper, brass or bronze are used to conceal joints, corners, angles, etc., instead of wood mouldings. This type of decoration is used in restaurants, bars, cafes, stores, soda fountains, beauty parlors, barber shops, store displays, bath rooms, kitchens, etc.

FIR 1 

Method of Laying Out Rooms for Wall Board 

The principal cause of unsatisfactory wallboard installations is the failure of the carpenter to follow the directions published by the manufacturer. To obtain satisfactory results, carefully follow manufacturers' directions. 

Estimating Wallboard Quantities. When estimating wallboard, make a rough sketch of each room, if possible, giving an elevation of each of the four walls and a plan showing the ceiling, similar to that illustrated. From this it is possible to obtain the number of lin. ft. of "headers" or nailing strips required, the size of each piece of wallboard, as well as the

number of lin. ft. of panel strips and moldings necessary to complete the job.

If the studs are not wide enough to form nailing pieces for the panel strips, a piece of wood, usually 1"x1", must be nailed to either side of the stud along the entire length and flush with the face of the stud. 

Method of Placing "Headers" or Nailing Strips for Wall Board. 

When estimating this class of work, care should be taken to obtain the exact number of lin. ft. of "headers" required as this is an important item in the cost of the work.

Placing Furring for Relief Ceilings.-Furring strips should be nailed at right angles to joists. Any convenient width of furring may be used but it must be wide enough to provide a nailing base to nail all edges of the decorative strips at least every 6". Furring may be of any No. 2 material, soft wood being preferable. Make sure that all furring strips are level.

With joists 16" on centers, a carpenter should cut and place 350 to 400 lin. ft. of furring strips per 8-hr. day, at the following labor cost per 100 lin. ft.:

As previously mentioned, it usually costs more to place a small piece of wallboard than a large one, as this generally calls for cutting and fitting above and below windows, around

door openings, etc., that requires considerably more work than placing a large piece of wallboard where no cutting and fitting is necessary. For this reason, estimating the labor cost by the sq. ft. is not the safest method to use, although it is the most common.

Where time in estimating is not a factor, the safest method is to lay out the work as shown in the accompanying illustration, dividing it into panels and then allow a certain length of time to place each piece of wallboard. For instance, in the illustration on this page, the room is 10'-8"x17'-0"x9'-0" ceiling,

and contains 679 sq. ft. of walls and ceilings, less 109 sq. ft. for door and window openings, or a net of 570 sq. ft. As laid out it requires 27 pcs. of wallboard for walls and ceilings. 

Estimating on the basis of 300 to 350 sq. ft. per 8-hr. day, it will require about 14 hrs. time to place the wallboard in the room, which is equivalent to 30 min. for each piece. A safe way to figure is to allow 20 to 30 min. for each piece of wallboard in the job, depending upon the class of work. 

Nails Required for Wallboard. When applying wallboard, 1" flat head nails are recommended. They should be driven around edges of panel about 6" apart. The center of the panels should be fastened with self-clinching fasteners, de- 

Illustrating Attractive Wall Designs Using Wallboard and Metal Joint Strips scribed in the next paragraph. The decorative or panel strips should be fastened with brads, (not nails) 1" to 1" long.

Brads should be applied every 4" about " back from the edge of the strip. Nailheads should be slightly countersunk with a very small nail set. Fill nail holes with whiting mixed with some of the sediment from bottom of can of paint of the color

WALLBOARD 

963 selected for the ceiling. Do not use putty as it is liable to result in oil discoloration through the paint. On the average job, figure about 1-lb. of nails per 100 sq. ft. of wallboard. 

Upson Self-Clinching Fasteners.-The Upson Company has perfected a patented fastener which does away with all nail 

Modern Decorative Treatment Using Wallboard and Metal Mouldings marks on the face of the board. Nailed to the studs and joists this fastener securely anchors the big panels of wallboard to the back, doing away with all nail holes. 

Panel Strips and Mouldings For Use With Wall Board.- 

Strips for working out decorative effects on walls or ceilings and for concealing the joints of wallboard may be of the same material as the wallboard or they may be of wood or metal, depending upon the effect desired.

The labor cost of placing wood or composition decorative strips over the wallboard will vary with the design of panel strip used, whether it consists of one, two or three members, the size of the panels and the design of the walls and ceilings, as the more cutting and fitting required the fewer lin. ft. of strips a man will place per day.

Applying Wallboard Over Old Plastered Walls and Ceilings. 

-In remodeling work where the wallboard is applied over old walls and ceilings, it is advisable to remove the old plaster wherever possible. This is inexpensive, seldom costing over

WALLBOARD 

965 $5 or $6 a room and makes a much better job. To obtain a first class job it is recommended that all interior trim, such as door and window casings, base, etc., be removed before applying the wallboard. It is also recommended that furring strips be placed over all old plastered walls, as this will straighten the walls and provide a much better base for securing the wallboard. 

Fig. A Fig. B Fig. C Fig. D Fig. E Fig. F 

After the furring strips have been placed, the cost of applying the wallboard will run about the same as given on the previous pages.

The labor cost of placing wood furring strips is given on page 959 under cost of "Placing Furring for Relief Ceiling."

Kinds of Wallboard.-There are many kinds of wallboard, fibre-board and gypsum board now on the market making it impossible to describe all of them in detail in a book of this kind. Some are made of wood pulp, wood fibre, cane fibre and some of gypsum compositions, manufactured under slightly different methods and varying slightly in appearance but all used for the same general purpose and all selling at approximately the same price for competing materials. 

All Celotex boards are manufactured by the Celotex Co.;

Temlock, Temboard and Temwood by the Armstrong Cork Products Co.; Masonite, Presdwood, Temprtile, etc., by the Masonite

Corp.; Nu-Wood Products by the Wood Conversion Co.; 

Weatherwood and Sheet Rock by the U.S. Gypsum Co.; Insulite products by the Insulite Co.; Beaver products by the Certainteed Products Co.; J-M Board by Johns-Manville; Gold Bond boards by National Gypsum Co., etc.

Wallboard Sizes and Costs.-Wallboard used for interior walls and ceilings is furnished in sheets 4 feet wide and 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 and 12 feet long and 4-in. thick. The -in. board costs about $45.00 per 1,000 sq. ft.; 4-in. thick, $55.00 to $60.00 and 1-in. thick, $65.00 to $70.00 per 1,000 sq. ft.

Wallboards 1-in. thick used for interior work are furnished in the same sizes as given above and sell for about $42.00 per 1,000 sq. ft. for the 6 and 12-ft. lengths and $45.00 per 1,000 sq. ft. for all other lengths.

Temboard DeLuxe and DeLuxe Quarterboard is 1-in. thick and similar to ordinary board but has a little greater density, costs about $56.50 per 1,000 sq. ft. for 6 and 12-ft. lengths and $62.00 per 1,000 sq. ft. for all other lengths.

Tile-Board. Same as wallboard except it has impressed in one face 4"x4" squares to represent tile. Figure same material quantities and labor costs as given for wallboard under similar conditions.

Bevel-Lap Plank.-Rectangular plank units with the two long edges provided with bevel-lap joints. Used for interior wall finish, wainscoting and similar treatment to combine insulation and decoration in one material.

Planks are furnished in two types-individual planks or multiple planks. Each type is furnished with beaded or bevel design, as illustrated.

Multiple plank are 1-in. thick, 4-ft. wide and 8-ft. long, with beads or bevels spaced uniformly (equal plank widths) 6, 8, 12 or 16-in. on centers. 

Plank-in. thick cost $60.00 to $65.00 per 1,000 sq. ft.; -in. thick, $72.00 to $75.00 and 1-in thick $80.00 to $85.00 per 1,000 sq. ft.

Placing Individual Plank.—The labor cost of placing individ ual plank will vary with the surface to which it is applied, length of walls, amount of cutting and fitting necessary, etc. 

Ceiling work costs more than wall work on account of working on a scaffold and placing the plank overhead. 

The most economical method of application is to a solid backing of plywood, wood boards or to other satisfactory nailing surface, as it is necessary to have nailing facilities every 6, 8, 10, 12 or 16 inches, depending upon width of the plank. In the event a solid backing is not available, it is necessary to place wood furring strips to provide for nailing the boards at edges and at ends, also for chair rails, wainscot cap and other ornamental strips.

Nail through face of the plank, never through bead or bevel. 

Bury nail heads below surface with properly gauged hammer blow or with a nail set.

The cost of wood blocking and furring is given on the previous pages of this chapter.

Insulating Tile 

Tile made of Temlock, Nu-Wood, Masonite, Celotex, Insulite, and other fibre composition are used for wall and ceiling finish. 

They are furnished with beveled edges and in sizes from 6x6-in. to 24x48-in. and may be used for obtaining ashlar effects on walls and tile effects on ceilings. abia quol d स

Method of Applying Fibre Tile on Ceilings

They may be applied direct to a wood backing or to furring strips on the walls and ceilings. When furring strips are used, the strips must be spaced to work out with the tile sizes. 

Nails should be driven through the tile at an angle to the surface of approximately 60 degrees. Reverse the angle of half the nails. Nail through the face of the tile, never through bevel. 

Bury nail heads below the surface with properly gauged hammer blow or with nail set. 

Insulating fibre tile in. thick cost $55.00 to $60.00 per 1,000 sq. ft.; -in. thick, $65.00 to $70.00 and 1-in. thick $75.00 to $80.00 per 1,000 sq. ft.

Nailing Recommendations For Wood Fibre Tile.-Galvanized wire brads are recommended. When they are not available, bright wire brads may be used.

Applying Fibre Tile Using Adhesives.-Special adhesives, known as "Adhestick," "Stickum," Armstrong's No. 500 Adhesive, etc., are available for applying fibre tile and plank. 

Bevel-lap tile and plank should be cemented to plaster with adhesive applied around all edges in spots of sufficient size and quantity to insure proper adhesion. The size and number of spots of adhesive will vary with the condition of plaster surface and size of tile. Large tile, such as 24x24-in. require spots of adhesive at the center as well as around the edges. Pressure should be applied over the spots of adhesive when sliding the tile into position. To form a good bond, the tile and plank should be worked into position with weaving or turning motion, starting one to three inches from final position. On ceiling applications where large tile are employed, use brads driven through the adhesive spots to assist in holding the tile firmly in place until the adhesive sets. Where irregularities in the plaster surface have been encountered and marked, apply adhesive to the proper thickness to insure a true surface. 

Fibre board and wainscot should be fastened to plastered surfaces with both adhesive and nails. Adhesive should be applied in spots about 1-in. in diameter and about 4-in. thick. These

spots should be spaced about 6 inches apart over the entire area of each piece. The board or wainscot should then be worked into position with a sliding, weaving motion, starting one to three inches from the final location, pressing firmly over the spots of adhesive. Whenever low spots are encountered in the plaster, enough adhesive should be used to shim out the low spots. The nails should be spaced every 4 to 6 inches around the 

Method of Applying Insulating Plank Using Adhesive edges and every 10 to 12 inches over the remaining area. Begin nailing at the center and work toward the edges. Use No. 17 gauge brads of proper length to secure anchorage, driven at an angle to the surface of approximately 60 degrees. Nails should be countersunk to be made practically invisible. 

Tile and plank may be applied to plaster board, insulating board, plywood or lumber. In each case the use of adhesive or a combination of adhesive and brads is recommended.

Labor Placing Fibre Tile Using Adhesive. The labor cost of placing fibre tile using adhesive or adhesive and nails will vary greatly with the skill and experience of the workman applying same, size of tile, etc. For instance, where an experienced man is placing the tile, and has a helper to build scaffold, unpack tile and apply the adhesive to the backs of the tile and the mechanic merely slides them in place, an experienced mechanic and helper should place 50 to 60 sq. ft. of 12x12-in. tile an hour but if one man is working alone and he must stop to apply the adhesive to each tile, set it in place and then drive several brads through them, 15 to 20 sq. ft. an hour would probably be the average. For this reason, conditions under which the tile are to be installed must be carefully considered before arriving at the labor cost. 

The design in which the tile are laid also affects the labor costs. For instance when tile are laid in herringbone pattern, it requires about twice as much time as for regular square or common bond. Diagonal patterns require about one-third more time than regular squares or common bond while tile laid in mixed ashlar designs require about 75 per cent more time than straight squares or common bond.

The quantities and costs given in the following table are based on using two men consisting of an experienced mechanic to place the title and one helper to build scaffold, unpack the tile and place them on the scaffold and to place the adhesive on the back of the tile ready for the mechanic. 

If the work is performed by inexperienced men, the labor costs as given, may be doubled.

Temwood, Presdwood, Hardboard, Panelboard There are a number of makes of board made of wood fibre or cane fibre pressed into board form under flat bed hydraulic presses that are much thinner and possess much greater strength than ordinary wallboard and are used for both interior and exterior work.

These hardboards are used for interior finish of walls and ceilings, cupboards, lining of closets, clothes chutes and similar purposes. 16 16 

They are usually furnished in 1", ", " and " thick, and from 4 to 12 ft. long. The " and " thickness comes in sheets 4x12-ft. only.

975 These hardboards or tempered boards are in no way comparable with ordinary wallboard, as it is a far more dense material, having greater tensile and transverse strength, greater resistance to abrasion, lower moisture absorption, and when properly applied, no warping or buckling. 

Bathroom Paneled with Presdwood and Metal Decorative Strips

Tempered Tileboard

Tempered tileboard is the same material as Panel board, Hardboard, Presdwood, etc., except that impressions have been made in the face of the board in 4″ squares, developing a tile pattern. This material is used for walls in bathrooms, kitchens, lavatories, restaurants, barber shops and similar places. This material is furnished in 4x12-ft. sheets. 

Tempered board or tileboard should be cemented to the walls, using Armstrong's Waterproof Linoleum cement or a cement of equal quality. The adhesive should be applied to the back of the boards with a saw-tooth trowel, the boards having first been cut to fit. Use shoring to hold the boards firmly until the adhesive takes a partial set. Where it is necessary to nail the board to the walls, small brads should be used where scored lines intersect.

Figure about 1 gal. waterproof cement per 100 sq. ft. of wall.

Metal Moulding For Wallboard 

Where a modern treatment is desired in connection with wallboard, panelboard, presdwood, etc., metal mouldings of various designs are extensively used. 

One type of metal moulding is the "Snap-On" *Metal moulding which consists of a metal "channel" or track which is nailed or screwed to the wall and then the finish metal moulding is merely pressed or "snapped" over the track which eliminates all exposed nails or screws.

The use of this metal does not require as careful fitting at the joints as the wallboard may be placed in the usual manner and the metal moulding is then placed over the joints and is wide enough to conceal them. 

These metal mouldings are furnished in Chromium, stainless steel, copper, bronze and brass, and in a variety of designs to meet practically any type of construction.

Items to Include When Making Up Wallboard Estimates.— 

When making up estimates on wallboard construction the following items should be included to insure a complete and dependable estimate: 

1. "Headers" or nailing strips to receive wallboard. 

2. Furring strips on walls and ceilings where necessary. 

3. Wallboard and labor placing same. 

4. Panel strips and labor placing same. 

5. Labor filling nail holes with plaster of Paris or crevice filler. 

6. Beam ceilings, ceiling cornices, plate rails, etc. 

7. Painting and decorating wallboard and panel strips. 

8. Nails. 

9. Profit.

PLASTER WALLBOARD 

Plaster or gypsum wallboard is made of gypsum, molded while in a plastic condition between two sheets of tough protective paper. 

Sheetrock with square edges is made, and in. thick; 32" and 48" wide and from 4'-0" to 12′-0″ long. The width fits standard 16 in. centering of studding and joists and the lengths readily adapt it to average ceiling heights. 

Tongue and groove sheetrock is madein. thick (longitudinal edges tongue and groove), 48 in. wide and 8, 9 and 10 ft. long.

It is particularly designed for those constructions where the board must be applied with the length at right angles to the framing members. 

*United States Gypsum Company

All framing for "headers" and furring for gypsum wallboard is practically the same as for fibre wallboard and the costs are the same. 

Nails should be 3d cement coated flat head common nails 

11" long but when applied over old plaster without the use of furring strips, use 6d cement coated flat head common nails 13" long. Tri-Jak for Assisting in Applying

Tri-Jak* for Applying Wallboard Ceilings.-The device illus trated reduces labor and cost of applying wallboard to ceilings and makes one-man application easy. 

It consists of 4 tempered spring-steel arms, with ball-bearing tips, mounted on a vertical shaft of hot-rolled steel, and the whole mounted on a tripod of heavy pipe with malleable iron ball feet. It will hoist board to a 11'-0" ceiling without using a platform.

Sheetrock* Reinforced Joint Systems.-The manufacturers* 

have developed two new systems of joint reinforcement, which add permanent joint concealment to its other advantages. The jointings between the boards are "laced" by reinforcing (either the new Metal "A" System or the Fabric System) embedded in a perfected joint cement of unusual strength and adhesiveness. 

The Metal "A" System of reinforcing consists of a perforated metal tape 1" wide and 250'-0" long, with 15 lbs. of joint cement, is sufficient to treat the joints of 500 sq. ft. of board surface. 

The Fabric System of reinforcing which consists of a specially woven and processed cloth fabric 2" wide and 250'-0" long, with 10 lbs. of joint cement, is sufficient to treat the joints of 500 sq. ft. of board surface. 

United States Gypsum Company.

Sheetrock finisher is a specially prepared material used to conceal joints, spot nail heads and repair surface abrasions. 

5 lbs. should finish joints and cover nailheads for 500 sq. ft. of Sheetrock.

Providing a first class job of crack filling and joint covering has been done, the walls and ceilings may be painted, calcimined, enameled or covered with lining cloth or paper, either with or without panels. It can also be decorated with Textone. 

Wood Grained Sheetrock*.-Wood Grained Sheetrock is repro duction by engraving and printing processes of the graining and color of a genuine wood surface. It is made in four finishes; walnut panels with a repeating pattern that can be matched, plain walnut, knotty pine and Douglas fir. The surfaces are true reproductions of the woods themselves if they were dressed and matched in large size panels.

The matched walnut panels are made 4 ft. wide x 9 ft. long only. The standard walnut, Douglas fir and knotty pine boards are 4 ft. wide and from 6 to 10 ft. long. Board are in. thick.

It can be cut in the same way that standard in. Sheetrock is cut, either by sawing or by scoring from the face side and breaking.

The method of erection is similar to the erection of standard Sheetrock where it is used with mouldings or panel strips. 

Price about $50.00 per 1,000 sq. ft.

Insulating Sheetrock*.-Insulating Sheetrock is standard § in. 

Sheetrock, upon the back of which is mounted a thin, smooth, bright sheet of aluminum. It is applied to the interior face of exterior walls, rafters or top story ceilings with the bright aluminum side next the framing members. It is furnished in the same sizes as standard Sheetrock and when the joints are reinforced and finished in accordance with the standard specifications, the interior surfaces may be papered or painted. 

Price 7 to 8 cts. per sq. ft.

Balsam Wool.-Balsam Wool is a flexible form of heat and sound insulation. It is made from new wood fibers, chemically treated to make it fire-resistant, moisture-resistant, and rodent and vermin proof. These fibers are permanently cemented together into a fleecy wool form. It is sealed on sides and edges with asphalt-coated creped kraft paper liners, which are flexible, wind-proof, water and moisture proof and folded over at the edges to form nailing flanges.

Balsam wool is also used as a sound deadener material because it has the ability to both absorb and reflect sound waves. 

This blanket form of insulation is furnished in thicknesses of -in., 1-in. and wallthick. The -in. and 1-in. wool is furnished in 16, 24 and 33-in. widths, while the wall thick wool comes in

Aluminum or Sheet Foil Insulation 

Another form of insulating material that has come into prominence recently are those composed of thin aluminum sheets or sheets of heavy paper covered with a mineral pigment and polished to a highly reflective surface. 

Their principle of insulating is as follows: This insulation consists of single or multiple sheets of pure aluminum or mineral pigment, highly polished, installed between wall studs, furring strips, ceiling joists or roof rafters. When heat tends to flow through such insulated structures, much of the radiant heat is reflected back toward its source. In summer, stifling outdoor

INSULATION 

989 heat is driven off. In winter, practically all supplied heat is retained in the house where it is needed. 

Metallation. Metallation is bright, polished, genuine sheet aluminum, cemented to one or both sides of heavy, tough kraft paper. 

Type "A" Metallation consists of sheet aluminum cemented to both sides of heavy, tough kraft paper with 14-in. plain paper margins exposed for installation between studs, joists or rafters, with paper edges nailed inside framing members to form a curtain of insulation between two dead-air spaces. It is furnished in rolls 17-in. wide, 176 ft. 5 in. long, containing 250 sq. ft. and weighing 18 lbs. Approximate price per roll $9.00 to $10.00, or 3.6 to 4 cts. per sq. ft. 

Type "B" Metallation consists of sheet aluminum cemented to both sides of heavy, tough kraft paper especially designed for application horizontally or vertically over studs, rafters or joists in a way that provides an air space on each side of the Metallation. Furnished in rolls 32-in. wide, 93 ft. 9 in. long containing 

250 sq. ft. or 25-in. wide and 120 ft. long, containing 250 sq. ft. 

Weight per roll 16 lbs. 

Price per roll, $9.00, or 3.6 cts. per sq. ft.

Type "C" Metallation consists of sheet aluminum cemented to one side of heavy, tough kraft paper and is especially designed for use as building paper, under sheathing or roof boards, and in types of construction in which only one surface can face an air space.

Furnished in rolls 32-in. wide and 93 ft. 9 in. long, containing 

250 sq. ft. or rolls 25-in. wide and 120 ft. long, containing 250 sq. ft. Weight 13 lbs. per roll. 

Price per roll $6.00, or 2.4 cts. per sq. ft. 

Silvercote Insulation Fabric.-Silvercote insulation fabric is manufactured from two external sheets coated with a mineral pigment and polished to a highly reflective surface. The sheets are laminated with specially prepared asphaltum and reinforced with an interlining of fabric imbedded in the lamination, consisting of a half inch mesh of strong jute cords. Two silverlike surfaces are exposed. It can be creased, folded and tucked into the most inaccessible places without injury. Silvercote insulation fabric weighs 75 lbs. per 1,000 sq. ft.

It is furnished in rolls of 250 and 500 sq. ft. Figure on approximately the same basis as given for metallation.

Insulating Lath 

Insulating lath are made by most manufacturers of building and wallboard. They are made of the same materials as the

building boards previous described and are sold under the trade names of Temlock, Celotex, Beaver, Insulite, J-M, Masonite,

Nu-Wood, Weatherwood, etc. 

They are furnished in different sizes by the various manufacturers but the most common sizes are 16x32-in., 16x48-in., 18x48-in., 24x48-in. and 1,, 1 and 12-in. thick. 

Method of Placing Insulating Lath. 

Most insulating lath are manufactured with the long edges shiplapped and all edges beveled to reinforce the plaster against cracking and eliminate unsightly lath marks. Some of these insulating lath are metal reinforced along the edges to reinforce the unsupported horizontal joint.

Insulating plasterboard lath, such as Insulating Rocklath, Gold Bond Aluminum Foil Insulating Lath, etc., consist of regular plasterboard lath with a thin sheet of aluminum attached to one side to provide insulating value. They are furnished in sheets 16x32-in., 16x48-in., 32x36-in. and and -in. thick.

Rock Wool Insulation 

Rock wool insulation is made of rock or silica, molten at high temperatures and blown into fine thread-like particles, which when cooled forms a wool-like substance that is used for in-

sulation between studs, ceiling joists and roof rafters, also for deadening between floors and partitions. Rock wool is fire-proof and vermin-proof.

Rock wool is furnished in loose form, in granulated form, in strips 15-in. wide, 2 and 4-in. thick and 9-ft. long. It is also furnished in bats 15x18-in. and 15x23-in. 3 or 3-in. thick to fill in the entire space between wood studs spaced either 16 or 

24-in. on centers. 

Rock Wool Bats.-Rock wool bats or "pillows" are recommended for use in new construction on account of their ease in handling and placing, as the 15-in. width fits in between studs without cutting. 

Rock wool bats are furnished in 15x18-in. and 15x23-in. sizes and 3 or 3ğ-in. thick, to fill in the entire thickness of 2x4-in. wood studs. Half bats the same size as given above except only 

2-in. thick are also obtainable.

The average density of rock wool bats is 4 to 5 lbs. per cu. ft.
