Strip Rock Wool.-Strip rock wool is furnished in strips 9-ft. long, 15-in. wide and either 2 or 4-in. thick.

One strip covers 11 sq. ft. not including space occupied by wood studs or 12 sq. ft. including space occupied by wood studs. 

Strip rock wool costs about ct. less per sq. ft. than rock wool bats and the labor cost will run approximately the same as for rock wool bats.

Loose or Bulk Rock Wool.-The covering capacity of loose or bulk rock wool will vary considerably, depending upon the density to which it is packed when placed in the walls, floors or ceilings.

The U. S. Bureau of Standards conductivity figure for rock wool is 0.27 b.t.u. at a density of 10 lbs. per cu. ft. 

Loose or bulk rock wool is usually packed in bags weighing 35 lbs. and containing 3 cu. ft. 

The covering capacity of bulk rock wool as given by most manufacturers is based on a density of 6 to 7 lbs. per cu. ft.

CORKBOARD INSULATION 

Corkboard is extensively used for insulating in packing plants, cold storage warehouses, freezing tanks, refrigerators, etc., and the cost will vary with the specifications covering the work and the location of same.

The following directions cover the erection of corkboard insulation in building construction of all kinds in general use and to secure satisfactory results, should be carefully followed. 

Portland Cement Mortar.-The portland cement mortar for erecting the corkboard should be made of any standard grade of portland cement mixed with clean, sharp sand in the following proportions: 

Wall Backing: 1:3 portland cement mortar requiring 5.00 bbls. of portland cement and 2.10 cu. yds. of sand per 1,000 sq. ft.

CORKBOARD INSULATION 

1005 

Ceiling Backing: 1:2 portland cement mortar requiring 6.66 

bbls. of portland cement and 1.86 cu. yds. of sand per 1,000 sq. ft. 

The mortar should be fairly stiff. Do not mix too much at one time and do not add any lime.

In erecting corkboard in portland cement mortar, it is essential that the cement backing be uniformly " in thickness over the whole surface of the board. At the same time no mortar must be allowed to get on the edges and ends. To facilitate the application of the cement backing the following suggestion is offered. 

Build a mortar board 4'-0"x3'-6". On top of the board nail 

2 parallel strips separated from each other by just the width of a full-size corkboard and " higher than the thickness of the T 

1 BOARDS

corkboard that is to be erected. One sheet of corkboard at a time can then be laid down between the strips, the mortar applied and a uniform bed, " thick, struck off by running a straight edge along the wooden strips, without any possibility of the mortar getting on the edges and ends. 

Asphalt. The proper grade of asphalt to be used in the erection of corkboard is very important. It must be odorless, as any material with an odor will taint food stuffs that may be stored in the insulated rooms. It should be an oxidized asphalt of 180° to 200° F. melting point and preferably made from a 

Mexican base oil.

Melt the asphalt in a large kettle outside the building. Transfer the molten asphalt in pails to the small dipping kettles that are placed close to where the cork is being erected. These kettles should be approximately 15″ wide, 40″ long, and 8" deep, and should be kept hot by two charcoal burners or oil heating equipment.

In insulating floors, roofs and tank bottoms, use pure molten asphalt only. All horizontal surfaces to be covered require ↓ lbs. of asphalt per sq. ft. of corkboard surface. 

Asphalt Cement.-Asphalt cement is used for walls, partitions and all vertical surfaces and is made by adding 4 per cent (by weight) of cork dust to the molten asphalt after it has been placed in the dipping pan and thoroughly mixed. This gives the asphalt greater adhesive qualities. Figure lbs. per sq. ft. of corkboard surface.

Nails or Impregnated Skewers.-All nails used in erecting corkboard should be galvanized wire nails. Ordinary wire nails should never be used. Where two courses of corkboard are erected in portland cement mortar, impregnated skewers may be employed instead of nails to hold the second course in position, but do not use either nails or skewers in erecting a single course of corkboard against brick, stone or concrete walls. Portland cement mortar or asphalt cement is all that is required. Thickness

METAL WEATHER STRIPS 

The cost of metal weather strips will vary with the type of window, whether double hung or casement, size of opening, thickness of sash, etc., as they all affect the material and labor costs. It will make considerable difference in the labor costs whether the weather strips are installed in an occupied or unoccupied building. Ordinarily a workman must use more care when working in an occupied building and for that reason it will require to hour more time per opening than when working in new or unoccupied buildings. 

The following quantities and costs are based on using men experienced in placing weather strips. *Lumber cost based on using temporary studs at least 4 times.

Metal Weather Strips for Double Hung Windows.-When weather stripping double hung windows, it usually requires a " wide track strip at the top and bottom of the window, the side strip for the lower sash is " wider than the width of the sash, while the side strip for the upper sash is " narrower than the width of the sash. The meeting rail has a zinc interlocking strip.

When estimating the quantities of weather stripping required take the distance around the window, plus the width, to take care of the meeting rail between the top and bottom sash. 

As an example, obtain the number of lineal feet of weather stripping required for a 4'-0"x6′-0″ window by adding 4'-0"+ 

4′-0″+4′-0″+6′-0″+6′-0″—24′-0″, or it requires 24 lineal feet of stripping for the window.

The lineal foot cost of metal weather strip for double hung windows will average as follows:

Sash 12 In.

Thick $0.054 

Sash 21 In.

Thick $0.05

24x.05 or $1.25.

CHAPTER XVI WOOD AND METAL LATHING, INTERIOR AND EXTERIOR PLASTERING, ORNAMENTAL PLASTERING 

Plastering costs vary widely depending upon the kind of materials used and the class of workmanship performed, and the estimator should consider these items carefully before pricing any plastering.

There are three distinct grades of plastering, and the estimator should possess a fair knowledge of the class of work required and estimate accordingly.

The first and cheapest grade of plastering and the one most commonly used on all types of ordinary buildings have the walls plastered without plumbing or "rodding," and are merely floated. Work of this class admits of variations and "waves" in the finish of " to ". This is the regular commercial grade of plastering and on the following pages is headed "Ordinary Work."

A better grade of plastering, such as required in high grade residences, apartments, hotels, schools, office buildings, etc., all walls are "rodded," and the finish plaster does not admit of variations or "waves" exceeding "to". This class of work is listed on the following pages under "."

The very highest grade of work is found only in the most expensive residences, court houses, Federal Government buildings, state capitol buildings, public libraries, etc., where all walls and ceilings together with all interior and exterior angles must be absolutely straight, and plumb and not admit of variations or "waves" exceeding "to". This is termed "Highest Grade Work."

Estimating Quantities of Lathing and Plastering.-Lathing and plastering are estimated by the square yard, but the method of deducting openings, etc., varies with the class of work and the individual contractor. 1018

PLASTERING 

1019 Many plastering contractors make no deductions for door or window openings when estimating new work, while others deduct for one-half of all openings over a certain size. 

Both lathing and plastering are estimated by the sq. yd. which is obtained by multiplying the girth of the room by the height, plus the ceiling area. Example: Obtain the number of sq. yds. of plastering in a room 12'-0"x18'-0", having 9'-0" ceilings. 18+18+12+12=60 lin. ft. of wall. 

60 × 9 540 Sq. Ft. Wall Area 12x18=216 Sq. Ft. Ceiling Area 756 Sq. Ft. Area of Walls and Ceiling 

756 9 Sq. Ft. 84 Sq. Yds.

When measuring spaces under pitched roofs where the opposite walls are not parallel and do not form a rectangular ceiling or where they are not straight or plumb from floor to ceiling and follow the pitch of the roof, the ceiling should be measured from the extreme lengths of wall to wall as if all walls were vertical and the walls should be measured from the floor to the highest point of the ceiling, as if all walls were vertical. 

Openings should be measured between grounds and no deductions should be made for openings less than 2'-0" wide, and then only one-half the area of each opening should be deducted. 

Many plasterers do not make any deductions for openings. 

The complete contents of store front openings should be deducted, and the contractor should figure 1'-6" wide for each jamb by the height, when the return or "reveal" is less than 1'-0".

For all beams or girders projecting below ceiling line, allow 1′-0″ in width by the total length as an extra for each internal or external angle, in addition to the actual area. 

Corner Beads, Moldings, Etc.-All beads, quirks, rule joints and moldings are measured by the lin. ft., from their longest extension with 1′-0″ extra added for each stop or miter. Corner beads should always be measured by the lin. ft. 

Plaster Cornices.-Plaster cornices should be measured by the total length of the walls. If the cornices are 1'-0" or less in girth, measurement should be made by the lin. ft., stating the girth of each cornice. If the cornices are over 1'-0" in girth, measurement may be made either by the sq. ft. of exposed face or by the lin. ft., stating the girth of each cornice.

Allow one lin. ft. for each internal miter and 3 lin. ft. for each external miter.

Enriched cornices (cast work) should be measured by the lin. ft. for each enrichment. 

Arches, Corbels, Brackets, Ceiling Freize Plates, Etc.-Arches, corbels, brackets, rings, center pieces, pilasters, columns, capitals, bases, rosettes, pendants, and niches are estimated by the piece. Ceiling freize plates should be estimated by the sq. ft.

Columns. Plain plastered columns should be measured by the lin. ft. or by the sq. yd., multiplying the girth by the height. 

Cement Wainscot.-Cement wainscot should be measured by the sq. ft. or sq. yd.

Circular or Elliptical Work.-Circular or elliptical work on a small radius should be estimated at double the rate of straight work.

WOOD LATH 

Wood lath should be estimated by the sq. yd. Inasmuch as it is customary to deduct only one-half the area of openings, it is not necessary to add any allowance for waste. When placing wood lath it is customary to allow" between each lath for a plaster key. 

A standard wood lath is 1" wide and 48" long, although they are furnished in three different sizes and lengths, as follows:

Labor Placing Wood Lath.-A lather should place 1,400 to 

1,600 1"x48" wood lath, (95 to 110 sq. yds.) per 8-hr. day and should also place 1,400 to 1,600 1"x48" wood lath (72 to 82 sq. yds.) per 8-hr. day.

In many localities lathers are paid by the thousand lath or by the sq. yd. When paid by the sq. yd. the cost may be easily obtained by dividing the price per 1,000 by 69 (69 sq. yds. per 

1,000 lath). Example: Find the sq. yd. labor cost with lathers paid $8.00 per 1,000 lath. $8.00-69-11.6 cts. per sq. yd.

In Chicago, a Union lather is supposed to place 100 sq. yds. of 1"x48" lath per 8-hr. day, as a minimum day's work. 

Nails Required for Wood Lath.-It requires 10 lbs. of 3d wire nails per 100 sq. yds. of 1" lath and 14 lbs. per 100 sq. yds. of 1" lath..

PLASTER BOARD AND ROCKLATH 

Rocklath is a solid sheet of gypsum encased in a tough fibrous covering, forming a uniform, strong, fire-resisting plaster base. 

Rocklath boards are made " thick and in two sizes, i.e., 16"x32" and 16"x48", 6 sheets to the bundle. Each bundle of 

32" boards contains 21 sq. ft. and weighs about 30 lbs. while each bundle of 48" boards contains 32 sq. ft. and weighs about 

45 lbs. Either size provides the usual vertical joint break (similar to that of wood lath) without cutting.

Nails Required for Rocklath.-Nails shall be 14" long. 13 gauge," flat head blued lath nails. Nails are spaced 4" apart, using 5 nails per stud. Nails at edges should be spaced " from edge. First nail to intermediate supports, then the ends. Butting ends must center over a support.

With studs spaced 16" on centers it will require 7 to 8 lbs of nails per 100 sq. yds. of rocklath and with studs spaced 12" on centers it will require 9 to 10 lbs. per 100 sq. yds. 

Labor Placing Rocklath.-A lather should place 90 to 110 sq. yds. of Rocklath per 8-hr. day on average work. 

INSULATING LATH 

There are a number of different makes of Insulating lath on the market, made of the same materials as the building and insulating boards bearing the same names. 

They are usually furnished in sheets 18"x48" or 24"x48" and in" and 1" thicknesses, having beveled edges and shiplapped to reinforce the joints. 

These materials are fully described on pages 995 to 997, under Insulation. 

A lather should place 90 to 110 sq. yds. per 8-hr. day, on average work.

METAL LATH AND FURRING 

Metal lath is used as a plaster base instead of wood lath when nailed to wood studs and joists, for solid plaster partitions, suspended ceilings, for reinforcing corners and joints of wood lath or plaster board, and furring for ornamental plaster beams and cornices.

The costs will vary according to the class of work on which it is used, the size of the rooms and the method used in placing hangers for suspended ceilings.

Metal Lath Suspended Ceilings.-When erecting suspended ceilings of metal lath and channels the following method is generally used:

Irrespective as to whether the suspended ceiling is used with a concrete, tile or wood floor, heavy wire or " round iron rods are usually used for hangers. When these hangers are placed in the structural slab it eliminates considerable cutting and drilling to secure hangers. Hangers are usually spaced about 

3'-0" on centers each way so that each hanger supports 8 to 9 sq. ft. of ceiling. The cost of the hangers will vary with their length or the distance the ceiling is suspended below the structural slab. 

Supports of 2" flat bar iron or 2" steel channels are then attached to the hanger rods, so that it requires about 3 lin. ft. of channel per sq. yd. of ceiling.

After the " or 1" channels have been placed, the metal lath is attached to the channels by means of tie wire running through the metal lath and over the channels. The scratch coat of plaster is then applied to the metal lath. laps and waste in cutting the metal lath.

Applying Metal Lath to Wood Joists.-In non-fireproof buildings where metal lath is applied to boiler room ceilings, engine rooms or other places requiring a semi-fireproof ceiling, metal lath is stapled to the wood ceiling joists. 

On work of this kind, a lather should apply 90 to 110 sq. yds. of metal lath ceiling per 8-hr. day.

Erecting Suspended Metal Ceilings. The labor cost of erecting suspended metal ceilings will vary with the method used in placing hangers, size of rooms, etc., as the larger the area the more work a lather can complete per day.

In average size rooms where hangers are placed in the structural floor slab, a lather should complete 35 to 45 sq. yds. of ceiling per 8-hr. day, but if it is necessary to drill holes in the concrete or tile to secure hangers, a lather will place only 

30 to 35 sq. yds. of suspended ceiling per 8-hr. day.

In closets, toilet rooms and other small spaces, a lather will complete only 20 to 25 sq. yds. of suspended ceilings per 8-hr. day.

Placing Metal Lath Ceilings Under Metal Tile and Concrete 

Joist Floor Construction.-In buildings having floors of metal tile and concrete joist construction, it is customary to place metal lath ceilings directly under the concrete joists. These ceilings are held in place by wire hangers placed in the floors before the concrete is poured. After the concrete floors are in place and the metal "pans" removed, " round iron rods, spaced about 12" on centers, are fastened to the hangers and the metal lath is then wired to the " pencil rods.

On work of this kind, a lather should place hangers in concrete slab, place pencil rods and complete 40 to 50 sq. yds. of metal lath ceiling per 8-hr. day.

Placing Ceilings of Ribbed Metal Lath.-There are a number of ribbed metal lath on the market having " or " ribs spaced about 4" on centers, which take the place of channel iron and metal lath in ceiling construction. These materials are formed from a sheet of metal that has been perforated to furnish a key for the plastering. The "ribs" are pressed out of the metal so that one sheet forms both the channels and lath. 

These ceilings are more expensive than ordinary channel iron and wire lath, on account of the extra cost of the ribbed lath.

In average size rooms where hangers are placed in the structural slab before the concrete is poured, a lather should complete 35 to 45 sq. yds. of ceiling per 8-hr. day, but if it is necessary to drill holes in the tile or concrete ceiling to place hangers, a man will place only 30 to 35 sq. yds. of suspended ceiling per 

8-hr. day.

In closets and other small spaces, a lather will complete only 

20 to 25 sq. yds. of ceiling per 8-hr. day.

Cornices. When placing metal furring consisting of channels and metal lath for ornamental plaster beams and cornices, a lather should bend all channel iron and place 50 to 60 sq. ft. of furring per 8-hr. day.

Placing Metal Corner Beads.-The cost of placing metal cor ner beads will vary with the manner in which they are placed and the grade of workmanship.

Placing Metal Picture Mold and Base Ground.-When placing metal picture mold or base ground to wood studs, a lather should place 250 to 300 lin. ft. per 8-hr. day, where the beads are straight and level.

Estimating Plaster Quantities 

The following pages contain covering capacities and quantities of the different kinds of plastering materials required and are based on manufacturer's specifications.

Prepared or "patent" plasters are sold by the ton and are packed in 80 and 100 lb. sacks. Each 100 lb. sack is equivalent to 1 cu. ft. When plaster is mixed with sand in the proportions of 1 to 1, 2 to 1, or 3 to 1, it means either, 1, 2 or 3 parts of sand are to be added to each 100 lb. sack of plaster. 

Covering Capacity.-The covering capacity of plaster necessarily depends upon conditions under which the plaster is

Bondcrete for Interior Concrete Surfaces.-Used for both scratch and brown coats applied over concrete surfaces. Bondcrete adheres to dry concrete because of its cementitious qualities and because it maintains a practically unchanging volume during the process of setting and hardening. It must not be applied to smooth concrete surfaces and must not be covered with a sanded brown coat-use only Bondcrete full to the grounds. 

It usually requires 1,700 to 2,200 lbs. of Bondcrete per 100 sq. yds. depending upon the regularity of the concrete surface and thickness applied.

Quantity of Putty Obtained from Various Plastering Materials 

The quantity of lime putty obtainable from one ton of lime will vary with the kind of lime used, whether lump quicklime, pulverized quicklime or hydrated lime, also upon the quality of the lime, as lime produced in different parts of the country will produce varying amounts of lime putty. 

Under average conditions the following quantities should be obtained.

PLASTERING 

1035 Covering Capacity of Lime Plaster.-There has been some confusion in the past regarding the covering capacity of lime plaster due to the lack of definite specifications covering the method of mixing and proportioning the materials. 

Lime plaster is usually proportioned by volume, using 1 volume of stiff, well aged lime putty to 2 volumes of dry sand, plus necessary hair or fiber for scratch coat.

For the brown coat, use 1 volume of lime putty to 3 volumes of dry sand, plus hair or fiber as needed. 

As will be noted from the above table, the volume of lime putty obtainable from various kinds of lime will vary considerably with the kind of lime used. The tables of costs on the following pages are based on the quantity of lime putty required per 100 sq. yds. 

Slight adjustments will be required where pulverized quicklime or hydrated lime are used.

One cu. ft. of sand is considered 100 lbs. or 2,700 lbs. per cu. yd.

Finishing Lime.-Use finishing lime for finish coat only in conjunction with gauging plaster.

Under average conditions one ton of Hydrated lime, when used in the proportion of 2 parts of dry lime to 1 part of dry gauging plaster by weight, should finish 500 to 700 sq. yds. or it requires 285 to 400 lbs. of dry hydrated lime and 145 to 200 lbs of dry gauging plaster per 100 sq. yds. of finish. 

A ton of quicklime mixed in the proportions of 3 parts lime putty by measure with 1 part of dry gauging plaster (equal to 1 part dry gauging plaster to 2 parts dry hydrated lime by weight) should finish about 1,000 sq. yds. or it would require about 200 lbs. quicklime and 100 lbs. gauging plaster per 100 sq. yds.

While published tables show that 28 lbs. of lump lime will produce as much putty as 43 lbs. of hydrated lime, when it comes to sand carrying capacity the best brands of hydrated lime will nearly offset this difference, and, pound for pound, will carry practically as much sand as lump lime.

Prepared Gypsum Trowel Finishes.-There are a number of prepared gypsum trowel finishes on the market which require only the addition of water to make them ready for use. A 

few of these are Universal White Trowel Finish, Adamant* Trowel Finish (White), Adamant* Slate Colored Trowel Finish Badger Trowel Finish and Red Top Trowel Finish. 

*United States Gypsum Company.

PLASTERING 

1037 Under average conditions, if mixed and applied in accordance with standard specifications, one ton will cover 350 to 400 sq. yds. of surface or it requires 500 to 575 lbs. per 100 sq. yds. 

Prepared Gypsum Sand Float Finishes.-There are a number of gypsum sand float finishes, such as Red Top* Silica Sand 

Float Finish (White), Adamant* Gray Sand Float Finish, Adamant White Sand Float Finish and Red Top* Sand Float Finish (gray). 

These finishes are ready for use when water is added and under average conditions one ton is sufficient for 250 to 275 sq. yds. or it requires 725 to 800 lbs., per 100 sq. yds. 

Estimating Labor Costs of Plastering 

Before it is possible to prepare an accurate estimate on the cost of any plastering job, the quality of work must be considered, as labor costs may vary from 25 to 100 per cent. 

The costs given on the following pages cover three distinct grades of workmanship from the cheapest to the very finest work. These three grades are fully described on page 1018. 

Applying Scratch Coat of Plaster.-A plasterer should apply 

150 to 175 sq. yds. of scratch coat per 8-hr. day, where just an ordinary grade of workmanship is required, and 125 to 150 sq. yds. per 8-hr. day where first grade workmanship is required. 

Applying Brown Coat.-Where just an ordinary grade of workmanship is required, a plasterer should apply 125 to 150 sq. yds. of brown coat per 8-hr. day, although on cheap work a plasterer will brown out 200 sq. yds. per 8-hr. day.

Where first grade workmanship is required, a plasterer should brown out 115 to 135 sq. yds. per 8-hr. day, while on the highest grade workmanship, a plasterer should apply 90 to 110 sq. yds. of brown coat per 8-hr. day.

Applying White Finish or “Putty” Coat.—On an ordinary job of white coating, a plasterer should apply 125 to 150 sq. yds. per 8-hr. day, but where first grade workmanship is required, a plasterer will apply only 75 to 100 sq. yds. per 8-hr. day.

Where the highest grade of workmanship is specified, a plasterer will apply 50 to 60 sq. yds. per 8-hr. day. 

Applying Sand Float Finish.-A plasterer should apply 90 to 110 sq. yds. of sand float finish per 8-hr. day, where just an ordinary grade of workmanship is required or 70 to 85 sq. yds. where first grade workmanship is required. 

United States Gypsum Company.

On the highest grade workmanship, a plasterer should apply 

45 to 55 sq. yds. per 8-hr. day.

Applying Finish Coat of Cement Wainscoting.-Where cement wainscoting is used in kitchens, bath rooms, laundries; corridors, etc., using "Keene's" cement, "Adamant", or other similar finishes applied over a brown coat of hardwall plaster or portland cement, a plasterer should apply 65 to 75 sq. yds. per 8-hr. day. 

If the wainscoting is blocked off into squares, 3″x6″, 4"x4" or 6"x6" to represent tile, a plasterer should block off 55 to 65 sq. yds. per 8-hr. day.

To apply the finish coat of plaster and block same off into squares to represent tile, a plasterer should complete 30 to 35 sq. yds. per 8-hr. day.

Where first grade workmanship is required, a plasterer should apply 50 to 60 sq. yds. of cement wainscot per 8-hr. day and should block off into squares 45 to 55 sq. yds. per 8-hr. day, or he should apply cement wainscot and block off into squares 

25 to 27 sq. yds. per 8-hr. day.

Where the highest grade workmanship is required, a plasterer should apply 35 to 45 sq. yds. of cement wainscoting per 8-hr. day, and block off 40 to 45 sq. yds. or he will apply cement wainscoting and block off 18 to 22 sq. yds. per 8-hr. day.

Special Prepared Finishes 

There are a number of prepared plaster finishes on the market that are ready for use by the addition of water. These may be applied over a brown coat of gypsum cement plaster and the cost of the material is the only additional cost. 

Where a special finish is specified, deduct the cost of the Finish White Coat as given under the ordinary plastering classification and add the cost of the special finish specified.

PORTLAND CEMENT PLASTER 

When applying portland cement plaster for interior work, it is customary to add a small percentage of lime to make the mortar work easier, and the quantities given on the following pages are computed on that basis. 

Some plasterers (not all) add more lime and less cement, and when this is done the costs should be reduced accordingly, as a plasterer will apply considerably more lime plaster than portland cement plaster. 

Labor Applying Scratch Coat.-A plasterer should apply 90 to 

110 sq. yds. of scratch coat per 8-hr. day where ordinary workmanship is required and 80 to 100 sq. yds. where first grade workmanship is required. 

Labor Applying Brown Coat.-When applying a brown coat of portland cement plaster, a plasterer will apply 70 to 90 sq. yds. per 8-hr. day where ordinary workmanship is required and 

60 to 75 sq. yds. where first grade workmanship is required. 

Labor Applying Finish Coat.—When applying the finish coat of portland cement plaster, a plasterer should apply 60 to 70 sq. yds. per 8-hr. day, where ordinary workmanship is required and 45 to 55 sq. yds. where first grade workmanship is required. 

Blocking Portland Cement Plaster into Squares to Represent Tile. If the finish coat of portland cement plaster is blocked off into squares, 6″x3", 4"x4" or 6″x6″ to represent tile, a' plasterer should block off 55 to 65 sq. yds. per 8-hr. day, where ordinary workmanship is required and 45 to 55 sq. yds. where first grade workmanship is required.

Running Portland Cement Base. On the ordinary job of portland cement base 4" to 6" high, a plasterer or cement finisher should complete 55 to 65 lin. ft. per 8-hr. day and where first grade workmanship is required, 45 to 55 lin. ft. per 8-hr. day.

American Caen Stone Cement Plaster 

The cost of Caen stone cement plaster will vary according to the thickness of the finish coat and the class of work, viz., whether plain or blocked off into squares to represent ashlar. 

On ordinary walls and ceilings that are not blocked off, the Caen stone finish coat may be as thin as ". However, on work that is blocked off into squares to represent ashlar, having flush joints of white cement, and where first class work is required throughout, the Caen stone finish coat should not be less than " thick.

Where ornaments and cornices are encased in Caen stone cement and plaster molds are used for the purpose, the molds should be toughened by painting them with linseed oil. If a gelatine mold is used on the work, the mold should first be painted with white lead and turpentine, as an application of this paint will render it much more durable. 

If it is desired to "age" and enrich the original color of the Caen stone cement, it should be polished with buttermilk. 

Estimating Quantities of Caen Stone Cement Plaster.-In 

Caen stone work the scratch and brown coats usually consist of hardwall plaster, which may be estimated on the same basis as other classes of interior plastering.

The quantities of Caen stone cement will vary with the brand of cement used and the thickness to which it is applied. 

If the finish is " thick, it will require 10 to 12 sacks (100 lbs. each) or 1,000 to 1,200 lbs. per 100 sq. yds. of finished work.

If the Caen stone cement finish coat is " thick, it will require 20 to 23 sacks (100 lbs. each) or 2,000 to 2,300 lbs. per 

100 sq. yds.

On average work allow 1 lbs. of Caen stone cement plaster per sq. ft. of surface. On first class work, where the finish coat is" thick, allow 2 lbs. per sq. ft. of surface. 

Labor Applying Caen Stone Cement Plaster.-The finish coat of Caen stone is applied over a brown coat of hardwall plaster. 

When figuring the labor cost of applying the finish coat of Caen stone, there are four distinct labor operations to receive consideration. The Caen stone must be applied in the usual manner and if the work is blocked off into squares and jointed to represent ashlar, the plasterers will have to mark the work off and cut the joints. These joints are usually filled with white 

Keene's cement to produce a contrasting color. After the joints have been filled it will be necessary to rub down the entire surface with sand paper to bring it to a smooth finish. 

The last operation is a very slow and expensive process, as the surface must be thoroughly rubbed until the joints and surfaces are uniform and smooth.

The labor cost on this work will vary with the ability of the mechanics. Plasterers experienced in Caen stone work will perform much more work than inexperienced men, and this should be considered when pricing the work. 

When applying the finish coat of Caen stone over the brown coat, a plasterer should apply 15 to 20 sq. yds. per 8-hr. day.

Cutting Joints in Caen Stone Cement Plaster. If the Caen stone is blocked off into squares to represent ashlar, it will be necessary to cut horizontal and vertical joints in the finish coat and fill them with white cement to produce a contrast. The labor quantities and costs on this work vary considerably, depending upon the methods and tools used. Where experienced men are employed, a plasterer should cut joints in 15 to 18 sq. yds. per 8-hr. day.

Filling Joints in Caen Stone Plaster.-After the joints have been cut, it will be necessary to fill them with white cement to produce a contrasting color between the joints and the Caen stone, and an experienced plasterer should fill joints in 30 to 

35 sq. yds. of wall per 8-hr. day.

Rubbing and Sanding Caen Stone. After the joints have been filled and before the plaster has set too hard, it will be necessary for the plasterer to rub the wall with sand paper or carborundum until the joints and wall present a smooth and uniform appearance. This is a slow and expensive process but is absolutely essential to obtain satisfactory results.

PLASTERING 

1075 

A plasterer should rub and sand 6 to 8 sq. yds. per 8-hr. day but if the walls are allowed to stand too long before rubbing, these labor costs may be doubled. Under ordinary conditions the rubbing should be performed with 24 to 36 hrs. after the joints have been filled.

When estimating the cost of ornamental plaster cornices, it is customary to measure the exposed girth of the cornice (not the height and projection), and estimate the work at a certain 

**Garden City Sand Company, Chicago.

PLASTERING. 

1079 price per lin. ft. if the cornice is less than 12" in girth and by the sq. ft. if over 12" in girth. 

Where metal lath and furring is required for plaster cornices, add for this work as given on the previous pages. 

If plaster cornices are enriched with egg and dart, dentils or other ornamental cast work stuck on the plain cornices, add for this work at a certain price per lin. ft. for each row of enrichment. When estimating the number of lin. ft. of plaster cornices, measurements should be taken from wall to wall, and one lin. to 1205 5 stage bilt arbeides Stencil Application ft. should be added for each internal miter and 3 lin. ft. for each external miter.

When running ornamental plaster cornices under 12" in girth, a plasterer should run 40 to 50 lin. ft. per 8-hr. day, depending upon the size and length of runs between miters, as it is much easier for a man to run cornices on long straight walls than where necessary to form a miter every 8'-0" to 10'-0". 

If cornices are enriched with egg and dart or other ornamental cast work, figure 20 to 25 cts. per lin. ft. for each row of enrichment.

On large plaster cornices, a plasterer should run 45 to 50 sq. ft. per 8-hr. day, depending upon size, design and length of runs. 

The above quantities do not include time applying scratch or brown coat, which should be estimated in the same manner as given for that class of work.

When running ornamental plaster cornices in Keene's cement, the labor cost will run about 25 per cent higher than for plain plaster cornices. This is due to the extra labor required working the cement mortar.

The labor cost of running cornices in portland cement will cost 2 to 3 times as much as plain plaster cornices or a man will run only 15 to 20 sq. ft. of cornice per 8-hr. day. 

English Trowel Finish 

Ornamental Plaster Beams.-When estimating the cost of ornamental plaster beams, the sides are estimated in the same manner as plaster cornices but the soffits of the beams (when plain) are estimated at about twice the cost of plain plastering, plus an additional charge for sticking ornaments or enrichments on same.

Where the beams have depressions or "rails", a plasterer should run 40 to 45 lin. ft. per 8-hr. day.

If cast plaster ornaments are stuck on the beam soffit, figure $1.00 to $1.25 per sq. ft. for this work.

The above quantities do not include any allowance for wood or metal furring, which should be added as given under "Metal 

Lath and Furring."

Modeling and Casting for Ornamental Plaster.-When making models for ornamental plaster, such as column and pilaster caps and bases, enrichments for cornices and beams, modillions, ceiling and wall panels, and other ornamental work, the cost

PLASTERING 

1081 will vary from $8.00 to $10.00 per sq. ft.

depending upon the detail. 

After the models have been made, the cost of casting and setting the ornaments in place is worth $1.00 to $1.25 per sq. ft. 

Cast Wall Panels.-Estimate the labor cost of modeling as given above and add $1.00 to $1.25 per sq. ft. for casting and setting the panel strips in place. 

Spanish Palm Finish 

Ornamental Plaster Caps and Bases.-When estimating ornamental plaster caps or bases for columns, pilasters, etc., where they vary from 2'-0" to 3'-0" in diameter and 3'-0" to 4'-0" high, obtain the area of the base or cap and estimate the modeling at $4.50 to $5.00 per sq. ft. After the models are completed, allow $12.00 to $15.00 for casting and setting each ornamental plaster base and cap. 

Circular or Elliptical Work.-Where necessary to run orna mental plaster cornices, beams, wall and ceiling panels, etc., to a radius of 50'-0" or more, estimate the cost of this work the same as straight work but where the radius is under 10'-0", double the cost of straight work. 

Placing Plaster Panel Molds.-Where ornamental plaster panel molds are run on walls or ceilings, a plasterer should run 

50 to 60 lin. ft. per 8-hr. day.

EXTERIOR STUCCO 

.211

Exterior stucco is generally composed of a portland cement base or one of the many magnesite stuccos on the market. 

Portland cement plaster should not be applied when the outside temperature is below 32°F. as freezing injures it, while magnesite stucco is mixed with a chlorine solution and is not affected by cold weather. 

The cost of either type of stucco will vary according to the materials used and the grade of workmanship required.

Portland Cement Stucco 

The cost of portland cement stucco will vary according to the class of work, as many plasterers (not all) add more lime than should be used for exterior work, as the lime makes the plaster spread much easier but results in an inferior job. 

Applying Scratch Coat of Portland Cement Stucco.-Where just an ordinary grade of workmanship is required, a plasterer should apply 90 to 110 sq. yds. of scratch coat per 8-hr. day or 

80 to 100 sq. yds. where first grade workmanship is required. 

Applying Brown Coat of Portland Cement Stucco.-A plasterer should apply 80 to 90 sq. yds. of brown coat per 8-hr. day, where just an ordinary grade of workmanship is required or 65 to 75 sq. yds. where first grade workmanship is required. 

Applying Trowel or Float Finish Coat of Portland Cement.— 

A plasterer should apply 40 to 50 sq. yds. of portland cement float finish per 8-hr. day, where just an ordinary grade of workmanship is required and 30 to 35 sq. yds. per 8-hr. day, where first grade workmanship is required. 

Applying Wet Rough Cast Finish to Portland Cement Stucco. 

-If a wet rough cast finish is used and the mortar and aggregate are thrown against the wall with a paddle or similar tool, a plasterer should complete 35 to 45 sq. yds. per 8-hr. day. 

Applying Pebble Dash or Dry Rough Cast.-When applying a pebble dash or dry rough cast finish where the aggregate is thrown against the wet cement or "butter" coat, a plasterer should apply about 40 sq. yds. per 8-hr. day.

Washing Exterior Stucco With Acid to Expose Crystals.— 

Where the finish coat of stucco contains granite, marble or crystal screenings, it is washed off with a solution of muriatic acid to expose the crystals. A man should wash 525 to 575 sq. ft. (58 to 64 sq. yds.) per 8-hr. day.

On some jobs it will be necessary to wash the walls two or three times to bring out the crystals satisfactorily, and in such instances the labor cost should be increased accordingly. 

A solution of commercial muriatic acid in the proportion of 

1:10 (1 part acid to 10 parts water) should be used.

"Stonekote" Exterior Stucco 

"Stonekote" is a portland cement for exterior use. It is furnished in a variety of colors and may be finished with various kinds of aggregate to produce either a float or rough cast finish. 

Estimating Quantities of "Stonekote".-The material quantities given below were furnished by the manufacturers* as necessary to produce a satisfactory job. 

Quantity of "Stonekote" Required for Scratch Coat.-"Stonekote" is furnished by the manufacturers with the sand added, requiring only the addition of water. 

Applied according to the manufacturer's directions it requires 35 bags (3,500 lbs.) of scratch coat material per 100 sq. yds. of actual surface. 

It costs $0.85 per bag (100 lbs.) f. o. b. Chicago. A charge of 15 cents is made for each bag, which is refunded when the empty bags are returned in good condition, prepaid.

Quantity of "Stonekote" Required for Brown Coat.-In 2-coat work, where the brown coat is applied over wood lath, brick or tile walls or in 3-coat work where applied over the scratch coat, it requires 2,500 lbs. of second coat material per 100 sq. yds. of actual surface. 

Brown coat material costs the same as scratch coat.

Oriental Stucco 

Oriental* Stucco is a prepared stucco furnished in various colors to obtain the rough texture finishes that are used so much at the present, such as Basket Weave or Spanish Finish, Rough Cast or California Mission finish, Sand Float or Colonial finish, Sponge or Stipple finish, Raked Trowel finish, Splatter Dash or 

Oak Bark Smooth and Rough finish. See pages 1076 to 1081.

The scratch and brown coats are applied in the usual manner while the special rough finishes are obtained by troweling in circular motion to show trowel marks, brushing with a large calcimine brush to obtain basket weave effect, stippling wet plaster with a slightly wet sponge or stippling brush, troweling the wall at right angles and scraping, or brooming walls with a fibre brush or whisk broom, according to the finish desired.

Oriental stucco may be applied over metal lath or self-furring wire fabric, Gyplap wall construction covered with galvanized steel wire reinforcement, brick or tile walls or over cement and concrete blocks.

Magnesite Stucco 

There are a number of magnesite stuccos on the market that can be used with wood lath, as 2-coat work is satisfactory on wood lath while metal lath requires 3-coat work. 

Magnesite is mined originally as a white rock; it is then calcined or burned and ground to a fine powder. 

Some magnesite stuccos are furnished in powder form with the mixing liquid (a chloride solution) furnished in steel drums. 

This liquid is mixed with the powder at the job and is ready to apply. Other brands of magnesite stucco are furnished in powder form with the dry chloride mixture incorporated in the stucco itself, and only water is added at the job and the stucco is ready to apply.

Some magnesite stuccos may be finished in either a float or pebble dash finish but many of them are finished in a pebble (dry rough cast) finish to make a satisfactory appearance. It is usually applied in 2 coats, each being about " thick, making a total thickness of ". 

Applying Brown Coat of Magnesite Stucco.-Where a good grade of workmanship is required, a plasterer should apply 100 to 120 sq. yds. of brown coat per 8-hr. day. 

Applying Float Finish of Magnesite Stucco.-A plasterer should apply 65 to 75 sq. yds. of float finish stucco per 8-hr. day.

Applying Second or "Butter" Coat of Magnesite Stucco for 

Pebble Dash.-When applying the second coat of magnesite stucco ready to receive the pebble dash, a plasterer should apply 

100 to 120 sq. yds. per 8-hr. day.

Applying Pebble Dash or Dry Rough Cast.-After the second coat of stucco has been applied and before it has set, it will be necessary to throw the pebbles or glass against the wet plaster to give the "dash" appearance. After the "butter" coat has

been applied, a plasterer should apply dash to 55 to 65 sq. yds. per 8-hr. day.

CHAPTER XVII PAINTING, VARNISHING AND DECORATING 

Estimates and bids on painting and interior decorating vary to a greater extent than most any other branch of building construction, and when one looks into the matter it is not surprising because carelessness in taking off the quantities from the plans is a fault common to painters. Then too, there are several kinds of painters, good painters, fair painters, poor painters and others who are just plain "daubers." There are painters who figure on "skinning the job" by applying one or two less coats of paint or varnish than called for by the specifications; others who figure on substituting cheap and inferior materials for those called for; and others who do not know how to do good work, so naturally one should expect a wide variation in figures.

Of course, a cheap or inferior job costs less than a first class job, and the buyer usually gets what he pays for. 

When preparing estimates on painting, consider the quality of materials and workmanship required and price the work accordingly.

METHODS OF MEASURING AND LISTING PAINTING QUANTITIES 

When estimating quantities of painting or interior finishing, the actual surface to be painted should be measured as accurately as possible from the plans or from measurements taken at the building. From these measurements it should be possible to estimate the quantity of materials required, but the labor quantities present a much more difficult problem, owing to the different classes of work and the difficulties encountered in applying the paint. For instance, the covering capacities of paint will be the same for a plain surface or a cornice, but the labor cost painting the cornice will be considerably more owing to the height of the cornice above the ground and the amount 1102

of "cutting" or "trimming" necessary. Care must be used when pricing any piece of work, as conditions on each job are different.

Clapboard Walls.-The actual area of all walls and gables should be obtained and stated in sq. ft. or by the square (100 sq. ft.). Add 10 per cent to actual surface measurement to allow for painting the under edge of boards. Do not deduct for openings. 

Brick, Wood, Cement or Stone Walls.-Obtain the actual area of all surfaces to be painted and reduce to sq. ft. or squares (100 sq. ft.). Make no deductions for openings unless very large.

Wood or Metal Cornices.-Obtain the actual girth of the cornice and multiply by the length, which will give the number of sq. ft. of surface to be painted. Add for necessary ladders or scaffolds, depending upon the height of the cornice and the difficulty in reaching it, as the labor costs on work of this kind are often doubled or trebled. 

Outside Blinds and Shutters.-Obtain the area of both sides of all outside blinds or shutters which gives the number of sq. ft. of surface to be painted. The labor cost on work of this kind will be 50 to 100 per cent more than straight work, on account of the extra labor involved and the small surface area. 

Porch Rail, Balusters, Etc.-When estimating quantities of porch rails or balustrade, multiply the length of the rail or balustrade by the height, and the result will be the number of sq. ft. to be painted. If the balustrade is to be painted on both sides, multiply by 2. The labor cost will vary with the detail of the work, but will often be 14 times the cost of straight work. 

Porch Columns and Pilasters. To obtain the quantity of painting on porch columns or pilasters, multiply the girth of the column by the height, and the result will be the number of sq. ft. of surface to be painted. If the columns or pilasters are fluted or paneled, the labor cost will often be 1 times the cost of straight work.

Wood or Metal Roofs.-To compute the area of roofs, multiply the width by the length and include the area of all gables or dormers. The pitch of the roof and the height of the building have considerable bearing on the labor cost. See chapter on Roofing for rules for measuring all kinds of roofs.

Lattice Work and Grills. Obtain the area in sq. ft. by multiplying the length of the lattice by the height. If painted on both sides, multiply by 2. 

Gutters and Down Spouts.-Obtain the girth or distance around the gutter or down spout, (which will vary from 1'-0" to 2'-0") and multiply by the length. The result will be the sq. ft. of gutter or down spout to be painted. The labor cost will vary with the amount of scaffolding necesary and the difficulty in reaching the work.

Door Frames. When estimating quantities of wood or metal door frames, multiply the width of the frame by the distance around it. The result will be the number of sq. ft. to be painted. Do not estimate any door frame less than 1'-0" wide, and if over 1'-0" wide, multiply by the actual width. 

Example: A door frame for a 3′-0″x7′-0″ opening. There will be two sides 7'-0" high and a top 3'-0" wide, 7+7+3=17 ft.

Multiply the length by the width, 17×1=17 sq. ft. of surface. 

Window Frames and Sash.-When estimating painting quantities for wood window frames and sash, add 2'-0" to both the length and width of the opening, to take care of the sides and heads of the frame and the outside casing or brick mold, and multiply to obtain the area. For instance, on a window opening 4′-0″x6′-0″ add 2′-0″ to both the width and height, which gives a window 6'-0"x8'-0", containing 48 sq. ft. of surface. 

Do not deduct for glass in the sash, as the labor cutting around edges more than offsets the few feet displaced by the glass.

Fancy Sash, French Doors and Windows, Casement Sash, Etc. 

-Sash having a large number of small lights require considerable time cutting around muntins, etc., and for that reason the work is usually priced 1 to 1 times the cost of straight work. Do not deduct for glass area.

Picture Mold and Chair Rail.-On picture mold, chair rail, etc., less than 6" wide, obtain the number of lin. ft. to be painted or varnished and multiply by 6" to obtain the number of sq. ft. 

Wood and Metal Base.-Wood or metal base 6" to 10" high should be figured as 1'-0" wide.

Wood Plate Rail, Cornices, Etc.-When estimating quantities of wood plate rail, wainscot rail and ceiling cornices, measure the girth of the member and if less than 1'-0" wide, figure as 1'-0".

If over 1′-0″ wide, multiply the actual girth by the length, viz., 1'-3"X200'-0" 250 sq. ft. 

Interior Doors, Jambs and Casings. -When estimating quan tities for interior doors, jambs and casings, add 2′-0″ to the width and 1'-0" to the height of the opening. This allows for painting or varnishing the edges of the door, the door jambs which are usually 6″ wide, and the casings on each side of the door which average from 4" to 6" wide. Example: On a 

3′-0″x7′-0″ door opening, add 2'-0" to the width and 1'-0″ to the height, which gives an opening 5′-0″x8′-0″, containing 40 sq. ft. on each side. Some painters figure all single doors at 

40 sq. ft. per side, or 80 sq. ft. for both sides, while others figure them at 50 sq. ft. per side or 100 sq. ft. for both sides. 

Do not deduct for glass in doors.

Interior Sash Doors, French Doors and Casement Windows. 

-When estimating quantities for door or window openings containing a large number of small lights of glass, such as French doors, casement windows, etc., take the size of the opening, and add 25 per cent for extra labor cutting around muntins, stiles, etc. Do not deduct for glass in doors or windows.

Interior Windows, Jamb Linings, Sash and Casings. When estimating painting quantities for windows and window trim, add 2′-0″ to the sides and length to allow for jamb linings, casing at the top and sides, and window stool and apron at the bottom. Example: If the window opening is 3′-0″x6′-0″, adding 2'-0" to both the width and length gives a window 5′-0″x8′-0″, containing 40 sq. ft. of surface. 

If the windows or sash are cut up with numerous small lights, requiring considerable cutting around muntins and division bars, add about 25 per cent to the cost of straight work. 

Stairs. When estimating quantities of paint or varnish for wood stairs, add 2'-0" to the length of treads and risers to allow for stair strings on each side of the stairs. A stair tread is 10" to 12" wide, riser is about 7″ high, and the average cove and under side of a stair tread 2″ in girth, so each tread should be figured 2′-0″ wide. Multiply the width by the length to obtain the number of sq. ft. of paint or varnish required for each step. Multiply the area of each step by the number of treads in the stair, and the result will be the number of sq. ft. of finish. Example: A flight of stairs containing 20 treads,

4'-0" long. Adding 2'-0" to the length of the treads to allow for the stringers, gives 6 lin. ft. in each tread, which, multiplied by the girth of 2'-0" gives 12 sq. ft. of surface in each step. 

Since there are 20 treads in the stairs, 12×20=240 sq. ft.

For painting the soffits of stairs, use same rules of measurement as given above.

Balustrades and Hand Rails with Balusters.-When estimat ing balustrades around well holes or stair hand rail and balusters, measure the distance from the top of the treads to the top of the hand rail and add 6″ for painting or varnishing the hand rail. Multiply the height of the balustrade by the length and the result will be the number of sq. ft. of balustrade. An easy method for computing the length of the stairs is to allow 

1 lin. ft. in length for each tread in the stairs. Example: If the hand rail is 2'-6" above the treads and the stairs contain 20 treads, add 6" to the height of 2'-6" to take care of the extra work on the hand rail proper, making a total height of 3′-0″. 

3×20=60 sq. ft. of surface for one side of the balustrade or 120 sq. ft. for two sides.

The balustrade around the stair well hole is easily estimated by multiplying the height by the length. 

This same method will apply when obtaining quantities for porch railings, etc.

On fancy balustrades having turned spindles which require considerable additional labor, use actual measurements as given above and add to allow for extra labor. 

Wood Ceilings and Wainscoting. When estimating quantities for wood ceilings, multiply the length by the width. Do not deduct for openings, such as skylights, etc.

For matched and beaded wainscoting, multiply the length by the height.

Floors. To compute the quantities of floors to be finished, multiply the length of each room by the width, and the result will be the number of sq. ft. of floor to be finished. 

Plastered Walls and Ceilings.-To obtain the area of any ceiling, multiply the length by the breadth, and the result will be the number of sq. ft. of ceiling. 

When estimating walls, measure the entire distance around the room and multiply by the room height. The result will be the number of sq. ft. of wall to be decorated. For instance, a 12′-0″x15′-0″ room has two sides 12′-0″ long and two sides

1107 15′″ long, giving a total of 54 lin. ft. If the ceilings are 9′-0″ high, 54X9=486 sq. ft. the area of the walls. 

Do not deduct for door and window openings.

Cases, Cupboards, Book Cases, Etc.-When estimating sur faces of cupboards, wardrobes, book cases, closets, etc., to be painted or varnished, obtain the area of the front and multiply by 3, which includes both inside and outside of doors and the back of the case. If the ends of the case are exposed, obtain the area of one end and multiply by 4, which includes the inside and outside of both ends. The top and bottom of the case may be computed by taking the area of the floor and multiplying by 2. If the shelves are to be finished, take the area of the bottom of the case and multiply by the number of shelves, which gives the number of sq. ft. of finish. 

After the areas of the different parts have been obtained as described above, add them together to get the total number of sq. ft. of surface to be painted. 

COVERING CAPACITY OF PAINTS 

It is difficult to say how many sq. ft. of surface one gallon of paint will cover, as there are several items that influence the covering capacity. By brushing the paint out very thin it will cover more surface than when applied thick. Dark paint will hide the surface better than light paint, and for that reason it can be brushed out thinner than the lighter colors. Also, a rough surface will require considerable more paint than a smooth surface.

Soft and porous wood will absorb more oil and require more paint than close grained lumber.

Another thing that must be considered are the ingredients entering into the paint. Different brands of paint vary in covering capacity or hiding power. This is due to the varying proportions of carbonate and hydrate used in the paint and to the varying degrees of fineness to which the lead is ground. 

Naturally, an inferior grade of paint consisting of one-half white lead and one-half of a more transparent pigment cannot possibly go as far as a paint consisting of pure white lead.

Priming Coat on Wood.-As mentioned above, a gallon of paint will cover less surface on soft porous wood than on close grained wood; also dark paint has a greater covering capacity than light paint.

The priming coat should be mixed thin in all cases, with sufficient oil to satisfy the wood, and with only enough pigment to provide a foundation for the succeeding coats. This will be found especially advisable when priming bass wood, white pine and poplar, as they require considerable oil to satisfy them. It is often difficult to make paint stick to yellow pine boards that are full of pitch.

Another thing the estimator must consider is the fact that paint has a greater covering capacity on smooth boards than on rough boards and a greater covering capacity on a wall of smooth dressed boards than on weatherboarded wall. 

If white or light colored tints are used for the priming coat on weatherboarding or matched boards, one gallon of paint should cover 450 to 500 sq. ft. of surface on soft or porous wood and 

500 to 550 sq. ft. on close grained wood. 

If dark colored paints, such as gray, tan, buff, drab, etc., are used for priming weatherboarding or matched boards, one gallon of paint should cover 500 to 550 sq. ft. of surface on soft or porous wood and 550 to 600 sq. ft. on close grained wood. 

If rough lumber is painted, the covering capacity will be greatly reduced, depending upon the surface of the lumber. 

Second or Subsequent Coats of Paint on Wood.-The varia tion in covering capacity due to the pores in the wood will not be so great in the second and following coats, although they will vary to a certain extent. 

If white or light colored tints are used, one gallon of paint should cover 500 to 550 sq. ft. on porous wood and 550 to 

600 sq. ft. on close grained wood. 

If dark colored paints, such as gray, tan, buff, drab, etc., are used, one gallon of paint should cover 550 to 600 sq. ft. of surface on porous wood or 600 to 650 sq. ft. on close grained wood.

Bear in mind that the above quantities are based on surfaced lumber and the covering capacity will be greatly reduced when applied to rough boards.

Estimating Paint Quantities on Old Work. When estimating old work, special attention must be given to the old surface as this will have considerable bearing on the covering capacity. 

If the old surface is hard and in good condition, it will be safe to figure 350 to 400 sq. ft. per gallon for white or light tint paints but if the old surface is very dry and worn through to the wood in many places, sufficient paint must be used in the

first coat to satisfy the surface, and not more than 250 sq. ft. can be covered properly with one gallon of paint. 

Two Coats of Paint on Wood.-Two coats of white or light colored paint should cover 240 to 265 sq. ft. of surface on porous wood and 260 to 290 sq. ft. on close grained wood. 

Two coats of dark colored paint, such as gray, tan, buff, drab, etc., should cover 265 to 290 sq. ft. of surface on porous wood and 290 to 315 sq. ft. on close grained wood. 

Three Coats of Paint on Wood.-One gallon of white or light colored paint should cover 175 to 200 sq. ft. with three coats.

One gallon of dark colored paint, such as gray, tan, buff, drab, etc., should cover 200 to 225 sq. ft. with three coats. 

Painting Brick and Concrete.—On brick or concrete surfaces that have not been resurfaced with cement, one gallon of white or light tint paint should cover about 225 sq. ft. of surface with one coat, while dark colored paints, such as tan, gray, buff, etc., should cover 275 to 300 sq. ft. per gallon, with one coat. 

When applied to rough cast plaster or stucco, one gallon of white or light colored paint should cover 150 to 175 sq. ft. with one coat, while dark colored paint should cover about 225 sq. ft. per gallon, with one coat.

To obtain the covering capacity of 2 or 3-coats of paint, use quantities given above for one coat and divide by 2 or 3, as required.

Painting Smooth Metal Surfaces. When painting smooth metal surfaces, such as gutters, downspouts, metal roofs, siding, etc., one gallon of pure red lead and oil paint should cover 1,500 to 1,800 sq. ft. with one coat.

After the first coat has been applied, one gallon of paint should cover 1,000 to 1,200 sq. ft. of surface for each additional coat. 

Painting Structural Steel.-One gallon of red lead and oil should cover 600 to 700 sq. ft. of structural steel for the first coat and 500 to 600 sq. ft. for the second or subsequent coats. 

A mixture of 33 lbs. of pure red lead and one gallon of oil produces approximately 1.42 gallons of paint.

Flat Wall Paint.-Flat wall paint is suitable for interior use only. It is usually factory mixed and any number of coats may be applied. It dries with a soft, velvety finish and may be used on old or new walls, wallboard, interior woodwork and similar surfaces.

A good grade of flat wall paint will cover 400 to 500 sq. ft. with one coat or 200 to 250 sq. ft. with 2 coats. 

Painting Smooth Plastered Walls and Ceilings.-When paint ing smooth plastered walls and ceilings with lead and oil paint, the covering capacity will vary with the thickness to which the paint is applied because on work of this kind it is possible to apply the paint thick enough to hide the surface with one coat. If the paint is mixed thin the covering capacity will be greater but it will require more coats of paint to hide the surface. 

One gallon of white or light colored paint should cover 550 to 600 sq. ft. with one coat; 275 to 300 sq. ft. with 2 coats and 200 to 

225 sq. ft. with 3 coats. 

One gallon of dark colored paint should cover 700 to 750 sq. ft. of surface with one coat; 350 to 375 sq. ft. with 2 coats and 

225 to 250 sq. ft. with 3 coats.

Painting Sand Finished Plastered Walls and Ceilings. When painting rough sand finished plaster, one gallon of white or light colored paint should cover 450 to 500 sq. ft. with one coat; 250 to 275 sq. ft. with 2 coats, and 175 to 200 sq. ft. with 3 coats. 

One gallon of dark colored paint should cover 600 to 650 sq. ft. of surface with one coat; 325 to 350 sq. ft. with 2 coats and 200 to 225 sq. ft. with 3 coats.

Covering Capacity of Wall Size.-The covering capacity of wall size will vary greatly with the material used. 

Glue size consisting of ground or flake glue and water will cover 900 to 1,000 sq. ft. of surface per gallon. 

Varnish size consisting of varnish, benzine or turpentine and a little paint, will cover 450 to 500 sq. ft. per gallon. 

Hard oil or gloss oil size consisting of rosin and benzine will cover 450 to 500 sq. ft. per gallon. 

Covering Capacity of Calcimine.-One gallon of calcimine should cover 250 to 275 sq. ft. of surface on smooth plastered walls and 200 to 225 sq. ft. on sand finished walls. 

When applied to brick walls, one gallon of calcimine should cover 150 to 175 sq. ft. of surface. 

Covering Capacity of Cold Water Paint.-Cold water paint is furnished in powder form and is mixed with cold water. It can be applied by hand or using a spraying machine.

Three pounds of cold water paint mixed with one gallon of water should cover 100 sq. ft. of surface. 

Shingle Stain. When staining wood shingles after they have been laid, one gallon of good stain should cover 150 sq. ft. of surface, one coat. 

The second and third coats will go farther, as the wood does not absorb as much stain as on the first coat and should cover 

200 to 225 sq. ft. per gallon.

One gallon of good stain should cover about 100 sq. ft. of roof with 2-coats or 65 to 75 sq. ft. with 3 coats. 

If the shingles are dipped in stain before laying, it will require 

3 to 34 gals. of stain per 1,000 shingles. When dipping shingles in stain, only two-thirds of the shingle need be dipped, as it is unnecessary to dip the end of the shingle that is not exposed. 

Covering Capacity of Oil and Spirit Stains.-When staining finishing lumber, such as birch, mahogany, oak, gum, etc., one gallon of stain should cover 500 to 550 sq. ft. 

One gallon of spirit stain should cover 450 to 500 sq. ft. 

Covering Capacity of Wood Fillers.-Liquid filler is usually used with close grained woods, such as pine, birch, etc., and one gallon should cover 500 to 550 sq. ft. 

It is necessary to use a paste filler to fill the pores of all open grained wood, such as oak, ash, walnut, mahogany, etc.

Where the wood is stained and filled at one operation, add sufficient stain to the filler to produce the desired shade. Take about 5 lbs. of paste filler, add enough stain to give it the desired color and then add turpentine or benzine to bring the mass to the consistency of a heavy paint. The usual proportion is about one gallon of liquid to 5 lbs. of filler. One gallon of combined stain and filler should cover about 300 sq. ft. of surface.

If paste filler is used on oak, one lb. of filler should cover about 40 sq. ft. of surface or it requires 2ª lbs. per 100 sq. ft. 

If paste filler is used on close grained wood, such as pine, birch, etc., one lb. of filler should cover about 45 sq. ft. or it requires 24 lbs. per 100 sq. ft. of surface. 

Covering Capacity of Shellac.-The covering capacity of shellac will vary with its purity but one gallon of good shellac should cover 550 to 600 sq. ft. of surface.

Covering Capacity of Varnish.—One gallon of good varnish should cover 400 to 450 sq. ft. of softwood floors with one coat; 

200 to 225 sq. ft. with 2 coats and 150 to 175 sq. ft. with 3 coats. 

When applied to hardwood floors, one gallon of good varnish should cover 500 to 550 sq. ft. with one coat; 250 to 275 sq. ft. with 2 coats and 200 to 225 sq. ft. with 3 coats.

When applied to softwood interior finish, one gallon of good spar finishing varnish should cover 450 to 500 sq. ft. with one coat; 200 to 225 sq. ft. with 2 coats and 150 to 175 sq. ft. with 

3 coats.

When applied to hardwood interior finish, one gallon of good spar finishing varnish should cover 550 to 600 sq. ft. with one coat; 275 to 300 sq. ft. with 2 coats and 200 to 225 sq. ft. with 

3 coats. 

Covering Capacity of Wax.-One gallon of liquid wax composed of turpentine and beeswax should cover 550 to 600 sq. ft. with one coat. 

One pound of good paste wax should cover 250 to 300 sq. ft. of surface with one application. 

Covering Capacity of Crevice Filler. The amount of crevice filler required to fill cracks in floors before painting will vary with the size of the cracks and the width of the flooring but on an average, one lb. of crevice filler should cover 20 to 25 sq. ft. of floor.

Covering Capacity of Varnish Remover.-The amount of varnish remover required to remove old varnish from floors and interior finish will depend upon the condition of the old work, but one gallon of good varnish remover should be sufficient for 250 to 300 sq. ft. of surface. 

Covering Capacity of Enamel.-When enamel is used for interior finish, the first and quite often the second and third coats consist of white lead and pure linseed oil. When lead and oil is used one gallon should cover 450 to 500 sq. ft. with one coat; 250 to 275 sq. ft. with 2 coats and 175 to 200 sq. ft. with 3 coats.

If prepared enamel undercoating is used for the base coats, one gallon should cover 400 to 450 sq. ft. with one coat; 225 to 250 sq. ft. with 2 coats and 150 to 175 sq. ft. with 3 coats.

On work of this kind the ground coats usually consist of lead and oil or prepared enamel undercoating, while the last one or two coats are enamel. The covering capacity of enamel

will vary with the brand used but one gallon of good enamel should cover 400 to 450 sq. ft. with one coat or 200 to 225 sq. ft. with 2 coats. 

Glazed Walls.-One gallon of good glazing liquid, colored with oil colors, should cover 500 to 550 sq. ft. of surface. 

Bronzing Radiators.-Bronze powder is mixed with banana oil or varnish and turpentine and is used for painting radiators, grilles, etc. It is usually mixed in the proportions of 6 ounces of powder to one pint of banana oil. One ounce of good powder should cover 20 to 25 sq. ft.

If aluminum or silver powder is used for radiators or grilles, 4 ounces of powder is usually mixed with one pint of banana oil. 

One ounce of good aluminum or silver powder properly mixed, should cover 25 to 30 sq. ft. of surface. 

Directions for Mixing Paint.-To "break up" lead quickly, easily, and smoothly, use the following method: Start by adding a very small quantity of oil-not more than one pint of oil to 100 lbs. of lead. With a good, strong, smooth paddle work the oil completely into the lead. Then add another pint of oil, and when this is thoroughly worked in, add additional oil -a quart at a time-working it thoroughly into the lead each time until you have worked in about 1 gallons of oil to 100 lbs. of lead. In breaking smaller quantities of lead, reduce the quantity of oil proportionately.

The mixture will now readily thin down with more oil into a perfectly smooth paint that is entirely free from lumps. The small amount of skin paint should then be removed by straining through a wire screen or cheese cloth.

Color should be partly thinned and added to the lead before the final thinning or it may be thinned to a fluid condition and added after the final thinning of the paint, but before straining. 

Add the driers before the final thinning.

The working qualities of the paint will be very much improved by straining and by allowing it to stand at least one day before using. 

The above method is not only labor saving, but it is the only way by which a high grade white lead can be properly broken. 

Adding a large quantity of oil at the start may cause the lead to "break up" lumpy. 

If you are not familiar with "breaking" pure white lead, be careful not to add too much oil when finally thinning down the paint. On account of the fineness of the lead*, it feels stiffer 

*Carter White Lead Co.. Chicago.

under the paddle than coarser leads with the same quantity of oil. You can determine its body by testing it under the brush. 

For dead flat effects, follow the above method, but use turpentine instead of linseed oil. However, first mix the lead with benzine or turpentine, and allow same to stand over night. 

Then skim off the oil which has risen to the top. In special cases it will be found desirable to pour off all the liquid and again mix the lead thoroughly with fresh benzine or turpentine, allow it to stand, and skim off as before. 

The following information relative to mixing lead and oil paints and the quantities as given on the following pages was furnished through the courtesy of one of the largest manufacturers of white lead in the country and is dependable. 

Soft Paste White Lead.-White lead is commonly furnished in Heavy Paste form which has to be broken up slowly as described above. However, most brands of white lead are now obtainable in Soft Paste form, where the lead is ground in linseed oil to a thinner consistency than the Heavy Paste, and when mixed with an equal quantity-measure for measure-of linseed oil, makes a paint of the same consistency as when 100 lbs. of Heavy Paste is thinned with 4 gals. of oil. 

When Soft Paste is used the time required "breaking up" the lead and mixing the paint is reduced one-half.

White lead Heavy or Soft paste are both the same price. 

Number of Gallons of Paint Obtainable from Any Mixture. 

-One hundred pounds of pure white lead will bulk 2 gallons, and 2 gallons plus the quantity of oil, turpentine, drier, and color added will give the number of gallons of paint produced by the mix. 

How to Mix Paints 

It is impossible to give a formula by which any color may be matched exactly, as this must depend upon the painter's eye. Tinting "colors in oil," as they are called, should be added cautiously and gradually and never at one time all that is called for by the formula. The color always looks darker in the pot than when it is spread out on a board; it also changes somewhat in drying, for which due allowance must be made. Also. tinting colors vary in strength with different makes, and there is no uniform standard of either strength or color sold under a common name.

Carter White Lead Co., Chicago.

The quantities of thinners specified on the following pages cover white paint mixed for the second and third coats on new work. Some additional thinner will be required for first coat work.

The time required mixing colors will vary with the ability of the painter and are based on using Heavy Paste white lead. 

If Soft Paste white lead is used, the mixing time may be reduced one-half.

Floor Paint.-To one gallon of white lead paint of any desired shade, add lb. of litharge which has been worked out smooth with a little of the paint. This will dry very hard, and should be mixed in the paint only when it is ready to be used, as litharge will cause paint to harden in the pot. 

A durable floor paint may be made by adding to the paint mixed as above a small amount of varnish-about a pint or a

quart of varnish to the gallon. If the floors are outside and exposed to the weather, spar varnish is preferable. If the floors are not exposed to the weather, add ordinary floor varnish.

Painting Brick, Stucco or Concrete.-When painting brick, stucco or concrete that is less than one year old, the surface should first be washed with a solution of 10 parts sulphate of zinc to 90 parts water to neutralize the causticity of the lime.

ESTIMATING LABOR COSTS .... 

$0.21

Perhaps in no other trade will labor costs vary to a greater extent than in painting and varnishing. On some classes of work the material costs are almost negligible, while the labor costs may make it one of the most expensive kinds of work. 

Naturally, the cost of the work will depend upon the grade of workmanship specified or upon the class of work the painting contractor figures on doing.

Some painters (not all) always figure on getting away with a little less than called for. For instance, if three coats of paint are specified on outside work, they will try to get away with two. If three coats of varnish are called for on the interior finishing, they will try to get away with one less; and if the work is to be rubbed down to an egg shell gloss, they figure on giving a coat of "flatine" instead of gloss varnish for the last coat, which will eliminate the rubbing time.

Every contractor must make a profit on his work if he is to remain in business, so when a painter submits an unreasonably low figure, it may be assumed that he has either made a mistake in his quantities or has figured on using inferior material and slighting the workmanship. 

In the large cities particularly, there are two classes of painters—those who make a specialty of "cheap" work, such as factory buildings, flat or apartment buildings, speculative work, and work of this class, and those who specialize in high class work. Naturally, the painter who figures the cheaper class of work is bound to be lower than the man who figures a first class job, as a painter can cover more surface per day when he just hits the "high spots" than when he is conscientious in his work and gives a good, honest job.

When preparing an estimate, the estimator should consider the above facts and price his work accordingly.

On exterior work, labor quantities and costs are given on only one class of work, but on interior finishing and decorating, costs are given on two grades of work, termed "Ordinary 

Work" for the cheaper grade and "" for the better grade.

FINISHING INTERIOR WOODWORK 

The greatest variations in costs will be found in interior finishing, as this is principally a labor proposition. For instance, where two, three or four coats of paint, enamel or varnish are specified, some painters will apply the entire number of coats without sanding between coats, regardless of specifications. 

This saves time but produces an inferior job. 

It is possible to make a fairly good job with poor materials if the workmanship is right but it is impossible to make a good job using the best materials if the workmanship is poor. 

To produce a first class finish on interior woodwork, it is necessary to sand or rub down between coats to produce a smooth surface to receive the following coats. The finish coat will then be smooth and without rough spots, dust marks, etc. 

It is practically impossible to obtain this finish without sanding between coats.

For the reasons given above, costs are given on two classes of work, and the estimator should use his judgment as to the class of work required. The cheaper grade of work is termed "Ordinary Work," while the better grade is termed "First 

Grade Work." Labor Glazing Plastered and Canvassed Walls 

Where walls of vestibules, dining rooms, living rooms, etc., are covered with canvas, Sanitas or similar wall covering, they are usually finished with a glaze finish. This consists of a ground coat of lead and oil paint applied in the usual manner, and then the finish coat of one or more colors is applied and blended with an ordinary stippling brush, a bunched cloth, a sponge or a rumpled piece of paper to bring out the high lights. 

The labor cost applying the ground coat is the same as given for plain painting on the same kind of walls, i.e., canvassed, wallboard, plaster, etc.

Where only one glazing color is used in addition to the base coat, a painter should glaze and high light 600 to 800 sq. ft. per 8-hr. day.

If more than one glazing color is used in addition to the base coat, a painter should glaze, high light and finish 400 to 600 sq. ft. per 8-hr. day.

ITEMIZED COSTS OF INTERIOR PAINTING 

The itemized costs given on the following pages include the specifications generally called for by architects and owners and furnish the contractor or estimator detailed information regarding every item entering into the cost of any class of painting. 

These costs are tabulated in such a way that local material prices and wage scales may be substituted in all instances. 

To compute the cost of paint in any locality, refer to the itemized costs given on the previous pages and insert local prices.

The following costs include sufficient material for the superficial area figured. If there are many large openings, the

quantity of paint may be reduced, depending upon the number and size of openings.

Painting Contractor's Overhead Expense and Profit.—Inas much as the painting on a building is usually sublet to a painting contractor, it will be necessary to add for the painting contractor's overhead expense and profit, which includes workmen's compensation and liability insurance, general office overhead, trucking, ladders and scaffold, drop cloths, profit, etc.

This item will vary considerably with the individual contractor, the size of the job, the size of the town or city in which the work is performed, and how anxious the contractor is to obtain the job, but under average conditions this will add 25% to 40% to the actual cost of the work. 

The costs on the following pages include 25% for overhead expense and profit but this may be changed to suit local conditions.
