Textone Wall Finishes.-Textone is a plastic decorating material applied by the painter and decorator. It may be applied over practically any interior surface, such as plaster, wallboard, paint, canvas, metal, wood, brick and concrete. It is furnished in powder form and mixed with water in the proportion of 1 pint of water to 1 lb. of Textone, to secure consistency that will produce the desired texture. It should be applied with a Dutch calcimine brush and laid on to a uniform thickness of " to ". Two men work to best advantage, one applying Textone and the other texturing.

There are several finishes obtainable, such as the brush finish, Early English finish, Spanish Palm finish, Stipple finish, Mission finish, Scroll finish, etc., and these are obtained by using wadded paper, a whisk broom, sponge, an ordinary wall stippler or the palm of the hand. 

Textone comes in white only but is readily tinted to any desired shade.

One lb. of Textone should cover 9 to 11 sq. ft. of surface for a medium texture (slightly more for finer textures). 

Inasmuch as hardened Textone is insoluble in water, care must be used to prevent spattering woodwork and other trim. 

To prevent this, a special adhesive tape is furnished in rolls 1" wide and 30 yards long for covering the edges of casing, base and other interior finish.

WALL PAPER AND PAPER HANGING Total 

*$1.17 .01%

Wall paper is estimated by the roll containing 36 sq. ft. The standard size roll is 1'-6" (18") wide and 24'-0" long, and contains 36 sq. ft. or 4 sq. yds. of paper. The double roll is just twice as long as the single roll, viz.: 48 ft., and contains 72 sq. ft. or 8 sq. yds. of paper. 

Estimating the Quantity of Wall Paper Required for any 

Room. When estimating the quantity of wall paper required for any room, measure the entire distance around the room in lin. ft. and multiply by the height of the walls or the distance from the floor to the ceiling. The result will be the number of sq. ft. of surface in the four walls. 

Make deductions in full for the area of all openings such as windows, doors, consoles, mantels, built-in book cases, etc. The difference between the area of the four walls and the area of the openings will be the actual number of sq. ft. of surface to be papered. 

When adding for waste in matching, cutting, fitting, etc., paper hangers use different methods and allow different percentages, contingent upon the height of the ceiling, the design of the paper, and the size of the pattern or figure, but an allowance of 10 to 15 per cent will prove sufficient in nearly all cases. 

When estimating the quantity of paper required for walls, bear in mind that it is not necessary to run the side wall paper

PAPER HANGING 

1187 more than one or two inches above the border, when a border is used. The height of the wood base should also be deducted from the total height of the wall. 

In rooms having drop ceilings, the depth of the drop should be deducted from the height of the wall, which will decrease the area of side wall paper in the same amount as it increases the quantity of ceiling paper.

If a border is required, measure the distance around the room and the result will be the number of lin. ft. of border. Dividing by 3, gives the number of yards of border required. 

When estimating the quantity of wall paper required for ceilings, multiply the width of the room by the length, and the result will be the number of sq. ft. of ceiling to be papered. 

In rooms having a drop ceiling, add the depth of the drop or the distance the ceiling paper extends down the side walls to the length and breadth of the room and multiply as described above. Example: A room measuring 16'-0″x20′-0″, having a drop ceiling extending 1'-6″ down the side walls should have 3′-0″ added to both the length and width of the ceiling as follows: The width of the room (16′-0″) plus the drop (1′-6″ on each end or 3'-0" for both sides of the room) equals the total width of the ceiling (19′-0″). The length of the room (20'-0") plus the drop (1'-6" on each end) equals the total length of the ceiling (23′-0″). The number of sq. ft. in ceiling is obtained by multiplying, 19×23=437 sq. ft. 

After the areas of both sidewalls and ceiling have been computed in sq. ft. divide by 36, and the result will be the number of single rolls of paper required; or by dividing by 72 gives the number of double rolls of paper required.

Paste Required Hanging Wall Paper.-The quantity of paste required for hanging wall paper will vary with the weight of the paper and the surface to which it is applied. 

Where light or medium weight wall paper is used, one gallon of paste should hang 12 single rolls of paper. 

If heavy or rough texture paper is used, it will often be necessary to give it two or three applications of paste to obtain satisfactory results. On work of this kind one gallon of paste should hang 4 to 6 single rolls of paper.

When making paste, care must be used when brown sugar, glue or blue vitriol is added to the mixture, as they will draw the color from many papers. 

There are a number of prepared pastes on the market containing all the necessary ingredients so that by adding water and boiling, the paste is ready for use. 

If prepared paste is used, one pound of dry paste should make 3 gallons of ready to use paste or 1 gallon of solid paste.

As stated above, the quantity of paste required will vary with the weight of the wall paper, but the following will prove a fair average for both light and heavy weight papers.

Placing Wall Paper Borders.-Wall paper borders are usually estimated by the lin. ft. or yd. and as the width varies from 3" to 18" there is never over one width required. 

The average size room requires 50 to 60 lin. ft. or 17 to 20 yds. of border.

Flexwood.-Flexwood is a genuine wood veneer cut to 1/85 of an inch, glued under heat and hydraulic pressure to cotton sheeting with a waterproof adhesive. A patented flexing operation breaks the cellular unity of the wood to produce a limp, pliable sheet which may be applied by hand to any smooth surface, flat or curved. Waterproof Flexwood cement, which makes a permanent bond, is used to apply Flexwood. Standard sizes of stock material are 18-in. and 24-in. widths and 8-ft. and 10-ft. lengths. 

The mechanics of installing Flexwood are as follows: the background is sized with Flexwood cement. Another coating of cement is brushed on the Flexwood which is then hung in the manner of any sheet wall covering. A stiff, broad knife, used with considerable pressure, smooths out the Flexwood, removes air spaces and furnishes the necessary contact. 

Some of the wood available in Flexwood are Mahogany, Walnut, Oak, Prima Vera, Knotty Pine, Orientalwood, Satinwood, Zebrawood, Rosewood, English Oak, Maple, Lacewood, etc. The cost of the material varies from 25 cts. to 75 cts, per sq. ft. depending upon the kind of wood.

It requires a skilled and thoroughly competent paperhanger to apply this material and the labor costs vary considerably with the design to be obtained.

Considerable time is usually required to lay out any room to obtain the desired effect, spacing of strips, etc. This is especially true where certain designs must be obtained on columns, walls and pilasters and where narrow strips of contrasting woods are used to obtain inlay effects.

On plain walls without inlays, a paperhanger experienced in this class of work should apply 125 to 140 sq. ft. of Flexwood per 8-hr. day, at the following labor cost per 100 sq. ft.: 1

Finishing Flexwood.-Flexwood will take any wood finish but where the natural color of the wood is desired, the Flexwood is given one coat of lacquer sealer, sanded lightly between coats and then given one coat of lacquer for a finish coat. 

One gallon of lacquer sealer will cover about 300 sq. ft. of surface, one coat.

CHAPTER XVIII ,  

While glass is not one of the largest items entering into the total cost of a building, it is a branch of work that requires a great deal of detail to prepare an accurate estimate, and for that reason should be figured with the utmost care. 

There are dozens of different kinds of glass and they are figured in almost as many different ways.

Plain window glass is figured from lists prepared by the glass manufacturers giving the price of each size light in both single and double strength, and discounts are quoted from this list price depending upon market conditions.

Plate glass and mirrors are also figured from plate and mirror lists issued by the different manufacturers and jobbers, from which certain discounts are quoted, depending upon market conditions.

Chipped glass, ribbed glass, wire glass, and many other kinds of fancy glass are estimated by the sq. ft. depending upon the size of the glass, thickness, etc. 

Estimating the Quantity of Glass Required.-When measur ing and listing the glass quantities for any job, always list each kind of glass separately, such as single strength, double strength, plate, mirrors, ribbed glass, etc., as they are all figured from different lists and take different discounts.. 

As far as practicable all sizes of each kind of glass should be listed separately as it will make it much easier when pricing the estimate.

Labor Glazing Window Glass.—In the larger cities the glass is usually sent to the job and the glazing is done in the building after the sash are fitted, but in the smaller cities and towns where stock sash are used, the sash are usually glazed in the mill before being sent to the job. It costs considerable less to glaze in the mill than on the job, so that this item should be taken into consideration when pricing the work. 1195

The labor cost of glazing will vary with the size and kind of glass, and whether set in putty or with wood stops, as it costs about twice as much to use wood stops as putty.

Labor Setting Plate Glass in Store Fronts.-The labor cost of handling and setting plate glass in store fronts will vary with the size of the glass, the length of the haul, etc. 

The average size plate glass used in modern store fronts requires 4 men to handle and set each light of glass. No matter how many lights of glass there are in the job, it will be necessary to allow time for 4 men, also a time allowance for glaziers going to the job and returning to the warehouse after completion, and time for truck and driver hauling glass from the warehouse to the job and return. 

Unless the job is considerable distance from the warehouse, an allowance of 2 hours time for each man going to the job and returning to the warehouse should prove sufficient, but in many instances this time may be reduced one-half.

It is customary for the truck and driver to remain on the job until the glass is set and return to the warehouse with the men, so that truck time should be figured on this basis.

Labor Glazing Steel Sash.-The labor cost of glazing steel sash will vary with the size of the glass, amount of putty required per light, and the class of work; i. e., whether sidewall sash, monitor sash, etc., also whether it is necessary to hoist the glass and erect special scaffolding to set it.

The time of year in which the work is performed will also influence the labor costs, as a glazier can set more glass in warm weather than during the winter months. The labor costs given below are based on summer glazing. For winter work add 10% to cost given.

Estimating the Cost of Plate and Sheet Glass, Mirrors, Etc. 

The price of glass is subject to frequent change due to fluctuations in the cost of manufacture, supply and demand, etc. 

While all prices and discounts have been revised to date of publication, it is advisable to consult your nearest jobber or dealer before quoting prices or submitting estimates.

All discounts quoted are applicable to the Central District of the United States and include delivery of glass within this territory, but for all points west of the Mississippi River and south of the Mason and Dixon line and in all of the New England States, it will be necessary to add freight from nearest factory or warehouse in the Central District to destination. 

Sheet Glass.-With the flat drawn window or sheet glass now made, there is no bow in the glass so that either side may be glazed out.

Weights of Sheet Glass.-Single strength sheet glass weighs about 1.4 lbs. per sq. ft. and double strength glass weighs about 2 lbs. per sq. ft.

Leaded and Art Glass 

When estimating leaded or art glass, odd or fractional parts of inches are charged as even inches of the next larger size; for example, a 124"x13" light will be charged as 14"x14".

Circles, ovals or irregular patterns will be charged at the rate of a square or rectangle which will contain them.

Beveled Plate Glass Leaded.-If beveled plate glass is wanted leaded in straight patterns, such as squares, hexagons, diamonds, etc., estimate the cost of this work at about $3.00 a square foot. 

If beveled plate glass is wanted leaded in circular or curved work, estimate the cost of this glass at about $3.25 to $3.75 a square foot.

If the leaded plate glass is wanted in elaborately cut flower designs and in other elaborate circular patterns, the cost will run as high as $8.00 a square foot.

Colored Art Glass Leaded. Leaded art glass furnished in colors may be had in many designs at $1.50 to $1.75 a square foot, which includes only straight work. 1 Landscape and water scenes in colored art glass will run from $3.75 to $5.00 a square foot.

Very elaborate designs of art glass in colors with flowers, fruits, etc., may be purchased at from $5.00 to $8.00 per sq. ft. 

The architect usually specifies an allowance of so much per square foot to cover the cost of all art glass in the building. 

Cost of Boxing Leaded or Art Glass.-Boxing either leaded or colored art glass is charged for at the rate of 15 cents a square foot of actual lid measurement of cases shipped, but the minimum charge for any box is 50 cents. 

Cost of Copper.—If the leading is to be electro plated for a copper finish, add 25 cents per square foot to the cost of plain leading. 

Cost of Wide Leading. For window glass leaded in heavy wide leading, add 25 per cent to plain leaded prices.

METAL STORE FRONT CONSTRUCTION 

Metal store fronts constructed of bronze, alumilited aluminum alloy, both drawn and extruded, and of stainless steel in drawn members only, are extensively used for display windows, as they provide the greatest display space with the least obstruction, which places them in high favor with all who use windows for display purposes.

In the larger cities the metal store fronts are usually erected by the concern furnishing the materials, while in the smaller cities and towns, store front erection is usually performed by carpenters.

Labor Erecting Metal Store Fronts.-The labor cost of in stalling metal store fronts will vary with the style of front, size, etc., as the larger and more elaborate the front the more labor required to install it. 

In the larger cities metal store fronts are installed by sheet metal workers but in the smaller cities and towns carpenters usually install them.

There is no set rule for estimating the cost of metal store fronts by the lin. ft. of material. A certain number of hours should be allowed for an average size store front for each type of construction and a proportionate addition or deduction for a larger or smaller store front should be figured therefrom. 

Figure 1. Metal Store Front Construction. 

The following costs cover installation of the metal portions of the store front and do not include any woodwork or carpentry labor in connection with same. This should be figured under Carpentry.

Installing Metal Work for Metal Store Front Similar to 

No. 1.-When installing the metal work for a store front similar to Figure 1, an experienced carpenter or sheet metal

worker should install all the metal work above the bulkhead for a 20'-0" store front in 14 to 16 hrs. Add 2 to 4 hrs. time for a store front 30'-0" wide.

If the transom bars are omitted and the large plates extend to the ceiling, without the use of a copper transom bar, deduct about 4 hrs. time from the above.

If the bulkhead of this store front is constructed entirely of metal panels, without movable sash, figure 20 to 22 hrs. time for bulkhead construction only. If movable sash are used in bulkhead, add 2 to 4 hrs. time.

If the transom bars are omitted and large plates extend to the ceiling, without the use of a metal transom bar, deduct about 4 hrs. time from the above.

CHAPTER XIX ROOFING, CORRUGATED ASBESTOS AND METAL ROOFING AND SIDING 

Roofing is estimated by the square containing 100 sq. ft. 

The method used in computing the quantities will vary with the kind of roofing and the shape of the roof. 

The labor cost of applying any type of roofing will be governed by the pitch or slope of the roof, size, plan of same (whether cut up with openings, such as skylights, pent houses, gables, dormers, etc.), and upon the distance of the roof above the ground, etc.

Rules for Measuring Flat Roofs.-When measuring flat roof surfaces that are to be covered with composition, tar and gravel, tin, metal or prepared roofing, the measurements should be taken from the outside of the walls on all four sides to allow for flashing up the side of each wall. The flashing is usually 6" to 1'-0" high. This applies particularly to brick, stone or tile buildings having parapet walls above the roof level. AL

FIZURE 1 Fig. 1. Flat Roof with Parapet Walls SECTION A-A 

On flat roofs projecting or overhanging beyond the walls of the building, the measurements should cover the outside dimensions of the roof and not merely to the outside of the walls. 1225

When estimating the area of flat roof surfaces, do not make deductions for openings containing less than 100 sq. ft. and then deductions should be made for just one-half the size of the opening.

Make deductions in full for all openings having an area of 

500 sq. ft. or more.

Example: The length of the building (as shown in Figure 1), is 50'-0", which is the distance from A to B. The width of the building from B to C is 20′-0″. Multiplying the length by the width, 50x20=1,000 sq. ft. By referring to Figure 1, you will note the building is only 48′-0″ long and 18'-8" wide between walls. The method of measuring the full length and width of the building is to allow for flashing up the side of the walls, which usually extends 6" to 12" high. 

PITER ALLIGAT SECTION THRU ROOT FIGURE 2 Fig. 2. Flat Roof Overhanging Walls. 

Figure 2 illustrates a building of the same size with projecting roof. The size of the building proper is 20′-0″x50′-0″, while the roof projects beyond the walls 2'-0" on each side, making the size of the roof 24'-0"x54′-0″. The roof area is obtained by multiplying the length of the roof (the distance from E to F), 54'-0", by the width of the roof (the distance from F to G), 24′-0″, making the total roof area, 54′-0″x24′-0″=1,296 sq. ft.

The skylights on both roofs measure 6'-0"x9′-0″ and contain only 54 sq. ft. each, so that no deductions should be made for these openings, as they contain less than 100 sq. ft. each and the

ROOFING 

1227 extra labor flashing up the sides of the walls more than offsets the cost of the small openings. 

Rules for Measuring Plain Double Pitch or Gable Roofs. 

To obtain the area of a plain double pitch or gable roof as shown in Figure 3, multiply the length of the ridge (A to B), by the length of the rafter (A to C). This will give the area of one-half the roof. Multiply this by 2 to obtain the total sq. ft. of roof surface. 

Example: Assume the length of the ridge (A to B), is 30′-0″ and the length of the rafter (A to C), is 20'-0". By multiplying (A to B), 30′-0″ by (A to C), 20'-0" equals 600. The area of one-half the roof is 600 sq. ft. 600x2=1,200 sq. ft. of roof. 20.0" 30'-o' 20-0" D

Roof

Rules for Measuring Hip Roofs.-To obtain the area of a hip roof as shown in Figure 4, multiply the length of the eaves (C to D) by the length of the rafter (A to E). This will give the number of sq. ft. of one end of the roof, which multiplied by 2 gives the area of both ends. To obtain the area of the sides of the roof, add the length of the ridge (A to B) to the length of the eaves (D to H). Divide this sum by 2 and multiply by the length of the rafter (F to G). This gives the area of one side of the roof and when multiplied by 2 gives the number of sq. ft. on both sides of the roof. 

To obtain the total number of sq. ft. of roof surface, add the area of the two ends to the area of the two sides. This total divided by 100 equals the number of squares in the roof.

€ £ ! G 

ROOF PLATT ELEVATION FIGURE 4 Fig. 4. Hip Roof 

Example: Assume the length of the eaves (C to D) is 20'-0" and the length of the rafter (A to E) is 20'-0". Multiplying (C to D) 20'-0" by the length of the rafter (A to E), or 10′-0″ equals 200 sq. ft., the area of one end of the roof. To obtain the area of both ends, 200x2=400 sq. ft. 

To obtain the area of the sides of the roof, assume the length of the ridge (A to B), is 15′-0″ and the length of the eaves (D to H), is 30'-0". Add (A to B) 15'-0" to (D to H) 30'-0", and the result is 45'-0". By taking the combined length of the ridge and eaves, of 45-22'-6", the average length of the roof. 

Assuming the length of the rafter (F to G) as 20′-0″, 22′-6″x 20′-0″ 450 sq. ft., the area of one side of the roof, which multiplied by 2 equals 900 sq. ft., the area of both sides of the roof.

Adding the area of the two ends to the area of the two sides gives 1,300 sq. ft. of roof area. .00.05

1229 The area of a plain hip roof running to a point at the top .. is obtained by multiplying the length of the eaves (B to E) by the length of the rafter (A to F). This gives the area of one end of the roof. To obtain the area of all four sides, multiply by 4.

Example: Multiply the length of the eaves (B to E), which is 30′-0″, by the length of the rafter (A to F), 10'-0", and the result is 300 sq. ft., the area of one end of the roof. 300x4=1,200 sq. ft., the area of the 4 sides.

Rules for Measuring Conical Tower Roofs and Circular 

Buildings. To obtain the area of a conical tower roof as shown in Figure 6, multiply the length of the rafter (A to B) by the distance around the eaves at B. As an example, assume the length of the rafter (distance from A to B) is 15'-0" and the diameter of the building at B is 20'-0”. 

To obtain the distance around the building, multiply the diameter by 34 or 3.1416. If the eaves project beyond the outside walls, and the diameter is given only to the outside walls of the building, add the length of the roof projection on both sides of the building to obtain the correct diameter. 

Example: If the diameter of the building (C to D) is 20'-0" and the eaves project 2'-0" on each side, the diameter of the building at the eaves would be 24'-0".

Multiplying 24′-0″ (B to E), the diameter of the building at eaves, by 3.1416, gives 75.3984, or approximately 75'-5" around the eaves at projection (B to E). 

To obtain the area of the roof, multiply the length of the rafter (A to B), which is 15′-0″, ( of 15 is 7) or 7'-6", by the distance around the eaves at B and E, which is 75'-5" or 75.4 feet, and the result is 565.5, or 565 sq. ft., the area of the roof. 

To obtain the area of a cylindrical or circular building, multiply the height by the circumference, or the distance around the building, and the result will be the number of sq. ft. to be covered. The circumference is obtained by multiplying the diameter (C to D) of the building by 34, or 3.1416. To obtain the area of the outside walls of a cylindrical building whose diameter is 20'-0" and the height 15'-0", 20x3.1416=62.832, or 

62'-10". Multiply 62.832 ft. (the distance around the building) by 15 ft. (the height of the building)=942.48, or 9421 sq. ft., the area of the outside walls.

ASPHALT SHINGLES 

Asphalt shingles are furnished in several styles and the labor cost of laying them will vary with the style of shingle used and the type of roof to which they are applied. (8) G 

Individual Asphalt Shingles. 

Individual asphalt shingles are furnished and laid in exactly the same manner as wood shingles, the only difference being their size.

Strip asphalt shingles are furnished in strips, each containing 3 or 4 shingles, so when laying them a man handles and lays 3 or 4 shingles at a time.

Wide space asphalt shingles are similar to individual shingles except they are laid in a different manner and do not require as many shingles per square as when laid in the regular manner.

Estimating Quantities of Asphalt Shingles.-Asphalt shingles are sold by the square containing sufficient shingles to cover 

100 sq. ft. of roof.

When measuring roofs of any shape, always allow one extra course of shingles for the "starters" at the eaves, as the first or "starting" course of shingles must always be doubled.

ASPHALT SHINGLES 

1231 Obtain the number of lin. ft. of hips, valleys and ridges to be covered with asphalt shingles and compute same as 1'-0" wide.

When using asphalt shingles for roofs, roll asphalt roofing of the same materials as the shingles are often used for forming valleys, hips and roof ridges. 

Individual asphalt shingles are 8" or 9" wide, 12" long, and when laid 4" to the weather requires 380 to 424 shingles per 100 sq. ft. It is customary to leave " space between each shingle. 270 b 91 pe as 1 

Strip Asphalt Shingles 

Strip asphalt shingles consist of strips of heavy asphalt roofing covered with red, green or variegated slate chips. Each strip is 10" or 12" wide and 36" long (sizes differ somewhat according to the brand used). These shingles are cut so that they look like individual shingles when laid. 

Strip shingles are laid 4" to the weather (the full length of the "cut-outs") and end touching end so that there is no space between the strips at the ends. 

As each strip of shingles is 36" long and laid 4" to the weather, one strip covers 144 sq. in. or 1 sq. ft. It requires 

100 strips of shingles to cover 100 sq. ft. of roof. 

Shingles 36"x10" give a double thickness at all points except at cutouts, while 36"x12" shingles give a double thickness at all points, including cutouts, and a three thickness roof at the point of hardest wear.

Wide space shingles are practically the same as individual shingles, the only difference being in the method of laying. 

They are usually 9" wide and 16" long and are laid with 5"

exposed to the weather. All shingles are laid 6" apart, with each shingle overlapping the two under shingles 1" on each side, forming a perfectly tight roof. 2510 

I Wide Space Asphalt Shingles 

You will note from the illustration that each shingle sags in the middle, thus closing up the space under it and preventing water blowing upward. Each shingle is laid 5" to the weather with a 6" "head-lap," so that one shingle covers 75 sq. in. of roof or it requires 192 shingles per 100 sq. ft. 

Estimating Quantities of Asphalt Shingles for Sidewalls.- 

When individual asphalt shingles are used for sidewalls they should not be exposed more than 3" to the weather with " space between each shingle. As individual shingles are usually 8" or 9" wide, one shingle covers 25 to 27 sq. in. or it requires 535 to 565 shingles per 100 sq. ft. This is 33 per cent or more shingles per 100 sq. ft. than are required for roofs. 

If individual asphalt shingles are placed lengthwise on sidewalls with the shingles laid 3" to the weather, one shingle covers 39 sq. in. of surface or it will require 370 shingles per 

100 sq. ft. This is about 14 per cent or less shingles than when laid lengthwise on the roof and exposed 4" to the weather. 

One square of individual shingles should cover 114 sq. ft. of sidewall surface when laid lengthwise. 

Always add an extra course of shingles for the "starters," as the first course must always be doubled to prevent leaking. 

When estimating sidewall shingles, the method of laying should be thoroughly understood, as most manufacturers sell their shingles at a certain price per square, based on the assumption that they are to be used for roofing.

ASPHALT SHINGLES 

1233 When strip asphalt shingles are used for sidewalls they should not be exposed more than 3" to the weather, and will require 33 per cent or more shingles than when used for roofing. If the strips are 36" long it will require 133 strips of shingles per 100 sq. ft. of sidewall. One square of strip shingles will cover only 75 sq. ft. on sidewalls. 

If wide space shingles are used for siding it is advisable to lay them lengthwise, exposing them 3" to the weather and spacing them 12″ apart. See that each shingle laps the two under shingles 2" on each side. Put 3 nails in each shingle, driving them 31" above the butt. Each shingle covers about 

84 sq. in. of surface, and it requires 172 shingles per 100 sq. ft. 

One square of shingles should cover 111 sq. ft. of sidewall.

SLATE ROOFING 

Roofing slate is furnished in a number of sizes, thicknesses and finishes to meet the architectural requirements of the buildings on which they are to be used. The four principal classifications are: Standard slate; Textural slate; Graduated slate and Flat slate roofs. 70 ids gitchie fandibbs di 1007 Strle IsmineT ad to t L 

Standard Slate Roofs

Standard Roofs.-Standard slate roofs are composed of slate approximately" thick (Commercial Standard Slate), of one uniform standard length and width, having square tails or butts laid to a line. Standard roofs are suitable for any building where a permanent roofing material is desired at a minimum cost. If desired, the butts or corners may be trimmed to give a hexagonal, diamond or "Gothic" pattern for all or part of the roof.

Textural Roofs.-The term "Textural" is used to designate slate of rougher texture than the Standard, with uneven tails 

Textural Slate Roofs or butts and with variations of thickness or size. In general, this term is not applied to slate over " in thickness. 

Graduated Roofs.-The graduated roof combines the artistic features of the Textural slate roof with additional variations

SLATE ROOFING 

1239 in thickness, size and exposure. The slate is so arranged on the roof that the thickest and longest occur at the eaves and gradually diminish in size and thickness until the ridges are reached. Slate for roofs of this type can be obtained in any combination of thicknesses from" to 1" and heavier when especially desired. 1-89TS Teutos adfast te OS toubab bis di wa 

Graduated Slate Roofs 

In addition to the usual standard sizes, slate above" thick are produced in lengths, up to 30". The graduations in lengths generally range from 24" to 12". The longest slate are used at the eaves and the length usually diminishes with the thickness. The variations in length will at once provide a graduation in exposure by using the standard 3" lap. To illustrate, a suitable range of lengths might be:

Flat Roofs. Flat roofs offer a wide field for roofing slate and are so designated whether or not they are used for "promenade" purposes.

Slate of any thickness may be used instead of slag or gravel as a surfacing material for the usual built-up type of roof. For ordinary roofs the Standard" slate are used but for promenade or extraordinary service, the slate should be " or " thick.

Slate for flat roofs are furnished in the following standard sizes: 6"x6", 6″x8″, 6″x9", 10"x6", 10"x7", 10"x8", 12″x6″, 12"x7" and 12"x8".

Estimating Quantities of Roofing Slate.-Obtain the net area of the roof in sq. ft. as described at the beginning of this chapter. Add 6″ to rafter length to allow for waste of normal roof. 

Deduct one-half the area of chimneys and dormers if over 20 sq. ft. and less than 80 sq. ft. Make no deductions if less than 20 sq. ft. and deduct 20 sq. ft. less than actual area if more than 80 sq. ft. 

Include area of dormer sides, sides of dormers if slated, slate saddles or other places where slate is used in addition to the main roof area. Include overhanging parts of dormers, etc. 

Add 1 sq. ft. for each lin. ft. of hips and valleys, for loss in cutting and fitting. 

Allow 2 to 15 per cent additional slate, depending upon the extent to which the roof is intersected by other roofs, dormers, walls, etc.

SLATE ROOFING 

1241 Divide the total of the above by 100, which will give the number of "squares" of roofing required.

Slate is always sold at the quarry on the basis of the quantity required to cover 100 sq. ft. or a "square" of roof when slate is laid with a 3″ head lap. If the roof is flat or other than 3″ lap is used, the quantity must be corrected to the equivalent amount required as though the 3" lap were used. 

Items to Be Included in an Estimate for Slate Roofing.-The following items should be included to make a complete and accurate estimate on slate roofing: 

1. Cost of slate (punched) on cars at the quarry. 

2. Freight from quarry to destination. 

3. Loading and hauling to storage yard. 

4. Unloading, piling and waste at storage yard. 

5. Loading and hauling to job, also unloading and piling at job. 

6. Placing on roof and laying, (a) roofing felt, (b) elastic cement, (c) nails, (d) snow guards or snow rails, (e) sheet metal, (f) labor, including compensation insurance, (g) waste in handling, cutting and fitting. 

7. Contractor's overhead expense, surety bond, if required, and profit on the work.

Labor Punching Slate.-The labor cost of punching slate on the job will vary with the size of the slate, as the larger the slate the fewer pieces required per square.

SLATE ROOFING 

1243 Slate may be obtained from the quarry punched and ready for use and this eliminates all punching on the job, but in the event the corners are broken in shipment it is not possible to reverse the slate after they have been punched. When punched on the job the best end of the slate may be used. 

If one slater is working on the job with a helper, the helper should punch the slate and carry them to the slater as fast as required. In instances of this kind, there should be no additional charge for punching. If, however, there is only one man working on the job, who must punch the slate and lay them, a man should punch one square of slate in 30 to 40 min. or 12 to

Labor Cost of Laying Roofing Slate.-The labor cost of laying roofing slate will vary considerably with the size of the slate, thickness, type of roof, etc., but when large thick slate are used for graduated roofs, the labor costs will run higher than when the same size slate are used on standard roofs. 

The size of slate best adapted for plain roofs are large, wide slates, such as 16"x12", 18"x12", 20"x12" or 24"x12". Slate from 16"x8" to 20"x10" are also popular sizes. For roofs cut up into small sections, the 14"x7" and 16"x8" are very popular. 

A roofing gang consisting of two slaters and one helper can work to advantage and perform the work more economically than one man working alone. In some localities the helper is considered an apprentice and is permitted to lay slate, in others he can only punch and carry the slate to the slaters. 

Laying 16"x8" Roofing Slate.-When working on plain roofs that do not require much cutting, 2 slaters and a helper should handle and lay 450 to 600 sq. ft. (4 to 6 sqs.) of 16"x8" slate per 8-hr. day. On more complicated hip or gable roofs, requiring considerable cutting and fitting for hips, valleys, dormers, etc., 2 slaters and a helper should handle and lay 

325 to 400 sq. ft. (34 to 4 sqs.) of 16"x8" slate per 8-hr. day. 

Laying 18"x9" Roofing Slate.-When laying 18"x9" slate on plain roofs, 2 slaters and a helper should handle and lay 500 to 650 sq. ft. (5 to 6 sqs.) per 8-hr. day.

On more complicated hip or gable roofs, requiring considerable cutting and fitting for hips, valleys, dormers, etc., 2 slaters and a helper should lay 350 to 425 sq. ft. (3 to 44 sqs.) per 8-hr. day. 

Laying 20"x10" Roofing Slate.-When laying 20"x10" slate on plain roofs, 2 slaters and a helper should handle and lay 550 to 650 sq. ft. (5 to 61 sqs.) of roof per 8-hr. day, but on more complicated roofs, requiring considerable cutting and fitting for hips, valleys, dormers, etc., the same gang would lay only 

400 to 450 sq. ft. (4 to 4 sqs.) per 8-hr. day. 

Laying 22"x12" Roofing Slate.-On straight roofs, 2 slaters and a helper should handle and lay 600 to 700 sq. ft. (6 to 7 sqs.) of 22"x12" slate per 8-hr day, but on the more complicated roofs, requiring cutting and fitting for hips, valleys, dormers, etc., the same gang would lay only 425 to 500 sq. ft. (4 to 5 sqs.) per 8-hr. day.

Laying Graduated Roofing Slate.-When laying graduated roofing slate from" to 4" thick and 12" to 24" long, considerable care is required in selecting the right slate for each course and laying them to obtain the desired effect. On work of this kind 2 slaters and a helper should handle and lay 200 to 250 sq. ft. (2 to 21 sqs.) of roof per 8-hr. day.

ASBESTOS SHINGLES 

Asbestos shingles* are made of asbestos fiber and portland cement, united under hydraulic pressure and cut to shingle shapes. They are furnished in a variety of different sizes, shapes and colors, so that the cost will depend upon the style and color of shingles used, method of laying and the size and shape of the roof.

When estimating quantities of asbestos shingles, the measurements are taken in the same manner as for shingle or slate roofs. The length of the eaves must be measured to obtain the number of lin. ft. of starters required, also the length of the hips and ridges, as either shingles or a special ridge roll will be required. Asbestos shingles are sold by the square containing sufficient shingles to cover 100 sq. ft. of surface. 

They are made in American, Hexagonal and Dutch Lap styles, in a uniform thickness of ". Tapered American Method shingles are also made with 1", 5", 7", 1″ and 1″ butts. 

*Varies according to locality. 

*Johns-Manville Co.

Method of Laying Asbestos Shingles American Method of Laying Asbestos Shingles.-When laying 

No. 5 or No. 10 shingles, apply under the roofing felt, one course of No. 51 (81"x17") shingles at eaves lengthwise and parallel with same, overhanging the eaves about 1". Apply the second course, using main body shingles, entirely covering the first course as shown in the accompanying illustration, breaking joints, after which proceed in the regular manner as with wooden shingles or slate, exposing 7" to the weather. For No. 

55 (exposed 7" to weather) and No. 190 and 200 (exposed 8" 

Copper clip enlarged scale

Hexagonal shingle on roof

Deta.ls of Ridge Roll C nst: uction to weather) use main body shingles for starters. Fasten each shingle in place with at least 2 galvanized iron or copper needle pointed shingle nails. Never drive nails down tight as it is only necessary to drive them firmly. Over the ridges and hips apply asbestos ridge and hip rolls with not less than 3" lap, fastened in place with special ridge roll fasteners furnished for the purpose or use "Boston" or "Chicago" hip and ridge method as shown in the accompanying illustration. 

Where ridge pole does not project high enough above the roof boards to allow direct application of ridge roll, it is necessary to put in a false pole to obtain a direct fastening through top of ridge roll. See illustration covering this construction. 

All chimneys, valleys, etc., should be flashed with copper or other approved material.

Hexagonal Method of Laying Asbestos Shingles.-The hex agonal or "honeycomb" method of applying asbestos shingles, in the thickness, is lower in cost than the American method. 

The hexagonal method apparently shows 6 sides of the shingle, thus overcoming the objections to severely straight lines and producing a pleasing effect. Hexagonal Method of Laying Asbestos Shingles. 

Apply one course of No. 17 asbestos shingles end to end, parallel with and overhanging the eaves 1", over which apply one course of No. 71 shingles, entirely covering the starter, No. 17, breaking all joints as shown in the accompanying illustration. 

Cover balance of roof with No. 70 shingles 16"x16", laid as shown, exposing 13"x13" to the weather. Securely fasten all shingles in place with galvanized or copper needle pointed nails, and fasten the points of the No. 70 main body shingles with special copper storm nails. Never drive nails down tight as it is only necessary to drive them firmly. All the main body shingles, i.e., the No. 70, should be laid with the diagonal lines on a 45-degree angle with the eaves. Over the ridges and hips apply asbestos ridge and hip rolls, with not less than 3" lap, fastening in place with special roll fasteners furnished for the purpose.

Dutch Lap Method of Laying Asbestos Shingles.-The Dutch 

Lap Method of applying asbestos shingles closely resembles the American Method in appearance yet approximates the cost of the Hexagonal method. 

Apply, under the felt at eaves, one course of No. 41 starter shingles (3"x17") parallel with and overhanging eaves 1", with each shingle overlapping preceding shingle approximately its length so that nail holes will occur one over the other. Cut the first starter to its original length and with a new hole punched 218" from the cut end, apply at the end of the roof to

ASBESTOS SHINGLES 

1261 overhang the gable 1". Fasten with a nail through the new hole. Then apply a full length starter to overlap the first starter one-half its length. Fasten both with a nail through coinciding holes. Proceed in a similar manner to end of roof. 

Completely cover starters and balance of roof with No. 40 shingles (17"x17") laid as shown, exposing 11"x14" to the weather, securing each shingle with 2 shingle nails and 1 storm anchor. The shingles are aligned on nail and storm anchor holes and therefore automatically establish a one-third side lap and 3″ head lap. Ridges, hips and exterior corners are ´finished with No. 18 asbestos ridge and hip shingles or asbestos ridge roll in the same manner as with other types of asbestos shingles.

Laying Asbestos Shingles 

The cost of laying asbestos shingles will vary with the size of the shingles, style in which they are laid, whether plain or complicated roofs, and upon the labor employed. 

Where possible, it is economy to work two mechanics and one helper in a crew, as a helper can keep two mechanics supplied with materials without difficulty and the quantities and costs given are on that basis. However, if one man is working alone, use the total number of hours per square for any type of roof and multiply by the current wage rate... 

Laying Asbestos Shingles by the American Method.-When laying 8"x16" asbestos shingles on plain hip or gable roofs, a crew consisting of two roofers and a helper should handle and lay 450 to 600 sq. ft. (4 to 6 sqs.) per 8-hr. day,

On complicated hip or gable roofs, the labor cost will be higher due to the necessity of cutting and fitting shingles. This additional labor will vary, depending upon how badly the roof is broken up, but a crew consisting of two roofers and a helper should lay 325 to 400 sq. ft. (3 to 4 sqs.) per 8-hr. day, unless very unusual conditions exist. 

Laying Asbestos Shingles by the Hexagonal Method.-When laying 16"x16" asbestos shingles by the Hexagonal method on fairly plain roofs, a crew consisting of two roofers and a helper should handle and lay 600 to 675 sq. ft. (6 to 62 sqs.) per 

8-hr. day.

On more complicated roofs, the labor cost will be higher due to the necessity of cutting and fitting shingles. This additional labor will vary, depending upon how badly the roof is broken up, but a crew consisting of two roofers and a helper should handle and lay 500 to 600 sq. ft. (5 to 6 sqs.) per 8-hr. day, unless very unusual conditions exist.

TIN AND METAL ROOFING 

Metal roofs include tin, copper, zinc, galvanized iron or steel or any of the special processes, such as Armco, Toncan, etc. 

When estimating quantities of metal roofing, the measurements are taken in the same manner as for other types of roofs. 

Where the metal roof is applied over flat roofs having parapet walls, an allowance of 1'-0" on each side and end of the wall should be allowed for flashing up to sides of the walls. 

If metal roofing is applied to a flat surface or pitch roof with overhanging eaves the measurement is taken to cover the entire roof surface. 

Do not make deductions for openings containing less than 100 sq. ft. and then deduct for just one-half the area of the opening, as the extra flashing costs as much as the roofing omitted.

Deduct in full for all openings containing over 100 sq. ft. 

Sizes of Sheets.-The common sizes of tin plates are 10"x14" or multiples of that size. The sizes generally used for roofing are 14"x20" and 20″x28″. The larger sizes are more economical to lay, but for flat roofs the 14″x20″ size is preferable,

A box of tin contains 112 sheets. 

For a flat seam roof, the edges of the sheets are turned in "to", locked together and well soaked with solder. The sheets should be fastened to the roof boards by cleats locked in the seams. These cleats are usually spaced about 8″ apart and 

2 nails are used in each cleat.

For flat seam roofing a 14"x20" sheet of tin, with edges turned up" on each side and end measures 13"x19" and contains 247 sq. in., but the covering capacity when locked to other sheets is only 12"x18" or 2314 sq. in. The number of sheets required to cover one sq. (100 sq. ft.) of roof is obtained by dividing 14,400 sq. in. (100 sq. ft.), by 231 sq. in. (1 sheet),

equals 62. It requires 62 sheets of 14"x20" tin to cover 100 sq. ft. of roof. 

Method of Laying Flat Seam Metal Roofing. 

Sheets measuring 20"x28" with the edges turned for flat seam roofing measure 19"x27" and when locked to other sheets have a covering capacity of 181″x261″ or 490 sq. in. It requires 29 sheets to cover 100 sq. ft. of roof. 

Tin for roofs may also be obtained in rolls 14″, 20″ and 28″ wide. When used for flat seam roofing the loss due to turning edges amounts to 13" on the width of any sheet. 

Tin in 14" rolls loses 13" or 11 per cent of its width due to turning edges and laps. When estimating roofs using roll roofing, take the area of the roof and add 11 per cent for waste. 

Another method is to take the length of the roof and divide by 121" (the net width of each sheet) and the result will be the number of strips of tin required. Multiply the number of strips by the length of each strip to obtain the quantity of tin required for any roof.

An example of this method is as follows: By referring to 

Figure 1, the actual dimensions of the roof are 18'-8″x48′-0″. 

Allowing 1'-0" on each side and end of the roof for flashing, the roof would be figured as 20'-8″x50′-0″. The roll tin will run the long way of the building so that each strip will be 50'-0" long. The width of the building is 20'-8″ or 248″ wide. Each strip of tin covers 12" in width, so it requires 20 strips of tin 50'-0" long to cover the roof.

The actual measurements of the sheets will be 11" less in width and length than the size of the sheet used. For instance, the actual covering capacity of a 24"x96" sheet will be only 

221″x941″ or 2,126 sq. in.

Standing Seam Metal Roofing.-Standing seam roofing re quires a larger allowance for waste than flat seam roofing. The standing seam, edged 11″ and 11″ takes 23" off the width and the flat cross seams edged ", take 13" off the length. 

If 14″x20″ tin is used, each sheet covers 11"x18" or 212.34 sq. in. It requires 68 sheets of 14"x20" tin per 100 sq. ft. of roof. 

If 20"x28" tin is used, each sheet covers 171"x26" or 463.59 sq. in. It requires 32 sheets of 20″x28″ tin per 100 sq. ft. 

If roll tin is used 23" should be allowed for the two standing seams. The end waste will vary with the length of the sheets.

Tin in 14" rolls loses 2" off the width due to the standing seams, making it necessary to add 20 per cent for waste. 

Another method is to take the width of the roof and divide by 111" (the net width of the sheet), and the result is the number of strips of tin required. Multiply the number of strips by the length of the roof to obtain the quantity of tin required. 

A Method of Laying Standing Seam Metal Roofing An example of this method is as follows: By referring to 

Figure 1, the actual dimensions of the roof are 18'-8″x48′-0″. 

Allowing 1'-0" at each end of the roof for flashing, the dimensions of the roof should be figured as 20'-8″x50′-0″. The rolls will probably run the long way of the building, so that each strip will be 50'-0" long. Each strip of tin covers 11″ in width or it requires 22 strips of 14″ tin 50′-0″ long to cover the roof.

COPPER ROOFING 

1277 

Estimating Quantity of Copper Required for Flat Seam Roof ing.-Copper roofing is estimated in the same manner as tin, the only difference being the variations in the amount of waste for the different size sheets. 

For a flat seam roof the edges of the sheets are turned in ″ to" and locked together. If the seams are soldered, care should be taken to see that the edges of the copper are well tinned before soldering. The sheets should be fastened to the roof boards by cleats locked in the seams. These cleats are usually spaced 8" to 12" apart and two nails used in each cleat. 

On cheaper work the nails are driven through the copper under the turned edges, but this should not be permitted. 

On flat seam roofing 11" should be deducted from the length and width of each sheet to allow for turning edges and lapping.

CORRUGATED STEEL ROOFING AND SIDING 

Corrugated steel is used extensively for roofing and siding steel mills, manufacturing plants, sheds, grain elevators and other industrial structures. 

It is made with ", 1", 21" and 3" corrugations but the 11" and 21" corrugations are most commonly used. SE 219902 8px" Jalo 9125

Methods of Placing Corrugated Metal Roofing.

CORRUGATED ROOFING AND SIDING 1281 

The sheets are usually furnished 26" wide and 6'-0" `to 10′-0″ long, but the 8′-0″ length is probably the most frequently used. 

When estimating quantities of corrugated siding or roofing, always select lengths that work to best advantage and be sure and allow for both end and side laps. 

Corrugated siding or roofing is nailed to the wood framework or siding when used on wood constructed buildings. When used as a wall and roof covering on structural steel framing, the corrugated sheets are fastened to the steel framework, using cleats of " or " band iron, which are passed around or under the purlins (which usually consist of channels, angles or Z bars) and riveted at both ends to the corrugated sheets. When angles are used for purlins, clinch nails are sometimes used for fastening the corrugated sheets. 

When used for siding one corrugation lap is usually sufficient, but for roofing two corrugations should be used and if the roof has only a slight pitch, the lap should be three corrugations.

When used for siding, a 1" end lap is sufficient, but when laid on roofs it should have an end lap of 3″ to 6″ depending upon the pitch of the roof. For a pitch a 3″ lap is sufficient ; for a pitch a 4″ lap should be used; and for a pitch a 5″ end lap.

When applying to wood sheathing or strips, the nails should be spaced about 8" apart at the sides. When applied to iron or steel purlins, the side laps should extend over at least 1 corrugations, and the sheets should be riveted together every 8" on the sides and at every alternate corrugation on the ends.

VARIOUS TYPES OF SHEETS. 

Types of Corrugated Asbestos Roofing and Siding.

TYPE Z 

The same materials that are used in forming the corrugated sheets are molded at the factory into special standard shapes to be used as ridge roll, corner roll, louvres and ventilators.

They are also furnished in flat sheets 36"x48", 42"x48" and 

42"x96" and " to 2" thick. Standard size corrugated sheets are made 42" wide and 3′-0″, 3′-6″, 3′-9″, 4′-0″, 4′-3″, 4′-6″, 4′-9″, 5′-0″, 5′-3″, 5′-6″, 6′-0″, 6′-6″, 7′-0″, 7′-6″, 8′-0″, 8′-6″, 9′-0″, 10'-0", 10'-6" and 11'-0" long, and approximately " thick.

Sheets can be furnished on special order cut to any desired length possible from the standard sizes. Special curved sheets can also be furnished with the following limitations: sheets may be curved longitudinally, the arc being formed along the direction of the corrugation; minimum radius when so curved 

60". Sheets may be curved crosswise, the arc being formed across the corrugations, minimum radius when so curved 24". 

Sheets may be curved either way but not in combination. 

The sheets are furnished in three types, as illustrated. The cut corner construction eliminates a thickness of material in the corner lap, thus allowing the sheets to nest perfectly at these points and permit them to be laid with side laps forming vertical lines. The inside and outside radii of the corrugations are the same, thereby allowing the sheets to nest perfectly at all laps.

Corrugated asbestos roofing may be laid on roofs pitched 2" to the foot and over. Asbestos roof putty should be used in all laps.

Supporting purlins or girts shall be spaced not to exceed 60″ center to center for roofing and 72" for siding. 

Method of Applying Corrugated Roofing and Siding 

Corrugated asbestos roofing and siding is applied directly over purlins and girts of skeleton frame construction or may be applied over solid wood sheathing.

When used as either roofing or siding, all sheets shall be lapped one corrugation at the sides and 6" at the ends. The size of the end lap is governed by the cut corner construction. 

The width of weather exposure of sheets for estimating purposes is 37.8".

Sheets shall be of proper length so that all end laps will occur over a purlin or girt and so that fasteners at ends of sheets will pass through both upper and underlying sheets. 

Fasteners especially designed for use in connection with this material can be furnished by the manufacturer*. The style of fastener to be used will be governed by the type, shape and

Labor Handling and Placing Corrugated Asbestos Roofing and Siding. The labor cost of handling and placing asbestos siding and roofing will vary according to the class of work, whether placed over wood or steel purlins or girts, size of sheets used and conditions under which the work is performed. 

The most economical organization for applying asbestos roofing and siding consists of one mechanic, 2 helpers and 3 laborers, and the labor costs given on the following pages are computed on this basis. 

The labor costs include all time necessary cementing joints and covering exposed fasteners with asbestos roof putty, also the time necessary placing ridge roll, corner roll, louvre blades, etc.

Placing Corrugated Asbestos Siding Over Wood Framing.— 

When placing asbestos siding in sheets 42″x48″ to 42″x60″ on wood framing, a crew consisting of mechanic, 2 helpers and 3 laborers should handle, place and fasten 7 to 8 sheets an hr. or 56 to 64 sheets per 8-hr. day. Inasmuch as the smaller sheets cover 11 sq. ft. minimum and the larger sheets 14 sq. ft. minimum, this is equivalent to 700 to 800 sq. ft. per 8-hr. day. 

When placing corrugated sheets 42"x72" to 42″x96″ on sidewalls, a crew should handle, place and fasten 6 to 7 sheets an hr. or 48 to 56 sheets per 8-hr. day. Inasmuch as the smaller sheets cover 173 sq. ft. minimum and the larger sheets 23 sq. ft. minimum, this is equivalent to 1,000 to 1,150 sq. ft. per 8-hr. day.

When placing corrugated asbestos siding 42″x48″ to 42″x60″

on steel framing, a crew consisting of one mechanic, 2 helpers and 3 laborers should handle, place and fasten 5 to 6 sheets an hr. or 40 to 48 sheets containing 500 to 600 sq. ft., per 8-hr. day

BUILT-UP ROOFING 

Built-up roofing consists of several plies of saturated felt and roofing pitch or asphalt, covered with slag or gravel. It may be used on flat roofs, roofs having only a slight pitch and where manufacturers' directions and the proper materials are used, for roofs having a pitch up to 9 inches to the foot. 

The specifications on the various types of roof vary widely, depending upon the surface to which the built-up roofing is applied and the service required. 

The cost of a built-up roof is governed by the pitch of the roof, size, plan (whether cut up with openings, skylights, pent houses, irregular roof levels, etc.), and the distance of the roof above the ground, as the higher the roof the higher materials must be hoisted, which increases the labor costs.

The rules for estimating quantities of built-up roofing are given in the first part of this chapter, under the heading "Rules for Measuring Flat Roofs." Roofing Contractor's Overhead Expense and Profit.-The quantities and costs on composition roofing given on the following pages are actual and do not include any allowance for roofing contractor's overhead expense and profit. 

According to a national survey made by the United Roofing Contractors of America, the overhead expense of roofers in Chicago and other large cities averages 25%. They recommend a 10% profit, in addition to the allowance for overhead. 

The estimator should use his own judgment as to the amount to be added for overhead and profit-it varies a lot among different contractors.

Quantity of Pitch or Asphalt Required for Built-Up Roofs.- 

The quantity of roofing pitch or asphalt required for any builtup roof will vary with the number of thickness or plies of felt used and the class of roof, i. e., whether a cheap or first-class built-up roof. All manufacturers of roofing materials include in their specifications sufficient materials for a first class roofbut all roofs are not applied according to these specifications. 

On certain types of industrial and speculative buildings, where price is a determining factor, competitive practices do not always produce a first class roof. On this class of work, some roofers merely mop an area sufficient to hold the next ply of felt, while on every first class roof plenty of pitch or asphalt should be used, sufficient to thoroughly mop each sheet of felt as in no instance should felt touch felt. 

On a first class roof, 25 to 30 lbs. of coal tar pitch or asphalt should be used for each mopping per 100 sq. ft. of surface and the last pouring in which the gravel or slag is imbedded, should use 40 to 75 lbs. of pitch or asphalt per 100 sq. ft. 

For the reasons given above, quantities and costs are given on two grades of roofing, "Ordinary Work" and "First Class" work. The estimator must use his own judgment as to the type of roof required on the structure under consideration.

Estimating the Quantity of Roofing Felt.-Asphalt or tarred felt for built-up roofing is furnished in 4 sq. rolls containing 432 sq. ft. and weighing 65 lbs. per roll for 15-lb. felt and 60 lbs. per roll for 14-lb. felt. 30-lb. felt which is generally used as the base sheet over wood construction when an asphalt specification is used is furnished in 2 sq. rolls containing 216 sq. ft. and weighing 65 lbs. These weights are those used on a bonded job in the best type of building construction. On small jobs where a bond is not required a roofer will occasionally use 12-lb. felt because of economy. 12-lb. felt is furnished in 4 sq. rolls containing 432 sq. ft. and weighing 52 lbs. per roll. The standard or preferable

BUILT-UP ROOFING 

1295 weight of felt on any first class built-up roofing job should be 

15-lb. felt.

When specifying the grade or weight of felt to be used it is customary to state that "felt shall weigh not less than 15 lbs. per sq." 15 lbs. per 100 sq. ft. is standard practice of all roofing manufacturers. Inasmuch as felt is furnished in 4 sq. rolls of 

432 sq. ft. there is 32 sq. ft. per roll or 8 sq. ft. per 100 sq. ft. allowed for laps.

In designating the weight of felt to be used, specify whether it is to be 14 lbs. per 100 sq. ft.; 15 lbs. per 100 sq. ft. or 30 lbs. per 100 sq. ft. If light weight felt is used, it should be specified as 12-lb. felt.

When estimating the quantity of felt required for any roof, an addition of 2 to 3 per cent to that included in the roll should be figured for laps, cutting and waste, or in other words figure about 110 sq. ft. of felt per 100 sq. ft. of roof, per ply.

Quantity of Roofing Gravel Required for Built-Up Roofs.- 

Roofing gravel should be uniformly embedded into a heavy top pouring of asphalt or pitch so that approximately 400 lbs. of gravel or 300 lbs. of slag is used per 100 sq. ft. of roof area. 

Where the incline of the roof is over 3" to the foot then it is customary to use not less than 250 lbs. of slag per 100 sq. ft. of roof.

Labor Applying Built-Up Roofing. The labor cost of hand ling materials and applying built-up roofing will vary with the specification used and the type of building to which the roofing is applied. On the low type of building, 1, 2 or 3 stories high, where there is no great distance from the ground to the roof

: deck, the labor for hoisting materials and supplying hot asphalt or pitch from the ground to the roof deck is considerably less than on a high building where there is a greater distance from the kettle to the roof.›

On low type buildings, a 5-man crew composed of 1 man at the kettle, 1. man carrying 'hot stuff,' 1 man rolling in felts, 1 man nailing in and 1 man mopping in, can lay the following areas per 8-hr. day: 

20 sqs. of 5-ply asphalt and gravel or pitch and gravel over wood roof deck, consisting of 1 sheathing paper, 2 dry felts and 13 plies of felt mopped in with a top pouring of pitch or asphalt and gravel surfacing. 

> 

20 sqs. of 4-ply asphalt and gravel or pitch and gravel over a concrete deck, all mopped including a top pouring of pitch or ‘asphalt and gravel or slag surfacing. 

24 sqs. of 4-ply asphalt and gravel or pitch and gravel over wood roof deck, consisting of 1 sheathing paper, 2 dry felts and 2 plies of felt mopped in with a top pouring of pitch or asphalt and gravel or slag surfacing. 

24 sqs. of 3-ply asphalt and gravel or pitch and gravel over concrete roof deck, all mopped and including a top pouring of pitch or asphalt and gravel or slag surfacing. 

The above figures apply to buildings up to 3 stories in height. 

On buildings of considerable height or if the roof surfaces are broken up with skylights, irregular roof levels, etc., the above quantities should be reduced about 25 per cent.

Type "A" buildings are the most convenient type of structure for application of built-up roofing. A low type of building from 

1 to 3 stories in height, straight, practically flat area not broken up by very many skylights or variations in the deck elevation. 

Type "B" buildings are not a convenient type of structure for the application of built-up roofing. A high type of building requiring considerable handling of materials to place them on the roof deck. Area of deck broken up by skylights or pent houses or

BUILT-UP ROOFING 

1297 saw-tooth deck construction, monitors, etc. Considerable variation in the deck levels or possibly a combination of flat areas and inclined areas.

On the average roof where the mopping between layers consists of mopping the width of the lap, a roofer should mop 100 sq. ft. of surface in 6 to 7 minutes.

On first grade work where the entire roof surface is mopped between each layer of felt, a man should mop 100 sq. ft. of roof in about 10 minutes.

After the roof surface has been mopped, a roofer should place roofing felt over 100 sq. ft. in about 6 minutes. 

After the last thickness of felt has been applied, it should require to -hr. roofer time to handle and hoist gravel, heat and hoist pitch, mop the roof surface. and apply gravel to one square of roof.

Where first grade workmanship is required, it should require 35 to 40 minutes for a roofer to handle pitch and gravel, mop the roof and spread gravel over one square of roof. 

Bonded Roofs.-Where standard materials are used, it is general practice with all manufacturers to make the following charges where a surety bond is required guaranteeing the roof for a period of years: $1.00 per square for a 20 year bond; $0.75 per square for a 15 year bond and $0.50 per square for a 10 year bond.

Quantity of Materials Required for Built-Up Roofs.-The quan tities of coal tar pitch, asphalt, felt, gravel, slag, etc., required for the various types are those recommended by manufacturers for the very best roofing and are included under all roofs headed 

"."

The quantities given under "Ordinary Work" are those commonly used by roofers on competitive work, although there is no set standard for this class of work. 

Prices on Roofing Materials.-Prices on roofing materials such as coal tar pitch, asphalt, felt, etc., vary according to market fluctuations, location of job, etc. Current material prices should always be obtained, where possible.

CHAPTER XX INTERIOR MARBLE AND STRUCTURAL SLATE 

To prepare an accurate estimate of cost of marble work, the estimator should understand the correct method of measuring and listing quantities from the plans; the manner in which the marble should be handled and set on the job, as well as the most economical and practical methods of handling the work.

When estimating marble wainscoting, it is incorrect to take the height of the wainscot from the floor to the cap and multiply by the number of lin. ft. because in all probability the wainscot is made up of three members, viz., base, die and cap, and each member should be estimated separately; the base and cap by the lin. ft. and the wainscot or die by the square or superficial foot.

The length and size of the pieces of marble has considerable bearing on the labor cost, because it usually costs as much to set a 6" piece as one 2'-0" long, so that a job made up of short pieces will cost more per foot than a job having a larger percentage of long pieces of marble. 

Trade Practice.-Trade practice in the marble industry re cognizes all marbles and stones commonly used for interior building purposes, as falling within one of four groups or Classifications, according to their respective characteristics and working qualities. Therefore, for purposes of standardization and clearer definition, the National Association of Marble Dealers has officially adopted these four classifications and defines them as follows: 

Group "A". Sound marbles and stones which require no "sticking,” “waxing," or "filling;" characteristically uniform and favorable working qualities.

Group "B". Marbles and stones similar in character to the preceding group but somewhat less favorable working qualities; occasional natural faults and requiring a limited amount of "waxing" and "sticking." 1320

INTERIOR MARBLE 

1321 Group "C". Marbles of uncertain variation in working qualities, geological flaws, voids, veins and lines of separation common; common shop practice to repair Nature's shortcomings by sticking, waxing and filling; "liners" and other forms or reinforcement freely employed when necessary. 

Group "D". Marbles and stones similar to the preceding group and subject to the same methods of finishing and manufacture but embracing those materials which contain a larger proportion of natural faults and a maximum variation in working qualities, etc. This group comprises many of the highly colored marbles prized for their decorative qualities. 

Below is a list of some of the more commonly used varieties of marbles and stones and the groups to which they belong :

Estimating Quantities of Marble Work. When measuring and listing quantities of marble work from the plans, there are several general rules that should be followed to insure accuracy. 

To accurately estimate the quantity of marble base, obtain the number of lineal feet of base, listing the various heights separately. All base under 1'-0" high is extended and priced on a lineal foot basis. All base 1′-0″ or over is extended and priced on a superficial foot basis. Always bear in mind that no piece of marble should be figured as being less than 1'-0" long, as it requires just as much time to set a 6" piece as one 2'-0" long. 

Short pieces are usually found around pilasters, door and window returns, etc.

Marble die is estimated by the square or superficial foot, and the labor costs computed in the same manner. When listing quantities, obtain the length of each run and multiply by the height, and the result will be the number of sq. ft. of die. If marble pilasters project beyond the face of the wall, list each projection according to its actual dimensions and if less than a 

6" projection, it should be priced as 6″ wide, but if the pilasters are over 6" wide, then use actual dimensions. 

Marble wainscot cap under 1'-0" wide or any marble under 1'-0" wide, should be measured by the lineal foot. 

Marble stair treads should be measured by the square or superficial foot, as they are ordinarily 12" or more in width. 

Be sure to mention length, width and thickness of all treads, type of nosing, etc.

Marble stair risers should be estimated by the lin. ft. giving length, height and thickness of each riser, as it costs practically as much to set a short riser as a long one. 

When estimating toilet stall work consisting of toilet backs, partitions, stall fronts, stiles, etc., the fronts should be estimated by the superficial foot if over 12" wide and by the lin. ft. if less than 12″ wide. Partitions and backs should be estimated by the superficial foot. Marble cap is usually estimated by the lin. ft. Some marble contractors figure toilet work at a certain price per stall, including all labor in connection with same, although most contractors recommend pricing on a square or lineal foot basis.

Marble column bases and caps formed of solid stock over 2"

INTERIOR MARBLE 

1323 thick, should be estimated at a certain price for each base or cap, mentioning the size and number of cu. ft. in each. 

Marble floor tile and border are usually estimated by the superficial foot, giving size of tile, such as 6″x6″, 9″x9″, 12″x12", etc. Small cr irregular sized tile, such as dots, etc., are estimated in the same manner, except that a notation should be made of the class of work, as it costs more to lay small and irregular shaped tile. 

Marble hand rail, moldings, etc., should be estimated by the lin. ft., giving the size of each, in order that the quantities may also be stated in cu. ft. if over 2″ thick. 

All classes of circular work, such as base, wainscot or die, should be estimated in the same units as straight work, except that circular work should be estimated separately, as it usually requires considerable more cutting and fitting than straight work.

All marble work cut and set "on the rake", such as stair wainscoting, wainscoting under stairs, etc., should be estimated by the superficial foot, using the largest dimensions. Work of this kind should be estimated separately as it is more expensive to set than straight work.

Handling and Setting Interior Marble.—Estimating the labor cost of handling and setting interior marble will depend as much upon the conditions under which the work is performed as any other class of construction work. The amount of labor handling, sorting and distributing the marble on the job before it is set should be considered, also whether it is necessary to hoist the marble above the first floor, as this will require considerably more handling. The average size of the pieces should be considered, such as the average length of base, size and thickness of wainscot, length of thresholds, treads, risers, caps, etc., as it costs almost as much to handle and set a short piece of marble as a long one. This is especially true on stock that can be handled by one man.

On practically all jobs it is necessary to have laborers handle the marble and distribute it ready for the setters, although in the larger cities all marble must be handled by marble setters and helpers. On large jobs a contractor may employ a "chain gang" composed of union helpers to handle the marble in the building. These men unload the marble from the cars

or trucks, unpack and store it in the building or distribute it to the location in the building where it is to be used. 

Hoisting Marble.-The Proposal sheet of practically all marble contractors belonging to the National Association of Marble Dealers states that the marble contractor shall have free use of the general contractor's hoisting facilities, runways, etc., so for this reason no allowance has been made for hoisting in the following estimates of cost.

However, if it is necessary for the marble contractor to pay for the use of hoist for hoisting marble to the upper floors of a building, figure about -hr. hoist time per 100 sq. ft. of marble.

Cartage on Marble From Cars to Job.-If the marble is furnished by an out of town mill and it is necessary to haul it in trucks from cars to the job, the cost will vary with the length of the haul but under average conditions should not exceed 3 to 5 cts. per sq. ft. If the marble is furnished by a mill located in the same town as the job, the price of the marble will probably include delivery to the job. 

Marble Contractor's Overhead Expense and Profit.—It is necessary to have a foreman on all jobs of any size to supervise the arrival, unloading and distribution of the stock, as well as to lay out the work and supervise the setting. 

On an average allow to -hr. foreman time to each hour setter's time, depending upon the size of the job and the number of setters employed.

Most small jobs will not require a foreman and no allowance should be made for same.

It will also be necessary to allow for overhead expense, such as liability and workmen's compensation insurance, office and traveling expense, profit, etc., which will vary according to the size of the job.

A fair allowance for overhead expense and profit is 20 to 30% of the actual cost of the work. 

Average Labor Cost Setting Interior Marble.-While the labor cost of marble setting will vary with the kind of material handled, some of the large producing marble companies estimate the setting cost of the entire job at a certain price per foot. 

The quantities for the entire job are taken, which include base, cap, wainscot or die, treads, risers, etc., and the labor priced at 55 to 75 cts. per sq. ft. as follows:

Setting Marble Base.-The cost of setting marble base will vary with the size of the rooms, whether straight walls or broken up with pilasters, piers, etc., and whether the job consists of long or short pieces of base.

Setting Circular Base.-Setting circular base having either rough or smooth bottoms will cost about one-half more than straight work of the same kind and set under similar conditions. 

There is usually considerable cutting and fitting on all circular work.

Setting Marble Wainscot or Die. The labor cost of setting marble wainscot or die will vary with the size of the pieces, the height of the wainscot or die, etc., as a marble setter will set almost as many lin. ft. of 5'-0" wainscot as 3'-0" wainscot. 

The labor cost handling stock will be increased somewhat, as it will require 2 to 4 laborers or helpers to handle each piece of marble and place it on the floor ready for the setter, while lighter stock, such as base, risers, treads, etc., can be handled by one man.

Setting Marble Toilet Stalls and Partitions.-The cost of handling and setting marble toilet stalls, backs, partitions. stiles, etc., will vary greatly with the individual job. On work of this kind the marble partition slabs are seldom less than 5'-0" in height and width and each slab contains 25 to 30 sq. ft. of marble. The backs are usually the same height as the partitions but not so wide and each back contains 16 to 20 sq. ft. of marble. The stall fronts or stiles are usually 6" to 8" wide and 6'-0" to 7'-0" high and extend to the floor to support the dividing partitions where metal standards are not used. 

As an average on toilet stall work, a good marble setter should complete about 4 stalls per 8-hr. day, after the marble backs are in place. Since the average partition contains about 

25 sq. ft. and each stile about 5 sq. ft., a setter and helper should set about 120 sq. ft. of marble per 8-hr. day, at the following labor cost for 4 complete stalls, exclusive of backs:

Laying Marble Floor Tile.-There are three labor operations to be considered when estimating the labor cost of setting marble floor tile, viz., the cement bed under the marble floor, labor handling and setting floor tile and the cost of rubbing or smoothing the floors after they have been laid.

Smoothing Marble Floors.-After the marble floors have been laid, it is necessary to rub them with carborundum stone to remove the uneven spots at the joints. On jobs of any size it is customary to use a rubbing machine powered by gasoline or electricity. The machine is operated by one man and runs back and forth over the floors and grinds them to an even surface using carborundum stone as an abrasive. *Depending upon union rules.
