Estimating Quantities of Interior Marble 

When estimating quantities of interior marble, any fraction of an inch will be treated as a whole inch when figuring. 

No piece of marble will be considered as being less than 6″ wide and 1'-0" long. 

Thickness.—Thicknesses given are approximate but not exact.

For slabs gauged to a given thickness, an extra charge of 10 per cent to the list price will be made.

Extra Lengths.-On slabs 10′-0″ to 12′-0″ long, add 10 per cent to list price; on slabs over 12′-0″ long, add 20 per cent.

Extra Widths.-On slabs over 5'-6" wide, add 10 per cent to list price.

Polished Both Sides.-Prices given are based on marble having one side polished unless otherwise noted. If both sides are to be polished, add 25 cents per sq. ft. for marbles in Group “A” and “B” and 45 cts. per sq. ft. for marbles in Group “C” and “D.”

Hone Finish.-Hone finish takes the same price as polished work.

Sand Finish.-If marble is finished with sand finish on one side only, deduct 10 cents per sq. ft. If sand finish on both sides, add 5 cents per sq. ft. 

Polished Edges. For each polished edge on " and 14" thickness, add 1" to measurement taken at right angle to the polished edge; on 1½" and 2″ thickness, add 2″.

Beveled or Rounded Edges.-For each beveled or rounded edge on " and 14" thickness, add 2" to measurement taken at right angles to the edge; on 1½" and 2" thickness, add 4",

INTERIOR MARBLE 

1339 

O. G. Molding.-For single member O. G. molding 75 cents per. lin. ft. of edge on " thick; 85 cents per lin. ft. on 14", and $1.05 per lin. ft. on 1½".

For each additional member, add 60 cents per lin. ft. of edge on " and 14", and 70 cents on 1½". 

Countersinking. For countersinking 14" deep or less, 65 cents per sq. ft. of surface. For each additional 14" deeper, or fraction thereof, add extra 45 cents per sq. ft. of surface. 

Grooving. For grooving 4" deep or less, 65 cents per lin. ft. for each groove. For each additional 14" deeper, or fraction thereof, add extra 45 cents per lin. ft. of each groove. 

Rabbeting. For rabbeting 4" deep or less, 50 cents per lin. ft. for each rabbet. For each additional 4" deeper, or fraction thereof, add extra 35 cents per lin. ft. of each rabbet. 

Special Cutting, Polishing, Drilling, Etc.-All special work other than listed above will be charged for extra. 

How to Figure Marble.-Find the cost of one piece of %" thick Alabama Clouded "A," polished one side with square cut edges, finished to size 6'-4"x1'-5".

Multiply 

Feet (1) x feet (6)=feet.... 

Feet (1) x inches (4) inches.. 

Inches (5) x feet (6)=inches.... 

Inches (5) x inches (4) inches.. 6'-4" 1'-5" 6'-0" 0'-4" .2'-6" 0'-2" 9'-0" 

Figured as 9′-0″@$1.35, $12.15, cost of piece.

Figure the same piece with one long and both short edges polished. Adding 1" for each of the 2 short edges makes the computing length 6'-6"; and adding 1" for the one long edge, makes the computing width 1'-6". 6'-6"x1'-6" equals 9.75 sq. ft. 

Another method is to use decimals, multiplying 6'-4" or 

6.33x1'-5" or 1.417, equals 8.969 or 9 sq. ft.

Designs for Slate Walks and Floors.

Irregular Flagging consists of irregularly shaped pieces of slate cut to sizes suitable for laying in walks, terraces, porches, etc. The size of the pieces range from 1 to 4 sq. ft. and the standard thickness for exterior installations is 1". 

Random Trimmed Rectangles are used where more formal installations are required, and are furnished with reasonably

STRUCTURAL SLATE 

1351 smooth surface in a range of sizes from 1 to 4 sq. ft. in a piece and no definite sizes may be specified. 

Fitted Trimmed Rectangles are similar to Random Rectangles in color and finish. The difference is that Fitted Rectangles are cut to certain exact sizes and may be all one size, such as 12"x12" where a uniform pattern is required, or they may be cut to fit a random pattern. 

Fitted Irregular Flagging is furnished ready to install, with no cutting on the job, and is generally furnished in localities where mechanics, who are familiar with cutting and installing slate, are not available.

CHAPTER XXI TILE FLOORS, WAINSCOTING AND MANTELS TERRAZZO AND COMPOSITION FLOORS, RUBBER TILE AND LINOLEUM FLOORS 

Practically all kinds of tile for floors and wainscoting are estimated by the sq. ft. except base and cap, which are estimated by the lin. ft.

When preparing an estimate on tile work, the size of the rooms or floor spaces in which the tile are to be laid should be considered because a tile setter can set more tile in one large room than in several smaller ones. A tile setter will seldom start work on a room late in the afternoon unless he is certain it can be finished before quitting time. 

The different kinds of tile also have considerable bearing on labor costs, as it is easier to lay " or 1" ceramic tile, mounted on paper, than 2", 3″ or 4" tile, unmounted, necessitating setting each piece of tile separately. 

When estimating wall tile, the size of the room, height of wainscoting and number of internal and external angles must be considered, as small rooms usually require more labor than large ones.

Estimating Quantities of Floor Tile.-All kinds of floor tile are estimated by the square or superficial foot, obtained by multiplying the length of each room by the width. Inasmuch as there are many kinds of floor tile it is advisable to mention the kind, as " hexagon, 1″ square, 2″ hexagon, 2″ square, 3″ hexagon, 3″ square, 4"x4" quarry tile, etc.

Tile base and cap are estimated by the lin. ft. obtained by measuring the entire distance around the room in which it is to be used. Make deductions for door openings but add for tile plinths, where required.

When preparing an estimate on tile work, the following items should be included: 1352

INTERIOR TILE 

1353 

1. Cost of tile delivered at the job. 

2. Cost of sand and cement for floor fill under tile. 

3. Labor mixing and placing cement floor fill. 4.

Labor laying floor tile and cleaning same at completion. 

5. Tile contractor's overhead expense, such as office expense, cartage, insurance, etc. 

6. Tile contractor's profit.

Labor Conditions Affecting Tile Costs 

Estimating the labor cost of setting floor and wall tile is purely a matter of judgment on the part of the estimator-a knowledge of the men who will work on the job and the market in which the work is to be performed. 

Tile setters seldom give a full day's work for a full day's pay and this was greatly aggravated during our last prolonged period of building prosperity. In the larger cities it had been their custom to come onto the job at 8 to 8:30 in the morning, stand around and smoke cigaretts for an hour or two and start laying tile about 9:30 or 10 o'clock in the morning.

They will probably finish what they consider a "day's work" by 2 or 2:30 o'clock in the afternoon and the balance of the day is spent in plain “loafing” until quitting time.

This condition is worse in some localities than in others but in cities where the Unions are exceptionally strong, the workmen do the smallest day's work and the labor costs are highest. 

Wages vary widely in different parts of the country, from $1.25 per hr. which is the national scale to $1.75 per hr. in some of the larger cities.

The costs given on the following pages are average for union mechanics but in localities where the men do a real day's work (if there are any), the daily output will be considerably increased.

Where quantities are increased, the estimator should be familiar with conditions prevailing in the localities in which the work is to be performed.

Placing Cement Floor Fill Under Tile Floors.-Cement floor fill under tile floors is usually placed by tile setters and helpers, one tile setter and one or two helpers working together. The fill is often placed a day or two in advance of the tile and is from 21" to 3" thick. One bbl. of cement and 1 cu. yd. of sand are required for 100 sq. ft. of floor fill.

When placing fill in large rooms, one setter and 2 helpers should place 450 to 500 sq. ft. per 8-hr. day, at the following cost per 100 sq. ft.:

Laying Ceramic Floor Tile.-When estimating the labor cost of laying" or 1" ceramic floor tile, the class of work and the size of the rooms should be considered. A tile setter will lay more plain floor tile than where a border is used, as it is not necessary to match the designs, although very few ceramic tile floors with borders are used today. It also costs less to lay tile in large rooms than in small rooms. 

When laying ceramic floor tile in corridors, store rooms, lobbies, and other large spaces, a tile setter and helper should lay 100 to 125 sq. ft. of tile per 8-hr. day, at the following labor cost per 100 sq. ft.:

Laying Ceramic Floor Tile in Small Rooms.-When laying 

" or 1" ceramic floor tile in bath rooms, small vestibules, etc., a tile setter and helper should complete 3 small rooms or 2 large rooms per 8-hr. day. When pricing this class of work consider the size of the rooms as this has a greater bearing on the labor cost than a sq. ft. price.

An average bath room contains 25 to 40 sq. ft. of floor. If a tile setter completes 3 rooms per 8-hr. day, he will have laid 

75 to 120 sq. ft. of tile but if he completes only 2 rooms per day, the labor cost will be increased one-half. It is not safe to figure over 2 rooms per 8-hr. day where the rooms contain 40 sq. ft. or more.

As previously mentioned in this chapter, it is not so much what a man can do as what he will do that must be considered. 

For instance, if two bath rooms have been completed by 2 or 3 o'clock in the afternoon, it is unlikely that the third room will be started because in most cases a tile setter will not start another room if he has to hustle to finish it by quitting time and the union rules do not permit overtime without one hour's interval between regular quitting time and before starting overtime, which is not tempting for a possible hour's overtime. Consequently, there is a day's pay for 75 to 80 sq. ft. of tile.

Estimating on the basis of 3 small bath rooms a day, the labor cost should run as follows:

Glazed and Enameled Wall Tile, Base and Cap 

The following rules should be observed when estimating quantities of wall tile, base, cap, etc.

INTERIOR TILE 

1361 To obtain the number of lin. ft. of base required, measure the entire distance around the room, making deductions in full for all door or other openings where base is not required. To this quantity add interior and exterior corners, stops, etc., also add a few pieces of base to allow for breakage when cutting.

Tile plinths should be estimated by the piece, according to the actual number required, which is usually 2 to a door. 

When estimating the quantity of wall tile required, measure the entire distance around the room and multiply by the height of the wainscot, which may be 3′-0″, 4′-0″, 5′-0″, 6′-0″, 7′-0″ or more feet high, and the result will be the number of sq. ft. of tile required. From this quantity deduct area of all door and window openings, space occupied by tub (where tile are not required), etc. When estimating wall tile, add for interior and exterior corners, and other fittings required as shown by the plans. All tile "trimmers" should be measured by the actual number required, as they are sold by the piece. 

Add a small percentage to the above to allow for breakage. 

Tile wainscot cap is estimated by the lin. ft. obtained by measuring the distance around the room, and deducting for door and window openings, where cap is not required. Add for exterior and interior corners, stops, etc. and a few pieces of straight cap to allow for breakage, etc.

Cement Back-Plaster or Bed for Tile Wainscoting.-When setting wall tile, the plaster contractor usually applies a scratch coat of portland cement plaster to the metal lath, brick or tile walls, ready for the tile contractor. The thickness of the cement plaster or bed varies with the straightness of the walls but a fair average is " to " thick.

The labor cost setting tile cove or base in small vestibules, bath rooms, etc., will vary with the size of the rooms, number of corners or angles and amount of cutting necessary. 

On work of this kind, a tile setter and helper should set cove or base in 4 small rooms per 8-hr. day without any trouble but some setters will complete only 3 rooms per day unless they are checked up regularly. For instance, if a tile setter has completed two rooms by 2 or 3 o'clock in the afternoon, rather than start another room which would require a little extra effort on his part, he will spend the balance of the day loafing. For this reason the most accurate costs are undependable, as they are contingent entirely upon the man performing the work.

When estimating the cost of setting tile cove or base in small bath rooms, vestibules, etc., containing 35 to 40 lin. ft. of base, a tile setter and helper should complete 2 rooms (70 to 80 lin. ft.) per 8-hr. day. If the rooms contain only 20 to

Labor conditions on this job were unfavorable, as marble and tile setters were scarce at the time this work was done. 

It was impossible to obtain anything but "floaters", who performed just as little work as was possible to hold their jobs. 

However, it was a rush job and it was necessary to make the best of conditions regardless of cost. 

The tile used in these floors were very uneven in thickness, resulting in rough and uneven floors, necessitating rubbing all floors by hand. The building was located outside of the city limits and electric power was not available, so the laborers used long poles with sandstone and carborundum stone fastened to the ends to rub all floors. A man rubbed about 40 sq. ft. of floor per 8-hr. day.

While the above costs show that a tile setter and helper averaged 90 sq. ft. of floor per 8-hr. day, it does not furnish an accurate record for future use or a comparison with the previously stated fact that a setter and helper will set either two or three rooms per day, which in this instance is equivalent to either 80 or 120 sq. ft. of tile per day.

All of the bath rooms in this building were practically the same size, and when the work was started the tile setters took things rather easy and laid tile in only 2 rooms requiring 80 sq. ft. of tile per 8-hr. day. Later on the contractor in checking his costs, saw where this rate of progress was going to leave him and after talking with the workmen on the job they immediately completed floors in 3 bath rooms (120 sq. ft.) per day. This merely illustrates how the human element enters into all building costs.

Setting 44"x4" Colored Wall Tile in Bath Rooms.-The two 

English type houses illustrated on pages 568 and 805, each contained two bath rooms about 5'-0"x7'-0" in size.

.481 TERRAZZO WAINSCOT, FLOORS, BASE AND BORDER 

The cost of terrazzo work varies with the size of the job, size of rooms or spaces where the floors are to be installed, floor designs, strips of brass or other non-rusting material, and method of laying the floors.

Two methods are used in laying terrazzo floors over concrete construction. One is to bond it to the concrete and the other to separate it from the structural slab. 

When the first method is used, the concrete fill is provided for by another contractor and should be left 2" below the finished floor. This concrete can be made of cement, sand and hard coal cinders in proportion of 1:1:6. Soft coal cinders must not be used. Slag, broken stone or gravel are also good aggregates for concrete fill under terrazzo floors. Before the terrazzo contractor installs his underbed, he must see that this concrete fill is thoroughly cleaned of plaster droppings, wood chips and other debris, and wetted to insure cohesion.

The second method is used in buildings where cracking is anticipated either from settlement, expansion and contraction or vibration. In this case the terrazzo contractor begins his work from the structural floor slab up. This method requires a thickness of at least 3". The concrete slab is covered with a thin bed of dry sand over which a sheet of tar paper is laid. 

Over the paper the underbed is installed as in the first method except that coarser aggregate can be used in the underbed, such as cinders or fine gravel where its thickness exceeds 21". When this method is used, the cracks originating in the structural slab are not likely to appear on the surface but terminate at the sand bed.

When terrazzo is laid over wood floors a thickness of not less than 2" is required. The floor should first be covered with tarred paper. Over this paper nail galvanized wire netting No. 14

TERRAZZO 

1395 gauge, 2″ mesh. Then lay the concrete underbed as specified under the second method.

The underbed for terrazzo consisting of 1 part portland cement and 4 parts sharp, screened sand shall be spread and brought to a level not less than" nor more than " below the finished floor. 

Into this underbed, while still in a semi-plastic state, install brass strips or preassembled decorative units, having proper bonding features. If strips other than brass are required, name the metal.

The terrazzo topping shall be not less than "nor more than 3" in thickness and shall be of granulated marble of colors selected. The topping shall be uniform in composition and the marble granule that appears on the surface shall be used for its entire thickness. The granule to be composed of such propor tions of Nos. 1-2-3 sizes as required. 

Composition for terrazzo mixture shall be in the proportion of 200 lbs. of marble granules to 100 lbs. of gray or white portland cement, mixed dry and water afterward added to make the mix plastic but not too wet. The mix shall then be placed in the spaces formed by the brass dividing strips and rolled into a compact mass by means of heavy stone or metal rollers until all superfluous cement and water is extracted, after which, it must be hand troweled to an even surface, disclosing the lines of the brass strips on a level with the terrazzo filling. 

When the floors have set sufficiently hard, they shall be machine rubbed, using coarse carborundum grit stones for the initial rubbing after which a light grouting of pure gray or white portland cement shall be applied to the surface, filling all voids, and allowed to remain until the time of final cleaning. 

Floors shall have the grouting coat removed by machine, using a fine carborundum grit, after which it must be thoroughly washed. Do not use acids in cleaning terrazzo floors.

Ramped or other surfaces in terrazzo floors so specified, shall be made anti-slip by the addition of an abrasive aggregate. For heavy duty floors, the proportion shall be 2 parts of abrasive to 3 parts of marble granule and the abrasive shall be mixed in the terrazzo topping for its entire thickness. For light traffic floors, the abrasive shall be sprinkled on the surface only, and show a proportion of 5 parts marble granule and 1 part abrasive aggregate.

Terrazzo Base.-Terrazzo base is usually coved at the floor and may be any height desired. If the base is to finish flush with

the finish plaster, a metal base bead shall be furnished and set by the plasterer. The base shall be divided approximately every 

4 lin. ft. using metal base dividers. The walls back of the base shall have a scratch coat of cement and sand mortar brought to a line" back of the finished face of the base, into which the base dividers shall be set. Base shall be finished with a very fine stone, so as to leave the surface at a hone finish. 

Terrazzo Partitions.—Where terrazzo partitions are used, metal lath construction shall be provided by the lathing contractor as follows: Erect forms of metal studding, placed not over 12" on centers and securely fastened at corners, at walls and over openings, and well bedded into floors. This framing to be covered with galvanized expanded metal lath. 

Plasterer contractor shall apply to the metal lath a scratch coat of 1 part portland cement and 2 parts sand, to within " of finish. Upon surfaces thus prepared, the terrazzo contractor shall apply and install the setting bed and terrazzo finish. The finished thickness of partitions shall not exceed 21". Terrazzo partitions shall be machine rubbed and brought to a smooth hone finish.

Terrazzo Wainscots.-Plaster contractor shall prepare with a plumb scratch coat of portland cement and sand to within " of finish. The terrazzo finish shall be applied in the same manner as specified for terrazzo partitions. Terrazzo wainscot shall be machine rubbed and brought to a smooth hone finish. 

Estimating the Cost of Terrazzo Work. In addition to the direct cost of labor and materials entering into terrazzo work, an allowance should be made to provide for wood grounds, carborundum stone for rubbing, wiring for electric power, depreciation on machines, use of hoist, cleaning up rubbish, freight and cartage on machines and tools. This will vary with size and location of job. 

The costs on the following pages are based on an average job containing about 3,000 sq. ft. as the labor on a small job containing 100 to 200 sq. ft. will run twice as much as on a job containing 5,000 sq. ft. 

Miscellaneous Job Costs, Overhead Expense, Profit, Etc.- 

The amounts included under miscellaneous job expenses to cover such items as wood grounds, carborundum rubbing stone, wiring for electric power, electric power, depreciation on machines, use of hoist, cleaning up rubbish, freight and cartage, etc., are

TERRAZZO 

1397 averages. On large jobs these amounts may be reduced somewhat but on small jobs they may be increased. An allowance of 3 to 5 cts. per sq. ft. or per lin. ft. should be figured to take care of the above items. 

The allowance of 20% for contractor's overhead expense and profit is taken as an average. On large jobs this percentage may be reduced to 10 or 15 per cent, while on small jobs it may be increased to 25 or 30 per cent.

The estimator should use his own judgment when allowing for the above items, based on local conditions at the time of letting the work.

Brass Strips in Terrazzo Floors and Base.-Brass strips or other non-rusting metals are used in practically all terrazzo floors and add to the cost in proportion to the quantity used. 

Standard brass strips B & S gauge No. 20 cost 4 to 5 cts. per lin. ft. including waste. 

Brass strips B & S gauge No. 14, cost 10 to 11 cts. per lin. ft. including waste.

The cost of brass strips per sq. ft. of floor will vary with the size of the squares or design and should be estimated accordingly.

Terrazzo base is jointed every 4'-0" with vertical brass joint strips. No. 20 gauge brass averages about 10 cts. per joint.

Estimating Quantities of Terrazzo Work.-Terrazzo floors are estimated by the sq. ft. and will vary from 2" to 3" thick, depending upon the sub-floor, as described in the previous paragraphs.

Terrazzo floor borders are estimated by the sq. ft. when over 

12" wide and by the lin. ft. when less than 12" wide.

Terrazzo base is estimated by the lin. ft. stating height. An allowance of l′-0″ should be made for each corner or miter. 

Double cove terrazzo base having 2 finished faces, such as ordinarily used under narrow partitions, shower stalls, etc., are estimated by the lin. ft. and the cost is double that of single cove base.

Terrazzo wainscot is estimated by the sq. ft. 

Terrazzo partitions having 2 finished faces, are estimated by the sq. ft. (measurement one side only) and the cost is double that of terrazzo wainscot.

Labor Placing Terrazzo Wainscot, Partitions, Floor and Base. 

-The labor cost of placing terrazzo work will vary with the

size of the rooms, design of the floor, size of the squares or pattern requiring brass strips, etc., as the smaller the squares, the more metal strip required and the higher the cost.

Method of Laying Out Floor to Receive Rubber Tile RUBBER TILE FLOORS AND BASE 

Rubber tile are extensively used for floors and base in offices, hotel lobbies, banks, theaters, churches, hospitals, kitchens, elevator fronts and cabs, corridors, etc. They are furnished in 3"x3",

When laying rubber tile over wood floors, the wood floor should consist of thoroughly dry and well-seasoned tongue-andgroove lumber not more than 3" wide laid diagonally and toenailed with about 1/32" joints close but not driven tight. 

When laying rubber tile over an old wood floor, all loose, defective or badly worn boards shall be replaced and face nailed. 

Any uneveness in the boards shall be planed or sanded smooth and even.

Over the wood base there shall be installed saturated asphalt felt weighing about 1 lbs. per sq. yd. which shall be securely affixed to the base with linoleum paste. Spread the paste with a rubber-edged paste spreader used for linoleum installations. 

Depending upon the condition of the sub-floor, the spreading capacity should be about 110 sq. ft. per gallon. After the saturated felt is laid, it should be thoroughly rolled with a threepiece 150-lb. linoleum roller.

The cement should be spread with a steel straight-edged trowel. Depending upon the condition of the sub-floor, the spreading capacity should be from 60 to 80 sq. ft. per gallon. 

The finished floor should be thoroughly rolled with a threepiece 150-lb. linoleum roller and any high edges tapped in place with a flat headed hammer.

Laying Rubber Tile. The cost of laying rubber floor tile varies with the size and shape of the room or space where the tile are to be laid, size of tile, kind of sub-floor, etc., as it is easier to lay tile in a large square room than one cut up with offsets, pilasters, bays, etc.; the size of the tile, as a man will lay more sq. ft. of large size tile than of the smaller sizes. 

When laying saturated felt over wood sub-floors, an experienced man should spread paste, lay and roll 250 to 300 sq. ft. of felt an hr. depending upon the room sizes. 

After the saturated felt has been laid (over wood floors), an experienced tile setter should lay and finish the following tile of various sizes per 8-hr. day:

ASPHALT TILE FLOORS 

Asphalt tile are made of asbestos fiber, mineral pigments and asphaltic binder. It is the only type of resilient flooring that can be used satisfactorily on concrete floors that are in direct contact with the ground, at or below grade. Hence it is suitable for basement rooms, as it does not become slippery when it is wet and is easily cleaned with soap and water. Asphalt tile are also used in residences, stores, offices and institutions where a low cost floor is desired.

They are furnished in sizes 3″x3″, 6″x6″, 6″x12″, 6″x24″, 9″x9″, 9″x18″, 12″x12″, 12"x24" and 18"x24", and are ", " and " thick and in a variety of colors.

16 When applied over old or new wood sub-floors, the wood floor shall be finished smooth and level and covered with a layer of saturated felt bonded to the wood with linoleum paste and then rolled thoroughly with a linoleum roller. The asphalt tile are then laid over the saturated felt, using an approved asphalt cement for bonding the tile to the saturated felt. 

When applied over concrete floors, the concrete floor must be smooth and even. If the concrete floors are at grade or subgrade levels, or where humidity conditions are extreme, the concrete shall be given one coat of primer after which the tile are laid in asphalt cement. 

Quantity of Linoleum Paste Required.-Depending upon the condition of the sub-floor, one gallon of linoleum paste should cover approximately 110 sq. ft. Costs about 40 cts. per gal. 

Quantity of Primer and Asphalt Cement Required.-When priming concrete floors, one gallon of primer should cover 150 to 200 sq. ft. of surface, depending upon the porosity of the surface. Price 60 cts. per gal.

One gallon of asphalt cement should lay 160 to 175 sq. ft. of

tile, depending upon the condition of the sub-floor. Costs about 

75 cts. per gal.

Labor Laying Asphalt Tile.-The cost of laying asphalt tile varies with the size and shape of the room or space where the tile are to be laid, size of tile, kind of sub-floor, etc., as a tile setter will lay more sq. ft. of tile in a large room than one cut up with pilasters, offsets, etc., also a man will lay more sq. ft. of large size tile than of the smaller sizes. 

When placing saturated felt over wood sub-floors, an experienced man should spread paste, lay and roll 250 to 300 sq. ft. of felt an hr. depending upon the room sizes. 

After the saturated felt has been laid (over wood floors), an experienced tile setter should lay the following quantities of tile per 8-hr. day:

.23 LINOTILE FLOORS 

Linotile is a dense yet resilient composition consisting of oxidized oils, powdered cork and color pigments thoroughly mixed and calendered into sheets which are later cut into tiles. 

Linotile is used for floors in residences, kitchens, bath rooms, offices, stores, banks, hospitals, schools and buildings where the floor must be sturdy and long wearing as well as colorful and attractive. 

The tile are furnished in numerous sizes from 3"x3" to 24"x36", "and" thick.

When laying Linotile over wood, the wood floors should be double and the top floor laid on the diagonal. Where top floors are omitted, the sub-floor should be covered with " Temwood* or "Temboard*, firmly nailed to the underfloor with 2d rosincoated nails 6" on centers.

The top floor must be true, even, level, clean, free from foreign matter and dry. 

*Cost of tile varies according to color and thickness.

*Armstrong Cork Products Co., Floor Division, Lancaster, Pa.

LINOTILE 

1413 When laid over concrete floors, the concrete floor shall be troweled to a smooth and even surface without expansion joints, and shall be thoroughly dry. 

Lining felt shall be pasted to the wood, Temwood or Temboard sub-floor, using linoleum paste with all seams butted and made tight. Over the felt, Linotile shall be laid in linoleum paste. The use of lining felt is optional on suspended concrete or non-absorbent subfloors. 

After the Linotile floor has been laid, it should be thoroughly rolled with a three-piece 150-lb. linoleum roller and any high places tapped with a flat-headed hammer. The entire floor should be sandbagged, with several layers of sand bags over high spots and irregular areas. At completion the floor should be washed with a solution of Armstrong's* Floor Cleaner, rinsed thoroughly with clear, cold water and given one thin coat of water emulsion-wax.

CORK TILE 

Cork tile* are made from high-grade pure cork shavings compressed and baked in molds. It is used for floors and wainscoting in offices, libraries, hospitals, schools and other places where footsteps must be muffled. 

They are furnished in a variety of sizes from 2"x2" to 12"x36", and" and " thick. Cork tile are supplied beveled or unbeveled.

With unbeveled cork tile, sanding the finished floor is usually necessary to offset unevenness of the subfloor. With beveled cork tile, the beveling conceals such irregularities, with the result that sanding is unnecessary and the smooth surface given at the tile factory is retained. 

The wood or concrete subfloor must be smooth and even before cork tile can be placed. A lining felt is used over wood 

*Armstrong Cork Products Co., Tile Floors Dept., Lancaster, Pa.

CORK TILE 

1415 subfloors but this is not necessary when applied over smooth, level concrete floors. 

After the floor has been laid and sanded (if unbeveled tile are used), the floor should be given a coat of Cork Tile Filler, followed by two coats of Cork Tile Finish (glossy or flat) and subsequent waxings with an approved water emulsion wax, or the floor may be finished by merely applying 3 applications of water emulsion wax and vigorously buffed by machine.

ACOUSTICAL TILE 

Acoustical tile are applied to ceilings and walls for the purpose of absorbing and deadening sound in offices, banks, auditoriums, and other spaces where the utmost in quiet is desired. 

Acoustical tile are made of many different materials, such as cork, wood fiber, cane fiber, specially processed stone, and other insulating materials. 

They are made in a variety of sizes, such as 6"x6", 6"x9". 

9"x9". 12"x12". 9"x18", etc., and vary from " to 2" thick, depending upon the materials used.

ACOUSTICAL TILE 

1417 Acoustical tile may be installed on sound, dry plaster, concrete, smooth wood securely nailed and on gypsum core board of small size (16"x32"). A good job can result only when the subbase is smooth and level, and erected so that it will not sag, warp, swell or shrink unduly. 

Method of Placing Acoustical Tile Using Adhesive 

Where the acoustical tiles are erected on a solid surface, the adhesive should be applied with a trowel or putty knife to the back of the tile in uniform "spots" about 2" in diameter and " thick. Four such spots evenly spaced are usually applied to the back of a 12"x12" tile. When applied where unusually high relative humidity is to be expected, such as in natatoriums, an approved waterproof cement should be used as the adhesive. 

A crew of at least two men is required to handle the work of installation efficiently, one man on the floor pasting the tiles and one man in the scaffold to place the tiles on the ceiling. 

The "spots" of adhesive should be kept back from the face of the tile about 1". Tiles should then be placed firmly against the ceiling about 1" from their final position and slid into place under pressure.

One gallon of Acoustical Adhesive (Water Resistant) or

1 Acoustical Cement (Waterproof) should be sufficient for about 40 sq. ft. of tile. The adhesive costs about 60 cts. per gal. and the cement about $1.25 per gal.

Labor Placing Acoustical Tile. The labor cost of placing acoustical tile on ceilings will vary with the size of the rooms or spaces where the tile are to be applied, pattern in which the tile are laid, height of scaffolding, etc.

The following quantities and costs are based on a 4 or 5-ft. scaffold consisting of horses and planks and laying tile in plain square or ashlar designs:

LINOLEUM FLOORS 

Within the past few years linoleum floors have become increasingly popular for use in offices, residences, restaurants, etc. 

This is due chiefly to the improved methods of laying and the attractive patterns produced by the manufacturers.* 

Inasmuch as linoleum floors are frequently specified for use in new buildings, it is important that the contractor be conversant with the various kinds of linoleum, methods of estimating, costs, etc.

What Linoleum Is.-Linoleum is a flooring material having foundation or back of burlap on which is imposed a body composition which has for its principal binder oxidized linseed oil incorporated with finely ground cork or wood flour, rosin. and various gums and pigments. There are five chief kinds of linoleum made at the present time, namely Plains, Prints, Jaspes.

Straight Line Inlaids, and Molded Inlaids, each of which is made by a different process and requires a different composition of ingredients in its manufacture. 

Plain Linoleum.-Plain linoleum is made in a wide range of thicknesses and is used for a variety of purposes: 6mm. Battle- 

*Armstrong Cork Products Co., Floor Division, Lancaster, Pa.

LINOLEUM FLOORS 

1421 ship," Battleship, " or heavy, medium and standard gauges. 

The 6mm. Battleship is the heaviest grade of Plain linoleum manufactured today. It is made in one color, brown, is very tough and durable, and is intended for enduring permanent installations where the service is unusually severe. It is laid principally on the floors of offices, stores, hospitals, banks, and similar places where there will be constant and trying wear. 

The "gauge of Battleship is manufactured for similar purposes and is made in six colors-brown, green, dark gray, terra cotta, black and chocolate.

The" or heavy, medium and standard gauges of Plain Linoleum are similar to Battleship linoleum, except that they may be obtained in a greater variety of colors-sixteen may be had in these three lighter gauges.

Cork Carpet.-Cork carpet is as the name implies a carpetlike material made of a body composition of cork and oxidized linseed oil imposed on a burlap back, but unlike Plain linoleum in the fact that it is not so dense, that is, very resilient, the cork being in much larger granules and is somewhat heavier in gauge. It is made 1″ thick and in two colors, brown and green. 

It is used in places where extreme quiet and underfoot softness is desired, such as in churches and certain working areas in post offices. 

Jaspe Linoleum.-Jaspe Linoleum has a striated, two-tone effect-colors running in streaks or lines parallel to the length of the goods. These streaks are obtained by working through calendar rolls two sets of color which have been only partially mixed together. It is made in three gauges, ", " or heavy and medium.

The appearance of Jaspe is unusual because the streaky two color effect relieves the monotony of the regular plains, yet it does not have the artificial touch of the various wood and parquetry patterns. With it most artistic results can be obtained. 

Inlaid Linoleum.-There are two general types of inlaid linoleum-molded and straight line. Their distinguishing feature is that the design goes all the way through to the back. 

Molded Inlaid Linoleum is made in three gauges, " or heavy, medium and standard. These thicknesses are about the same as 

Plain Linoleum. The designs are formed by means of stencils through which the granulated "mix" is pressed. One of these metal stencils is prepared for each color, as many being required as there are colors in the pattern.

Straight Line Inlaid Linoleum.—Straight line inlaid is similar to molded inasmuch as colors go all the way through to the back. 

Molded inlaid, however, does not have the markings of each particular figure so clearly outlined. When the several colors are all pressed together there is a tendency to each one to "flow" somewhat into the one next to it. The markings of straight line linoleum, however, are sharply defined. This result is obtained by rolling out sheets of the various colors required and dieing out pieces from them to conform to the pattern to be made. These pieces are then set automatically into the design on the burlap back. Straight lines of these goods are very clean cut with pleasing appearance. This kind of linoleum can be used for installations of the highest grade. 

Parquetry Inlaid Linoleum.-Parquetry inlaid is a form of straight line inlaid which gives, as the name suggests, an appearance of a wood parquet floor. Parquetry has an extremely striking effect, and can be used on very fine installations. While perhaps it is not as good artistically as Jaspe, it still can be employed with very gratifying results in the best of rooms which lend themselves to this treatment. All parquetry is made in the " or heavy gauge.

Marble Inlaid Linoleum.-Together with the regular straight line linoleum might be classified the marble inlaid patterns. 

This type of linoleum is made under the regular straight line process. The blocks, however, have the fine graining similar to that of natural quarry marble and create a very handsome and striking effect. These marbles are available in a variety of colors and make exceedingly handsome rooms when bordered with a harmonizing color of plain linoleum.

All-Over Marble Linoleum.-This type of marble patterns differs from the Marble Inlaid Linoleum in that it is not made up of blocks but produced in a solid sheet 6 ft. wide and approximately 90 ft. long, the entire sheet being marbleized. This is known as Marbelle linoleum and lends itself remarkably well to custom floor work in much the same way as plain linoleum is used. The bright, varied colorings give them a wide range of decorative possibilities, being made in four gauges-1 medium and standard and in eighteen colorings. 3" 169 1", Embossed Inlaid Linoleum.-Embossed inlaid linoleum is a form of molded inlaid linoleum. It is, however, strikingly different from anything that has ever been achieved in the history of linoleum making. Instead of having a smooth surface

LINOLEUM FLOORS 

1423 it is embossed—that is, the tiled blocks are raised above the cement interliners in the pattern. These designs come in a variety of colors with irregular spotted motifs of bright tile placed here and there to relieve any monotony of the design. 

This linoleum is the first step to achieve what is known as texture in any linoleum surface. When it is laid properly it is almost impossible to distinguish it from actual tile flooring, although it has all the resilience and sanitary qualities of durable linoleum.

Raybelle Linoleum. This type of linoleum is different from anything ever seen before. It is not an imitation of wood or marble as are the Jaspes and Marbelles, but joins these materials as a new basic type of linoleum. It is made in three gauges-heavy or ", medium and standard, and eight color combinations. It makes an exceedingly attractive all-over floor, either with or without border treatment, combining very well with the plain colors.

Printed Linoleum.-Printed linoleum merely has the pattern printed on the surface. It is cheaper than inlaid linoleum but if properly cared for, will give satisfactory service. 

Good Linoleum Laying.-Linoleum may often be ruined by poor laying. Manufacturers have realized this salient fact and have tried to remedy the difficulty. The Armstrong Cork Company has conducted various research studies and investigations for the past fifteen years on this problem and has determined certain methods of laying which are recommended to the public and to the linoleum trade. Briefly the recommendations on laying are: 

1. To insure that linoleum will give absolute satisfaction on a wood floor, bond it over a lining of unsaturated deadening felt of approved weight. 

2. Do not bond linoleum direct to a wood floor. 

3. On concrete, linoleum may safely be bonded direct, without a felt lining, although linoleum is not recommended for concrete floors that are in direct contact with the ground.

Laying Linoleum Over Wood.-Inasmuch as the floor boards in an ordinary wood floor are subject to expansion or contraction due to changing weather conditions, it is not advisable to bond linoleum direct to wood. For a wood base a layer of deadening felt should first be pasted upon it. The felt

Laying Linoleum Over Concrete.-Linoleum may often be cemented direct to concrete. However, the concrete must be troweled to a smooth and even finish. When deadening felt is used, linoleum paste is applied to both the floor and the felt to bond the felt to the floor and the linoleum to the felt.

It should be remembered, however, that linoleum should never be bonded directly to a concrete floor which has contact with the ground. It is almost impossible to eliminate moisture from a basement floor. Moisture on a floor causes mildew or mold, disintegrates linoleum paste, and will in time injure the linoleum.

Estimating Quantity of Linoleum Required.-In estimat ing the number of strips of linoleum needed to cover the specified spaces, plan to use the waste falling off in one room wherever it will fit to advantage in another. In so doing however, never cause more than one additional seam. 

Too many seams often spoil a good job. Plan to use your strips of linoleum in such a manner that a minimum number of seams is necessary. 

The accompanying illustration shows just how the linoleum should be estimated from the plans and listed on the estimate sheet.

CHAPTER XXII SHEET METAL WORK 

Sheet metal work in its many branches is a highly specialized business, because the greater part of the work is performed in the shop and the fabricated materials are sent to the job ready to erect. For that reason an estimate on sheet metal work must take into consideration the cost of the finished materials at the shop or delivered to the building site, plus the labor cost of erection.

Estimating Quantities of Sheet Metal Work 

The data given on the following pages will assist the estimator in measuring quantities from the plans and listing them on the estimate sheet.

Metal Gutters and Eave Trough.-Metal gutters and eave trough are furnished in numerous designs, from 2" to 12" in size. When estimating quantities, obtain the number of pieces of each size gutter and the length of same, as the estimate should state the lin. ft. of each size. 

Metal Conductor Pipe or Down Spout.-Metal conductor pipe is furnished both round and square and from 2" to 6" in size. 

When estimating quantities, measure the distance from the roof to the ground, which will be the length of each down spout. 

After the quantities have been obtained in this manner, list the total number of lin. ft. of each size. 

Metal Conductor Heads.-Metal conductor heads are made in various styles, shapes and sizes. They are usually furnished in galvanized iron or copper.

Conductor heads are generally used on buildings having flat roofs where a cast iron conductor pipe is placed inside the building and installed by the plumbing contractor. When placed on the outside of a wall at the roof level, an opening is usually left in the masonry wall at the low point of the roof to allow the water to pass through the wall opening into the conductor head and down the conductor pipe. 1432

SHEET METAL 

1433 When estimating conductor heads always note style and size of each head and the material specified, as there is considerable difference in cost between galvanized iron and copper. 

Metal Flashing and Counter Flashing.-Flashing and counter flashing is furnished in tin, galvanized steel or copper. They are measured by the lin. ft. when less than 12" wide and by the sq. ft. when over 12" wide.

Metal flashing used in connection with a flat roof deck covered with felt or composition roofing usually extends 6″ to 12″ up the side of the brick fire wall and projects under the roofing the same distance. A counter flashing is then placed over and above this flashing. The upper edge of the counter flashing is inserted in a raggle or slot formed in the brick or stone wall. 

After the counter flashing has been placed, it is calked with cement or mortar to prevent water from getting back of the flashing and running under the roof.

On many jobs using felt or composition roofing, the felt is run up the wall about 12" and mopped. The metal counter flashing is then placed to extend down over the felt, which prevents water from getting back of the flashing and running under the roofing. 

Where metal counter flashing is used, it is necessary to cut an open joint or raggle in the mortar joint of the masonry wall. 

Metal flashing should be estimated by the lin. ft. (stating the width) if less than 12" wide and by the sq. ft. if over 12" wide. The kind of metal used should also be stated. 

Counter flashing should be estimated by the lin. ft. but the estimate should state the width and kind of metal used. 

The cost of cutting raggles should be estimated by the lin. ft. 

Metal Valleys and Hips.-Metal valleys and hips are frequently used with certain types of shingle and slate roofs. They are either continuous metal strips of a certain size or small shingles of tin, galvanized iron or copper.

They should be estimated by the lin. ft. stating the width of the valley or hip and the kind of metal used. 

Metal Ridge Roll, Hip Roll and Cap.-Metal ridge roll, hip roll and cap should be estimated by the lin. ft. giving the width, gauge and kind of metal.

Metal Ventilators.-Metal ventilators for roofs and skylights should be estimated at a certain price for each ventilator, f.o.b. factory or erected. Always state size and type of ventilators required, as there are numerous kinds on the market at varying prices.

When estimating the cost of ventilators in connection with metal skylights, first ascertain whether the skylight price includes the price of the ventilator, as some types of hip or gable skylights include the cost of the ventilator. 

Metal Skylights.-When estimating metal skylights, consider the following: Type of skylight, whether single or double pitch or hip skylight; with or without ventilators or side sash; kind of glass, and whether a metal curb is required. 

The size of each skylight should be noted, as many firms figure the cost of skylights at a certain price per sq. ft. when they contain over 60 sq. ft. and at a certain price per skylight when they contain less than 60 sq. ft. 

Metal Cornices.-Sheet metal, zinc and copper cornices may be estimated by the lin. ft. if less than 12″ in girth and by the sq. ft. if over 12" in girth.

The girth of metal cornices is obtained by measuring the girth line of the metal to obtain the actual quantity of metal required for one lin. ft. of cornice or by measuring the depth of the cornice, plus the wall projection. The approximate girth of a cornice may be obtained by adding the projection and height together, which gives the number of sq. ft. of metal required per lin. ft. of cornice.

When there are enrichments of galvanized steel, zinc or copper on the cornice, they should be estimated separately and added to the cost of the straight run cornice. 

When estimating a cornice requiring miters, add one lin. ft. for each miter. 

Do not estimate any cornice less than 12" in girth.

Labor Placing Sheet Metal Work 

The costs given on the following pages are for the erection of various kinds of sheet metal work on the job. Add cost of the fabricated material, contractors' overhead expense and profit. 

Sheet Metal Contractors' Overhead Expense and Profit.—It is customary for general contractors to sub-let their sheet metal and cornice work to sheet metal contractors, and for this

SHEET METAL 

1435 reason it will be necessary to add a percentage to the actual labor costs to cover rent, office expense, cartage, tools and other items of overhead expense. This will vary with the individual contractor and competitive conditions at the time of letting the contract but a fair average should run from 15 to 25 per cent of the actual cost of the work. 

The percentage to be added for profit will also vary with the contractor and business conditions as a firm without much work in the shop will figure much closer than one that is busy. 

A fair allowance for a sheet metal contractor's profit should be 10 to 15 per cent of the actual cost of the work. 

The total allowance for overhead expense and profit should not exceed 25 to 30 per cent of the actual cost.

Placing Hanging Gutter or Eave Trough.-This cost will vary with the slope of the roof, distance above the ground and the method used in hanging the gutter.

On wood constructed buildings having hip or gable roofs, metal hangers or supports are placed over the gutters or eave trough and fastened to the eaves under the shingles or other roofing. The eave trough or gutter must always slope in the direction of the down spout, in order to drain satisfactorily, On hip or gable roofs having eaves 20'-0" to 25′-0″ above the ground, a tinner and helper should place 80 to 100 lin. ft. of gutter per 8-hr. day, at the following labor cost per 100 lin. ft.:

Cutting Raggles in Masonry Walls.-The labor cost of cutting raggles in brick walls will depend entirely upon the kind of mortar used and the condition of the mortar at the time of cutting the raggles.

If the brick are laid in portland cement mortar, it will cost more to cut the raggles than when laid in lime mortar. Also, if the raggles are cut within 24 hrs. after the brick are laid, the labor cost will be much less than cutting them two or three weeks later.

Ventilating Skylights.-Ventilating skylights are used in factories, foundries, machine shops, garages, dairies, laundries and

SHEET METAL 

1441 in any other type of building requiring economical light and ventilation. They are furnished in any type of metal desired, galvanized copper-bearing steel, aluminum or copper, depending upon the nature of the building on which they are to be used. 

Normally, for building of ordinary construction, the standard 18-gauge galvanized copper-bearing steel is furnished. Should the building be of reinforced concrete or steel and concrete construction, the non-corrosive aluminum or copper construction should be furnished. 

Race CORDRACATION GER CANTERE 

ada autteen 70%

Section Through Ventilating Skylight 

These skylights are of gable type as illustrated and are furnished in standard widths of 4'-0" to 20'-0" and any desired length in multiples of 2'-0". Standard widths in multiples of 

2'-0" are usually carried in stock to facilitate prompt delivery. 

It is standard practice to interpret the size of a skylight as being outside to outside of curb dimensions. 

The length of the ventilating sections depend upon the width of the skylights; 4'-0", 6'-0" and 8'-0" widths having maximum ventilating sections of 40'-0" each controlled from one operating station; 10'-0" and 12'-0" wide skylights have maximum ventilating sections of 30'-0" in length; 14'-0" and 16'-0" widths have 

40'-0" maximum lengths, and 18'-0" and 20'-0" widths have 

30'-0" maximum ventilating sections.

A Mechanical operating device consisting of either loose rod or chain control is furnished as required, so that the skylight can be readily controlled from the floor. All skylights under 

30'-0" in length are arranged for full length ventilation. Longer skylights are arranged with ventilating sections as required. *Vent-O-Lite Company, Ventilating Skylights, Chicago, Ill.

The cost of ventilating skylights vary with their size and number of ventilating sections in each skylight. Small skylights 

6'-0" to 8'-0" wide and up to 30'-0" long, containing one ventilating unit on both sides, constructed of 18-gauge galvanized copper-bearing steel and glazed with 4″ ribbed wire glass, will cost from $1.15 to $1.75 per sq. ft. Larger skylights, 10'-0" and 

12'-0" wide will cost from $1.00 to $1.50 per sq. ft. installed complete with glass. Skylights over 12'-0" in width will cost from $0.95 to $1.50 per sq. ft. The above prices are based on installation in Chicago.

For jobs in other locations, add freight and installation costs. 

The skylights weigh approximately 10 lbs. per sq. ft. including glass, and the installation costs will average about 12 cts. per sq. ft. of flat horizontal area. 

Either puttied or puttyless glazing construction can be secured. 

Puttied construction is regularly furnished at the above prices. 

Puttyless glazing, consisting of the glass being bedded between layers of impregnated asphalt felt, with the glazing assembly secured with brass stud bolts and cap nuts, costs about 6 cts. per sq. ft. additional.

In estimating the cost of ventilating skylights, the principal thing to remember is: The smaller the area of the skylight, the higher the price per sq. ft.

METAL CEILINGS AND SIDEWALLS 

Metal ceilings and walls are constructed of sectional units of sheet steel stamped in various designs and painted. There are two classes of metal ceilings and walls, known as "continuous ceilings and sidewalls" and "panel ceilings and sidewalls."

Continuous ceilings and sidewalls include those that have all nailing points on a level with the ceiling or wall line. They may be applied directly to wood sheathing without the use of furring strips; but when applied over old plaster, studs, joists, etc., furring strips are necessary and must be placed as explained in the following paragraphs.

Panel ceilings and sidewalls have sunken panels or plates of various depths. Most of these designs must be applied to furring strips, irrespective of the surface to which they are applied. Furring strips 1"x14" are ordinarily used on this class of work, but in all cases the strip must be of sufficient thickness to allow for the depth of the metal panel.

SHEET METAL 

1443 Before applying a metal ceiling over an old ceiling er te joists, the ceiling must be furred down to a level surface. It is also essential that the furring strips running both lengthwise and crosswise of the room be centered to the nailing points in the metal ceiling plates.

Furring strips should always be placed at right angles to the joists and the cross furring or headers should run parallel to the joists. The longitudinal furring strips should be placed 

12" to 24" on centers, depending upon the width of the metal. 

The cross or end furring strips should be spaced the length of each sheet of metal ceiling, as the metal sheets must be nailed at both the ends and sides. 

Estimating the Quantity of Wood Furring Strips. If wood furring strips for ceilings or walls are spaced 24" on centers both lengthwise and crosswise, it will require 110 lin. ft. of furring strip per 100 sq. ft. of wall or ceiling. 

Furring strips 24" on centers lengthwise and 48" on centers crosswise will require 85 lin. ft. of strip per 100 sq. ft. of wall or ceiling.

Furring strips 24" on centers lengthwise and 96" on centers crosswise will require 70 lin. ft. of strip per 100 sq. ft. of wall or ceiling.

Furring strips 12" on centers lengthwise and 96" on centers crosswise will require 120 lin. ft. per 100 sq. ft. of wall or ceiling. 

Estimating Quantities of Metal Ceiling and Side WaH.-When measuring any room for a metal ceiling, multiply the length of the room by the breadth, and the result will be the number of sq. ft. of metal ceiling required without cornices or drops. 

If there is a cornice or drop in the ceiling, add twice the depth of the cornice (measured from the bottom of the foot mold to the ceiling height) to both the length and breadth of the room, and multiply the length by the breadth. The result will be the number of sq. ft. of metal ceiling and cornice required for the room. 

Example: A store room 18′-0″x40′-0″ in size having a metal ceiling and cornice that drops down the side of the wall 1'-0". 

As this cornice is on both sides and both ends of the room, it will be necessary to add 2'-0" to both the length and breadth of the room, which will make the room 20'-0"x42′-0″ in size, 20×42=840 sq. ft. of ceiling and cornice for the room.

Do not deduct for openings in ceilings, such as skylights, stairways, etc., having an area of less than 50 sq. ft. 

When estimating the quantity of metal sidewall or wainscoting required for any room, measure the entire distance around the room in lin. ft. and multiply by the height of wainscoting. To obtain the height of sidewalls, measure from the bottom of the foot mold at ceiling to the top of the wood base at the floor. Multiply this by the number of lin. ft. of wall and the result will be the number of sq. ft. of metal sidewall required. 

Example: A room 18'-0"x40′-0″ in size having a 12'-0" ceiling.

In the ceiling measurement previously given the cornice drops down 1'-0" on the sidewalls. In addition, assume that the wood base is 6″ high, making a total deduction of l′-6″ from the total height of 12′-0″, which leaves 10'-6" to be covered with metal.

The distance around the room should be obtained by adding twice the length and twice the breadth together, which totals 

116 lin. ft.: 116′-0″ × 10′-6″-1,218 sq. ft. of metal sidewall required for the room.

When estimating metal wainscoting or sidewall for any room, do not deduct for openings containing less than 25 sq. ft. 

When computing wainscoting and sidewall, the contractor must make provision in his estimate for loss of material due to waste, etc.

Metal ceiling cornices are usually estimated by the lin. ft. of cornice of a specified width.

TIN CLAD Fire Doors 

Tin-clad fire doors are used in factory, mill and warehouse buildings and may be either sliding or swinging, having fusible links and automatic closing devices.

Sliding doors and lap type swinging doors in brick walls do not ordinarily require a steel frame but they may be necessary with tile walls. Flush type swinging doors require a frame. 

Standard 3-ply (25%" thick) doors are ordinarily used but 

2-ply (134" thick) are also furnished.

Method of Calculating the Area of Fire Doors.-For flush doors, multiply the width of the opening in feet by the height of the opening in feet. 

Square Top Lap Doors. Obtain size of door by adding 8″ to width and 4″ to height of opening, then multiply width of door in feet by height of door in feet. 

Inclined Top Lap Doors. Obtain width of door by adding 8" to width of opening and obtain height by adding 8" to height of door for doors up to 4'-0" wide and 12" for doors up to 

6'-0" wide. Multiply width of door in feet by height of door in feet.

CHAPTER XXIII STEEL DOORS AND WINDOWS,  AND TRIM 

; Steel windows are furnished in a great variety of styles and sizes, depending upon their use and the type of building in which they are to be used. These windows have been standardized by the steel window industry to eliminate waste and duplication in manufacturing.

When estimating solid steel windows, refer to the illustrations showing the styles and sizes available in each type, as to arrangement of lights, ventilators, etc., and price them as given in the price lists.

The country has been divided into two zones by the manufacturers, as given on the following pages, so when figuring net costs, be sure to apply the discounts applying to the zone in which the windows are to be used. 

Labor Erecting Steel Windows.-The labor cost of erecting steel windows will vary with the class of labor used, size of the individual units and the job working conditions.

Continuous sash require about 4-lb. of putty per sq. ft. of sash..

Continuous Steel Windows.-Continuous steel windows are used in monitor and saw-tooth roof construction where the windows are set on a slope. Their advantage lies in the fact that they provide quickly and easily a continuous opening from one end of the building to the other, at the same time furnishing a canopy of steel and glass which admits ample daylight and excludes the weather. 

The two commonly used type of continuous steel windows are top hung and fixed. Top hung continuous windows require mechanical operators.

Continuous steel windows are from 3′-0″ to 6′-0″ high and vary in price from 21 cts. per sq. ft. for the 6'-0" heights to 

30 cts. per sq. ft. for the 3′-0″ heights, for either fixed or top hung windows.

Mechanical operators for continuous sash cost from $1.70 to $1.80 per lin. ft. depending upon the length of the run. Runs from 

60 to 100 ft. will take the higher price while runs of over 100 ft. will take the lower price. Add erection costs.

Labor Erecting Continuous Steel Windows.-Working under average conditions, an experienced iron worker should set 

200 to 250 sq. ft. of windows per 8-hr. day, at the following labor cost per 100 sq. ft.:

All corners are welded and the hardware is bronze. Other important features are the large glass lights and the open-in ventilator at the sill, which deflects the incoming air and prevents drafts.

Residence Steel Casement Windows 

Steel casement windows are extensively used in residences, apartments, hotels, schools, etc. They are made from specially

rolled steel sections which are attractive in appearance. Casement windows are delivered at the job completely assembled, with a priming coat of paint. The hardware is usually delivered unattached and is applied after erection and painting. Hinges are usually of the extension type to permit washing the window from the inside.

Wood Surrounds for Steel Casement Windows 

Wood Surrounds are a combination buck and brick mould in one single piece. They make the installation of casements in brick veneer easy and at the same time provide a pleasing outside window trim. Wood surrounds are made of clear heart redwood and are shipped in exact sizes with all corners mitered or mortised ready for attachment to the casement. No further cutting is necessary. Necessary wood screws for attaching the wood surrounds to the casement are included.

Home Development Steel Casements Home Development Steel Casements 

The Home Development window was designed primarily for homes where cost is of paramount consideration. Horizontal lines are accentuated. Hardware and screens are simple in

STEEL WINDOWS 

1491 design. Sections used in its manufacture are the same as those used in the production of Residence casements. 

The nominal glass size is 16"x12" as compared with the 

8"x12" glass size of the Residence casement, as there are no vertical muntins used.

The screen used with this window is the side hinged type but because of new window hardware it fits flat against the window even when the window is closed. Only two screws are used in attaching the screen which saves time in removing for storage. 

The locking handle is attached to the casement frame and locks through the window section. Clean-type friction hinges hold the ventilator in any open position and make it possible to wash the outside of the glass from within the room. 

Prices include mastic cement, glazing clips, bronze plated malleable hardware, wood screws or strap anchors for installation into wood or masonry, drilling for standard shade brackets and preparation for side hinged screens. 

Screen List prices include steel frame, side hinged screen with 16 mesh bronze cloth, and screws for attaching to window.

Steel Accordion Folding Doors 

Steel accordion folding doors are furnished as standard practice with four leaves per opening. Each pair of leaves fold at side, either inwardly or outwardly as ordered by the buyer. 

The door leaves are made of heavy seamless tubular rails and stiles, welded and re-enforced at all corners. 

The steel window panels may be furnished in any height desired, or may be omitted entirely and heavy gauge plate continued for the entire height.

The glass in the windows is glazed using steel glazing angles. 

The door manufacturer furnishes and includes in his quotation all necessary hardware, including tracks, trolleys, hinges, cane bolts, etc.

The standard opening dimensions are the inside measurement of structural door frames. The door manufacturer does not furnish door frames. These should be included in the miscellaneous iron work and installed with the progress of the masonry or structural steel work.

The price of accordion folding doors varies with the size, quantity, etc., but the following net prices on several of the more common sizes will give the estimator a fair idea of their cost.

The labor cost of erecting steel doors will vary with the locality in which the work is performed, labor scale, size of doors, etc., but on an average, the erection costs will run from

Wicket doors permitting convenient entrance or exit may be furnished at approximately $80.00 additional cost per door opening. Wicket doors are equipped with cylinder locks.

Electrically driven operators, controlled by push buttons, located at one or more convenient points on the interior of the building, may be installed for an additional cost of $400.00 to $450.00 per opening.

This type of door is in great favor on railroad and industrial plant projects where their rugged construction guarantees the elimination of any break-down or mechanical failure.

The possibility of utilizing the large portion of the opening for glass area and the tight construction provided by standard weathering equipment furnished by the manufacturer also serves to eliminate unusual heat losses. 

Glass and glazing is not included in the above prices and should be estimated as given under "Glass and Glazing."

HOLLOW METAL DOORS AND TRIM 

The following data and prices were furnished by one of the largest manufacturers* of hollow metal doors and trim in the

United States. . 

All of the prices given are for single units. Varying discounts will be allowed for different quantities of the same units. 

The greater the number of units of one kind, the greater the discounts. Where there are 10 or more units of one kind required, deduct 10 per cent from the prices given. 

Glass and hardware are not included in prices given, but the hardware is fitted on all work free of charge. 

All materials are furnished with a ground coat finish, according to the following specifications:

Materials and Workmanship.-All steel and iron used in the construction of the proposed work shall be thoroughly protected from the elements by being treated in full compliance with the following requirements. 

The material required for the several coats and processes of enameling will be referred to as primer, filler and ground coat, each of which shall be of the very best quality procurable in the market and specially prepared for this class of work. The chemical properties of the ingredients used are to be carefully 

Dahlstrom Metallic Door Co., Jamestown. N. Y.

tested for final and lasting results, so that when the work is finished the enamel will stand rigid hammer and bending tests without flaking or cracking, and shall be impervious to water tests. 

Each coat is to be baked in properly heated ovens in varying degrees as determined by experience to give the most satisfactory results in wearing qualities and elasticity. 

All baked enamel finish shall be applied in a smooth, clean and neat manner by skilled workmen, and all colors and varnishes shall be kept clean and free from specks and dust. 

METAL GLASS GLASS METAL GLASS METAL METAL VOJ DESIGN I DESIGN 2 DESIGN 8 DESIGN 4 DESIGN S METAL GLASS GLASS METAL GLASS METAL METAL METAL H METAL DESIGN 6 DESIGN 7 DESIGN 8 DESIGN DESIGN 10 GLASS METAL METAL GLASS METAL METAL METAL DESIGN I DESIGN 12 DESIGN 18 GLASS METAL DESIGN 14 DESIGN 15 Various Designs of Hollow Metal Doors

All exposed surfaces of the work shall be thoroughly washed with naphtha and sandpapered with emery cloth or fine sandpaper until free from all oil, dirt, rust and impurities and an entirely clean surface is obtained. 

Immediately thereafter the work shall be given a priming coat of enamel, thoroughly applied to all accessible portions of the work inside and out, baked to a proper degree of hardness and made smooth.

All exposed surfaces requiring a high finish shall then receive two coats of mineral filler, finely ground and mixed with linseed oil to a proper consistency to fill all voids and construction marks in the surface of the work. The filler to be ground or rubbed down with lump pumice stone and water to obtain a true and even surface before the ground coat is applied. 

One coat of ground enamel of uniform character throughout and of approved color shall then be applied and baked hard, leaving the work ready to receive the final finish to be applied after it is erected in the building. 

Classes of Finish.-Hollow metal doors and trim are furnished in the following classes of finish: 

Class "A"-Plain colors such as Dark Green, Dark Olive, Maroon, Chocolate, Black, Sea Green, Dark Brown. 

Class "B"-Plain colors such as White, Light Gray, also 

Cream, Light Blue and any light colors except Carmine. 

Class "C"-Stippled enamel such as Copper Verde Antique,

Bronze Verde Antique. 

Class "D"-Grained finishes such as Light Mahogany, Tuna 

Mahogany, Dark Mahogany, Dark Birch, Cherry and American 

Walnut Straight Grain. 

Class "E"-Grained finishes such as Medium Oak, Light Oak, Dark Oak, Circassian Walnut, Light Ash, Dark Circassian 

Walnut, Pine and Straight Oak, Bronze Stipple and Gum Wood.

CHAPTER XXIV STRUCTURAL AND MISCELLANEOUS IRON AND STEEL, STEEL JOISTS AND ROOF CONSTRUCTION 

The preparation of a structural steel estimate involves a great deal of work on account of the large amount of detail involved in listing the quantities from the plans, computing the weights of the various sections, cost of making shop drawings and detailing the steel, estimating the cost of shop fabrication, freight, cartage, and the labor cost of erecting the steel on the job.

The structural steel framework of a building usually consists of grillage, cast iron column bases, built-up columns, girders, beams, lintels, roof trusses, etc., which are fabricated from standard shapes, such as angles, "I" beams, channels, "Z" bars, "H" columns, plates, rods, etc., in combinations designed to give the required strength.

Estimating Quantities of Structural Steel 

When estimating the quantity of structural steel required for any job, each class of work should be estimated separately, i.e., column bases, columns, girders, beams, lintels, trusses, etc., as they all involve different labor operations in fabrication. 

Columns can be estimated closely by estimating the main members as shown on the plans, including bases, caps, splices, connections, etc. For columns without cover plates, figure 1 to 

3 lbs. per lin. ft. for rivet heads and 5 to 8 lbs. per lin. ft. where cover plates are used.

All standard connections can be taken from manufacturers' hand book and be sure to include rivets and bolts for connecting steel to steel.

When figuring cast iron column bases, figure as shown on the plans and add about 10% for fillets and overrun, except on very large castings when 5% to 7% overrun is sufficient. 1509

Plate girder details are often estimated by percentages but usually consist of stiffeners, fillers and shelf angles. The most satisfactory method is to figure all members as shown on the plans and add 21% to 5% for rivet heads. 

There is considerable more variation in roof trusses owing to the large amount of details required. These ordinarily weigh from 15% to 25% as much as the main members, while in special cases they may run as high as 25% to 35%.

Beams can be figured as shown on the plans, adding all necessary connections, which can be obtained from manu facturers' hand book. 

In addition to the structural framing of the building, it is often necessary for the structural steel contractor to furnish numerous miscellaneous items, such as base plates, loose lintels, anchor bolts, coal chutes, coal door covers, etc., although they are set in place by other contractors. 

Items to be Included in a Structural Steel Estimate.—When preparing an estimate on structural steel, the following items should be included to obtain the erected price: 

1. Cost of structural steel shapes at the mill. 

2. Freight on structural steel shapes from rolling mill to fabricating shop. 

3. Cost of making working drawings and detailing steel ready for the shop. 

4. Cost of assembling and fabricating shapes into columns, girders, beams, trusses, etc. including templates in connection with same. 

5. Cost of applying one or more coats of shop paint. 

6. Shop overhead expense and profit. 

7. Freight on fabricated steel from shop to destination. 

8. Cartage on steel from shop or cars to job. 

9. Cost of erecting steel, including plant rental, setting up and removing derricks, hoisting engines, unloading steel at site, erecting steel, field riveting or bolted connections. 

10. Cost of painting structural steel after erection. 

Estimating Cost of Structural Shapes at Rolling Mill.-After the quantities have been listed from the plans, it will be necessary to compute the cost of the steel sections required. 

All prices on structural steel are based on mill shipment from rolling mills in Pittsburgh, Bethlehem, Chicago, etc., depending upon the location of the mill where the steel is purchased, plus freight from rolling mill to fabricating shop.

The rolling mills bill materials at the weights given in their hand books but exercise the right to a 21% variation, either above or below the tabulated sectional area. Contracts on a pound basis often contain the provision that payment shall be made by scaled weight but no excess greater than 2% of the total calculated weight will be paid for. 

Where steel is wanted in a hurry, it is often necessary to purchase same from jobbers' stocks, which usually costs from 1 to 14 cents per lb. more than when purchased from mills. 

Another item that must be considered when pricing steel work is the base price on standard sections and the additions thereto. 

Example: Assuming the base price of steel is 2 cts. per lb. or $40.00 per ton, find the cost of 1"x1"x" steel angles. The standard classification of extras given on the following pages shows that angles of this size cost 15 cts. per 100 lbs. more than the base price or $2.15 per 100 lbs.

Structural steel prices change so often, depending upon market conditions, that latest quotations should always be obtained before figuring jobs of any size. 

Cost of Making Working Drawings and Detailing Structural 

Steel. The cost of making shop or working drawings for steel structures will vary with the type of building, weight of steel, amount of duplication, etc. The ton cost will run considerably less where fairly heavy shapes are used than on light structures using lattice columns, large light weight trusses, etc., as the latter type of construction requires considerable detailing without involving much tonnage. 

Steel skeleton construction, such as office buildings, hotels, etc., without unusual features can usually be detailed for $3.50 to $7.50 per ton.

Ordinary mill and factory buildings consisting of columns, lintels, light trusses and crane runs, requiring considerable detailing without much duplication, will cost from $3.50 to $9.00 per ton.

Theaters, churches and other structures of this class will cost from $8.00 to $25.00 per ton for details. 

When detailing plate girders, roof trusses, beam work and other special work, figure the cost of the work by the number of sheets of details required, figuring $40.00 to $50.00 for each 

24"x36" sheet.

Shop Painting of Structural Steel. After the steel has been fabricated it is customary to give it a coat of paint before it leaves the shop.

The cost of painting is usually estimated at a certain price per ton and the quantity of paint required and the surface area to be covered will vary with the class of steel. Ordinary structural beams contain 225 to 275 sq. ft. of surface per ton; plate girders 125 to 175 sq. ft. of surface per ton, while trusses contain 275 to 325 sq. ft. of surface per ton. The average for a job will vary from 175 to 225 sq. ft. per ton of steel. 

A gallon of paint will cover 350 to 600 sq. ft. of surface, depending upon the kind of paint used. A gallon of red lead and oil should cover 600 to 700 sq. ft. of surface for the first coat and 

500 to 600 sq. ft. on the second coat. 

Sufficient red lead and oil paint and labor necessary to paint one ton of structural steel (200 sq. ft.) with one shop coat of paint should cost as follows: gal. red lead and oil...

Shop Overhead Expense and Profit.-After the actual cost of the various items making up a structural steel estimate have been computed, including shop drawings, assembling and fabricating, shop painting, etc., it will be necessary to add for shop overhead expense and profit. This includes such items as office expense, rent, estimating, interest, depreciation, insurance, advertising, etc., and will vary with the shop and the amount of work on hand. Drafting room overhead will vary from 10% to 25% of the actual cost of the work, while shop overhead will often be 30% to 50% the actual cost of fabrication. These items have been included in the drafting room and shop fabrication costs given on the following pages but to this it will be necessary to add 10 per cent for business administration, office overhead and sales expense, plus 10 per cent additional on the total cost for profit.
