Mill and Shop Inspection of Structural Steel.-Where the structural steel is inspected by one of the testing laboratories, the usual charges for this work are as follows: 

Mill inspection is usually figured at $0.30 to $0.40 per ton and shop inspection from $0.50 to $0.75 per ton. Where both mill and shop inspection are let to one firm, a common price is $1.00 per ton for both.

Field Inspection of Structural Steel. Where field inspection of the erection and riveting of the structural steel is required, figure $85.00 to $100.00 per week for salary and expenses of a field inspector, plus transportation to and from job. 

Erection of Structural Steel 

The field cost of handling and erecting structural steel is difficult to estimate. This is due to a number of reasons, such as weather conditions, strikes, delays in receipt of materials, storage facilities, size and type of building, equipment available, labor conditions, amount of riveting, etc. *This item varies as described on previous pages. **Fabricating costs vary according to amount of shop labor required as given under cost of the various fabricating operations.

Any one of the above items may cause a considerable variation in the estimated labor costs and for that reason should be carefully considered when preparing the estimate. 

Hauling Structural Steel From Shops or Cars to Job.-The cost of hauling structural steel from the shop or cars to the job will vary with the facilities for loading trucks at cars, distance of haul, weight of steel members, etc. 

If steel is hauled by horse drawn trucks, a two horse load will vary from 2 to 3 tons but motor trucks will haul from 5 to 

10 tons per load.

The average cost of hauling structural steel is $1.50 to $2.50 per ton.

Plant and Equipment for Steel Erection.-The equipment required for steel erection will vary considerably with the size and type of building.

Skeleton frame buildings up to 100'-0"x100′-0″ in size will require one derrick to unload the steel from the trucks and erect it in place, while buildings of irregular shape, such as "L" shape, "U" shape, etc., will probably require additional derricks, as one derrick can handle a job 100′-0″x100'-0" but if the job is 75'-0"x125'-0" it will probably require two derricks to set the job, while a "U" shape building may require 3 derricks. 

Where the buildings have set backs at certain story heights, as required by many cities, it will often require 2 derricks on the job, one to unload the steel and hoist it from the street and another to set the steel. 

At the present time it costs $500.00 to $750.00 to set up and remove a hoisting engine, derrick, compressor outfit, etc., for a one derrick job, with additional derricks at approximately the same cost.

On buildings covering considerable ground area, such as high schools, auditoriums, mill and factory buildings, etc., up to 

3 or 4 stories high, it is often more economical to use a derrick crane, mounted on a motor truck or a railroad car, depending upon location of the job. Where a movable crane can be used to advantage, that is the most economical method to use, as the crane can be moved about at slight expense.

The more rivets that can be driven from one scaffold, the greater the number driven per day.

Actual Costs of Structural Steel Work 

The costs given on the following pages are taken from actual jobs, and compiled so that they may be used in any locality. 

Erecting Steel on a Two Story Wall Bearing Building, Mas silon, Ohio. On a two story store and office building erected in Massillon, Ohio, all of the structural steel framing consisted of 6-inch "H" columns one story high, with 12 and 15-inch “I” beams framing into them at the first and second floors. All of the steel on the first floor was set in place without the use of a derrick. On the second floor a small hand operated “A” frame derrick was used to hoist the steel into place. 

At the time this work was performed there were no structural iron workers to be obtained, and all the steel was set by carpenters and laborers.

The entire job contained 31 tons of steel, and the labor cost handling, erecting and bolting one ton of steel averaged as follows:

Erecting Steel on a Nine Story Wall Bearing Apartment 

Building, Chicago.-On a 9-story apartment building erected in 

Chicago, the structural steel was of skeleton type except the ends of the beams were carried on the exterior masonry walls. 

This job was started during the autumn months and was carried on through the winter with the usual amount of cold weather, ice and snow to contend with, so the conditions were not the best for making a low cost record. Furthermore, it was not possible to erect the steel to the best advantage, as the progress of steel erection was contingent upon the progress made in building the masonry walls. It was not possible to set the steel until the masonry walls for each story had been completed.

All of the steel was hoisted from the ground to the upper story by a boom fastened to the hoisting tower and operated from a nigger head on the hoisting engine. After the steel was placed on the floor, it was hoisted in position using hand operated derricks. The building was 9 stories high, and all connections were riveted by hand.

Labor Erecting Steel Stacks. When estimating the labor cost of erecting steel stacks for office buildings or other buildings of this type, where the stack extends from the ground to the top of the building and is either built into the building or placed on the outside of one of the rear walls, there are several items to be taken into consideration; viz., the length and weight of each section of stack, the facilities for hoisting and placing, and the amount of rigging necessary. 

Where each section of the stack weighs 500 to 1,000 pounds, it is customary to place a small gin pole on the roof of the building and lift each section in place. 

Three or four iron workers should set up all necessary rigging in one day, ready to place the sections. After the derricks and rigging have been placed ready to start hoisting, the gang should handle, place and bolt one 15 to 20 foot section of stack in 4 hours, or 2 sections (30 to 40 lin. ft.), per 8-hour day.

How to Estimate the Cost of Structural Steel in any Locality. 

-All prices on structural and reinforcing steel from mill are based on shipment from Pittsburgh, Pa., or Chicago. When computing the freight charges from mills to point of delivery, add freight from Pittsburgh, Pa., or Chicago to your city, and the result will be the cost of the steel f.o.b cars your city. 

As an example of the method used, suppose we wish to obtain the price of reinforcing steel in carloads from mills at Chicago for delivery in St. Louis, Mo.

Price of steel, f.o.b. cars mills, Chicago 

Freight rate per 100 lbs. Chicago to St. Louis 

Total cost per 100 lbs.

Rate Total 

$2.30 $2.30 .24 .24 $2.54

Bear in mind that mill shipments should always be in full carload lots, and the freight rate on less than carloads is considerably higher.

How to Estimate the Cost of Structural and Reinforcing Steel 

Purchased from Jobber's Stock.-Where the steel is wanted in a hurry or in less than carload lots, it is customary to purchase same out of warehouse or jobber's stock from the nearest city having such stocks.

In instances of this kind the price of the steel at destination may be computed by taking the price of the steel at mills, Pittsburgh or Chicago plus freight from mills to city from which the steel is purchased. This will give the jobber's cost of the steel. 

At the present time an allowance of $1.25 to $1.50 per 100 pounds or $25.00 to $30.00 per ton should be added to mill prices to allow for jobber's handling charge, overhead expense. and profit. This will give the selling price of the steel at jobbing center, to which it will be necessary to add freight (either local or carload rate) from jobbing center to destination. The total will be the delivered price of the steel.

As an example, compute the cost of 100 pounds of steel purchased from St. Louis stock and shipped to Fort Worth, Texas.

Estimating the Weight of Wrought Iron, Steel, or Cast Iron 

When tables of weights are not handy, the following rules will prove of value to the estimator when computing the weights of wrought iron, steel, or cast iron. 

Weight of Wrought Iron.-One cubic foot of wrought iron weighs 480 pounds. One square foot of wrought iron 1-inch thick weighs 40 pounds. One square inch of wrought iron one foot long weighs 3 lbs.

To find the weight of one square foot of flat iron of any thickness, multiply the thickness in inches by 40, and the result will be the weight of the iron in pounds. 

To find the weight of one lineal foot of wrought iron bar of any size, multiply the cross sectional area in square inches by 3, and the result will be the weight per lineal foot. 

Weight of Steel.-One cubic foot of steel weighs 489.6 

pounds, or 2 per cent more than wrought iron. One square foot of steel 1-inch thick weighs 40.8 pounds. A piece of steel 

1-inch square and one foot long weighs 3.4 pounds.

To find the weight of one lineal foot of steel bar of any size. multiply the cross sectional area in square inches by 3.4, and the result will be the weight of the steel in pounds. If the weight per lineal foot is known, the exact sectional area in square inches may be obtained by dividing the weight by 34 

Weight of Cast Iron.-One cubic foot of cast iron weighs 

450 pounds. One square foot of cast iron 1-inch thick weighs 

37½ pounds. A piece of cast iron 1-inch square and one foot long weighs 3% pounds. One cubic inch of cast iron weighs 26 pound.

STEEL JOISTS 

Steel Joists were developed primarily to take the place of wood construction. In recent years the Underwriters and Building Departments have recognized the merits of this construction from the point of fire resistive and structural qualities with the result that this type of floor construction has not only replaced wood to a great extent but other types of fire resistive floor construction to an equal extent. 

ORIENT FINISH EXANSON RODS O-T OPEN TRUSS JOISTS- 

4921 0181 

TAI SOOS DIAMOND RIB LATH Open Truss Steel Joist* Construction With Finished Floor of Cement. 

" Diamond Rib Lath for Floor and Ceiling.

Steel Joists fall into two classifications, namely: Open Web 

Joists and Strip Steel Joists. The Open Web Joist is manufactured by welding chord members, consisting of Tee Sections, Angles or bars, with round bar web members to form a Warren Truss. The Strip Steel Joist consists of a plate web member and angle flanges welded together to form a plate girder. 

When steel joists are used in strictly fireproof construction, it is necessary to place a 2" to 4" slab of concrete on metal lath over the joists and a plastered ceiling on metal lath beneath the joists.

Where a wood floor is required, wooden nailing screeds supported on screed clips are imbedded in the concrete slab and the wood flooring is then nailed to the screeds. 

Steel Joists may also be used in semi-fireproof construction by nailing the wood sheathing directly to screeds attached to 

Truscon Steel Co., Youngstown. O.

STEEL JOISTS 

1545 the joists without the use of a protective concrete slab. A few manufacturers of steel joists have met the demand for this type of construction by fabricating a nailer joist with the wood "O-TOPEN TRUSS E91 STEEL JOISTS 26 DIAMOND RID LATH 

Open Truss Steel Joist Construction with finished floor of wood secured by means of screeds placed at right angles to the joists and elevated to provide for concrete underneath. " Diamond Rib Lath for floor and ceiling. screed attached in the shops by the use of lag screws, bolts or, as in the case of one manufacturer, by the use of a special U-shaped top chord into which the wood screed is firmly imbedded. 

Open Truss Steel Nailer Nailed ho 7 

Joist Construction 

Direct to Nailer Joists.

With Wood Sub-Floor

In the latter method the screed rests directly on the top chord of the joist and is secured against any possible vertical or lateral movement by the upturned flanges of the top chord which are pressed into the wood screed. One of the greatest objections to wood lumber when used in ordinary dwellings and apartment buildings is the shrinkage of the joists which permits the finished floor to drop 1/4" to 3%" below the wood base, door jambs, casings, etc., giving an unsightly appearance that is difficult to overcome. In the manufacture of nailer joists with special U-shaped top chord into which the wood screed is firmly imbedded. The screeds are made of kiln-dried yellow pine which precludes the possibility of any shrinkage. These wood screeds are also impregnated with a waterproofing solution to prevent their absorption of any moisture. 

Open web joists may be used to great advantage in all types of light occupancy buildings. The open web construction greatly facilitates the placing of plumbing, conduits, etc., making unnecessary the need of a furred ceiling or heavy fills on top of the structural slab. 

WELDED STEEL FABRIC CEMENT -PLATE GIRDER JOISTS RIB LATH Plate Girder Steel Joist Construction With Cement Floor Finish. 

" Diamond Rib Lath for Floor and Ceiling.

Steel joists may also be used in mill construction to replace structural steel purlins with a resulting economy of materials, using nailer joists for supporting wood deck and all-steel joists for steel deck. The joists are provided with sag rods and bearing plates for bolting to supporting trusses when necessary. 

Strip steel joists may be used wherever open web joists are permitted with approximately the same structural economies. 

No strip steel joist is manufactured which corresponds to the open web nailer joist. Where wood screeds are necessary they must be attached in the field. In strip steel joist construction

STEEL JOISTS 

1547 the conduits must be threaded through holes punched in the web of the joists, placed in a fill on top of the joists or suspended below the joists and covered with a furred ceiling. 

Estimating Steel Joists.-Steel Joists and related products are generally sold by the manufacturer directly to the contractor and when preparing general contract estimates the most satisfactory method is to send plans or sketches to the manufacturer or his agent thus assuring a sub-bid based on an economical layout and design and one which includes the necessary accessories such as lath, clips, ceiling extension rods, bridging, etc.

In his quotation the manufacturer will note the tonnage of joists, sq. ft. of lath, etc. which will enable the contractor to figure the necessary cartage and labor of erection. The universal method of figuring the labor of erection is to add a unit amount per ton of joists and per sq. ft. of lath. The cost of joist erection including placing of accessories varies from $6.00 to $15.00 per ton depending on labor conditions, location and type of building. If joists are to be welded to the structural steel a unit price of 10 cts. to 15 cts per joist will generally cover the cost of making two ½" welds on each end of the joists. The cost of placing the top lath will vary from 5 cts. to 10 cts. per sq. yd.

When making preliminary estimates, the cost of joist construction may be taken from one of the following tables. The unit prices used in each case are noted in the table and adjustments may be made for differences in freight and labor costs. 

These tables are based on the use of Open Web Joists but the Plate Girder Type may be substituted with little variation from the costs shown.

Labor Setting Steel Joists.-The labor cost of handling and setting steel joists is usually estimated by the ton, based on the total weight of the joists to be placed. 

This cost will vary considerably, depending upon the type of building, size of joists, length of spans, amount of handling and hoisting necessary, etc.

It is much cheaper to set joists on long straight spans and large floor areas, such as garage and factory buildings, office buildings, etc., than on residences and other irregularly constructed buildings.

All steel floor joists must be bridged according to manufacturer's standards.

On an ordinary job of steel floor joists of regular construction and fairly long spans, two men working together should handle and place 5,000 to 6,000 lbs. of joists (including bridging), per 8-hr. day, at the following labor cost per ton:

JUNIOR STEEL BEAMS 

1557 

JUNIOR STEEL BEAMS* 

Junior beams are light weight rolled structural I-beams which are used as floor beams or roof purlins in residences, schools, stores, apartments, hospitals and all types of light occupancy structures. 

They are rolled from billets to man ufacturers' standard specifications for structural steel for buildings by highly perfected methods, resulting in a structurally perfect section. It is produced in sizes having depths of 6″, 7″, 8″, 9", 10", 11″ and 12" and with flanges varying in width from 

178" for the 6" steel joists to 3" for the 12" joists. The properties of these new sections are given below:

Expanded metal lath can be applied direct to the tops and bottoms of rolled steel joists and securely fastened by an especially designed hand tool and heavy wire clips, the operation of attaching the lath being much more rapid than other methods of applying metal lath.

When metal lath is applied to the top of rolled steel joists, concrete can be poured, using the lath as the only form work needed, and the cost of lumber and the erecting of wood forms and their removal after the concrete has set are all done away with. By back-plastering the under side of the metal lath, it can be made to serve as satisfactory reinforcement for the slab, rib lath being used where the rolled steel joists are set farther apart than the usual spacing of wood joists. Clips for holding wood nailing strips can be attached direct to the tops of the steel joists.

Where the joists rest on walls, bearing partitions, or on top of girders, no attachment to supports is necessary, but adjust- 

Jones & Laughlin Steel Co.

able cross bridging of heavy wire is furnished, the same as with other steel joists. Where the rolled steel joists must frame flush on top with supporting girder, the method of installation is to drop the joists into steel stirrups hung from the main supports, no coping of flange of joists being necessary. Similar stirrups are used where the joists are framed with their tops at any other level than flush with the tops of supporting girders. 

Little or no fabrication of steel joists is necessary, but material is furnished cut to any desired length, and coped when absolutely necessary. It is carried in stock in lengths up to 

42'-0" and is painted with a heavy coat of asphaltum.

Method of Laying Ferrobord Steel Roof Deck

STEEL ROOFDECKS 

1559 

FERROBORD STEEL ROOF DECK 

The Ferrobord* type of steel roof deck is so formed that each sheet interlocks with the adjoining sheets to form a continuous deck over the entire roof. 

When insulated and waterproofed, it is adaptable to any type and shape of roof and is used in the industrial, commercial, railroad and institutional fields. This method of roof construction has been successfully applied on factories, boiler houses, blacksmith shops, foundries, power houses, warehouses, garages, armories, stadiums, exhibition buildings, field houses, schools and hospitals, stores, shops, etc., and on hangars and airdomes in the aeronautical field. Many installations have 

Spot Welding Ferrobord Steel Roofdeck to Steel Purlins. 

Truscon Steel Co.

been made on apartment houses, theaters, and other types of monumental structures. 

Ferrobord roofdeck is adaptable to flat and pitched roofs and curved roofs with a minimum radius of 40'-0". 

Ferrobord is furnished in 18, 20, 22 and 24 gage Armco ingot iron or copper bearing steel, in 6" widths, 14" and 14" deep and in any desired length, the only restriction being shipping facilities. 

It is fastened to structural members with purlin clips that clamp over the flanges of the structural roof members or they may be spot welded to the structural members, thereby eliminating all mechanical clips.

Labor Erecting Ferrobord or Similar Roofdeck.-Ferrobord roofdeck is secured to the steel purlins by spot welding or specially designed clips. The labor cost of applying same will vary from 1 to 2 cts. per sq. ft. depending upon the type of building and the prevailing wage scale.

CHAPTER XXV. 

ELECTRIC FREIGHT AND PASSENGER ELEVATORS, MECHANICAL REFRIGERATION 

Elevator construction is such a highly specialized business that it is almost out of the question to expect any one except an experienced elevator engineer to prepare an estimate on equipment of this kind. 

There is no standard price for elevator equipment, as each time the capacity changes, the price changes, and when speed differs, the price differs. The travel, the number of openings, the kind of cab, the location of the job, all affect the price. 

For example, an elevator can be Hand Cable control (H. C.), Car Switch control (C. S.), Push Button control (P. B.), Dual 

Control, a combination of both Car Switch and Push Button, or Hold-In-Button control (H. I. B.), which is a cross between 

Car Switch and Push Button. There are three classes of Hold- 

In-Button controlled elevators.

The prices on the same equipment are subject to some variation also, as a Push Button job in Chicago might cost approximately the same as a Car Switch job in South Dakota or some other place where it is necessary to add freight, board, room, and expenses of the men erecting the equipment. 

In figuring passenger elevators, the capacity is generally figured on one passenger for every 2 sq. ft. of platform and 

150 lbs. is used as the average weight of each passenger. 

For freight elevators, manufacturers figure 100 lbs. per sq. ft. of platform, except to meet special conditions where large size platforms with minimum carrying capacity are required, such as furniture warehouses, garages, etc.

Essential Information for Figuring Elevators.-The following information is essential to enable the elevator manufacturer to prepare an intelligent estimate on the elevators required for any building: 1563

1. Name of Building, Location, Name of Owner, Architect. 

2. Kind of service and control. 

3. Capacity of elevator. 

4. Speed of elevator. 

5. Total travel of eleva tor in feet. 

6. Travel in floors, num ber of openings. 

7. Location of elevator machinery. 

8. Kind of electric cur rent available.

CHAPTER XXVI. 

HEATING AND AIR CONDITIONING 

Within the past few years tremendous strides have been made in the methods of heating buildings and with the introduction of humidifying and air conditioning still greater progress has been made.

Furnace or warm air remains the cheapest method of heating buildings and improvements in this method have been made by the introduction of "fans or blowers" to force the air through the ducts. Some systems incorporate air filters and water pans to extract the dust from the return air and moisten same before returning it to the rooms. 

Most "air conditioning" systems are duct systems using supply and return ducts to each principal room. These systems are usually furnished with air filters to extract the dust from the return air, and moisten it through humidifying pans, and again distribute it through the building by means of fans or blowers. 

While these systems are commonly known as air conditioning systems, they are really "humidfying systems" as they do not cool the rooms during hot weather. 

A complete air conditioning system heats, humidifies and conditions the air in the winter and cools and dehumidifies the air in the summer. Systems of this kind require the use of refrigerating apparatus, which is not only expensive to install but also quite expensive to operate.

Other systems use steam and hot water heat with radiators in part of the structure and hot air or ducts in the balance of the structure. These are known as "split" systems. 

It is practically impossible to go into the various systems in a book of this kind because each manufacturer has his own methods and equipment and costs vary widely, also each job must be laid out separately and varies with the room exposure, length of runs, insulation, etc., so that it really requires a thoroughly experienced heating and ventilating engineer to lay out each job before it can be estimated. 1570

HEATING 

1571 Boilers are now designed for burning special fuels, such as hard coal, soft coal, oil, gas, etc., and the costs vary with boiler sizes, accessories, such as domestic hot water heaters, thermostatic controls, etc.

The ordinary cast iron radiators standing in the room are almost a thing of the past in modern residential heating and new concealed convection type radiators are now used. These are all items that effect costs. 

Copper piping is now used for both heating and plumbing and the cost of this work depends to a large extent upon the experience of the contractor installing same. Mechanics familiar with sweating joints and installing copper piping can install this work rapidly, while those who are not accustomed to its use, will spend considerable time on it. 

For the above reasons, the estimator should be familiar with the requirements of the trade in order to prepare intelligent estimates.

Modified or Winter Air Conditioning Systems 

It is almost impossible for the average estimator to compute the cost of a modified air conditioning system for any building unless he knows just what system is to be used as practically all manufacturers use different methods of estimating and the industry is so new that no set standards have been established. 

In determining the amount of radiation required, it is necessary to make an accurate layout of each room, computing the amount of infiltration through doors and windows, exposed wall areas, exposed floors and ceilings, duct losses due to length of runs, insulation of walls, ceilings and ducts, duct resistance, velocity, etc., so that it is really a job for a person thoroughly experienced in this class of heating.

For the above reasons, a general idea of the requirements, sizes and costs of a modified air conditioning system can only be given in this chapter.

Modified or Winter Air Conditioning.-Modified or winter air conditioning is descriptive of the method of heating and ventilating, combined with an air filtration and humidification, now commonly used for the heating of homes. 

Each system consists of a direct fired heating unit, similar to the old style gravity furnace, a slowly revolving blower automatically controlled, and a supply and return system of ducts so arranged as to insure a complete change of air in each principal room of the house at intervals, usually 10 to 15 minutes each.

The unit may be gas, oil or coal fired. Gas or oil fired units designed for that particular fuel operate at high efficiency, although satisfactory, if less efficient results may be obtained through the use of conversion burners installed in units primarily designed for solid fuel. 

Coal fired units may be hand fired or used with automatic stoking devices with success and low fuel costs. However, this type of heating differs from gas or oil fired apparatus in that it is semi-automatic in nature. 

Thermostatic control of heating apparatus is highly desirable and invariably used. Automatic controls vary the supply of heat in accordance with demand set up by a thermostat located in the living portion of the home. Usually the blower commences operation automatically when the heated air in the generating unit has reached a pre-determined temperature and cuts out after the source of heat has been shut down and the temperature in the head or bonnet dropped to a pre-determined point. 

Design of air conveying systems of this kind presents an engineering problem which can only be solved with a reasonable degree of accuracy by a competent designer. The heat loss of the building, room by room, is established and the volume of heated air required for certain intervals establishes data from which a duct system can be designed with due regard for velocities, static pressures and delivery temperatures. 

Costs vary widely. Methods of estimating similarly vary. 

However, most of the methods used hinge very closely upon the type of building as to shape, the number of outlets and inlets, and the poundage of fabricated metal work involved. 

Houses are classified for this purpose into two general groups or types. No attempt is made to establish data covering unusual types of architecture or for other than standard kinds of con struction. 

Type "1" is that group described as the conventional rectangular building consisting of two floors and basement, which can be heated by a total number of openings, both supply and return, ranging from 10 to 25. Total cost of this type of house range from $6,000.00 to $12,000.00 in the Chicago area and from 10 to 20 per cent less in the smaller towns and cities. 

Type "2" includes that group of homes irregular in shape, with garage usually a part of the structure and wings or extensions at an angle to the main structure. These homes are usually in the higher cost brackets. The number of openings required varies from 25 to 60. Invariably this type of home

HEATING 

1573 requires localized temperature control, consisting of 3 or more zones under separate thermostatic control. 

Costs per opening for Type "1" houses are established from an estimate of sheet metal averaging 70 lbs. per opening. If return ducts are entirely of metal and the building structure not used insofar as possible for return trunks, this poundage should be raised to 80 lbs. per opening. 

For Type "2" structures without zone control, poundage per opening is figured at 85 lbs. If return ducts are wholly of metal, this figure becomes 90 lbs. If zone control is used add 10 lbs. per opening to the foregoing.

For a conventional house of standard structure rectangular in shape, with two main floors, the following openings or supply and return data is established:

If the sheet metal workers are able to install their duct work without unnecessary delay on the part of other trades, considerable time and money could be saved on this portion of the work.

Special Insulation.-Ducts in unexcavated spaces or in unheated attic spaces, both supply and return, should be insulated with not less than ½" of adequate insulating material. This material is furnished in flexible form and averages about 25 cts. per sq. ft. applied. 

Electrical Work.-Custom varies with respect to the supply and installation of electrical circuit from meter to fused safety switch adjacent to unit. Likewise for the connection of blower motor to 110 volt controls and also for the 22 volt wiring to thermostat when used. Most often the job electrician runs the 

110 volt service to the safety switch adjacent to unit. From this point it is handled as a sub-contract under the heating contractor and represents a cost of from $30.00 to $50.00 for complete wiring installation of all controls and motors.

Carpentry. The carpentry or cutting and framing to provide for ducts, etc., is invariably a part of the cost figured by the general contractor and is seldom, if ever, included as a part of the heating contract.

Approximate Costs of Air Conditioning Systems. Where an approximate cost of installing air conditioning systems is desired, including complete cooling units, the following will prove of value to the estimator as it is the experience of one of the foremost contractors installing air conditioning equipment. 

When installing complete air conditioning systems in hotels, office buildings, stores, etc., the cost will run about $1.50 per sq. ft. of floor area to be conditioned.

In restaurants, hotel dining rooms and other spaces subject to excessive heat or having south and west exposures, will often run 50 per cent more than the average given above. 

Where the size of the cooling or refrigerating units are known, the cost will run about $400.00 per ton of refrigerating capacity. 

For instance, an installation requiring 100 tons of refrigerating capacity will cost about $40,000.00 for the system installed complete.

WARM AIR HEATING 

Ordinary warm air heating is used only in the lowest cost buildings and when warm air is used in the better class buildings, it is usually a modified air conditioning system as described on the previous pages. 

When estimating warm air heating, the usual procedure is to obtain the total number of cubic feet in the building to be heated and allow a certain percentage for glass area and exposed wall surfaces. Most of the concerns manufacturing furnaces give the number of rooms in the house together with the maximum number of cubic feet the furnace will heat, but all manufacturers advise using a larger furnace than is actually required so that in extreme cold weather it will not be necessary to force the furnace to obtain sufficient heat. 

There are two methods of warm air heating. The one method uses a furnace with hot air pipes running to the various rooms, with a register in the wall or floor of each room. This method has its advantages where there are numerous rooms closed off from one another and it is desirable to heat certain rooms without heating the entire house. 

The pipeless method uses only one large register in the floor directly over the furnace, which should be placed near the center of the house. The theory of this system is that the

warm air rises driving the cold air to the floor. The one register in the floor contains both a cold and warm air chamber so that the cold air is drawn into the register and into the furnace, heated and expelled through the warm air register. This system should be used only in houses that are thrown open and having a free circulation of air at all times. 

Estimating the Size of Furnace Required.-When estimating the size of furnace required to heat any building, take the entire cubical contents of the building to be heated. Size up the building for the number and size of the windows, also the exposure of the building and make a liberal allowance for these conditions. 

For instance, a one story cottage or bungalow 30x55 feet having 9 foot ceilings, would contain 30x55x9 or 14,850 cubic feet. Making allowance for four exterior walls and approximately 20 windows and doors, it would be advisable to purchase a furnace having a capacity of 18,000 to 22,000 cubic feet, to insure plenty of heat in extreme weather. 

When estimating heating plants using a pipe furnace, it will be necessary to obtain the number of lineal feet of pipe running from the furnace to the registers in the various rooms. 

A two story building will require some square or rectangular pipes between the stud partitions leading to the second story. 

The number of lineal feet of each size should be listed, the number of register faces and frames, lineal feet of smoke pipe, elbows, dampers, collars, etc.

The following is a summary of the items to be included when preparing an estimate on warm air heating:

Furnace Pipes, Elbows, etc.

STEAM AND HOT WATER HEATING 

Because of different conditions surrounding the installation of heating apparatus, it is impossible to give any set rule that can be accepted, without modification, for all kinds of buildings to be heated. It is necessary to take into consideration all of the conditions in and around any building, and additions or deductions made to suit the requirements, no matter what rule may be used for figuring.

HEATING 

1581 

Methods of Computing Heating.-The most advanced method of figuring heating and the one that is generally used by heating engineers is the B.T.U. Method. This method is based on replacing the heat loss through exposed walls, doors and windows, floors, ceilings, etc., and uses so many factors, based on the type of construction that it is impossible to go into detail in a book of this kind, as intricate and elaborate formulas are used for both warm air, steam and hot water heating. In fact, if the entire subject of heating was thoroughly covered, it would require a book nearly as large as this one. For this reason only approximates can be treated in this chapter. 

The following rules for computing steam and hot water heating have been used successfully for many years before the advent of the B.T.U. method. 

Nearly all rules are based on 2 to 5 pounds steam pressure and temperature of 180 degrees for water, as indicated at the boiler when the outside temperature is at zero. When systems are designed for a lower heat temperature at the boiler (vapor, vacuum, etc.), it is necessary to provide additional radiation in accordance with the best practice of the different systems. 

It is general practice to consider 70 degrees as the standard for inside temperature and zero for the outside. When there is a greater difference between the inside and outside temperature, one per cent should be added to the radiation for each degree of difference. 

Many contractors make the mistake of installing too little radiation. A little extra surface will give greater economy and insure a first class working system, as well as a satisfied owner. 

An apparatus of ample size can be regulated to give economy, which cannot be done if the apparatus is too small and requires forcing.

The following rules have been found to give good results, but are not guaranteed. By using these rules and providing for additional radiation on the cold sides of building and making allowances for poor construction, loose-fitting windows, doors, etc., good results will be obtained.

Rule for Computing Steam and Hot Water Heating. This rule is based on outside temperature at zero and inside temperature at 70 degrees for walls 12 inches thick. Corrections should be made for varying conditions as stated below:

C equals contents in cubic feet.

W equals exposed wall surface in square feet. 

G equals glass (windows and doors) area in square feet. 

R equals radiation in square feet.

Steam 

(6C) + (80 W) + (300 G') 1000 =R 

Water 

(6C) + (80 W) + (300 G') 600 -R Example. A given room has 50 square feet of glass area, 220 square feet of wall and 1,800 cubic feet of space. Substituting the figures in place of letters in formula above: (6X1800)+(80 × 220) + (300 × 50) 

1080017600 + 15000 1000 

1080017600 + 15000 600 1000 

43.4 square feet of steam radiation = 72.3 square feet of hot water radiation.

Corrections for Varying Temperatures and Local Condi tions. Add one per cent of radiation for each degree below zero outside or above 70 degrees inside. Subtract one per cent for each degree above zero outside or below 70 degrees inside. 

When estimating the radiation in rooms where a greater or less amount of heat is required use the following corrections to C for rooms as listed when figuring residence work: 

For halls and dining rooms, use 10 C. 

For bath rooms, use 20 C.

For bed rooms, use 5 C. 

For all rooms on the sides receiving prevailing winds the radiation should be increased 10 per cent. Walls exposed to unheated rooms and spaces use 40 W instead of 80 W as given above.

The rule as given above is based on a 12-inch brick wall or good frame construction.

If an 8-inch brick wall is used with plaster applied direct to brick, use 120 W instead of 80 W. If the 8-inch brick walls are furred for lath and plaster, figure the same as 12-inch. 

For 12-inch brick wall, use 80 W; for a 16-inch wall use 70 W; and for a 20-inch brick wall, use 60 W.

1583 Solid cement and concrete block construction when plastered directly on wall should be figured same as 8-inch brick. If there is an air space between wall and plaster, figure the same as 12-inch brick. 

Brick veneer buildings should be figured the same as 12-inch brick walls.

Figure skylights the same as windows. If double windows are used, figure 140 G instead of 300 G.

When figuring the radiation in churches and auditoriums, use the formula as given above and multiply by the factors given below for the various sizes of buildings.

For computing minimum quantities of radiation for vapor systems at 70 degrees F. with the outside temperature at 10 degrees below zero, add twenty per cent (20%) to the amount of radiation for steam heating.

Flow Control Hot Water Heating Systems.-This method of hot water heating has largely superseded the older gravity or "open" type of hot water heating system. It is a complete combined automatic water heating and domestic water supply system for year 'round use. It's major advantages are instantaneous heating response, exceptionally high efficiency, low first cost, fuel economy and completely automatic operation. 

The flow control valve makes the boiler a reservoir of high temperature water, in that it prevents circulation through the system when heat is not required. A circulator or pump attached to the main near the boiler forces this hot water through the mains the instant the room thermostat calls for heat. When the thermostat is satisfied the circulator ceases to operate and the flow control valve stops all circulation of hot water, thus preventing overheating and needless heat losses.

The flow control hot water heating system requires approximately 20 per cent more radiation than is figured for steam heat. The mains are smaller reducing the cost of pipe, fittings and labor installing same.

All in all, a flow control hot water heating system costs a trifle less than the older gravity systems requiring large radiators and piping.

Any old gravity hot water heating system can be converted into a flow control system at a nominal expense.

Rule for Computing Boiler Sizes.-After the total number of square feet of radiation has been obtained, the size of the boiler should be computed.

Practically all boiler manufacturers rate their boilers, giving maximum heat output under full drive and also the recommended load, which represents the attached load, including piping, which may be placed on the boiler in accordance with accepted installation standards for economical operation. 

A cast-iron up-draft boiler should be 80 to 100 per cent larger than the actual amount of radiation in radiators and coils. 

A cast-iron down-draft boiler should be 60 to 65 per cent larger than the actual amount of radiation in radiators and coils. 

A steel fire-box, up-draft boiler, set in brick, should be 35 to 40 per cent larger than the actual amount of radiation in radiators and coils.

A steel fire-box boiler, brickset, up-draft with approved furnace, should be figured on the same basis as a steel downdraft boiler of similar number. 

A steel fire-box, brickset or portable down-draft boiler should be 40 per cent larger than the actual amount of the radiation in radiators and coils.

The quantities given above are approximates and should be used only when exact boiler sizes for the particular boiler specified are not obtainable.

In computing boiler sizes for buildings heated to lower than -10° to 70° F. multiply the amount of cast-iron column radiation necessary to maintain the required temperature by the following co-efficient before adding the percentage given in rule for computing boiler sizes.

Rule for Computing Boiler Sizes for Direct-Indirect and 

Indirect Radiation. For computing boiler sizes for directindirect and indirect radiation, reduce same to basis of direct by adding 25 per cent to direct-indirect and 50 per cent to indirect, then use the factor of safety as called for on direct radiation.

Regarding Steam Boiler Installation. It is recommended on all installations of steam boilers that drain valves be placed on the returns and that the condensation from such returns be discharged into the sewer for a period of 3 days to one week • after starting fire, thereby clearing system of grease and dirt.

At the end of this period the boiler should be thoroughly washed and blown out.

Boiler Capacity.-Boiler output is defined as the number of sq. ft. of standard direct column radiation or its equivalant in 

B.t.u., which a boiler will supply at its outlet in one hour, under standard conditions. 

240 B.t.u. represents one sq. ft. of standard direct column steam radiation. 

150 B.t.u. represents one sq. ft. of standard direct column water radiation.

Boiler Horsepower.-One boiler horsepower is defined as the evaporation of 34 lbs. of water per hour from a feed water temperature of 212 degrees into steam at 212 degrees. is equal to 34.5x970.4-33478.8 B.t.u. per hour.

One boiler horsepower is equal therefore to ft. of steam radiation. 33478.8 240 This =139 sq. 

Note that boiler horsepower is not derived from engine horsepower. 

1 horsepower hour=2545 B.t.u.

To find the B.t.u. output per hour of a steam boiler, multiply the output in sq. ft. by 240.

To find the B.t.u. output per hour of a water boiler, multiply the output in sq. ft. by 150.

To find the output in sq. ft. of steam radiation, divide the output in B.t.u. per hour by 240.

To find the output in sq. ft. of water radiation, divide the output in B.t.u. per hour by 150.

Estimating Pipe and Fittings. To prepare an intelligent estimate on the cost of any heating plant, the entire job should be laid out using the quantity of pipe of each size required; connections, such as elbows, tees, nipples, valves, etc., should all be figured separately. This requires considerable labor and a man must thoroughly understand his business to figure with any degree of accuracy.

HEATING 

1591 When estimating the quantities of piping required for any heating plant, the risers, mains and returns must be figured, together with all connections to and from the boilers. These will vary according to the system used and the type of building. 

A one-pipe steam heating system should have the highest point in the main directly over the boiler, and from this point it pitches down around the circuit until it drops to the floor or enters the boiler. The more pitch the better, but there should be at least one inch in 20 feet. The lowest point in the steam main, where it drops to enter the boiler or to the floor, should not be less than 14 inches above the water line of boiler and the more the better.

Branches for radiators should be taken from top of main, using a nipple and elbow or a nipple and a 45-degree ell, and should pitch up to the radiator.

Connections for steam should never be taken from side of main, as this will cause water hammer and syphoning of the water of condensation in the steam main into the radiator. 

Each radiator should be supplied with a good Disc radiator valve and a good automatic air valve, and each return main should also have an automatic air valve where it drops to enter boiler. 

If branches are longer than 8 or 10 feet, they should be one size larger than the upright connecting pipes. Where mains drop to floor, a pipe two sizes smaller can be used to return to boiler. Risers for either steam or water should be plumb and straight and if exposed in a room, and it is necessary to use couplings on same, the couplings should be at a uniform height from floor.

The valve on a steam radiator should be either wide open or tightly closed to prevent radiator filling with water. 

In a two-pipe system of hot water heating the highest return rises from boiler to radiator, the lowest point being at the boiler and the highest point at the end of the main. These pipes may be reduced as the branches are taken off, care being taken not to reduce too rapidly. Each radiator should be fitted with a

hot water radiator valve, union elbow and a good loose key compression air valve. All pipes should be well supported, so that no pockets or depressions will occur to retard or trap the circulation. All mains, both for steam and hot water, should run about 4 feet from wall to allow for expansion. 

Sizes of Pipes.—When estimating steam heating, the size of the main may be determined by taking the total amount of direct radiation to which add 25 per cent for piping and from this total extract the square root, dividing same by 10, which gives the size of the main to use. This is for one pipe work. 

For two pipe work one size less is sufficient and the return can be one or two sizes less than the supply. A steam main should not decrease in size but very little according to the area of its branches.

An example of the above method is as follows: A job contains 400 feet of direct steam radiation. By adding 25 per cent for piping, the result is 500 square feet. Extracting the square root of 500, gives 22.4. Divide 22.4 by 10 equals 2.24 or it will require a 2½-inch steam main.

Prices of Cast Iron Radiation 

Cast iron radiation is sold by the sq. ft. based on the ratings as given above. The sq. ft. price is the same regardless of width, height or length of standard radiators.

Cast iron radiation is subject to frequent price change, due to fluctuations in the price of cast iron.

The following prices are effective at time of publication but when figuring each job it is advisable to obtain current prices from your local distributor.

Standard cast iron radiation 30 cts. per sq. ft. subject to a cash discount of 5% and to a further discount of 5% in carload quantities. Rocky Mountain and Pacific Coast points about 10% higher. Extreme South about 5% higher. 

Wall radiators about 10% higher than standard radiation.

Radiant Convectors and Enclosures Radiant convectors combine convection heating with quickacting and comfortable radiant heating. They are formed of cast iron with finned sections and water backed radiating fronts. Radiant Convectors of Various Widths 

They are furnished in 4 widths and may be concealed in wall recesses or partly concealed, projecting into the room a short distance.

They are furnished in units from 13" to 602" long, in 4 widths, 318", 57%", 734" and 9" and in 24″, 26″, 29″, 32″, 35″, and 38" 

heights. 

The enclosures or fronts of the convection units are constructed of strongly braced furniture steel, accurately fitted to size. Five types of enclosures are furnished, all primed for painting. 

Complete enclosures are used for partially recessed or for free standing units, also for full recess where enclosure overlaps adjacent wall finish ½" at top and sides. 

Panel fronts are used in full recess or when used in a partial recess, the front is furnished with metal flange on top and sides to enclose space between panel front and wall finish. 

The table on the following page gives the sizes and ratings of the various convector units. 

The present price on radiant convector units is 28 cts. per sq. ft. of radiation only and does not include front panels or fronts.

Types of Standard Enclosures and Panel Fronts for Radiant Convectors 

Trade prices of standard enclosures and panels are based on the average size enclosure or panel on each order. The average size enclosure or panel is obtained by dividing the total number of sq. ft. of steam or water E. D. R., in the job by the total number of enclosures ordered. The total price of the enclosures on each order, therefore, equals the total sq. ft. of steam or water, E. D. R. ordered, multiplied by the price per sq. ft. of the average size enclosure.

Copper Pipe 

Copper pipe is used to a considerable extent for heating work and the cost depends upon the experience of the contractor installing same. Mechanics familiar with this class of work can install it rapidly, while those who are not accustomed to its use will spend considerable time on it, as it is an entirely different technique than installing steel pipe..

The price of the pipe itself is subject to wide fluctuations, due to the price of copper so that prices on copper pipe and fittings should ALWAYS be obtained for each job. 

Copper pipe is furnished in 3 weights, as follows: 

Heavy Copper Pipe (Government Type "K") for underground service, such as water, gas, steam, oil lines, industrial uses, also interior plumbing.

Standard Copper Pipe (Government Type "L") for interior plumbing and heating. 

Light Copper Pipe (Government Type "M")) for low pressure interior plumbing.

Estimating the Cost of Pipe and Fittings. To estimate the cost of pipe and fittings required for any heating plant, obtain the total number of square feet of radiation in the job (based on cast iron radiation) and figure at 20 cents per square foot.

This is based on prices of pipe as given on the previous pages. 

For each 5% increase or reduction in price of pipe, add or deduct 1 cent per square foot.

For bungalows and one story residences having short pipe runs, figure the cost of the pipe and fittings at 15 cents per square foot of radiation (based on standard cast iron radiation). For each 5% increase or reduction in price of pipe, add or deduct 34-cent per square foot of radiation. 

1 If wrought iron pipe is used instead of steel, figure the cost of pipe and fittings at 30 cents per square foot of radiation (based on standard cast iron radiation).

An example of the method used in estimating the cost of pipe and fittings is as follows: For a job containing 1,400 

square feet of standard radiation, take 20 per cent of 1,400 gives 280, or the pipe and fittings would cost $280.00. 1 The above allowances for pipe and fittings do not include radiator valves, floor and ceiling plates, boiler fittings, expansion tanks, etc., but only the pipe and fittings required for roughing-in-the job.

LABOR INSTALLING HEATING PLANTS 

The labor cost of installing steam, hot water, vapor and vacuum heating systems is usually figured on the basis of the number of radiators (commonly termed units) in the job, and estimated at a certain price per radiator (unit). This allowance includes all necessary labor to rough-in the job, set and connect boiler, set and connect radiators, and complete the job ready to operate.

N This allowance varies with the type of heating system. whether a one or two-pipe system and the class of building in bizipo of 19 which it is installed. >

Asbestos Cement for Boiler Covering 

'Asbestos should be applied to a warm surface. About 24 hours before using, mix with water to the consistency of thin mortar, enough asbestos for the first coat, which should be one-half of the entire thickness of the covering. Cover the boiler, throwing on by handfuls with just enough force to make it stick without packing too solidly. The more loosely it is applied the more effective. When the first coat is thoroughly dry, apply the second coat in the same manner, having a thicker consistency. The third coat should be applied with a trowel and brought to a smooth finish. It is important for good results to allow each coat to thoroughly dry before applying the next. A canvas or heavy muslin jacket can now be pasted over the asbestos and made moisture-proof by painting with asphaltum. This will insure a permanent covering.

Painting and Bronzing Radiators 

Radiators are usually finished in aluminum or gold bronze or one of the many colors of radiator enamel now furnished for the purpose.

Before the radiators are bronzed they should be thoroughly brushed with a steel brush to remove any possible rust scale and then given a coat of primer, which should be used to give best results. It acts as a filler and furnishes a smooth surface upon which to apply the finishing coat. 

After the priming coat has been applied, mix the bronze powder with the bronzing liquid to the consistency of cream. Apply it with a fitch brush (bear hair), and if possible cover the surface with one stroke of the brush. Do not work it any more than is absolutely necessary. Applying bronze when the radiators are warm improves the luster.

Maroon gloss Japan is used for factories, public buildings. and other structures requiring a durable radiator coating. This should be applied with an ordinary flat bristle varnish brush and one coat is sufficient. No priming is necessary.

Radiator enamels are furnished in a variety of colors, such as white, ivory, oak brown, black, silver gray, light blue, navy blue, dark green, moss green, vermillion and maroon. When light shades of enamel are used radiators should first be given one coat of primer and two coats of enamel. When dark shades of enamel are used, three coats of enamel should be used without primer. Do not apply enamel too thick as two thin coats are much better than one thick. Enamel should be applied when radiators are cold and heat should not be turned on for at least 

24 hours thereafter.

Keep the radiator liquid can closed tight when not in use because if left uncorked a very short time it evaporates and thickens and becomes worthless. Do not get any bronze in the liquid can, as the smallest particle will turn it green. 

Covering Capacity of Bronze and Enamel.-One gallon of radiator primer should cover about 250 square feet of radiation. 

One pound of gold or color bronze and one quart of bronzing liquid should cover 250 to 300 square feet of radiation.

One pound of aluminum and one-half gallon of bronzing liquid should cover 550 to 600 square feet of radiation.

One gallon of maroon Japan should cover 250 to 300 square feet of radiation with one coat.

One gallon of radiator enamel should cover 250 square feet of radiation with one coat.

MECHANICAL STOKERS 

Means to reduce coal consumption, lower boiler operating costs and eliminate the smoke nuisance are easily made possible through the use of mechanical stokers. Stokers are used in connection with boilers from 75 horse power in size to those of giant proportions in Central power stations.

The Chain Grate type of stoker, of which there are several makes, is the generally accepted type of stoker for all coals of a bituminous character. Natural draft is employed. During the past few years forced draft has been incorporated in the construction features of some makes of Chain Grate stokers, thus making possible the added ability to use practically all, if not all, the various grades of anthracite coal, mine sweepings and so-called coke braize. 

In addition to the type mentioned there is also a so-called 

Underfeed Stoker, of which 4 or 5 makes are on the market: it is necessary to use forced draft with this type as the depth of the fuel bed is generally 4 to 10 or 12 times that employed on chain grates.

In principle of operation the Chain Grate stoker travels as an endless chain in the form of grate bars or links, conveying the green coal into the furnace at the front, where it becomes ignited, travels through the entire length of the furnace, forms into fine ash and thence is discharged into an ash pit. The 

Underfeed Stokers employ a stationary grate bed, inclined, and a series of rams or plungers which force the green coal beneath and up into the body of the furnace fire. Ash and clinkers are discharged at the rear end through rotary clinker grinders, power operated.

The Underfeed type of stoker was developed in the Eastern part of the United States where anthracite coal is generally predominant. It is used also in the Central Western territory to some extent, where certain coals will permit. 

The choice of the type of stoker to be used depends largely on the character of coal which is available. A survey of the steam generating stations in the States West of Central Ohio shows the Chain Grate stoker a general favorite. In the 

Eastern territory of the United States it may be said the reverse is true. Regarding stoking equipment for residences and apartment buildings; these buildings all employ small size boilers operating on very low pressure with very minor demands for steam in quantity, consequently firing by the well known hand shovel prevails, although there are several small stokers now on the market for domestic use.

Methods of determining the size of stoker best suited for the work involved are based principally on the character of coal to be used, the horse power size of the boiler selected, and the required horse power or rating at which the boiler will operate.

MECHANICAL STOKERS 

1627 As an example, assume the coal to be bituminous, of 11,000 B. T. U. (British Thermal Units heat value), also accept an efficiency percentage of 70 per cent, and the latent heat of evaporation at 970. Then, B. T. U. x boiler efficiency per cent

Latent Heat of Evaporation Pounds of Water Evaporated per pound of coal, or 

11,000 x 70 970 

8 lbs. (nearly).

One Horse Power is equivalent to the evaporation of 34½ lbs. of water, from and at its temperature of 212 degrees F. 

Therefore, 34½ divided by the figure 8 above gives 4.3 lb. of the specified coal as the amount required to produce one horse power at 70 per cent boiler efficiency. All of these figures are very conservative and will represent a typical or average case. 

Further assume the boiler size as 500 Horse Power and to operate continuously at, say, 150 per cent of rating, or 750 Horse

Power. The amount of coal required then will be 750x4.3 or 

3225 lbs. per hr., or approximately thereto, depending largely on the B. T. U. uniformity. 

Continuing, it would be regarded as good practice to consider as being present a draft of about 3 to 4 of an inch water column over the furnace fire bed, in this case, making possible the burning of about 35 to 45 lbs. of bituminous coal per hr. per sq. ft. of grate surface. 

Assuming the furnace width of the boiler as 11 ft., and the stoker as 10 ft. wide, and a burning rate of only 30 lbs. of coal per sq. ft. per hr., it would require a furnace grate area of 3225 = 107 sq. ft.

approximately, or a stoker size commonly 30 rated as 10x11 ft. 

If the actual furnace draft present is known then the determining of the size of grate required is not so much a problem of guessing or assuming.

In the case of so-called underfeed stokers where forced draft is required the area of the grate would generally be about 80 per cent of that given in the example above, the forced draft providing a means for a still greater rate of burning coal per sq. ft. of grate.

So far as stoker costs are concerned it may be said the Natural Draft Chain Grate type prices are generally about 10 per cent less than the Underfeed Stokers with their required 

Forced Draft fans. 

At the present time Natural Draft Chain Grate prices are about $11.00 per nominal Horse Power, installed, for boilers as small as 225 H. P., reducing to about $9.50 per Horse Power for the 500 Horse Power sizes, exclusive of masonry work, which is really a part of the boiler contractors' work. 

Forced Draft Chain Grate Stokers, installed with required fan equipment, will cost about 20 to 25 per cent more than Natural Draft types, although the grate area of the former may be about 10 per cent less. There is so wide a range in prices and operating characteristics in stoker equipment that in every case the stoker manufacturers' advice should be sought and accepted.

CHAPTER XXVII. 

PLUMBING, SEWERAGE AND GASFITTING 

To prepare an accurate detailed estimate on plumbing and sewerage requires a working knowledge of the trade because all work must be laid out on paper and the number of lineal feet of each kind of pipe estimated separately, such as tile or cast iron sewers, soil and vent pipe, water pipe, gas pipe, drains, valves, pipe fittings, etc. Inasmuch as very few, if any, general building contractors or estimators possess this knowledge, it makes it doubly difficult for them to prepare more than an approximate estimate on the various kinds of plumbing work.

In making up an approximate estimate on plumbing, the average contractor counts the number of fixtures in the job and multiplies at a certain price per fixture, and that is usually the extent of the estimate. Before going into the matter of detail estimating, average prices will be given on plumbing fixtures installed in the building:

Approximate Prices of Plumbing Fixtures Installed in the 

Building. The method commonly used to obtain approximate costs on plumbing work is to count the number of fixtures in the job, such as kitchen sinks, lavatories, water closets, bath tubs, shower baths, laundry tubs, hot water tanks or heaters, etc., and estimate them at a certain price per fixture, installed.

This method of estimating has become more complicated during recent years, due to the great changes that have been made in plumbing fixtures both as to style, materials and color. 

Building code requirements vary widely in different localities and this has a great influence on costs, as do the rates of wages paid in different parts of the country. 

For this reason the installed prices of plumbing fixtures given in the following paragraphs can only be approximates and should be regarded as such; also all prices are based on using white fixtures, similar to those shown in the illustrations and any changes or additions for colored fixtures, cabinet sinks, lavatories, etc., should be made in accordance with the detailed fixture prices. 1629

The approximate prices given include complete roughing-in inside the building, together with all necessary tile drains and sewers inside the building and extending 20 ft. on the outside. 

The difference in cost between individual bungalows and houses and apartment buildings is due to the fact that in apartment building construction, one stack will often suffice for two or more sets of fixtures, while in individual houses, separate stacks are usually required for each group of fixtures. One set of laundry tubs in the basement is often sufficient for 3 apartments. This also applies to sewers, as in apartment building construction, one sewer will be sufficient for 2 or more apartments, which reduces the cost. 

The approximate prices given are based on material prices as given in this chapter and plumbers' wages at $1.62½ per hour. 

In one or two story houses, using bath room fixtures similar to those illustrated in Fig. 1, consisting of a porcelain enameled cast iron bath on legs, a porcelain enameled cast iron wall lavatory and a vitreous china washdown closet outfit; a porcelain enameled roll rim kitchen sink with single drainboard, a 2-compartment granitine laundry tub and a hot water heater with gas connection or connected to heating boiler, should average $80.00 to $90.00 per fixture or $480.00 to $540.00 for the job complete.

Using the same grade of fixtures in a 2 or 3-story apartment building, the cost should run from $75.00 to $85.00 per fixture, or $375.00 to $425.00 per apartment.

In one or two story houses, using bath room fixtures similar to those illustrated in Fig. 2, consisting of a porcelain enameled cast iron pedestal lavatory, a vitreous china closet outfit, a porcelain enameled cast iron recess bath; a porcelain enameled cast iron apron kitchen sink with single drainboard, a 2 or 3compartment granitine laundry tub and a hot water heater with gas connection or connected to heating boiler, should average from $90.00 to $100.00 per fixture or from $540.00 to $600.00 for the complete job.

Using the same grade of fixtures on a 2 or 3-story apartment building, the cost should run from $85.00 to $95.00 per fixture or from $425.00 to $475.00 per apartment.

In one or two story houses, using bath room fixtures similar to those illustrated in Fig. 3, consisting of a vitreous china pedestal lavatory, a vitreous china siphon jet closet combination, a porcelain enameled cast iron corner bath with shower complete as illustrated; a double drainboard kitchen sink with

PLUMBING 

1631 apron, a 2 or 3-compartment granitine laundry tub, a gas-fired storage water heater or connected to heating boiler, should average from $100.00 to $110.00 per fixture or from $700.00 to $770.00 for the complete job, Using the same grade of fixtures on a 2 or 3-story apartment building, the cost should run from $95.00 to $105.00 per fixture or from $570.00 to $630.00 per apartment. 

In one or two story houses, using bath room fixtures similar to those illustrated in Fig. 4, consisting of a vitreous china lavatory with chromium legs, a one-piece vitreous china closet combination and a porcelain enameled cast iron recess bath with shower complete; a double drainboard kitchen sink with apron, a 2 or 3-compartment granitine laundry tub, a gas-fired storage water heater or connected with heating boiler, should average from $110.00 to $120.00 per fixture or from $770.00 to $840.00 for the job complete. 

Using the same grade of fixtures on a 2 or 3-story apartment building, the cost should run from $105.00 to $115.00 per fixture or from $630.00 to $690.00 per apartment. 

In one or two story houses, using bath room fixtures similar to those illustrated in Fig. 5, consisting of a vitreous china wall lavatory, a vitreous china closet combination, a porcelain enameled cast iron recess bath with shower complete; a single drainboard kitchen sink with apron, a 2 or 3-compartment granitine laundry tub, a gas-fired storage hot water heater or connected with heating boiler, should average from $95.00 to $105.00 per fixture, or $665.00 to $735.00 for the job complete. 

Using the same grade of fixtures on a 2 or 3-story apartment building, the cost should run from $90.00 to $100.00 per fixture or from $540.00 to $600.00 per apartment. 

Approximate Cost of Plumbing and Sewerage for Public 

Garage Buildings.-The plumbing and sewerage in a public garage building is usually an item of considerable importance, on account of the large amount of sewerage required, heavy castings for wash racks, gravel basins, grease traps, triple basins, etc. 

On a garage building about 100'x125′ in size, having two lines of sewers, hot water heater, wash rack apparatus, 2 toilets and lavatories, heavy cast-iron clean out basins, grease traps, floor drains, cast iron down spouts, cast-iron triple basins, etc., the cost should run from $2,000.00 to $2,500.00 for the job complete, depending upon the specification and location of the work.

Preparing Detailed Plumbing Estimates 

When preparing detailed estimates on plumbing, it is necessary to list the quantity of each class of work separately, such as the number of lineal feet of 4″, 6″, and 8" sewers, and fittings; number of lineal feet of each size soil pipe, vents and fittings; number of lineal feet of galvanized water pipe and fittings of different sizes; number of valves of the various kinds and sizes; number of each type of fixture required, such as hot water heaters, laundry trays, kitchen sinks, slop sinks, bath tubs, lavatories, water closets, shower baths, etc., together with a list of fittings and supplies required for each. 

The following is a list of items the plumbing contractor should include in his estimate:

Estimating Quantities and Costs of Sewer Work.-Sewerage is estimated by the lineal foot, obtained by measuring the number of lineal feet of each size sewer pipe required, such as 

4", 6", 8″ and 12" pipe, and all fittings should also be listed in detail, giving the number of ells, Y's, T's, etc. 

Cast-iron sewer pipe is estimated in the same manner as tile sewer pipe.

Most plumbers estimate their sewer work at a certain price per lineal foot, including excavating, sewer pipe and labor. 

This is all right on ordinary jobs that do not require more than the usual amount of deep excavation, but if there is an exceptionally large amount of deep excavation (from 7 to 15 feet deep), then the excavating should be estimated separately. 

Undoubtedly the best method is to estimate the number of cubic yards of excavating required for sewers, based on a trench 18" wide by the required depth. Refer to Chapter on Excavating for labor costs excavating for trenches. 

Where 4 to 12-inch sewer pipe is used, an experienced sewer man should lay 10 to 12 lineal feet of pipe an hour or 80 to 96 lineal feet per 8 hour day, and the labor cost per 100 lineal feet should average as follows:

Estimating Quantities of Cast Iron Soil Pipe, Down Spouts, 

Stacks and Vents.-When estimating soil pipe, stacks, vents, etc. note the number of stacks and length of each, listing the number of lineal feet of each size pipe; the number of pieces.

size, and kind of fitting required, and price them at current market prices. The labor cost placing cast iron pipe is given on the following pages,

Estimating Quantity of Pipe and Fittings.-When estimating the quantity of black or galvanized pipe, list the number of lineal feet of each size pipe required, such as ½”, ¾”, 1″, 1¼”, 1½", 2″, 2½", 3″, etc., and estimate at the current market price.

After the cost of the pipe has been computed, take 75 per cent of the cost of the pipe to cover the cost of all fittings required. 

Brass or copper pipe and fittings should be estimated in the same manner as galvanized pipe. See chapter on "Heating."

Estimating the Quantity and Prices of Valves.-All valves of the different sizes should be listed on the estimate separately, stating the number of each size required, and pricing them at the current market price.

Estimating the Quantity of Fixtures.-Each type of fixture such as sinks, lavatories, laundry trays, water closets, bath tubs, drinking fountains, shower baths, hot water tanks and heaters, house pumps, bilge pumps, vacuum cleaners, etc., should be listed separately and priced at the current market prices. 

Labor Roughing in for Plumbing.-The usual practice among plumbers is to allow a certain percentage of the cost of the roughing materials to cover the labor cost of installing them, and this will vary with the type of building and grade of work. 

The total cost of the roughing in materials, such as castiron soil pipe, down spouts, stacks, vents, and fittings; also all black and galvanized pipe and fittings, all valves, increasers. tees, Y's, % bends, nipples, and in fact all pipe required to rough in the job is computed, and then the labor cost is estimated at a certain percentage of the cost of the pipe. 

In medium price bungalows and residences, the labor cost of roughing in the job will vary from 65 to 75 per cent of the cost of the roughing in materials, with 70 per cent a fair average. 

In apartment buildings of non-fireproof construction, the labor cost of roughing in will average about 75 per cent of the cost of the roughing in materials, while on high grade fire-proof construction, the labor cost roughing in will run from 90 to 100 per cent of the cost of the roughing in materials.

PLUMBING 

1635 In public garages, the labor cost roughing in the job will average about 80 to 90 per cent of the cost of the roughing in materials. 

Sewer work is estimated separately from roughing in.

Labor Handling and Placing Plumbing Fixtures.-The labor cost handling and placing all kinds of fixtures, such as laundry tubs, kitchen sinks, lavatories, bath tubs, shower baths, water closets, drinking fountains, etc., is usually estimated at 25 per cent of the cost of the fixtures. 

Plumbing Contractor's Overhead Expense and Profit.- 

Plumbing contractors like to add 10 per cent to the cost of their work for overhead expense, and an additional 10 per cent for profit, but frequently the jobs are let on the basis of a straight 10 per cent, or 10 and 5 per cent, depending upon the competition and how badly the contractor needs the work.

Garbage Disposall Units.-The Disposall does away with the kitchen garbage can. It is a self-contained unit attached to the kitchen sink to form an enlarged drain into which all kitchen food wastes can be placed. 

The unit consists of a housing in which is contained a propellor and shredding mechanism. A 4 h.p. motor is directly connected to the propellor and shredding mechanism and supplies the power for operating the waste unit. 

Waste material can be accumulated in the upper receptacle of the unit until a normal charge is collected or it may be operated to dispose of the material immediately. The capacity of the waste receptacle is 1 qt. 

Waste material passes through a series of shredders where they are reducd to a fine pulp. This pulp then passes into a revolving strainer disc through which it is forced centrifugally

into a chamber below and around the flywheel. Fins on the flywheel centrifugally force the pulp into the outlet passage connected to the drain line which carries the waste to the sewer. Cold water from the faucet flowing through the unit during the grinding operation thoroughly flushes the waste down the drain.

This unit is shown in the "cutout" portion of the electric dish washer illustrated above. 

The price of this unit is $134.00. The plumbing contractor receives a trade discount of 18% to 20% from the above. Fig. 1.

CHAPTER XXVIII. 

ELECTRIC WIRING 

Most electricians performing ordinary work, estimate the cost of wiring at a certain price per outlet, including conduit, wire, outlet boxes, plates, etc., depending upon the class of work. If there are exceptionally long runs of conduit or wiring, an extra charge per outlet is made to cover additional conduit, wire and labor.

Electrical contractors performing the largest work usually estimate the number of lineal feet of the different size conduit required, the number of lineal feet of each size wire, the number of outlet boxes, switches, etc., but to do this it is necessary for the estimator or contractor to possess a working knowledge of the business, which is seldom found among building contractors and estimators. 

Power wiring should be estimated by an experienced electrical engineer and for that reason will not be dealt with in this book. 

The data given on the following pages is intended to cover the ordinary classes of building construction, giving the cost per outlet for the various kinds of wiring. Knob and tube work is generally used in towns and the smaller cities and is run exposed between floor and ceiling joists and stud partitions, in either frame or masonry and frame construction.

In the larger cities it is necessary to run all wire in rigid or flexible conduit and this class of work is more expensive than knob and tube work

When installing electrical work in reinforced concrete buildings, the labor cost is considerably higher than in wood construction, as it is necessary to lay all work out on the wood forms and before the partitions are erected, and for this reason considerable care must be exercised in laying out and installing the work.

In buildings using floors of combination clay tile, metal tile or other forms of tile and concrete joist construction, the labor cost is still higher than on straight concrete construction, on account of it being necessary to place conduit around tile or metal pans, in joists, etc., which requires considerable extra labor. 1656
